summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
summary.authors: Jian Dai
summary.field_subfield: High-energy nuclear physics / QCD matter
summary.executive_summary: This letter investigates gluon radiation emitted during the hydrodynamic stage of deconfined hot QCD matter, or quark-gluon plasma (QGP), which is central to interpreting relativistic heavy-ion collisions at RHIC. The medium-induced radiation has been extensively studied in the context of final-state partonic energy loss, or jet quenching, where spatially extended nuclear matter affects the fragmentation and hadronization of hard partons, and essentially all high transverse-momentum hadronic observables are affected at collider energies. The degree of medium modification characterizes the hot QCD matter in the deconfined phase, and this effect emerges in principle from thermal QCD, though different approximation schemes yield consistent results. Gluon radiation has also been considered in the context of gluon density saturation in the initial stage, where a strongly interacting gluonic atmosphere is crucial for rapid local thermalization. The time evolution of the RHIC fireball influences observable particle production spectra, and given a strong initial interaction, the resulting state is modeled as a relativistic fluid undergoing hydrodynamic flow, for which generalized fluid mechanics characterizing the long-distance transport of color charges has been developed. The authors previously discovered single skyrmion solutions in color fluid and found an expanding skyrmion case consistent with the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of these non-static configurations is an important characteristic, motivating the calculation of the radiation spectrum in a semiclassical approach. The main results are a fast fall-off in the ultraviolet side of the spectrum, a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and a long tail in the infrared. The paper reviews nonabelian fluid mechanics, calculates the nonabelian current for the soliton solution, computes the semiclassical gluon radiation, and compares the spectrum with other approaches. The color current is derived from a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, with the configuration described by a group element field U and velocity field omega. The equation of state is approximated as epsilon = 3p, describing radiation, and the free energy density is obtained by integrating the ideal fluid formula. The expanding soliton solution is specified with a scale R(t) and a small parameter lambda = tau/R0. The semiclassical amplitude is computed using the lowest-order interaction between the classical current and a free quantum gluon field, and the radiation spectrum is derived from the density of states and energy distribution. The numerical results are presented for lambda = 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5, showing the density of states and energy spectrum as functions of kappa. The comparison with other approaches reveals differences in the infrared behavior, which stems from the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 rather than being infinitely large. The hydrodynamical approach also opens possibilities for addressing the eccentricity of the elliptic flow, which will be the topic of follow-up work. The work was supported by a CUNY Collaborative Research Incentive grant, and the author benefited from mentoring by V. P. Nair.

The comparison with other approaches reveals differences in the infrared behavior, which stems from the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 rather than being infinitely large. The hydrodynamical approach also opens possibilities for addressing the eccentricity of the elliptic flow, which will be the topic of follow-up work. The work was supported by a CUNY Collaborative Research Incentive grant, and the author benefited from mentoring by V. P. Nair.

Research Context
The study addresses gluon radiation during the hydrodynamic stage in the evolution of deconfined hot QCD matter or quark gluon plasma (QGP). Medium-induced gluon radiation has been thoroughly explored in the context of final-state partonic energy loss or jet quenching. Spatially extended nuclear matter affects the fragmentation and hadronization of hard partons produced in relativistic heavy ion collisions. Essentially all high p⊥ hadronic observables are affected at collider energies, and the degree of medium modification characterizes the hot QCD matter. Gluon radiation has also been considered in the context of gluon density saturation in the initial stage, where a strongly interacting gluonic atmosphere is crucial for rapid local thermalization. The time evolution of the RHIC fireball can influence observable particle production spectra. Given a strong initial interaction, the resulting state is modeled as a relativistic fluid undergoing hydrodynamic flow. Generalized fluid mechanics characterizing the long-distance physics of color charge transport has been developed for this purpose. The authors previously discovered single skyrmion solutions in color fluid and found an expanding skyrmion case consistent with the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of these non-static configurations is an important characteristic of this color skyrmion.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to calculate the gluon radiation spectrum for the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in the quark gluon plasma. The authors hypothesize that the expanding skyrmion configuration, consistent with the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball, produces a characteristic gluon radiation pattern. The predicted outcome is a radiation spectrum with a fast fall-off in the UV side, a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and a long tail in the IR. The authors expect a hierarchy between the partonic coupling gYM and the effective coupling geff, enabling a free parton picture. The authors predict that the infrared behavior in their case is softer than in prior work, due to the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0. The authors anticipate that the medium-induced gluon radiation is characterized by a frequency omega_C significantly larger than the characteristic momentum 1/R0. The authors hypothesize that their hydrodynamical approach opens up possibilities to address the eccentricity of the elliptic flow. The authors predict that the difference in infrared behavior arises from the medium size being taken to be infinitely large in prior work versus characterized by R0 here.

Methodological Details
The study models the transport of color charges in the volume of nuclear size using a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism. The configuration of the fluid is described by a group element field U, which shows up in the velocity field omega. The Lagrangian density includes the coupling of the abelian charge current to an external gluon field with an effective coupling geff. The authors consider only one abelian charge current, which means that U takes value in an SU(2) group. The equation of state is approximated as epsilon = 3p when the temperature is relatively high, describing radiation. The free energy density is obtained by integrating the ideal fluid formula, with beta as a dimensionless constant of integration. The expanding soliton solution is specified with a scale R(t) ≈ R0(t/τ + 1)4/3θ(t), valid provided τ ≪ R0. A small parameter lambda = tau/R0 is defined to characterize the expansion. The hedgehog ansatz is specified for the solution, with the stereographic map defining sin phi and cos phi. The sign in the expression of cos phi signifies a topological charge which is the skyrmion number. The authors take the positive sign, corresponding to the skyrmion number +1 or a skyrmion. The nonabelian current is derived by expressing the abelian current jµ in terms of the velocity omega through the equation of motion. The current has a natural form of a multipole expansion due to the skyrmion orientation in the color space. The authors only consider the effect of the lowest mode, with higher polarization effects to be considered elsewhere. The spherically symmetric part in the current is contained only in the third component, with P6(s) = 1 − 7s2 + 7s4 − s6. The lowest order semiclassical amplitude is given by the interaction of the classical current with a free quantum field for gluon. The gluon factor is given by the wave function with the color and helicity parts phi and epsilon summed over eventually. The spatial Fourier transformation is completed analytically, yielding the amplitude with B(k) = π2A(k)/120 and Q4(x) = 5x2 − 5x3 + x4. The parameter eta is defined as omegaτ/(kR0)3/4, and with the onshell condition omega = k, eta = lambdaκ1/4 where kappa is R0k. The radiation spectrum is derived from the density of states n = 4πk2 sum over c,h of |M|2. The number distribution is dN = sum over c,h of |M|2 d3k, and the energy distribution is dE/dk = alpha lambda2 kappa1/2 |fM_lambda(kappa)|2. The parameter alpha is defined as (2π5/225)(g2eff/β6). The numerical results for lambda = 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5 are given in Figure 1.

The study begins with a brief review of the nonabelian fluid mechanics before calculating the nonabelian current for the soliton solution. The semiclassical gluon radiation is calculated using the lowest order amplitude iM = geff<1| integral d4x Jaµ Âaµ|0>. The gluon self-interaction in terms like F aµν F aµν is omitted, allowing the authors to work with a free parton picture. The gauge coupling becomes the coupling between a classical current and a free quantum field for gluon. The authors specify R(t) in the amplitude equation to the form given in Eq. (7), yielding the integral with Q4(t4/3). The authors perform the spatial Fourier transformation analytically, completing the calculation of the amplitude. The authors derive the density of states and energy distribution from the amplitude, enabling the calculation of the radiation spectrum. The numerical results are computed for lambda = 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5, and presented in Figure 1. The comparison with other approaches is carried out in Section 4, revealing differences in the infrared behavior. The authors note that the gluon radiation by the expanding medium itself is not included in the popular approach of modeling the medium as static scattering centers. The authors estimate the quenching parameter to be 0.04 to 0.16 GeV2/fm, and L is the in-medium path length of a hard parton. The authors plan to address the eccentricity of the elliptic flow either intrinsically by considering the nonabelian color current or exogenously by considering the gluon radiation patterns.

Key Results
The density of states and energy spectrum are calculated for lambda = 1/5 (Black), 2/15 (Deep Gray), and 1/15 (Light Gray). The spectrum shows a fast fall-off in the UV side, a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and a long tail in the IR. The number density asymptotic in small k is ∼1/√k, as shown in Figure 2. The difference in infrared behavior arises from the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 in this case. The infrared behavior in this case is softer than in prior work, where the medium size is taken to be infinitely large. The characteristic momentum in this case is 1/R0, which is significantly smaller than the medium-induced radiation frequency omega_C. The quenching parameter is estimated to be 0.04 to 0.16 GeV2/fm, and L is the in-medium path length of a hard parton. The hierarchy between the medium-induced gluon radiation spectrum and the gluon radiation spectrum by the medium is established. The density of states n is given by alpha R0 lambda2 kappa−1/2 |fM_lambda(kappa)|2. The energy distribution dE/dk is given by alpha lambda2 kappa1/2 |fM_lambda(kappa)|2. The parameter alpha is defined as (2π5/225)(g2eff/β6), incorporating the effective coupling and the constant of integration. The authors note that the popular approach of modeling the medium as static scattering centers does not include the gluon radiation by the expanding medium itself.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The fast fall-off in the UV side of the spectrum indicates that high-energy gluon radiation is suppressed. The smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy suggests a characteristic energy scale for the radiation. The long tail in the IR indicates that low-energy gluon radiation extends over a wide range. The softer infrared behavior arises from the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0, which is finite. The hierarchy between the medium-induced gluon radiation and the gluon radiation by the medium reflects the different physical mechanisms. The hydrodynamical approach opens up possibilities to address the eccentricity of the elliptic flow, which is an important observable. The expanding skyrmion configuration provides a model for the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. The semiclassical approach allows the calculation of the radiation spectrum without including gluon self-interaction. The free parton picture simplifies the calculation by treating the gluon as a free quantum field. The multipole expansion of the current enables the consideration of the lowest mode, with higher polarization effects to be considered elsewhere.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors only consider the effect of the lowest mode, with the effects of higher polarization to be considered elsewhere. The gluon radiation by the expanding medium itself is not included in the popular approach of modeling the medium as static scattering centers. The authors do not report the specific values of the effective coupling geff, which is needed for the calculation. The authors do not report the specific values of the quenching parameter ˆq and the in-medium path length L. The authors do not report the specific values of the density of states n and the energy distribution dE/dk for the different values of lambda. The authors do not report the specific values of the amplitude iM and the function fM_lambda(kappa). The authors do not report the specific values of the parameter eta and the small parameter lambda. The authors do not report the specific values of the skyrmion number and the topological charge.

Claims
The expanding skyrmion configuration provides a model for the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball, and the gluon radiation pattern is an important characteristic. The expanding skyrmion case is consistent with the expanding nature of the fireball generated in RHIC experiments. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of these non-static configurations is an important character of this color skyrmion. The authors calculate the radiation spectrum in a semiclassical approach to characterize the gluon radiation.  The hydrodynamical approach opens up possibilities to address the eccentricity of the elliptic flow. The expanding skyrmion configuration provides a model for the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball.
The infrared behavior in this case is softer than in prior work, due to the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 rather than being infinitely large. The asymptotic of the number density in small k is ∼1/√k, as shown in Figure 2. The difference comes from the fact that the medium size is taken to be inﬁnitely large in [6] while in our case the medium size is characterized by the soliton size R0. The IR behavior in our case is softer.  The softer infrared behavior reflects the finite medium size characterized by the soliton size R0. The difference in infrared behavior arises from the different assumptions about the medium size.
The hierarchy between the medium-induced gluon radiation and the gluon radiation by the medium reflects the different physical mechanisms. The characteristic momentum in this case is 1/R0, which is significantly smaller than the medium-induced radiation frequency omega_C. In general omega_C is signiﬁcantly larger than the characteristic momentum in our case 1/R0. So there is a hierarchy between the medium induced gluon radiation spectrum and the gluon radiation spectrum by the medium.  The hierarchy reflects the different physical mechanisms of the two types of radiation. The characteristic momentum 1/R0 is significantly smaller than the medium-induced radiation frequency omega_C.

Robustness And Ablation Notes

Three Takeaways

The strongest evidence is the fast fall-off in the UV side, the smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and the long tail in the IR. 3. The future path is to address the eccentricity of the elliptic flow either intrinsically by considering the nonabelian color current or exogenously by considering the gluon radiation patterns.

summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study of a lunar occultation of a carbon-rich AGB star
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.

The dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell is Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K.
The radial density gradient of the best-fit models is close to r^-2, consistent with radiatively driven mass loss.
The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate.

Executive Summary
This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars supplies much of the heavy elements and solid particles in the interstellar medium. The mechanisms of AGB mass loss are thought to involve radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but details are poorly understood. Studies of circumstellar shell structure can clarify uncertainties about mass-loss processes. Molecular line and deep imaging studies have revealed periodic mass-loss variations producing 'rings' in radial distributions. Angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec are required to study the inner regions of circumstellar shells. Lunar occultation and multi-aperture interferometry have pushed resolutions to the milli-arcsecond level. Most interferometric observations have been made in only one or two broad bands, limiting spatial and spectral detail. AFGL 5440 is a carbon-rich AGB star with a well-characterized distance and photometry.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 can be fit by a single-size model or require a circumstellar shell. The authors hypothesize that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell from mass loss. They predict that a full radiative transfer model is needed to fit both the occultation fringes and the spectral energy distribution. They predict a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with Tmax around 950 K. They predict a density gradient close to r^-2 for a radiatively driven wind. They predict that the IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate.

Methodological Details
The study observed a lunar occultation of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440 (aka OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344). Observations were made during an immersion occultation event on 28 Aug 2001 at approximately 02:44:00 UT. The Moon elevation was 36 degrees, the Sun was 17 degrees below the horizon, and the lunar phase was 0.72. The position angle of the occultation on the lunar limb was 54 degrees. Observations were made with the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument is a long/wide slit, high-speed spectrophotometer using a NaCl prism to disperse light onto a 32x100 pixel portion of a 256^2 InSb array. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector is read-out every 8 msec, with photon integration over essentially the full 8 msec time. The observations cover the 1 - 4µm spectral region with resolving power varying from about 20 to about 100. The time resolution of 8 msec permits an effective angular resolution of a couple milli-arcsec. The plate scale in the spatial direction is 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm and background-limited longward of 3µm. A typical observation consists of taking 5000 frames centered on the occultation event. The buffer holds the most recent 5000 frames to accommodate errors in predicted occultation times of up to 10 seconds. The comparison stars IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2) were observed on 29 Jun 2001 and 26 Aug 2001. The data reduction uses a cross-correlation algorithm to shift images to the same wavelength/pixel scale. Sky subtraction uses sky measurements on either side of the stellar spectrum from the long slit. The end result is a sequence of about 100 light curves with a few hundred frames centered on the event. Wavelength calibration fits the NaCl dispersion function to the J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima. The wavelength calibration accuracy is probably good to ±0.01 lambda throughout the 1 - 4µm region. The fringe pattern is a convolution of blurring parameters including aperture, integration time, bandwidth, and source size/structure. The standard procedure is to model the blurring parameters with various source models to find the best fit. The approach was to choose input parameters and vary the dust optical depth to find the best fit to the energy distribution. The dust composition was assumed to be carbon-rich, typically a combination of amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite. The critical parameters are the dust temperature at the inner radius and the radial density gradient. The outer radius makes essentially no difference at wavelengths less than 60µm as long as it is at least 100 times the inner radius. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model. The dust temperature at the inner radius of the dust shell is Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit the occultation fringes at the longer wavelengths. The radial density gradient of models with a reasonable fit was close to r^-2. Models with a density gradient of r^-1.8 came closer to producing the IRAS 60µm flux but did not fit the 5 - 20µm energy distribution well. Models with a density gradient of r^-2.2 can fit the energy distribution out to 20µm but have worse fits to the IRAS 60µm flux. The optical depth for best fit at the fiducial wavelength of 5µm was typically in the range 0.3 - 0.6. The best-fit optical depth at 5µm is 0.5 ± 0.1. The best-fit dust composition included a small amount of SiC with comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite. The physical inner radius of the dust shell is 3.7x10^14 cm, or an angular radius of 11 mas at 2.25 kpc. The angular diameter of the central star is of order 3 mas. The dust mass-loss rate implied by the derived optical depth and density dependence is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. The best-fit model utilized roughly equal amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite in addition to a small amount of SiC. The dust emissivity is epsilon proportional to lambda^-1.3, consistent with amorphous carbon-rich dust. The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit by any similar model without graphite. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The gas mass-loss rate derived by Groenewegen et al. (2002) is 3.1x10^-5 solar masses per year. Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observations separately resolve the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell. The dust density gradient is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The inner radius constraint follows from the fact that dust cooler than 900 K cannot emit sufficiently to produce the required 3 - 4µm emission. The inclusion of graphite was driven by its relatively flat emissivity between 10 and 50µm, enabling the fit to the IRAS 60µm flux. The failure to fit the 60µm flux may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate from the time when the far-IR-emitting dust was ejected. This result is contrary to the large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The proposed higher past mass-loss rate is comparable to the period of fluctuation seen by Mauron & Huggins (2000) for IRC+10216. The models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. The inclusion of graphite is contrary to the large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The discrepancy around 1.7µm for IRC+00233 has no good explanation and may be due to systematic noise or a real photospheric difference. The data are limited by spectral resolution and signal-to-noise ratio to accuracies on the order of ±2 mas. The wavelength calibration accuracy is probably good to ±0.01 lambda, but no flux calibration was attempted. The predicted times of occultation events are often in error by as much as 10 seconds. The study did not attempt to extract details of the stellar photosphere or a thorough examination of all possible dust size/composition models. The study did not try to find any better than superficial agreement with the IRAS LRS data. The range of optical properties for different forms of amorphous carbon was not explored. The distance of 2.25 kpc is assumed, and the angular radius of 11 mas depends on this value.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study explored more than 200 models to understand the effect of varying input parameters. Models with a maximum dust temperature below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit the occultation fringes at the longer wavelengths. Models with a density gradient of r^-1.8 came closer to producing the IRAS 60µm flux but did not fit the 5 - 20µm energy distribution well. Models with a density gradient of r^-2.2 can fit the energy distribution out to 20µm but have worse fits to the IRAS 60µm flux. The outer radius makes essentially no difference at wavelengths less than 60µm as long as it is at least 100 times the inner radius. We found that we could obtain reasonably good fits with either the MRN or KMH grain size distributions. Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for a 4.5 mas uniform disk model for a subset of the wavelengths observed. Figure 2 shows the chi-squared and signal-to-noise ratio as a function of wavelength over the entire observed band. Figures 3 and 4 show the fits for HD 155292. summary.title: On Generalized Entropy Measures and Pathways
summary.authors: A.M. Mathai and H.J. Haubold
summary.field_subfield: Mathematical statistics / information theory
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a unified framework connecting statistical independence, generalized entropies, and pathway models. It begins by re-examining the product probability property (PPP), arguing that the term 'independence' is a misnomer and that additivity of entropy is not guaranteed by PPP alone. Instead, additivity arises specifically when the entropy is defined via a logarithmic functional form, which itself is forced by a recursivity postulate. The authors then introduce several generalized entropies of order α — Rényi, Havrda-Charváat, Tsallis, and Mathai's entropy — all of which reduce to Shannon entropy as α → 1. They show that logarithmic entropies are additive while power-law entropies are non-additive, with the coefficient a(α) quantifying non-additivity. The maximum entropy principle is used to derive probability models: fixing the first moment yields power laws and Tsallis q-exponentials, while escort densities and Mathai's entropy yield generalized beta and gamma forms. Crucially, Mathai's entropy produces a general pathway model that encompasses Tsallis statistics, superstatistics, Maxwell-Boltzmann, Gaussian, Weibull, and Wigner distributions as special cases. The paper also derives the differential equations satisfied by these pathway densities and connects Mathai's entropy to Kerridge's measure of inaccuracy and directed divergence. The central thesis is that non-additivity is the natural process in statistical mechanics, and additivity is an artifact of the logarithmic recursivity assumption.

The central thesis is that non-additivity is the natural process in statistical mechanics, and additivity is an artifact of the logarithmic recursivity assumption.

Statistical independence is traditionally defined via the product probability property. Shannon entropy is characterized by its additivity and extensivity properties. Non-additivity is important in statistical mechanics even under statistical independence.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Does statistical independence (PPP) imply additivity of entropy? Is the logarithmic form of Shannon entropy a consequence of a recursivity postulate? Do generalized entropies reduce to Shannon entropy as α approaches 1? Is Mathai's entropy non-additive while its dual measure is additive? Does maximizing Mathai's entropy yield pathway models with exponential and power law behavior?

The paper uses discrete multinomial populations with probabilities summing to one. The product probability property is defined as P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). The recursivity postulate partitions the m-th event into independent sub-events. Shannon entropy is defined with natural logarithm (base e). Rényi entropy of order α is defined for α ≠ 1, α > 0. Havrda-Charváat entropy of order α is defined for α ≠ 1, α > 0. Tsallis entropy of order α is defined for α ≠ 1, α > 0. Mathai entropy of order α is defined for α ≠ 1, −∞ < α < 2. Mathai's additive entropy of order α is defined for α ≠ 1, −∞ < α < 2. The bivariate joint entropy is defined over m×n probability arrays. The trivariate case extends to m×n×r probability arrays.

The joint entropy relation is derived as Fm,n,α = Fm,α + Fn,α + a(α)Fm,αFn,α. The coefficient a(α) equals zero for Rényi and Mathai's additive entropy. The coefficient a(α) equals α−1 for Mathai's entropy Mk,α. The trivariate relation includes quadratic and cubic cross terms. The functional equation fα(x) + bα(x)fα(y/(1−x)) = fα(y) + bα(x)f(x/(1−y)) is used. The boundary condition is fα(0) = fα(1). The coefficient bα(x) equals (1−x)2−α for Mathai entropy. The continuous Mathai entropy is defined via an integral of [f(x)]2−α. The Lagrangian functional U = [f(x)]α − λ[f(x)] is optimized. Fixing the first moment yields the power law form. The escort density is defined as µ[f(x)]α with µ−1 = ∫x[f(x)]αdx. Mathai's pathway model is f(x) = c xγ−1[1 − s(1−α)xδ]1/(1−α). The Maxwell-Boltzmann density arises for δ=2, γ=3, α→1. The Gaussian density arises for δ=2, γ=1, α→1. The Wigner function requires 1 < q < 3.

All generalized entropies reduce to Shannon entropy as α → 1. Mathai's entropy Mk,α is non-additive while M∗k,α is additive. The joint entropy relation is Mm,n,α = Mm,α + Mn,α + (α−1)Mm,αMn,α. The coefficient a(α) equals α−1 for Mathai's entropy. Additivity holds when a(α) = 0 and non-additivity when a(α) ≠ 0. The logarithmic form of Shannon entropy is a consequence of the recursivity postulate. Additivity is an artifact of the logarithmic functional form, not of independence. The paper notes that Havrda-Charváat and Tsallis entropies are difficult to produce densities. The definition of independence via PPP is inconsistent with the sure event. The paper acknowledges that there are no independent events for n = 3, 5, 7. The trivariate case illustrates non-extensivity even under statistical independence.

Additivity is due to logarithm, not independence. Logarithm of a product is the sum of logarithms. Logarithmic entropies are additive when a(α) = 0. Non-additivity is the natural process in statistical mechanics.
The recursivity postulate forces the logarithmic functional form for Shannon entropy. The recursivity postulate yields a weighted sum. The result is a logarithmic function. The recursivity postulate determines the logarithmic form. The recursivity postulate is one of several possible postulates. Characterization theorems rely on the recursivity property.
Mathai's entropy Mk,α is non-additive while its dual measure M∗k,α is additive. Mathai's entropy is non-additive. Mathai's additive entropy is additive. The coefficient a(α) equals α−1 for Mathai's entropy. Mathai's additive entropy has a(α) = 0. Mathai's entropy yields pathway models.

The Maxwell-Boltzmann density arises for δ=2, γ=3, α→1. The Gaussian density arises for δ=2, γ=1, α→1. The Wigner function requires 1 < q < 3. The pathway model requires specific parameter values. summary.title: The Return of a Static Universe and the End of Cosmology
summary.authors: Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer
summary.field_subfield: Cosmology (physical cosmology / observational cosmology)
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/conceptual essay (no empirical data, simulations, or experiments)
summary.executive_summary: This paper is a theoretical, argumentative essay rather than an empirical study, so it contains no participants, measurements, or numerical results in the usual sense; its 'results' are logical and physical consequences derived from extrapolating the standard cosmological model forward in time. The authors, Lawrence M. Krauss and Robert J. Scherrer of Case Western Reserve University and Vanderbilt University, argue that as the current Lambda-CDM universe is extrapolated forward, all evidence of Hubble expansion will disappear, so that future observers in our 'island universe' will be fundamentally incapable of determining the true nature of the universe. They identify three observational pillars of modern cosmology—the observed Hubble expansion, the detection of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the determination of the abundance of elements produced in the early universe—and describe how each will vanish for a far-future observer. They note that all cosmological models with a non-zero cosmological constant will approach a de Sitter universe in the far future, and they re-examine the practical significance of this ultimate de Sitter expansion, pointing out a new consequence: from the perspective of any observer within a bound gravitational system, the static version of de Sitter space outside that system will eventually become the appropriate physical coordinate system. They argue that in a time comparable to the age of the longest-lived stars, observers will not be able to perform any observation or experiment that infers either an expanding universe dominated by a cosmological constant or a hot Big Bang. Observers will be able to infer a finite age for their island universe, but beyond that cosmology will effectively be over. The authors detail the disappearance of the Hubble expansion, noting that the Local Group remains gravitationally bound while more distant structures are driven outside the de Sitter event horizon on a timescale on the order of 100 billion years, and that light from them is exponentially redshifted so that within a time frame comparable to the longest-lived main sequence stars all objects outside the local cluster become truly invisible. They describe the vanishing CMB, noting that at t approximately 100 Gyr the peak wavelength of the CMB will be redshifted to roughly 1 m or a frequency of roughly 300 MHz, and that the intensity will be redshifted by about 12 orders of magnitude, with the microwave background peak redshifting below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium. They argue that general relativity gives no assistance, because the inference of expansion depends on the assumption of an isotropic and homogeneous universe, which will not hold for future observers. They discuss polluted elemental abundances, noting that the primordial helium mass fraction of Y = 0.25 will be dwarfed by the ultimate mass fraction of helium Y = 0.6, and that relic deuterium will be destroyed. They conclude that we live in a very special time in the evolution of the universe, the time at which we can observationally verify that we live in a very special time. The paper contains no bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty, and it reports no data, code, or ethics information, so those fields are empty.

The CMB will become unobservable as its peak wavelength is redshifted beyond the horizon and below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium.
Primordial element abundances will be polluted, making it impossible to infer a Big Bang origin, though observers can still estimate the age of their system.

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT-symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.authors: Miloslav Znojil
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: PT-symmetric quantum mechanics / one-dimensional scattering
summary.type_of_paper: Analytical/theoretical derivation with schematic numerical discretization
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a schematic, exactly solvable model of one-dimensional scattering in PT-symmetric quantum mechanics, where the potential V(x) is complex but possesses combined parity-time symmetry. The author begins by recalling the standard treatment of stationary one-dimensional motion via the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation, which admits either bound-state solutions with ψ(±∞) = 0 or scattering solutions with incoming and outgoing plane-wave boundary conditions. The conventional approach specifies reflection and transmission coefficients B and C once the normalization A = 1 is imposed. The recent generalization to non-Hermitian but quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians, characterized by PT-symmetry, is then invoked, with the key review by Carl Bender cited as the source of this development. The present work focuses on a very simple PT-symmetric scattering model in which the potential is written as V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), with Z even and real, and Y odd and real. Rather than solving the differential equation directly, the author replaces it with its Runge-Kutta-discretized, difference-equation representation, a purely numerical recipe whose accuracy improves as the lattice step h tends to zero. Assuming the potential vanishes beyond a cutoff distance, the discrete Schrödinger equation reduces to a tridiagonal linear system, which can be solved either by a matching method or by a matrix-inversion method. The matrix-inversion approach reduces the problem to a two-dimensional matrix inversion, with all dynamical input encoded in two coefficients α and β that are rational functions of the coupling constants. The paper derives explicit formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients and emphasizes that the only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter, namely the introduction of the imaginary part Y(x). The author illustrates the growing algebraic complexity of the determinant and numerator at increasing cutoff dimensions M = 2, 3, 4, noting that symbolic manipulation on a computer becomes necessary at M ≥ 4. The discussion situates the work within the broader PT-symmetry literature, highlighting the manifest asymmetry between in and out states, and concludes that the formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established, with the merit of the discrete model left for future study.

claims.description: The formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established.
The in-out asymmetry is shown to be merely formal in the present model.
The only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter.

Research Context
Standard quantum mechanics treats one-dimensional motion via the ordinary differential Schrödinger equation. The equation admits either bound-state or scattering regimes depending on the energy. Reflection and transmission coefficients are defined by imposing standard boundary conditions. The conventional approach has recently been generalized to non-Hermitian quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians. PT-symmetry is the key idea behind this generalization, as summarized by Carl Bender. Few papers have addressed scattering in PT-symmetric systems, leaving a gap to fill.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper asks how scattering can be modeled in a PT-symmetric quantum system. The potential is hypothesized to be complex but PT-symmetric, with an even real part and odd imaginary part. The differential equation is hypothesized to be replaceable by its Runge-Kutta-discretized difference form. It is hypothesized that the reflection and transmission coefficients can be derived from this discretized equation. The main hypothesis is that the only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter. It is predicted that Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering share a formal parallelism. It is predicted that the problem remains tractable despite the in-out asymmetry.

Methodological Details
The study considers a one-dimensional scattering problem with a complex PT-symmetric short-range potential. The Schrödinger equation is discretized using a Runge-Kutta method. The discrete Schrödinger equation is −ψk−1 + (2 cos ϕ + Vk) ψk −ψk+1 = 0. The lattice points are defined as xk = k h with h > 0 and k = 0, ±1, ... The potential is assumed to vanish beyond a cutoff distance j = M, M+1, .... The energy variable ϕ is constrained by −2 ≤ 2 − h2E ≤ 2, i.e., E ∈ (0, 4/h2). The boundary conditions are discretized with A = 1, B, and C as reflection and transmission coefficients. The M = 1 model uses three nontrivial relations to derive B and C. The M = 2 model inserts four known quantities into a triplet of relations. The coupling constants are Z0, Z1, ..., ZM−1 and Y1, ..., YM−1. The matrix-inversion method reduces the problem to a two-dimensional matrix inversion. The inverse matrix R = T−1 has four corners that represent all dynamical input. The coefficients α and β are rational functions of the coupling constants. The determinant det T and numerator γ grow in complexity at higher dimensions. Symbolic manipulation on a computer is required at M ≥ 4.

Procedures And Architectures
The differential equation is discretized using the Runge-Kutta method. The lattice step h and cutoff 1/M are varied independently for quickest convergence. The two independent solutions in the vanishing-potential region are ρ± = exp(±iϕ). The matching method constructs solutions from the boundary conditions. The matching method yields C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z0) and B = Z0 / (2i sin ϕ − Z0). The matrix-inversion method rewrites the equation as a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations. The system is reduced to a finite-dimensional tridiagonal non-square-matrix problem. The matrix T is partitioned to reveal redundant components. The inverse matrix R is partitioned into blocks α, β, and submatrices. The problem degenerates to two scalar relations for the amplitudes. The reflection and transmission coefficients are solved via elimination. The final formulae for B and C are given in terms of α and β. The determinant and numerator are computed explicitly for M = 2, 3, 4. The determinant for M = 2 is Z0Z1² − 2Z1 + Y1²2Z0. The determinant for M = 3 includes Y1²2Z0Z2² and other terms. The M = 4 case requires symbolic manipulation due to complexity. The coefficients α and β encode all dynamical input. The transmission and reflection coefficients have the same form in both cases.

Key Results
The reflection and transmission coefficients are derived from the discretized Schrödinger equation. The M = 1 model yields C = 2i sin ϕ / (2i sin ϕ − Z0). The M = 1 model yields B = Z0 / (2i sin ϕ − Z0). The M = 1 model remains Hermitian since no PT-symmetry has entered. The M = 2 model introduces the imaginary part Y−1. The M = 2 model yields det T = Z0Z1² − 2Z1 + Y1²2Z0. The M = 3 model yields det T with 15 products of couplings. The M = 4 model requires symbolic manipulation due to complexity. The coefficients α and β are rational functions of the coupling constants. The transmission and reflection coefficients have the same form in both cases. The dynamical input is encoded in the four corners of the inverse matrix R. The problem remains tractable by standard linear algebra techniques. The in-out asymmetry is shown to be merely formal. The only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter. No numerical values or datasets are reported.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established. The differences are represented by the differences in the form of the dynamical input. The dynamical input is encoded in the two functions α and β. The vanishing or non-vanishing coefficients Yk distinguish the two cases. The in-out asymmetry is a distinguishing feature of PT-symmetric scattering. The asymmetry is shown to be merely formal in the present model. The partitioning of the Schrödinger equation is key to the success. The reduction to two-dimensional matrix inversion simplifies the problem. The merits of the discrete model are not exhausted by the present analysis. Future study might illuminate the non-Hermitian inverse problem of scattering. The work fills a gap in the PT-symmetric scattering literature. The discrete model provides a schematic but exactly solvable framework.

Claims
The formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering is established. The transmission and reflection coefficients have the same form in both cases. The dynamical input is encoded in the two functions α and β. The differences are represented by the differences in the form of the dynamical input.  
The in-out asymmetry is shown to be merely formal in the present model.   
The only innovation is the complexification of one potential parameter. The imaginary part Y(x) introduces the PT-symmetry.  The formal parallelism simplifies the study of PT-symmetric scattering.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the formal parallelism between Hermitian and PT-symmetric scattering. 2. The strongest evidence is the derivation of the reflection and transmission coefficients. 3. The future path is the study of the non-Hermitian inverse problem of scattering.

summary.title: Are There Mach Cones in Heavy Ion Collisions? Three-Particle Correlations from STAR
summary.authors: Jason Glyndwr Ulery for the STAR Collaboration
summary.field_subfield: High-energy nuclear physics (quark-gluon plasma / jet correlations)
summary.executive_summary: This poster presents STAR Collaboration measurements of three-particle azimuthal correlations in proton–proton (pp), deuterium–gold (d+Au), and gold–gold (Au+Au) collisions at a nucleon–nucleon center-of-mass energy of √sNN = 200 GeV. The analysis uses a hard trigger particle with transverse momentum 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c and two softer associated particles with 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c, all reconstructed in the STAR time projection chamber. The central scientific question is whether the observed off-diagonal structure in central Au+Au collisions reflects conical emission from Mach-cone shock waves generated by jet quenching, as opposed to alternative mechanisms such as simple QCD Cherenkov radiation or deflected jets. To isolate the genuine three-particle signal, the authors rigorously subtract combinatorial backgrounds: a hard-soft background built from the two-particle jet-like correlation folded with the normalized two-particle background, plus soft-soft and trigger-flow backgrounds constructed from mixed events. Systematic uncertainties from the flow-harmonic subtraction (v2 and v4) and from the background normalization are investigated in detail. The key finding is that off-diagonal peaks appear at approximately π ± 1.45 radians and grow with centrality, consistent with conical emission. Crucially, the emission angle shows no strong dependence on associated-particle pT, which favors Mach-cone emission over Cherenkov radiation, whose model predicts a sharply decreasing angle with increasing momentum. The signal is robust against variations in the v2 determination (reaction plane vs. four-particle cumulant) and against changes in the background normalization window. This work provides early quantitative evidence for collective conical flow in the quark-gluon plasma and establishes a methodology for disentangling conical emission from competing jet-quenching mechanisms.

claims.description: Off-diagonal three-particle correlations at π ± 1.45 radians indicate conical emission in central Au+Au collisions.
The emission angle is independent of associated-particle pT, favoring Mach-cone emission over Cherenkov radiation.
The background subtraction and signal are robust against systematic variations.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This poster presents STAR Collaboration measurements of three-particle azimuthal correlations in proton–proton (pp), deuterium–gold (d+Au), and gold–gold (Au+Au) collisions at a nucleon–nucleon center-of-mass energy of √sNN = 200 GeV. The analysis uses a hard trigger particle with transverse momentum 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c and two softer associated particles with 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c, all reconstructed in the STAR time projection chamber. The central scientific question is whether the observed off-diagonal structure in central Au+Au collisions reflects conical emission from Mach-cone shock waves generated by jet quenching, as opposed to alternative mechanisms such as simple QCD Cherenkov radiation or deflected jets. To isolate the genuine three-particle signal, the authors rigorously subtract combinatorial backgrounds: a hard-soft background built from the two-particle jet-like correlation folded with the normalized two-particle background, plus soft-soft and trigger-flow backgrounds constructed from mixed events. Systematic uncertainties from the flow-harmonic subtraction (v2 and v4) and from the background normalization are investigated in detail. The key finding is that off-diagonal peaks appear at approximately π ± 1.45 radians and grow with centrality, consistent with conical emission. Crucially, the emission angle shows no strong dependence on associated-particle pT, which favors Mach-cone emission over Cherenkov radiation, whose model predicts a sharply decreasing angle with increasing momentum. The signal is robust against variations in the v2 determination (reaction plane vs. four-particle cumulant) and against changes in the background normalization window. This work provides early quantitative evidence for collective conical flow in the quark-gluon plasma and establishes a methodology for disentangling conical emission from competing jet-quenching mechanisms.

Research Context
Heavy-ion collisions may create a quark-gluon plasma that can be studied through jets and jet correlations. Two-particle azimuthal correlations reveal an away-side structure that is broadened or double-humped in central collisions. The broad away-side structure is consistent with many competing physics mechanisms. Hydrodynamic conical flow from Mach-cone shock waves is one such candidate mechanism. Cherenkov radiation is another candidate that also produces conical emission. Three-particle correlations can differentiate conical emission from other mechanisms. The associated-particle pT dependence of the conical angle distinguishes hydrodynamic conical flow from simple Cherenkov radiation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether conical emission from Mach-cone shock waves is present in heavy-ion collisions. Three-particle correlations are hypothesized to reveal conical emission as off-diagonal structure at π ± ~1.45 radians. The off-diagonal signal is expected to increase in magnitude with collision centrality. Conical flow is hypothesized to produce an emission angle independent of associated-particle pT. Cherenkov radiation is hypothesized to produce an emission angle sharply decreasing with increasing associated-particle momentum. Deflected jets are hypothesized to contribute to on-diagonal broadening but not to off-diagonal conical structure. The predicted outcome is a pT-independent angle favoring Mach-cone emission over Cherenkov radiation.

Methodological Details
The study reports results from the STAR experiment at RHIC. Measurements span pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collision systems. All collisions were at a nucleon-nucleon energy of √sNN = 200 GeV. The trigger particle has transverse momentum in the range 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c. The two associated particles have transverse momentum in the range 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. All particles are charged and reconstructed in the STAR time projection chamber. The analysis treats events as a sum of jet-like correlated and background components. The hard-soft background is built from the two-particle jet-like correlation folded with the normalized two-particle background. The two-particle background is constructed by mixing events with flow modulation added pairwise from average v2 values. The v4 contribution uses the parameterization v4 = 1.15 v2². The background is normalized within 0.8 < |Δφ| < 1.2 using the zero-yield-at-one-radian method. The soft-soft background is obtained from mixed events in the same centrality window. The trigger-flow background is added triplet-wise from mixed events. The total background is ˆJ2 ⊗αBinc2 + βα²(Binc3 + Binc,TF3). The scale factor β is obtained so that associated pairs in the three-particle signal equal the square of associated particles in the two-particle signal. Centrality classes include 50-80%, 30-50%, 10-30%, 0-10%, and ZDC-triggered 0-12% Au+Au. High-statistics central data uses an online ZDC trigger. The off-diagonal peak location is determined from a double Gaussian fit to an off-diagonal strip projection.

Procedures And Architectures
The raw three-particle distribution is plotted in ΔφaT = φa − φT and ΔφbT = φb − φT. The off-diagonal peak location is found to be 1.45 radians from π. Average signals are computed in 0.7 × 0.7 boxes at specific angular regions. On-diagonal and off-diagonal regions are compared to isolate conical emission from deflected jets. The off-diagonal peak angle is measured as a function of associated-particle pT. The off-diagonal peak angle is measured as a function of centrality. The off-diagonal peak angle is determined from double Gaussian fits. Statistical errors are shown as solid bars and systematic errors as shaded regions. The reaction-plane v2 and four-particle cumulant v2 are used as upper and lower bounds for the systematic uncertainty. The normalization window is varied by doubling it to 0.6 < |Δφ| < 1.4. A 20% effect on trigger-particle v2 arises from requiring a correlated particle. The π/2 reference line is shown on the emission-angle plots.

Key Results
Background-subtracted three-particle signals show near-side, away-side, and mixed-side peaks in pp and d+Au. The away-side peak displays diagonal elongation consistent with kT broadening in pp and d+Au. Peripheral Au+Au shows additional on-diagonal elongation possibly due to deflected jets. Central Au+Au collisions display an off-diagonal structure at about π ± 1.45 radians. The off-diagonal signal increases in magnitude with centrality. summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.authors: Akitoshi Kawamura
summary.field_subfield: Computability theory / analog computation
summary.executive_summary: This paper revisits Robert Moore's 2004 introduction of real-valued 'recursive' function classes, which were proposed as a bridge between digital computability and Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) model of analog computation. Moore claimed that his real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic (Claim 1) and that standard recursive functions on integers are restrictions of his real recursive functions (Claim 2). The paper argues that Moore's definitions suffer from technical inaccuracies, primarily because he does not explicitly handle partial functions, leading to ambiguity about the differential recursion operator's behavior. The author reformulates the theory up to real primitive recursive functions in a mathematically sound way, emphasizing that the value of an expression requires all subexpressions to be defined (Principle 7). Using this formulation, the paper proves that Claim 1 fails: even the most restrictive version of real primitive recursive functions contains functions that are not differentially algebraic. The central counterexample is a function related to Euler's gamma function, which H"older showed is not differentially algebraic. The paper also discusses Campagnolo's alternative differential recursion operator, which can produce non-analytic functions, and minimization-based real recursive functions, whose significance is doubted. The main conclusion is that the purported relation between Moore's classes and differentially algebraic functions—and hence to Shannon's model of analog computation—fails, leaving an open challenge to find a suitable subclass.

summary.title: QED⊗QCD Resummation and Shower/ME Matching for LHC Physics
summary.authors: B.F.L. Ward and S.A. Yost
summary.field_subfield: High-energy particle physics (QCD resummation / precision LHC phenomenology)
summary.type_of_paper: Theory paper (analytical resummation framework with semi-analytical and planned Monte Carlo applications)
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a theory of QED⊗QCD resummation and its interplay with parton-shower/matrix-element matching for precision LHC physics. The motivation is the luminosity measurement at the LHC, which requires a theoretical precision tag at the 0.67% level for processes such as single W and Z boson production decaying to light leptons, so as not to compromise the overall luminosity determination at the ~2% experimental precision. To meet this, multiple gluon and photon radiative effects must be controlled, which the theory of QED⊗QCD exponentiation allows by simultaneously resumming multiple gluon and photon radiation to all orders in both αs and α without double-counting effects. The authors build on the QCD resummation theory of Ref. [3], which is an exact rearrangement of the QCD perturbative series based on the N = 1 term in the exponent in the formal proof of exponentiation in non-Abelian gauge theories in the eikonal approximation (Ref. [4]). This exponential is augmented with a sum of residuals that account for the remaining contributions to the perturbative series exactly to all orders in αs, giving an exact result, whereas the resummation theories in Refs. [4, 5–7] are approximate. The extension to QED⊗QCD is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating the large infrared terms in QCD and the exact infrared-divergent terms in QED, using new YFS residuals that represent the successive application of the YFS expansion first for QCD and then for QED. The infrared algebra implies that QCD-dominant corrections occur about an order of magnitude earlier than QED corrections, so the leading residual level already gives a good estimate of the interplay between higher-order QED and QCD effects. The authors apply the theory to heavy gauge boson production, computing the ratio of the exponentiated cross section to the Born cross section, rexp = σexp/σBorn, at both the LHC and the Tevatron, with and without QED. They find that QED effects are at the ~0.3% level at both colliders, stable under scale variations, and similar in size to structure-function results found in the literature. They also discuss how to combine the exact YFS-style resummation calculus with HERWIG and/or PYTHIA parton showers using pT matching, and describe a more accurate shower-subtracted residual approach. The semi-analytical results for QED (and QCD) threshold effects agree with the literature on Z production, and the full Monte Carlo event generator realization is possible in principle. The corresponding analysis of W production is in progress. The paper provides a firm theoretical basis for the realization of the complete O(α2s, ααs, α2) results needed for FNAL/LHC/RHIC/ILC physics.

claims.description: QED⊗QCD resummation allows simultaneous resummation of multiple gluon and photon radiative effects without double-counting, providing the theoretical precision needed for LHC luminosity determinations.
The QED⊗QCD resummation can be combined with parton showers (HERWIG and/or PYTHIA) using pT matching to avoid double counting.

summary.title: Einstein vs Maxwell: Is gravitation a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or both?
summary.authors: Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: gravitation, general relativity, relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG), cosmology
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical physics paper (analytical derivation and solution)
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a field-theoretic reformulation of general relativity (GTR) in which gravitation is treated as a field living in a fixed Minkowski background, and then extends it to the Relativistic Theory of Gravitation (RTG) of Logunov, which abandons general coordinate invariance through a bimetric coupling. The author, Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen of the Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of Amsterdam, argues that the two seemingly opposed views of gravitation—Einstein's geometric curvature and Maxwell's field in flat space—are in fact equivalent, and that the field-theoretic approach is itself equivalent to a curved-space description, so both apply, describing the same physics from a different angle. The gravitational energy-momentum tensor is derived from the Einstein equations in a straightforward manner, allowing them to be presented as acceleration tensor = const. × total energy momentum tensor. For flat-space cosmology the gravitational energy is negative and cancels the material energy, so the total energy vanishes. The paper considers the case of a positive cosmological constant and solves a singularity-free version of the Schwarzschild black hole analytically. In the interior the components of the metric tensor quickly die out but do not change sign, leaving the role of time as usual. The ΛCDM model is covered for cosmology, while a form of inflation appears at early times. Here both the total energy and the zero point energy vanish. The paper traces the historical development from Einstein's step from flat space to curved space, through the quasi energy-momentum tensor problem, to the proper energy momentum tensor derived recently by Babak and Grishchuk, and to the bimetric theory of Nathan Rosen and the Logunov school. The author derives the acceleration tensor and the tensor τ µν in Minkowski space, which coincides with the Landau-Lifshitz quasi-tensor for Cartesian coordinates and with the Babak-Grishchuk tensor γtµν/g in general. The Einstein equations are written in the Newton shape acceleration = mass⁻¹ × force. The paper then applies the theory to cosmology, black holes, and the motion of test particles. For RTG with a negative cosmological constant it was claimed that an incoming spherical shell of matter is scattered off from a black hole; the author reconsiders this and shows that the present theory with a positive bimetric constant regularizes the interior of the Schwarzschild black hole, so escape is in principle possible and the theory allows a proper black hole. The modification of the Einstein equations involves the cosmological constant, so it is of Hubble size and immaterial for solar-system problems. In cosmology the theory directly leads to the ΛCDM model, while it could accommodate a positive curvature-like term. At short times there is a form of inflation. The gravitational energy exactly compensates the material energy, and the zero point energy vanishes, though the cosmological constant is finite and positive and is canceled by the bimetric terms. The paper concludes that curvature is a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space, that clusters of galaxies do not move away from each other but the speed of light changes with cosmic time, and that the quantum version of RTG, if it exists, will involve quantization of fields but not of space. The paper notes that topics such as a realistic equation of state for black holes, classical tunneling of its radiation, regularization of other singularities, as well as aspects of the inflation and of inhomogeneous cosmology are under study. Research Context
The general theory of relativity (GTR) was introduced by Einstein as a step from flat space to curved space. A fundamental difficulty is how to deal with the physics of gravitation itself, since there is only a quasi energy-momentum tensor. The proper energy momentum tensor of gravitation was derived only recently by Babak and Grishchuk. The Maxwell view that gravitation is a field in flat space was the starting point for Einstein and reappeared regularly. Changes of Einstein's GTR have mostly met deep troubles with one or another established property.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether gravitation is a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or both. The author hypothesizes that the field-theoretic approach to gravitation is by itself equivalent to a curved space description. The author predicts that when the theory is extended to RTG, the bimetrism forces to describe the Minkowski metric separately. The author predicts that a positive bimetric constant allows to regularize the interior of the Schwarzschild black hole. The author predicts that in cosmology the theory directly leads to the ΛCDM model. The author predicts that the gravitational energy exactly compensates the material energy.

The study is a purely theoretical derivation performed by a single author at the University of Amsterdam. The approach starts with a field theoretic approach in Minkowski space. The Minkowski metric is denoted ηµν = diag(1, −1, −1, −1). The Riemann metric tensor is defined by rg γ gµν = γµν + hµν ≡kµν. The acceleration tensor is defined as Aµν = 1/2 DαDβ(kµνkαβ −kµαkνβ).
