This feature distinguishes the two paradigms, unlike the angular power spectrum where the values are the same. The authors believe that the numerical techniques developed can be used in various contexts other than just calculating the bispectrum. Overall, the paper provides a rigorous analytical and numerical treatment of the B-mode auto-bispectrum due to matter bounce, demonstrating that while it can in principle distinguish bounce from inflation, the signal is extremely difficult to detect due to its very low SNR.

Research Context
The CMB is a relic of early Universe events and helps decipher primordial perturbations. The CMB field is assumed to be statistically isotropic and Gaussian, so all information is in two-point correlations. Non-Gaussianities make odd correlations nonzero, providing information about early Universe physics. Inflation is the most remarkable cosmological model, providing nearly scale-invariant spectra and solving horizon and flatness problems. Despite tighter constraints, many inflationary models remain unruled out, motivating alternatives. Bouncing cosmologies offer an alternative to inflation, with matter bounce giving rise to scale-invariant power spectra. Power spectra are identical for inflation and matter bounce, making higher-order correlations necessary for distinction. Perturbations freeze outside the horizon in inflation but grow in matter bounce, encoding differences in higher-order correlations. Prior work studied the B-mode auto-bispectrum in generalized slow-roll inflation, showing only higher-order Galileons boost tensor bispectra.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper investigates the CMB B-mode auto-bispectrum due to matter bounce Universe. The B-mode auto-bispectrum can only be generated by tensor perturbations, i.e., the gravity waves. The authors study B-modes in a minimally coupled Einstein frame for simplicity. The authors obtain an analytical expression for the B-mode auto-bispectrum and numerically evaluate it. The authors hypothesize that, similar to inflation, the signal-to-noise ratio is small and difficult to detect in future experiments. The authors hypothesize that the bispectra for inflation and matter bounce are different for all three limits—squeezed, folded, and equilateral. The authors hypothesize that the bispectrum can distinguish the two paradigms, unlike the angular power spectrum. The authors hypothesize that the numerical techniques developed can be used in various contexts other than just calculating the bispectrum.

Methodological Details
The analysis is performed in a minimally coupled Einstein frame for simplicity. The CMB field is characterized in terms of Stokes' parameters: I, Q and U. The temperature field I (or T) is a spin 0 field under rotation of the coordinate system. The polarization fields Q and U transform as spin ±2 fields under rotation. The edth differential operator is used to obtain spin 0 fields E and B modes from Q and U. The E and B modes are defined using the edth operator applied to Q and U. The B-mode auto-bispectrum Bl1l2l3 is defined in terms of the three-point correlations of B-mode harmonic coefficients. The three-point correlation of primordial perturbations is expressed with a delta function enforcing momentum conservation. The function f is written as G(k1,k2,k3) times a sum over permutations involving polarization tensors. The bispectrum is nonzero only for ∑li = odd and when all li's are different. The bispectrum is calculated for ∑li = 33, implying 114 possibilities in total for the triple (l1,l2,l3). Due to symmetry, only one of the six permutations needs to be evaluated. The explicit constant C appears in the bispectrum expression, with C ∼10−26. The transfer functions are obtained from the CAMB software. Planck 2018 cosmological parameters are used in the analysis. The tensor-to-scalar ratio is set to r = 0.01 for the bispectrum plots. The SNR is computed using the expression from Ref. [20]. The SNR is computed for lmax = 100. The bispectrum values are obtained after dividing by the square of the tensor amplitude, i.e., P2T. The shape function is normalized to unity for comparison.

Procedures And Architectures
The paper is structured into sections covering theory, bispectrum, numerical computation, results, and conclusion. The relation of three-point correlation function of spherical harmonic coefficients is obtained in terms of the three-point function of primordial perturbations. The analytical form of the bispectrum due to matter bounce is obtained in section III. The numerical computation techniques are discussed in section IV. The numerical computation is done with the help of the transfer functions obtained from the CAMB software. The steps for calculating the bispectrum involve choosing li and Li's that satisfy the Wigner 3j and 9j symbol requirements. In addition to the conditions in Eq. (13), ∑Li = even must hold because of the presence of I0,0,0L1,L2,L3. Four integrations are performed: one over x and three over ki's. For separable form, the integral Ix(n,l,L) is evaluated for different values of x. For inseparable form, the Laplace transform is taken and another variable y is introduced. The integrals are stored in an array for the relevant values of n, l and L for given x (and y). The integral evaluation part can easily be parallel implemented. The binary search method is used to retrieve integrals while doing integration over x (and y). The binary search method relies on two theorems derived in Appendix A1. The Wigner 3j and 9j symbols are computed using two methods. The first method for Wigner 3j calculation is the Rasch Algorithm, based on the Regge symmetries. The Rasch method employs 36 out of 72 symmetries. By computing and storing one symbol, 36 other symbols are determined as well. The fgsl software, a fortran version of gsl, is used for the evaluation of the symbols. fgsl gives a segmentation fault at larger values of l. wigxjpf software is used for the bispectrum evaluation at larger values of l while calculating SNR. Wigxjpf software calculates these symbols using prime number factorization. The condition ∑li = 33 along with the Wigner 9j symbol gives 114 possibilities on the triple (l1,l2,l3). The bispectrum is the same modulo a phase sign for different permutations of (l1,l2,l3), reducing computation to 1/6. The numerical computation of bispectrum involves integration over 4 (or 5) integrals. Both the trapezoidal and rectangular integration methods were checked and give the same answer.

The B-mode power spectrum due to inflation and matter bounce cannot be used to demarcate between the two. The bispectra for inflation and matter bounce are different for all three limits—squeezed, folded, and equilateral. The peaks of the bispectrum in both cases appear at the permutations of (l1,l2,l3) = (2,15,16). In case of inflation, the highest value of the bispectrum is found to be ∼6 × 10−11. In case of bounce, the highest value of the bispectrum is about ∼5 × 10−23. The highest absolute value of B-mode bispectrum due to inflation, as per Fig. 4, is ∼6 × 10−11, occurring at (l1,l2,l3) = (2,15,16). The B-mode auto-bispectrum due to matter bounce is about 10−12 times smaller than the inflation value. The SNR for standard inflation at r = 0.01 and lmax = 100 is ∼10−5. For bounce at r = 0.01 and lmax = 100, the SNR is ∼10−18. The SNR due to bounce is ∼10−13 times smaller than due to inflation. The SNR for scalar-to-tensor ratio r = 0.01 and lmax = 100 for inflation is ∼10−5. For matter bounce, the SNR ratio is smaller by a factor of ∼10−13. The shape functions for the two cases exhibit stark differences as can be seen in Fig. 5. The SNR is calculated in Figure 3 for tensor-to-scalar ratio r ∈{0.1,0.01}. The bispectra values are obtained after taking tensor to scalar ratio r = 0.01.

summary.title: An Investigation of the KF-type Lorentz-Symmetry Breaking Gauge Models in N = 1-Supersymmetric Scenario
summary.authors: H. Belich, G. S. Dias, J.A. Helayel-Neto, F.J.L. Leal, W. Spalenza
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical particle physics / supersymmetry and Lorentz violation
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes two supersymmetric realizations of the Kostelecký-Krauss-Freedman (KF) type Lorentz-violating gauge action in an N = 1 framework. The authors note that the Standard Model Extension is a natural framework for studying Lorentz violation, and that the gauge sector contains a CPT-even tensor Kµνκλ with Riemann-like symmetries. They state that the action S = −(1/4)∫d⁴x KµνκλFµνFκλ is Lorentz-violating because the tensor has a non-zero vacuum expectation value. The central contribution is showing that supersymmetrizing this action can be done via either a chiral superfield or a vector superfield. In the chiral case, they derive that the background superfield must be chiral, imposing the constraint ξµ = ∂µS, and that the K-tensor depends exclusively on the scalar component S. They observe that no ζ-condensate or G-dependence appears in the K-tensor expression. In the vector case, they use a vector superfield to accommodate the background vector ξλ, noting that the content of partners is richer in this case than in the chiral background. They derive the component field actions Sboson, Sfermion, and Scoupled for both proposals. They emphasize that SUSY is readily seen to be broken by the background in both cases, though they do not have elements to decide whether SUSY breaking occurred before Lorentz-symmetry violation. They argue that Lorentz-symmetry violation, as originated at a more fundamental level in the string framework, cannot be dissociated from SUSY. The paper concludes by raising the question of the influence of the Lorentz-violating background on the spectrum, and the need to avoid non-physical excitations such as tachyons and ghosts. They note that the breaking of Lorentz-symmetry signals the violation of the former, and that a model with contemporary breaking of SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry remains to be built. This is a purely theoretical work with no experimental data, numerical results, or datasets, and no bibliography is provided in the supplied text.

claims.description: The KF-type Lorentz-violating gauge action can be supersymmetrized using either a chiral or a vector superfield.
In the chiral case, the K-tensor depends exclusively on the scalar component S, ensuring its constancy.
In the vector case, the background is richer, with fermion condensates that mix χ and Ψ.
Both proposals break SUSY through the background, though the ordering of SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry breaking is not determined.

summary.title: Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy
summary.authors: P. Nemes-Incze, Z. Kónya, I. Kiricsi, Á. Pekker, Z.E. Horváth, K. Kamarás, L.P. Biró
summary.field_subfield: Nanoscience / Materials characterization (STM of functionalized carbon nanotubes)
summary.executive_summary: Sidewall functionalization of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) is a versatile route to tune their electronic properties and interactions with the environment, broadening applications in sensors, medicine, and composites. However, refining these applications requires a clear picture of the changes functionalization induces—surface topography, band structure, doping—rather than only global spectroscopic averages. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and its Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS) mode offer spatially resolved, energy-resolved information at the atomic scale, but this potential remains largely untapped for functionalized CNTs because of sample stability issues. Functional groups reduce the contact area with the substrate, weakening the anchoring force, so the metal tip can move tubes and even brush them out of the scan area. Immobilization via strong chemical bonds (e.g., Au–S chemistry) is not universally applicable and may perturb the tube electronic structure. This work presents a simple solution: sandwiching functionalized multiwalled CNTs (MWCNTs) between few-layer graphene (FLG) flakes in a CNT–FLG composite (buckypaper). The clamping FLG layer restricts tube movement, enabling stable, reproducible CITS measurements on a well-studied CNT–graphite system with nearly matched work functions, so no significant substrate doping is expected. Using a Veeco Multimode III SPM in CITS mode with mechanically cut Pt/Ir tips, the authors acquired energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps and dI/dV spectra. They found that acid oxidation and functionalization preferentially advance along the zigzag crystallographic direction on large-diameter MWCNTs (~15 nm), providing experimental evidence for a crystallographic preference in oxidation reactions. High-conductance regions show graphitic dI/dV curves and atomic resolution with superstructure patterns indicating defect scattering, while low-conductance regions correlate with surface protrusions and are attributed to defective or intensely functionalized areas where the sp2 π lattice is destroyed. The sample is globally p-doped (~0.25 eV Fermi level shift) due to acid adsorption and oxygen-containing species, but functionalized sites show asymmetry suggesting charge transfer. The technique also enables in situ studies under gas or vapor environments, aiding understanding of gas sensing with functionalized nanotube networks.

summary.title: Nonlinearity in the dark: Broadband terahertz generation with extremely high efficiency
summary.authors: Ming Fang, Nian-Hai Shen, Wei E.I. Sha, Zhixiang Huang, Thomas Koschny, and Costas M. Soukoulis
summary.field_subfield: Terahertz photonics / nonlinear metamaterials and metasurfaces
summary.executive_summary: Terahertz (THz) technology has advanced rapidly since the emergence of quantum-cascade lasers and ultrafast photoconductive switches, yet efficient and compact THz emitters/detectors remain challenging. Conventional nonlinear optical rectification and difference-frequency generation (DFG) in inorganic crystals suffer from narrow bandwidth, phase-matching limitations, spectrum gaps, and low emission intensity. Metasurfaces of split-ring resonators (SRRs) have shown broadband gapless THz emission up to 4 THz with conversion efficiency comparable to 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystals, but the nonlinear response remains weak. This work reveals a fundamental limit of conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces, governed by dissipative and radiative damping due to linear scattering, which limit the local near-field amplitude and thus THz emission intensity. The authors propose a dark-mode-assisted perfect-absorbing metasurface that eliminates linear radiation damping while maintaining constructive interference and effective radiation of the nonlinear components. The design combines a resonant dark-state metasurface that drives nonlinear SRRs in the near field with a specific spatial symmetry enabling destructive interference of the radiating linear moments, plus perfect absorption via simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling of the pump radiation to the dark mode. Numerically, the study demonstrates a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of ~2.4 x 10^-11 m/V, one order of magnitude larger than previously reported SRR metasurfaces, corresponding to more than 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power. The proposal offers a paradigm of high-efficiency tunable nonlinear meta-devices and paves the way to revolutionary THz technologies and optoelectronic nanocircuitry. The study is theoretical, using a self-consistent FDTD calculation based on the hydrodynamic model and Maxwell's equations, and explicitly acknowledges that the simplified spatially infinite surface model is less suitable to predict practical absolute numbers observed in experiments.

claims.description: A dark-mode-assisted perfect-absorbing metasurface can eliminate linear radiation damping while maintaining nonlinear radiation, yielding giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility and enhanced THz generation.
The reference SRR metasurface provides a benchmark for comparison, showing conversion efficiency comparable to 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystal.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Terahertz (THz) technology has advanced rapidly since the emergence of quantum-cascade lasers and ultrafast photoconductive switches, yet efficient and compact THz emitters/detectors remain challenging. Conventional nonlinear optical rectification and difference-frequency generation (DFG) in inorganic crystals suffer from narrow bandwidth, phase-matching limitations, spectrum gaps, and low emission intensity. Metasurfaces of split-ring resonators (SRRs) have shown broadband gapless THz emission up to 4 THz with conversion efficiency comparable to 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystals, but the nonlinear response remains weak. This work reveals a fundamental limit of conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces, governed by dissipative and radiative damping due to linear scattering, which limit the local near-field amplitude and thus THz emission intensity. The authors propose a dark-mode-assisted perfect-absorbing metasurface that eliminates linear radiation damping while maintaining constructive interference and effective radiation of the nonlinear components. The design combines a resonant dark-state metasurface that drives nonlinear SRRs in the near field with a specific spatial symmetry enabling destructive interference of the radiating linear moments, plus perfect absorption via simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling of the pump radiation to the dark mode. Numerically, the study demonstrates a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of ~2.4 x 10^-11 m/V, one order of magnitude larger than previously reported SRR metasurfaces, corresponding to more than 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power. The proposal offers a paradigm of high-efficiency tunable nonlinear meta-devices and paves the way to revolutionary THz technologies and optoelectronic nanocircuitry. The study is theoretical, using a self-consistent FDTD calculation based on the hydrodynamic model and Maxwell's equations, and explicitly acknowledges that the simplified spatially infinite surface model is less suitable to predict practical absolute numbers observed in experiments.

Research Context
THz technology has gained significant progress in sensing, imaging, and communication. Efficient and compact THz emitters/detectors are urgently demanded. Conventional nonlinear THz sources suffer from narrow bandwidth and low intensity. Metasurfaces offer freedom to design subwavelength atoms as building blocks. Resonant nonlinearity and local field enhancement coexist in meta-atoms. SRR metasurfaces generate broadband gapless THz emission up to 4 THz. The nonlinear optical response reported is still fairly weak. A fundamental improvement in nonlinear efficiency is critical.

Research Question And Hypothesis
What fundamentally limits conversion efficiency in nonlinear metasurfaces? Can linear radiation damping be eliminated while maintaining nonlinear radiation? Can a dark-mode-assisted perfect-absorbing metasurface circumvent the efficiency limit? Will the design yield giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility and enhanced THz extraction? Will THz energy extraction be enhanced by two orders of magnitude?

Methodological Details
The study is a numerical/theoretical proposal without experimental data. The design uses two gold SRRs on a thin silicon slab. The silicon slab is periodically punctuated by metal walls. The unit cell length is 800 nm. The unit cell width is 240 nm. The silicon slab thickness is 100 nm. The SRR thickness is 50 nm. The operation wavelength is tuned around 1.5 µm. The TE2,0 mode is selected for operation. The sheet conductivities were calculated with a scanning step size of 5 nm. The model uses the hydrodynamic model for the electron gas. The simulation uses self-consistent FDTD calculation. The driving frequency equals the resonant frequency of the dark mode. The pulse duration is 140 fs. The peak amplitude is 2 x 10^7 V/m. The spectral width is approximately 3.2 THz.

Procedures And Architectures
The metasurface combines a resonant dark-state metasurface with nonlinear SRRs. The dark state is a low-loss dielectric element in a silicon film. The metal walls quantize the modes of the dielectric slab. The TE2,0 mode has an anti-symmetric electric field profile. The dark mode cannot directly couple to the incident plane wave. Coupling is achieved via non-resonant weak SRR scatterers. The SRRs create equivalent electric and magnetic effective surface susceptibilities. Balancing electric and magnetic coupling allows impedance match. Critical coupling eliminates the linear transmitted field. The metasurface is characterized by electric and magnetic sheet conductivities. The ideal perfect absorbing sheet fulfills ζσ(e)s = ζ^-1σ(m)s = 2. The optimal case is at ∆x1 ~ 70 nm and ∆x2 ~ 470 nm. The polarization currents are decomposed into symmetric and anti-symmetric sets. The nonlinear process is second order in the electric field. The linear radiation cancels in the far field while nonlinear radiation adds constructively. The THz signal is described by the second-order nonlinear susceptibility. The THz spectrum peaks at ω = 2/τ with bandwidth ∆ωFWHM ≈ 2.31/τ.

Key Results
The optimal configuration achieves absorption as high as 94%. The effective nonlinear susceptibility is ~2.4 x 10^-11 m/V. The traditional SRR metasurface susceptibility is ~1.7 x 10^-12 m/V. The reported 1.6 x 10^-12 m/V is consistent with prior work. The THz enhancement is more than 120-fold. The THz enhancement is inversely proportional to linear radiation damping. The generated THz signal amplitude increases linearly with pump intensity. The design shows dramatic emission enhancement over conventional SRR. The nonlinear susceptibility is more than one order of magnitude larger. The configuration would generate over two-order enhanced THz emission. The reference SRR metasurface matches 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystal. The THz radiation is polarized along the x-axis. The THz emission is emitted perpendicular to the metasurface on both sides.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Radiative and dissipative damping limit the local near-field amplitude. The ratio of THz signal to scattered pump is proportional to near-field amplitude. The dark mode eliminates linear radiation damping. The nonlinear components maintain constructive interference and effective radiation. The design tackles the efficiency limit in two crucial aspects. The design eliminates radiative damping of linear scatterings. The design enhances local field for nonlinear signals. The new concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes. The flexibility in tailoring meta-atoms opens new opportunities.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is theoretical without experimental verification. The model considers a spatially infinite surface under plane-wave illumination. The model is less suitable to predict practical absolute numbers. Conversion efficiency depends on many experimental factors. The comparison is within the same numerical simulations. The dimensions of the SRRs are not critical. The discussions to the case with substrate are in Supplemental Material. The thermal damage threshold estimation is in Supplemental Material.

Claims
A dark-mode-assisted perfect-absorbing metasurface can eliminate linear radiation damping while maintaining nonlinear radiation, yielding giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility and enhanced THz generation. The design eliminates linear radiation damping. The nonlinear components maintain constructive interference. The effective nonlinear susceptibility is ~2.4 x 10^-11 m/V. The THz enhancement is more than 120-fold. The nonlinear susceptibility is more than one order of magnitude larger. The study is theoretical without experimental verification. The model is less suitable to predict practical absolute numbers. Conversion efficiency depends on many experimental factors. The design offers a paradigm of high-efficiency tunable nonlinear meta-devices. The new concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes. The flexibility in tailoring meta-atoms opens new opportunities.
The reference SRR metasurface provides a benchmark for comparison, showing conversion efficiency comparable to 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystal. The reference SRR metasurface matches 0.2 mm-thick ZnTe crystal. The traditional SRR metasurface susceptibility is ~1.7 x 10^-12 m/V. The reference nonlinear response is still fairly weak. The proposed configuration should show much better performance in real experiments.

Data And Code Availability
The study is theoretical without experimental data. The details are in the Supplemental Material.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The THz enhancement is inversely proportional to linear radiation damping. The optimal case is at ∆x1 ~ 70 nm and ∆x2 ~ 470 nm. The dimensions of the SRRs are not critical. The TE2,0 mode is selected for operation.

Ethical Considerations
The study acknowledges support from funding agencies.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the designed dark-mode THz emitter and principle of operation. Figure 2 shows the equivalent current sheet. Figure 3 shows the scattering properties of the metasurface. Figure 4 shows the terahertz enhancement of the design. The absorption reaches as high as 94%. The effective nonlinear susceptibility is ~2.4 x 10^-11 m/V.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a dark-mode-assisted perfect-absorbing metasurface that eliminates linear radiation damping. 2. The strongest evidence is the giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of ~2.4 x 10^-11 m/V. 3. The future path is high-efficiency tunable nonlinear meta-devices for THz technologies.

summary.title: Reduced residence time of droplet impact on heated surfaces
summary.authors: Song Rong, Shiquan Shen, Tianyou Wang, and Zhizhao Che
summary.field_subfield: Fluid dynamics / multiphase heat transfer
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, with a focus on reducing the residence time—the interval between the moments a droplet visually contacts and visually detaches from the substrate. The authors identify a new bouncing mode, termed the bouncing-with-spray (BWS) mode, which dramatically shortens the residence time compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing (RB) mode. The BWS mode arises from the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, which creates holes that cause the liquid film to recoil into fragments, thereby reducing the recoiling distance and time. This mechanism is induced by heat, making it simple and reliable, as it avoids surface degradation and complex fabrication of microstructures. The study uses water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, with Weber numbers varied from 10 to 180. The residence time reduction is found to be independent of liquid viscosity, and the BWS mode reduces the residence time by about 40% compared with the RB mode. A theoretical model is proposed to describe the transition between the two modes in the film boiling regime, yielding a scaling law (ΔT ∼ V⁻¹) that agrees well with the experimental data. The model also explains the transition in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into the impact dynamics and potential applications in spray cooling, anti-icing, self-cleaning, and corrosion resistance.

The residence time reduction is independent of liquid viscosity.
The scaling law ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ agrees well with the experimental data.

The authors identify a new bouncing mode, termed the bouncing-with-spray (BWS) mode, which dramatically shortens the residence time compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing (RB) mode. The BWS mode arises from the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, which creates holes that cause the liquid film to recoil into fragments, thereby reducing the recoiling distance and time. This mechanism is induced by heat, making it simple and reliable, as it avoids surface degradation and complex fabrication of microstructures. The study uses water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, with Weber numbers varied from 10 to 180. The residence time reduction is found to be independent of liquid viscosity, and the BWS mode reduces the residence time by about 40% compared with the RB mode. A theoretical model is proposed to describe the transition between the two modes in the film boiling regime, yielding a scaling law (ΔT ∼ V⁻¹) that agrees well with the experimental data. The model also explains the transition in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into the impact dynamics and potential applications in spray cooling, anti-icing, self-cleaning, and corrosion resistance.

Research Context
Droplet impact occurs ubiquitously in nature and industrial applications. Impact on heated surfaces is affected by heat transfer and phase change. summary.title: Real-Time Ramsey Interferometry in Fractional Quantum Hall States
summary.authors: Tal Goren and Karyn Le Hur
summary.field_subfield: Condensed matter theory; fractional quantum Hall physics
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a theoretical protocol for probing the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall edge states using Ramsey interferometry. The authors argue that a two-pulse voltage modulation applied across a quantum point contact (QPC) generates an interference term in the current noise that oscillates with the dynamical phase accumulated between the pulses. The central claim is that this interference pattern directly reveals the fractional charge of the tunneling particles and provides access to their time-domain Green's functions. The method is developed for both Laughlin states with filling factor nu = 1/(2n+1) and for the non-Abelian 5/2 fractional quantum Hall case, where it can distinguish between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states. The paper derives the current-current correlation function using the Keldysh formalism and applies the stationary phase approximation to obtain explicit expressions for the noise under the Ramsey voltage modulation. Two tunneling geometries are considered: point-like tunneling of fractional quasiparticles through the bulk of a Hall bar, and momentum-resolved tunneling between separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel and acquire a momentum boost from the magnetic field. The authors show that the Ramsey signal amplitude decays with the delay time t0 in a way that reflects the Green's function of the tunneling particles, and that this decay is not due to a finite lifetime of the excitations but rather measures the envelope of the wave-function in time. The paper contrasts Ramsey interferometry with Mach-Zehnder and Hong-Ou-Mandel geometries, arguing that the continuous scanning of the time delay t0 makes Ramsey interferometry advantageous for measuring Green's functions. The theoretical results are presented as a proposal for future experiments, with no numerical simulations or experimental data reported. The work is grounded in chiral Luttinger liquid effective theory and cites extensive prior literature on fractional quantum Hall physics, interferometry, and Green's functions.

The central claim is that this interference pattern directly reveals the fractional charge of the tunneling particles and provides access to their time-domain Green's functions. The method is developed for both Laughlin states with filling factor nu = 1/(2n+1) and for the non-Abelian 5/2 fractional quantum Hall case, where it can distinguish between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states. The paper derives the current-current correlation function using the Keldysh formalism and applies the stationary phase approximation to obtain explicit expressions for the noise under the Ramsey voltage modulation. Two tunneling geometries are considered: point-like tunneling of fractional quasiparticles through the bulk of a Hall bar, and momentum-resolved tunneling between separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel and acquire a momentum boost from the magnetic field. The authors show that the Ramsey signal amplitude decays with the delay time t0 in a way that reflects the Green's function of the tunneling particles, and that this decay is not due to a finite lifetime of the excitations but rather measures the envelope of the wave-function in time. The paper contrasts Ramsey interferometry with Mach-Zehnder and Hong-Ou-Mandel geometries, arguing that the continuous scanning of the time delay t0 makes Ramsey interferometry advantageous for measuring Green's functions. The theoretical results are presented as a proposal for future experiments, with no numerical simulations or experimental data reported. The work is grounded in chiral Luttinger liquid effective theory and cites extensive prior literature on fractional quantum Hall physics, interferometry, and Green's functions.

Research Context
Fractional quantum Hall states host excitations with fractional charge and statistics. Edge states are described by a chiral Luttinger liquid effective theory. Ramsey interferometry has been suggested to probe mesoscopic and strongly correlated systems. Ramsey interferometry has been applied to one-dimensional quasicondensates, spin ensembles, and Rydberg atoms. The 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state is of major interest for topological quantum computation. The Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states are competing candidates for the 5/2 state. Recent experiments support the particle-hole Pfaffian state at filling factor 5/2.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper asks whether Ramsey interferometry can probe the dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles. The hypothesis is that a Ramsey two-pulse voltage modulation generates an interference term in the current noise oscillating with the dynamical phase. The authors predict that the interference pattern reveals the fractional charge of the tunneling particles. The authors predict that the interference pattern provides access to the Green's function of the fractional quasiparticles in the time domain. The authors predict that momentum-resolved tunneling provides information on the speed of the quasiparticles. The authors predict that Ramsey interferometry can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states. The authors predict that the Ramsey signal amplitude decays with the delay time t0 in a way reflecting the Green's function.

Methodological Details
The system is modeled using a chiral Luttinger liquid effective theory. The Laughlin states considered have filling factor nu = 1/(2n+1) where n is an integer. The fractional quasiparticle charge is q = e*nu with creation operator expressed by bosonic chiral fields. An electron is composed of nu-1 fractional quasiparticles. The commutation relations ensure correct anti-commutation for electrons and fractional statistics for quasiparticles. Two QPC geometries are considered: point-like tunneling and momentum-resolved tunneling. The tunneling Hamiltonian for a QPC at x=0 is given by the expression with dynamical phase. The dynamical phase is defined as the integral of the charge times the voltage over time. The Planck constant is fixed to hbar = 1 throughout the calculation. The Keldysh formalism is applied to describe the non-equilibrium system. The current-current correlation function is symmetrized on the two branches of the Keldysh contour. The current noise is defined as the Fourier transform of the correlation function. The stationary phase approximation is used to evaluate the main contributions to the integral. The Green's functions of the tunneling particles are defined in the time domain. The Ramsey voltage modulation consists of two short pulses separated by delay time t0 on a constant voltage. The pulse durations are assumed much smaller than the delay time t0. The pulses are approximated by Dirac delta functions. The calculation assumes Planck constant hbar = 1 and does not report numerical values.

The current operator between the two edges is derived from the tunneling Hamiltonian. The current-current correlation function is computed to second order in the tunneling amplitude D. The stationary conditions for the first term require the derivative of the phase plus omega to vanish. The stationary conditions for the second term require the derivative of the phase minus omega to vanish. For positive voltage modulation and positive frequencies, the noise comes from the second term. The double-integral is approximated by the integrand at equal voltage times. The resulting noise expression involves the Green's functions of the tunneling particles. The Ramsey noise expression includes an interference term oscillating with the delay time t0. The charge in the formula is the dressed charge in the fluid. The amplitude of the oscillations provides information on the Green's functions. The Green's functions of the fractional quasiparticles are given by the expression with the sine function. The function chi is defined in terms of the Keldysh indices and the sign function. The noise under the Ramsey modulation is given by the expression with the cosine factor. In the high temperature limit the amplitude decays exponentially with the delay time. The Ramsey signal probes the time-dependent dynamical phase of fractional quasiparticles. The interference pattern reveals the fractional charge of the tunneling particles. The amplitude of the oscillations provides information on the Green's functions. The decay of the Ramsey interference measures the envelope of the wave-function in time. The decay is not due to a finite lifetime of the excitations. The fractional quasiparticle is an eigen-state of the Hamiltonian with energy epsilon = v*q. The formation of interferences in time allows one to measure the charge conjugated to the electric field. The Ramsey signal is a result of interferences between two tunneling events at the same QPC. The time delay t0 can be scanned continuously in contrast to the length of the Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The Ramsey interferometry is advantageous for measuring the Green's function. The phase detected by the Mach-Zehnder is determined by the magnetic flux enclosed by the two arms. The Ramsey interference is determined by the dynamical phase accumulated by the particles. Mach-Zehnder interferometers can probe the charge fractionalization and statistics of quasiparticles. The number of quasiparticles in the bulk is difficult to control in Mach-Zehnder experiments. Ramsey interferometry involves only a single QPC and does not depend on bulk quasiparticles. The Ramsey interferometry does not detect exchange statistics. summary.title: BanStereoSet: A Dataset to Measure Stereotypical Social Biases in LLMs for Bangla
summary.authors: Mahammed Kamruzzaman, Abdullah Al Monsur, Shrabon Das, Enamul Hassan, Gene Louis Kim
summary.field_subfield: Natural Language Processing / Computational Social Science (bias evaluation in multilingual LLMs)
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a fill-in-the-blank dataset designed to measure stereotypical social biases in large language models (LLMs) for the Bangla language. The authors argue that bias research has been dominated by English-centric resources, and that culturally and linguistically adapted datasets are necessary to develop more equitable language technologies. To address this gap, they localized content from three existing datasets—StereoSet, IndiBias, and Kamruzzaman et al.’s (2024b) GenAssocBias dataset—alongside freshly curated regional data, producing a resource tailored to the Bangla-speaking community. The final dataset contains 1,194 sentences spanning nine bias categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The authors describe the translation process, which involved GPT-4 with few-shot learning followed by review by four native Bangla-speaking annotators, and detail several Bangla-specific translation modifications, such as adding gender-specific phrases and substituting English names and city references. They also address five pitfalls identified by Blodgett et al. (2021), retaining only sentences for which at least three annotators reached consensus. The paper then reports experimental results obtained by evaluating four multilingual LLMs—GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B—on both the Bangla and English versions of the dataset, using three prompting templates. The results reveal significant biases across all models and categories, with Mistral generally performing the least biased and GPT-4o the most biased on average. The authors note that overall, there is no consistent, major difference in model biases between Bangla and English, though notable exceptions exist, such as Mistral successfully handling caste bias in Bangla but not in English. They interpret these findings as evidence of a degree of cultural sensitivity that depends on the language of communication. The paper concludes by emphasizing the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems and highlighting the necessity of extending bias research beyond English. The authors also acknowledge several limitations, including incomplete regional representation, a focus on binary gender, translation inaccuracies, small category sizes, the exclusion of categories such as sexual orientation, socio-economic status, and disability, and the potential impact of models' limited Bangla proficiency on evaluation outcomes.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a fill-in-the-blank dataset designed to measure stereotypical social biases in large language models (LLMs) for the Bangla language. The authors argue that bias research has been dominated by English-centric resources, and that culturally and linguistically adapted datasets are necessary to develop more equitable language technologies. To address this gap, they localized content from three existing datasets—StereoSet, IndiBias, and Kamruzzaman et al.’s (2024b) GenAssocBias dataset—alongside freshly curated regional data, producing a resource tailored to the Bangla-speaking community. The final dataset contains 1,194 sentences spanning nine bias categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The authors describe the translation process, which involved GPT-4 with few-shot learning followed by review by four native Bangla-speaking annotators, and detail several Bangla-specific translation modifications, such as adding gender-specific phrases and substituting English names and city references. They also address five pitfalls identified by Blodgett et al. (2021), retaining only sentences for which at least three annotators reached consensus. The paper then reports experimental results obtained by evaluating four multilingual LLMs—GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B—on both the Bangla and English versions of the dataset, using three prompting templates. The results reveal significant biases across all models and categories, with Mistral generally performing the least biased and GPT-4o the most biased on average. The authors note that overall, there is no consistent, major difference in model biases between Bangla and English, though notable exceptions exist, such as Mistral successfully handling caste bias in Bangla but not in English. They interpret these findings as evidence of a degree of cultural sensitivity that depends on the language of communication. The paper concludes by emphasizing the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems and highlighting the necessity of extending bias research beyond English. The authors also acknowledge several limitations, including incomplete regional representation, a focus on binary gender, translation inaccuracies, small category sizes, the exclusion of categories such as sexual orientation, socio-economic status, and disability, and the potential impact of models' limited Bangla proficiency on evaluation outcomes.

Research Context
Bias in LLMs has been widely studied, but most bias datasets are predominantly English-centric. Existing bias datasets have been proposed for various languages, but research on Bengali remains sparse. Recent studies have revealed undesirable biases and stereotypes in state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs. Prior Bengali bias work has primarily addressed gender and religious biases rather than a broader spectrum. There is a lack of a dataset that comprehensively covers a broad spectrum of bias categories within the Bengali cultural context.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether stereotypical biases are prevalent in multilingual LLMs when evaluated on Bangla, and whether these biases differ from those observed in English. The authors hypothesize that significant stereotypical biases exist across multiple social categories in Bangla, reinforcing the necessity for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets. The authors predict that models will exhibit varying degrees of bias across categories, with some categories showing high bias and others showing relatively low bias. The authors predict that model biases in Bangla will not differ consistently and majorly from those in English, though language-specific differences may emerge. The authors hypothesize that certain models may demonstrate language-dependent cultural sensitivity, such as handling caste bias in Bangla but not in English.

Methodological Details
The study presents BanStereoSet, a dataset designed to evaluate stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. The dataset consists of 1,194 sentences spanning 9 categories of bias: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The StereoSet dataset provided data for the race, gender, religion, and profession bias categories. The beauty, beauty in profession, and ageism bias categories were derived from Kamruzzaman et al.'s (2024b) GenAssocBias dataset. The caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias dataset. The regional bias category was freshly curated by the authors. For StereoSet, only the intrasentence subset was considered because it holds the same structure as GenAssocBias. English sentences were translated into Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning to enhance translation accuracy. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators, fluent in English, reviewed each translation for accuracy. All intrasentence StereoSet examples and 250 samples from each bias type in GenAssocBias were included. Only the caste-related examples from IndiBias were used. Gender-specific phrases 'ekjon purush' (a man) and 'ekjon mohila' (a woman) were added to maintain gender distinctions; this modification was applied to 76 sentences. English names such as 'John' and 'Judy' were substituted with Bengali names like 'Mehedi' and 'Sumiya'; this change affected 12 sentences. References to US cities like 'Boston' were replaced with Bangladeshi cities such as 'Dhaka'; this adjustment was made in 6 sentences. The authors addressed five pitfalls from Blodgett et al. (2021): meaningful stereotype, misaligned stereotype, invalid perturbations, incommensurable groups and attributes, and text is not naturalistic. These pitfalls affected 47, 9, 15, 58, and 35 sentences of the final dataset, respectively. Corrections were performed manually and underwent discussion between all annotators. Only sentences for which at least three annotators reached a consensus were retained. For caste data, the 'sent-more' column was used for stereotype options and the 'sent-less' column for anti-stereotype options, with manually curated unrelated options. Regional data curation used a human-LLM partnership, retaining data only if at least three out of four annotators agreed on its appropriateness. Attribute collection started with 17 major cities in Bangladesh, using ChatGPT to generate 10 stereotypical, 10 anti-stereotypical, and 10 unrelated attributes for each city. The category sizes are: Race 241, Gender 178, Religion 56, Profession 206, Ageism 134, Beauty 130, Beauty Profession 126, Caste 60, and Region 63.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors evaluated the Bangla dataset using four multilingual LLMs: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B. Three prompting templates were used: a baseline template and two paraphrases. The baseline prompt instructed the model to select the appropriate word from the options based solely on the context, without considering the order of the options. The baseline prompt required a single, plain Bangla text with the answer and no explanation. Following Gupta et al. (2023), the main results were averaged across all three prompting templates. To compare Bangla results with English, the authors ran the four models using the English version of the dataset. For the English version, the authors used the modified English sentences, corrected Bangla-translated sentences, and zero-shot learning. Results are presented as a percentage (%) of responses that align with stereotypical judgments, excluding unrelated engagements. The authors exclude unrelated engagements because in the StereoSet dataset unrelated terms are included solely to assess the desired behavior. The desired behavior is for models' stereotypical responses to be close to 50%, indicating uniform treatment of stereotype and anti-stereotype attributes. For StereoSet-derived categories, the desirable percentage of stereotypical responses is lower than 50% due to extremely negative attributes. The authors interpret a fair or unbiased model's stereotypical engagement as ideally close to 50%, with StereoSet-derived categories leaning more towards 0%.

Key Results
On average, GPT-4o exhibits more stereotypical responses compared to other models, while Mistral exhibits the least. Mistral performs the best on 7 of the 9 bias categories, often by considerable margins. Llama performs best in the remaining 2 bias categories. All models show high levels of profession and region bias and relatively low levels of religion bias. Similar broad patterns are observed in English, with Mistral remaining the least biased model on average. In English, Gemma is now the most biased model. In English, gender, profession, caste, beauty, beauty profession, and region all show high levels of bias in all models. In English, all models continue to show low levels of bias in religion and handle ageism relatively well. On average, GPT-4o and Gemma models are more biased in Bangla sentences, while Mistral and Llama are more biased in English. Overall, there is no consistent, major difference in model biases in Bangla and English. Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla, but not in English, suggesting language-dependent cultural sensitivity. In the Gender category, GPT-4o shows 76.80% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 81.12% in English. In the Race category, GPT-4o shows 68.88% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 61.53% in English. In the Profession category, GPT-4o shows 72.53% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 73.50% in English. In the Religion category, GPT-4o shows 55.55% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 47.16% in English. In the Caste category, GPT-4o shows 76.27% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 78.78% in English. In the Beauty category, GPT-4o shows 92.38% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 94.11% in English. In the Beauty Profession category, GPT-4o shows 75.75% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 70.45% in English. In the Ageism category, GPT-4o shows 63.80% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 55.81% in English. In the Region category, GPT-4o shows 82.14% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 11.53% in English. The average stereotypical engagement across all categories is 73.78% in Bangla versus 63.77% in English for GPT-4o. For Mistral, the average stereotypical engagement is 55.41% in Bangla versus 59.94% in English. For Llama, the average stereotypical engagement is 64.09% in Bangla versus 65.54% in English. For Gemma, the average stereotypical engagement is 69.73% in Bangla versus 66.03% in English.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results indicate that all models exhibit significant biases across multiple social categories in Bangla, reinforcing the necessity for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets. The lack of a consistent, major difference in model biases between Bangla and English suggests that models handle bias similarly across languages, though notable exceptions exist. The finding that Mistral can handle Caste bias in Bangla but not in English suggests a degree of cultural sensitivity that is dependent on the language of communication. The results underscore the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems. The findings emphasize the necessity of extending bias research beyond English and developing datasets that reflect diverse linguistic and cultural realities. The results show promise in LLM capability to handle bias in less common languages as well as they do in English. The stark gap between popular models in their ability to handle bias highlights the need for further research and development.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh, as biases can vary markedly between different areas. The dataset's focus on binary gender (man and woman) representation restricts its ability to address biases concerning non-binary or gender-nonconforming identities. Challenges in translating stereotypes from English to Bangla may lead to inaccuracies or cultural mismatches. The relatively small size of certain categories, such as region bias, might limit the comprehensiveness of the bias evaluation. The dataset did not include other crucial categories such as sexual orientation, socio-economic status, or disability. The dataset predominantly captures explicit biases, which may neglect more subtle or underlying biases. The effectiveness of language model evaluations using this dataset could be compromised by the models' limited proficiency in Bangla, which might skew the results. The absence of gendered pronouns in Bangla complicates the accurate conveyance of gender nuances in sentences. The English translation provided for understanding purposes only is not actually included in the experiments.

Claims
BanStereoSet is a comprehensive, culturally adapted dataset for measuring stereotypical social biases in Bangla LLMs. The dataset consists of 1,194 sentences spanning 9 categories of bias. The dataset encompasses a broad spectrum of biases, including race, gender, and religion. The authors address five pitfalls from Blodgett et al. (2021). The authors retained only sentences for which at least three annotators reached a consensus. The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh. The dataset did not include other crucial categories such as sexual orientation, socio-economic status, or disability. The dataset facilitates the exploration of stereotypical bias across different social categories. The dataset potentially guides the development of more equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts. The dataset underscores the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems.

All models continue to show low levels of bias in religion in English and handle ageism relatively well. Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla, but not in English. The results reinforce the necessity for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets. The results underscore the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for training equitable AI systems. The results emphasize the necessity of extending bias research beyond English.

On average, GPT-4o and Gemma models are more biased in Bangla sentences, while Mistral and Llama are more biased in English. Mistral can successfully handle Caste bias in Bangla, but not in English. In the Region category, GPT-4o shows 82.14% stereotypical responses in Bangla versus 11.53% in English. The finding suggests a degree of cultural sensitivity that is dependent on the language of communication. The results show promise in LLM capability to handle bias in less common languages as well as they do in English. The results emphasize the necessity of extending bias research beyond English.

Data And Code Availability
City names and attributes used for region data curation are shown in Figure 4 in Appendix A. For further details on the models and results for each individual prompting template, see Appendix B. See Table 3 in Appendix C for unrelated engagement results.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors present main results averaged across all three prompting templates, following Gupta et al. (2023). The authors provide detailed results for each individual prompting template in Appendix B. The authors provide unrelated engagement results in Table 3 in Appendix C. The authors exclude unrelated engagements because in the StereoSet dataset unrelated terms are included solely to assess the desired behavior.

Key Figures Tables
Table 2 presents the three prompting templates used in the experiments. Table 3 presents unrelated engagement results in Appendix C. Figure 4 shows city names and attributes used for region data curation in Appendix A.

Three Takeaways

summary.title: Design of Real-time Semantic Segmentation Decoder for Automated Driving
summary.authors: Arindam Das, Saranya Kandan, Senthil Yogamani, Pavel Krizek
summary.field_subfield: Computer Vision / Efficient Neural Networks for Automated Driving
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology + Dataset (decoder design with proprietary dataset)
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses the under-studied problem of designing efficient decoders for real-time semantic segmentation on embedded platforms, where most prior work has focused on task-specific encoders. The authors argue that decoders are computationally expensive and that a task-independent, lightweight encoder can be shared across multiple tasks, with the decoder responsible for learning the semantic information that a generic encoder lacks. They propose a novel non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning, combining 1D and 3D kernels with multiple skip connections to distribute high gradient flow during back-propagation, and a family of decoders built on this layer. The encoder is a 10-layer VGG-style network pre-trained on ImageNet, and the study focuses on four classes: lanes, curb, road, and void. Experiments are conducted end-to-end using the Keras framework with the Adam optimizer on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. The authors report that careful experimentation with decoder design choices yielded a 10% improvement in mean IoU over a baseline configuration, with larger gains of 12% and 18% for the difficult lanes and curb classes respectively. They also demonstrate that the proposed decoder improves IoU over a standard FCN decoder with less than 2ms increase in runtime, satisfying the automotive power constraints. The paper contributes both a dataset (proprietary, owned by the authors' organization) and a decoder design, though the dataset is not publicly released. The authors note that their encoder consumed most of the runtime because it is wider than the decoder, and they discuss trade-offs between accuracy and runtime. Limitations include the proprietary nature of the dataset, the absence of data augmentation, the constant dilation rate of 1, and the lack of reported random seeds or detailed hyperparameter sensitivity analyses. The paper concludes by proposing future work on a systematic family of meta-architectures with a fixed run-time budget, learned using meta-learning techniques. Overall, the study makes a focused contribution to efficient decoder design for embedded semantic segmentation, demonstrating that decoder architecture choices can have a large impact on performance while remaining within strict runtime budgets.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper addresses the under-studied problem of designing efficient decoders for real-time semantic segmentation on embedded platforms, where most prior work has focused on task-specific encoders. The authors argue that decoders are computationally expensive and that a task-independent, lightweight encoder can be shared across multiple tasks, with the decoder responsible for learning the semantic information that a generic encoder lacks. They propose a novel non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning, combining 1D and 3D kernels with multiple skip connections to distribute high gradient flow during back-propagation, and a family of decoders built on this layer. The encoder is a 10-layer VGG-style network pre-trained on ImageNet, and the study focuses on four classes: lanes, curb, road, and void. Experiments are conducted end-to-end using the Keras framework with the Adam optimizer on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. The authors report that careful experimentation with decoder design choices yielded a 10% improvement in mean IoU over a baseline configuration, with larger gains of 12% and 18% for the difficult lanes and curb classes respectively. They also demonstrate that the proposed decoder improves IoU over a standard FCN decoder with less than 2ms increase in runtime, satisfying the automotive power constraints. The paper contributes both a dataset (proprietary, owned by the authors' organization) and a decoder design, though the dataset is not publicly released. The authors note that their encoder consumed most of the runtime because it is wider than the decoder, and they discuss trade-offs between accuracy and runtime. Limitations include the proprietary nature of the dataset, the absence of data augmentation, the constant dilation rate of 1, and the lack of reported random seeds or detailed hyperparameter sensitivity analyses. The paper concludes by proposing future work on a systematic family of meta-architectures with a fixed run-time budget, learned using meta-learning techniques. Overall, the study makes a focused contribution to efficient decoder design for embedded semantic segmentation, demonstrating that decoder architecture choices can have a large impact on performance while remaining within strict runtime budgets.

Research Context
Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel and is used in automated driving, augmented reality, and medical imaging. CNN architectures have grown in complexity, but embedded platforms impose computational bounds that require efficient models. Prior efficient-network research has largely focused on task-specific encoders, leaving decoder design under-explored. Unlike classification and detection, decoders are computationally expensive for semantic segmentation. Existing segmentation architectures typically pair an encoder with a decoder, with the encoder extracting features and the decoder reconstructing the output. Early decoders mirrored the encoder, while newer architectures use smaller decoders with additional encoder-to-decoder connections. Prior works such as SegNet pass max-pooling indices and Unet passes intermediate feature maps to the decoder. Dilated convolution is widely used to grow the receptive field exponentially without losing resolution. Most prior methods do not use a task-independent lightweight encoder, nor do they support multi-task learning.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to design an efficient decoder for real-time semantic segmentation on embedded platforms. The authors hypothesize that a task-independent, lightweight encoder can be shared across tasks, with the decoder learning the missing semantic information. They hypothesize that a novel non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning will perform well for under-represented classes. They predict that cascaded skip connections will enable high gradient flow, making the decoder suitable for real-time embedded deployment. They predict that careful decoder design will yield a substantial improvement over a baseline configuration. They predict that the proposed decoder will improve IoU over a standard FCN decoder with minimal runtime increase. They predict that reducing the number of feature maps will keep the decoder within the runtime budget.

Methodological Details
The study uses a proprietary dataset owned by the authors' organization, with samples shown in Figure 4. Each image in the dataset has a dimension of 1280x384 pixels. The dataset consists mostly of highly varied urban scenes with diverse lighting and dense shadows. The study focuses on four critical classes: lanes, curb, road, and void (everything else). The dataset is divided into Training, Validation, and Test sets of 3016, 981, and 1002 images respectively. Each sample has a single-channel annotation where each pixel has only one class label. The encoder is a task-independent, 10-layer VGG-style classifier pre-trained on ImageNet. The encoder uses convolution layers with 5x5 kernels followed by Batch-Normalization and ReLU. The encoder produces a total of 256 feature maps in its last layer. Convolution with stride 2 followed by max-pooling is used to reduce the problem space. The network is implemented using the Keras framework. The Adam optimizer is used with a weight decay of 0.9 and a batch size of 4. Training starts with an initial learning rate of 0.0005 using a polynomial decay strategy over 350K iterations. Dropout is not used in the model. Experiments are executed on an NVIDIA Titan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. No data augmentation technique is performed during training. The encoder is trained from scratch on ImageNet before transferring weights for the segmentation task. The authors note that the encoder consumed most of the runtime because it is wider than the decoder.

Procedures And Architectures
The proposed network has two parts: an encoder and a decoder, as shown in Figure 1. The encoder extracts features from various dimensions, reducing the problem space as it becomes deeper. The decoder consumes feature maps from the last and intermediate layers of the encoder to reconstruct the input space. Deconvolution layers are used instead of max-unpooling, as in SegNet and ENet. The decoder is designed to learn semantic features extensively to overcome the lack of semantic exploration in the encoder. The non-bottleneck layer contains both 1D and 3D kernels, with 3x3, 5x5, and 1x1 kernels. The non-bottleneck layer has two variants: type-1 and type-2, differing in the use of dilated convolution. The type-2 variant uses dilated convolution with kernel sizes of 3x3 and 5x5. The dilation rate is kept constant at 1 to avoid the computational cost of dilated convolution. Multiple skip connections distribute high gradient flow during back-propagation. The encoder-decoder architecture downsamples feature maps from 256 to 4, as the study concentrates on 4 classes. After the first deconvolution layer, non-bottleneck layer type-1 is used twice. After the second and third deconvolution layers, non-bottleneck layers of type-2 are used twice and once respectively. No non-bottleneck layer is used after the fourth deconvolution. Intermediate feature maps are pulled from the second and third last convolution layers of the encoder. The optimal decoder configuration is detailed in Figure 2 and used in Figure 3. The authors consider group convolution as a potential alternative to reduce encoder runtime. They note that aggregated residual transformation shows adverse effects for lightweight networks.

Key Results
The optimal decoder configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441, the highest among all variants. The optimal decoder achieves a mean class accuracy of 0.6588 across the four classes. The optimal configuration improves curb IoU to 0.4696, the highest among all variants. The optimal configuration improves lanes IoU to 0.5304, the highest among all variants. The optimal configuration improves road IoU to 0.9314, the highest among all variants. The optimal configuration improves void IoU to 0.9689, the highest among all variants. The (2N2)(2N2)(2N2)(2N2) configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.742, the second-highest. The (2N2)(2N2)(2N2) configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7323. The D8 decoder achieves a mean IoU of 0.727, outperforming D1 (0.7255). The D1 decoder achieves a mean IoU of 0.7255, the baseline among the named decoders. The D7 decoder achieves the lowest mean IoU of 0.6458, due to poor curb performance. The D7 decoder achieves a curb IoU of 0.2911, the lowest among all variants. The overall improvement over the baseline configuration is 10% in mean IoU. The improvement for the lanes class is 12% over the baseline. The improvement for the curb class is 18% over the baseline. The proposed decoder improves IoU over a standard FCN decoder with less than 2ms increase in runtime. The proposed decoder improves IoU especially for the key classes (lanes and curb). The non-bottleneck layers work better for curb despite a slight deterioration for lanes. The (2N1)(2N1)(2N1)(2N1) configuration achieves a curb IoU of 0.6343, higher than D1 (0.6228). The (1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2) configuration achieves a curb IoU of 0.6338.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study demonstrates that decoder design choices have a large impact on segmentation performance. The optimal configuration improves difficult classes (lanes and curb) more than easy classes (road and void). The non-bottleneck layer helps learn semantic information that the generic encoder lacks. The multiple skip connections enable high gradient flow, making the decoder suitable for embedded platforms. The decoder covers a significant portion of the overall computation of the network, so its design is critical. The proposed decoder improves IoU over a standard FCN decoder with minimal runtime increase, satisfying automotive constraints. The study shows that reducing feature maps keeps the decoder within the runtime budget. The authors argue that efficient decoder design is a critical aspect for real-time automated driving. The non-bottleneck layer is generic and can be used for any segmentation task. The study suggests that the encoder being task-independent is a key enabler for multi-task learning.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset is proprietary and owned by the authors' organization, so it is not publicly available. The paper does not report the train/test split ratio explicitly, only the set sizes. No data augmentation is performed, which may limit generalization. The dilation rate is kept constant at 1, though incremental rates could improve accuracy. The encoder consumed most of the runtime because it is wider than the decoder. The study focuses on only four classes, limiting broader applicability. The paper does not report the exact runtime values, only the less than 2ms increase. The non-bottleneck layers are non-repetitive between two deconvolution layers, which may limit generalization. The study does not compare against other state-of-the-art decoders beyond FCN.

Claims
Efficient decoder design is critical for real-time semantic segmentation on embedded platforms. Decoders are computationally expensive for semantic segmentation. Efficient network design is a critical aspect for automated driving. The decoder covers a significant portion of the overall computation of the network. The encoder consumed most of the runtime because it is wider than the decoder. The proposed decoder improves IoU over a standard FCN decoder with less than 2ms increase in runtime. The study demonstrates that decoder design choices have a large impact on performance.
A task-independent, lightweight encoder can be shared across tasks, with the decoder learning the missing semantic information. The encoder is designed to be task-independent and share features across tasks. The decoder learns semantic features extensively to overcome the encoder's lack of semantic exploration. The non-bottleneck layer removes the gap of learning semantic information in the encoder. Most prior methods do not use a task-independent lightweight encoder. The proposed non-bottleneck layer is generic and can be used for any segmentation task. The study supports multi-task learning practice.
The optimal decoder configuration achieves a 10% improvement in mean IoU over a baseline configuration. The optimal configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441. The improvement for lanes is 12% and for curb is 18%. The overall improvement is 10% from a baseline performance. The D7 decoder achieves the lowest mean IoU of 0.6458, due to poor curb performance. The non-bottleneck layers work better for curb despite a slight deterioration for lanes. The study suggests that decoder design can play a critical role for segmentation tasks.

Data And Code Availability
The dataset is proprietary and owned by the authors' organization, so it is not publicly available. The code is not reported as publicly available in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors experimented with multiple decoder variants, all reported in Table 1. The (2N2)(2N2)(2N2)(2N2) configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.742, the second-highest. The (2N2)(2N2)(2N2) configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7323. The (2N1)(2N1)(2N1)(2N1) configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7284. The (1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2) configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.731. The D8 decoder achieves a mean IoU of 0.727, outperforming D1 (0.7255). The D1 decoder achieves a mean IoU of 0.7255, the baseline among the named decoders. The D7 decoder achieves the lowest mean IoU of 0.6458, due to poor curb performance. The D3 decoder uses a batch size of 8, whereas D2 uses a batch size of 4. The D6 decoder uses a batch size of 4, whereas D5 uses a batch size of 8. The D4 decoder does not use 1x1 convolution even before 3x3 and 5x5 convolution. The D2 decoder does not use the second skip connection from the encoder.

Ethical Considerations
The dataset is proprietary and owned by the authors' organization, raising concerns about data sharing. The dataset consists mostly of urban scenes, which may limit diversity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the typical encoder-decoder architecture of a CNN-based semantic segmentation network. Figure 2 illustrates the non-bottleneck layers, with type-1 (left) and type-2 (right) variants. Figure 3 shows the CNN-based encoder-decoder architecture used for the semantic segmentation task. Figure 4 compares the proposed optimal decoder against a standard FCN decoder, with input images, ground truth, and outputs. Table 1 presents the results of different decoder variants with the non-bottleneck layer and VGG10 as encoder. Table 1 reports the average class accuracy and average class IoU score for each decoder configuration.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a novel non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoders for efficient real-time semantic segmentation. 2. The strongest evidence is the 10% improvement in mean IoU over a baseline configuration, with 12% and 18% gains for lanes and curb. 3. The future path is to build a systematic family of meta-architectures with a fixed run-time budget, learned using meta-learning techniques.

summary.title: Statistical mechanics of two-dimensional foams
summary.authors: Marc Durand
summary.field_subfield: Soft matter physics / statistical mechanics of cellular materials
summary.executive_summary: This paper applies the methods of statistical mechanics to two-dimensional (2D) foams subjected to macroscopic agitation, treating them as athermal systems analogous to conventional thermodynamic systems. The central novelty is the introduction of a new state variable, the total cell curvature, which plays the role of energy in standard statistical thermodynamics. The author argues that, unlike energy, the total number of sides and the total cell curvature are the relevant conserved quantities describing the macroscopic state of a foam. Building on the pioneering work of Edwards on granular matter and the microcanonical and grand-canonical ensembles, the paper derives an analytical expression for the probability distribution of the number of sides of a cell of given area. This expression recovers, in a certain limit, the semi-empirical distribution previously conjectured by other authors. The theory then enables the correlation of topological disorder (distribution of sides) with geometrical disorder (distribution of sizes), and the predictions are compared with experimental data from Quilliet et al. The model reproduces the experimental distributions well, including the relationship between the relative standard deviations of sides and areas. The paper is notable for containing no free parameters in the thermodynamic limit, although a free parameter is introduced for comparison with finite experimental samples. The formalism is proposed to be extendable to three-dimensional foams and to coarsening and coalescing foams. The work contributes a rigorous statistical-mechanical framework that improves upon earlier models that relied on ad-hoc interaction potentials, empirical laws, or the maximum-entropy formalism, and it explicitly incorporates the curvature sum rule that previous models had ignored. The paper also discusses the physical and geometrical constraints of foams, including Plateau's laws, Laplace's law, Euler's rule, and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, and it clarifies the distinction between bounded and unbounded foams. Overall, the paper provides a theoretically grounded, reproducible description of foam states that links microscopic configurations to macroscopic observables through well-established statistical-mechanical principles.
