summary.title: Anomalous Hall effect from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
summary.authors: Longju Yu, Hong Jian Zhao, Yurong Yang, Laurent Bellaiche, and Yanming Ma
summary.field_subfield: Condensed matter physics / magnetoelectric transport
summary.executive_summary: The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a topology-related transport phenomenon that enables efficient probing of magnetic orders, making it valuable for spintronics and memory readout. AHE is well established in ferromagnets and antiferromagnets with magnetization, and it can be induced by external fields capable of inducing magnetization through magnetoelectric coupling. Recent studies have demonstrated electric-field-induced AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling, such as the layer Hall effect and electric Hall effect. However, the AHE arising from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored. This work uses a group-theoretical approach to establish a phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field-driven AHE in crystalline materials. The symmetry analysis demonstrates that both type-I and type-III magnetic point groups exhibit spontaneous AHE or electric-field-induced AHE from linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The authors highlight that nonlinear magnetoelectric AHE is accommodated by a wide spectrum of magnetic point groups, where the anomalous Hall conductivity component is achieved by applying uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric field and is reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. Following the theory and confirmed by first-principles calculations, the authors suggest that Cr2O3 and CoF2 are representative materials towards the electric-field-induced AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The work emphasizes the important role of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in creating exotic transport phenomena and offers alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders.

claims.description: A large variety of magnetic point groups host an AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric field from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling.
The electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic orders.
Cr2O3 and CoF2 are candidate materials hosting the electric-field-induced AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling.

The work emphasizes the important role of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in creating exotic transport phenomena and offers alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders.

Research Context
The anomalous Hall effect is a fundamental transport phenomenon where an applied voltage induces a transverse Hall current response. AHE is now an important platform for exploring topology-related transport properties and offers an efficient way to probe magnetic order. AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets with specific magnetic configurations. Antiferromagnetic materials with symmetry-allowed weak or tiny magnetization likewise enable AHE. Magnetoelectric coupling, linear or nonlinear effect, are interesting avenues for electric-field driven AHE. Recent studies demonstrate that gate voltage can induce AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling. The electric-field induced AHE arising from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether AHE can originate from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling and which magnetic point groups host it. The hypothesis is that a large variety of magnetic point groups host an AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric field from nonlinear coupling. The predicted outcome is that such electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. The authors predict that Cr2O3 and CoF2 are candidate materials hosting the aforementioned AHE. The theory predicts that the anomalous Hall conductivity component is achieved by applying uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric field. The authors hypothesize that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling plays an important role in creating exotic transport phenomena. The predicted outcome is that our work offers alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders.

Methodological Details
The study is based on a group-theoretical approach to establish the phenomenological theory for AHE in crystalline materials. The analysis covers the entire 122 magnetic point groups, as detailed in Supplementary Note 2. Among these MPGs, 32 type-II MPGs exhibit time-reversal symmetry and forbid magnetization. The authors list the 90 type-I and type-III MPGs with respect to the anomalous Hall conductivity components in Table I. The anomalous Hall conductivity is expressed as an integral over the Brillouin zone involving the Berry curvature. The Berry curvature is denoted by Ωγ,nk with n being the band index and k being the wave vector. The Hall vector M is defined as (σzy, σxz, σyx) and behaves like the magnetization vector. The Onsager reciprocity relation requires that σαβ(+L) = σβα(−L). The effective magnetic field Bαeff is expanded with respect to electric field in a series. The effective magnetic fields for the 90 type-I and type-III MPGs are derived in Supplementary Note 2. The candidate materials Cr2O3 and CoF2 have no more than 10 ions per primitive cell. Cr2O3 has a N´eel temperature of 307 K and belongs to the ¯3′m′ MPG. CoF2 has a N´eel temperature of 39 K. The materials are selected from the MAGNDATA database. The first-principles calculations are supported by the high-performance computing center of Jilin University.

summary.title: Powers of Ideals and the Cohomology of Stalks and Fibers of Morphisms
summary.authors: Marc Chardin
summary.field_subfield: Commutative algebra / Algebraic geometry
summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a short, self-contained proof of a refinement of the classical result of Kodiyalam and Cutkosky, Herzog and Trung on the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of powers of ideals over standard graded algebras. The central object is the limit lim_{t→∞}(end(H^i_{A+}(I^t M)) + i − t d), which the author shows exists for every i and is at least the initial degree of M for some i. The main contribution is Theorem 5.3, which identifies this limit, for ideals generated in a single degree, as the maximum end degree of the i-th local cohomology of the stalks of the projection π from the closure of the graph of the rational map defined by the generators to its image. This proves a conjecture of Huy T`ai H`a and generalizes the result of Eisenbud and Harris for ideals primary to the graded maximal ideal in a standard graded algebra over a field. A further consequence is Corollary 1.2, giving a geometric criterion for the regularity of the saturation of powers of an ideal (equivalently, powers of ideal sheaves) to be eventually linear. The second half of the paper compares the cohomology of the stalks and the cohomology of the fibers of a projective morphism, showing that for families of projective schemes that are close to being flat, the maximum of the regularities of the stalks and the maximum of the regularities of the fibers agree, and that the maximum regularity of the stalks bounds above the one for the fibers under a weaker hypothesis. These results are stated in terms of a newly introduced notion of regularity over a scheme, generalizing the usual notion with reference to a polynomial extension of a ring. The paper is purely theoretical and contains no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational results; all statements are proved theorems, lemmas, and propositions.

summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang
summary.field_subfield: Photonics / Topological photonics
summary.executive_summary: Topological valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to control electromagnetic waves, but prior work has been confined to two dimensions, where light confinement along the third dimension is achieved non-topologically (e.g., total internal reflection), leading to out-of-plane losses and planar-only light manipulation. This paper introduces a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework featuring a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Unlike 2D systems with a single pair of valleys characterized by scalar valley Chern numbers, the 3D systems exhibit triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors develop a 3D photonic crystal with a diamond-like lattice composed of perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods, and break inversion symmetry by adjusting sphere diameters to open a complete photonic bandgap. summary.title: Systems of Hecke eigenvalues on subschemes of Shimura varieties
summary.authors: Stefan Reppen
summary.field_subfield: Number theory / arithmetic geometry (Shimura varieties, mod p cohomology)
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes a uniform principle for the mod p fiber of abelian-type Shimura varieties at hyperspecial level: the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in coherent cohomology with coefficients in automorphic line bundles are identical whether computed on the whole special fiber or on any Hecke-equivariant subscheme. The central object is the special fiber SK of the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model of a Shimura variety of abelian type at good reduction, equipped with the prime-to-p Hecke action. Prior work by Goldring-Koskivirta and by Terakado-Yu proved analogous equalities but only for subschemes that are smooth of dimension 0, such as the zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum or zero-dimensional central leaves. The present work generalizes these results to higher-dimensional and possibly singular subschemes, and to nonclosed subschemes and noncompact Shimura varieties. The main theorem (Theorem A) states that for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK of SK, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the direct sums of H0 over the L-dominant characters eta of the automorphic line bundles V(eta) are the same on SK and on YK. The proof introduces a novel three-step strategy: a refined going-down argument, a new further going-down argument, and the unchanged going-up argument of the prior literature. The refined going-down argument relates Hecke eigenforms on the Shimura variety to Hecke eigenforms of the sheaf of differentials via the conormal exact sequence, building on Ghitza. The new further going-down argument is the key innovation: because higher-dimensional and singular subschemes lack a nowhere vanishing Hecke-invariant section and have a conormal sequence that is neither exact nor locally free, the author intersects the subscheme with the smallest length stratum it meets nontrivially and successively removes nonsingular points to obtain a smooth closed subscheme ZK that admits a nowhere vanishing Hecke-equivariant section. This step crucially uses the existence of Hasse invariants, in contrast to the going-down argument of the prior literature. The going-up argument of the prior literature then applies verbatim to relate eigenvalues on ZK to YK and SK. The results apply in particular to the closures of Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, Newton strata, and central leaves, including higher-dimensional central leaves. The paper also treats nonclosed subschemes and noncompact Shimura varieties, requiring Hodge type or properness in some cases, and provides a corollary for Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves. The framework relies on G-zip theory, automorphic vector bundles, and the theory of Hasse invariants, and it extends to toroidal compactifications under an ampleness assumption. The work is purely theoretical with no numerical experiments, datasets, or code, and it contributes a conceptual unification rather than empirical findings.

summary.title: Enabling Real-Time Conversations with Minimal Training Costs
summary.authors: Wang Xu, Shuo Wang, Weilin Zhao, Xu Han, Yukun Yan, Yudi Zhang, Zhe Tao, Zhiyuan Liu, Wanxiang Che
summary.field_subfield: Natural Language Processing / Conversational AI
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology with human evaluation and benchmark experiments
summary.executive_summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed human-computer interaction, powering applications such as question answering and coding assistance. However, conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interaction during response generation. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed duplex models that can dynamically adapt to user input, facilitating real-time interactive feedback. However, these methods typically require substantial computational resources to acquire the ability. To reduce overhead, this paper presents a new duplex decoding approach that enhances LLMs with duplex ability, requiring minimal additional training. Specifically, the method employs parallel decoding of queries and responses in conversations, effectively implementing a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method significantly enhances the naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions with minimal training costs. The authors consider two scenarios: non-awakening interaction and interruption interaction. The model should filter out background dialogues or non-query input, and if the user interrupts with another question during an ongoing generation, the model should pause its current output to immediately address the latest query. The authors introduce DUplex decOding (DUO), a novel channel-based parallel decoding mechanism that equips LLMs with duplex capabilities. The approach enables simultaneous autoregressive output generation and input preprocessing. Furthermore, two state tokens are designed to signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored. The proposed method requires only minimal additional training to learn the state of the query. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, the authors test DUO based on human evaluation and standard benchmarks. The results show that the method significantly enhances the naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions with minimal training costs. The authors utilize MiniCPM-2.4B as the foundation model and construct 10K samples to train the model. The authors note that their dataset is significantly smaller than the one used in MiniCPM-Duplex, which consists of approximately 5,000K samples. The training of MiniCPM-Duo uses a 1e-5 learning rate, a constant learning rate scheduler, a batch size of 112, and a maximum length of 4,096. MiniCPM-Duo is trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 25 minutes, whereas MiniCPM-Duplex is trained for 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The authors conducted 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions with each model and enlisted three participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree, to assess the dialogue histories. The evaluation criteria included responsiveness, human-likeness, faithfulness, factuality, and overall experience. On standard benchmarks, MiniCPM-Duo achieves comparable results with MiniCPM-Duplex and MiniCPM, preserving the model's original capabilities to a greater extent. The authors study how MiniCPM-Duplex performs when trained on the same scale dataset as MiniCPM-Duo, and the performances drop. The authors present a case study demonstrating the model's adaptive behavior in response to user interactions and silences during the query and generation processes. While DUO demonstrates promising results, the study has limitations, with a significant constraint lying in the scope of multimodal testing. The experiments primarily focused on language models, potentially limiting the generalizability of findings to other domains.

The model should filter out background dialogues or non-query input, and if the user interrupts with another question during an ongoing generation, the model should pause its current output to immediately address the latest query. The approach enables simultaneous autoregressive output generation and input preprocessing. Furthermore, two state tokens are designed to signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored. The proposed method requires only minimal additional training to learn the state of the query. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, the authors test DUO based on human evaluation and standard benchmarks. The results show that the method significantly enhances the naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions with minimal training costs. The authors utilize MiniCPM-2.4B as the foundation model and construct 10K samples to train the model. The authors note that their dataset is significantly smaller than the one used in MiniCPM-Duplex, which consists of approximately 5,000K samples. The training of MiniCPM-Duo uses a 1e-5 learning rate, a constant learning rate scheduler, a batch size of 112, and a maximum length of 4,096. MiniCPM-Duo is trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 25 minutes, whereas MiniCPM-Duplex is trained for 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The authors conducted 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions with each model and enlisted three participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree, to assess the dialogue histories. The experiments primarily focused on language models, potentially limiting the generalizability of findings to other domains.

Research Context
Large language models have revolutionized human-computer interaction. Applications include question answering and coding assistance. The quality of these interaction experiences is important. Traditional turn-based chat systems inherently limit the interactive experience. Current human-AI interactions follow a turn-based pattern. One party passively waits while the other responds. Interruptions are facilitated through manual interventions. Human conversations involve simultaneous listening and thinking. Recent studies have proposed duplex models to address this challenge. These methods typically require substantial computational resources. The designed procedure diverges substantially from the backbone model.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question concerns enabling duplex ability with minimal training. DUO is a novel channel-based parallel decoding mechanism. The approach enables simultaneous autoregressive output generation and input preprocessing. Two state tokens are designed to signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored. The proposed method requires only minimal additional training to learn the state of the query. The method employs parallel decoding of queries and responses in conversations. This effectively implements a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy. The hypothesis is that the method enhances naturalness and human-likeness. The hypothesis is that this occurs with minimal training costs. The model should filter out background dialogues or non-query input. If the user interrupts, the model should pause its current output to immediately address the latest query. The method should handle both non-awakening and interruption interactions.

Methodological Details
The authors consider two scenarios: non-awakening interaction and interruption interaction. The model should filter out background dialogues or non-query input. If the user interrupts, the model should pause its current output to immediately address the latest query. The foundation model is MiniCPM-2.4B. 10K samples are constructed to train the model. The dataset is significantly smaller than MiniCPM-Duplex, which consists of approximately 5,000K samples. MiniCPM-Duplex is used as the baseline since both are derived from the same checkpoints. The learning rate is 1e-5 with a constant learning rate scheduler. The batch size is 112 and the maximum length is 4,096. The loss is calculated on the state tokens and output. MiniCPM-Duo is trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for about 25 minutes. MiniCPM-Duplex is trained for 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The decoding strategy is implemented based on the repository https://github.com/thunlp/Ouroboros. The input channel predicted tokens α are set to 4. Human evaluators assess four aspects: responsiveness, human-likeness, faithfulness, and factuality. Responsiveness evaluates whether the model responds to user queries. Human-likeness assesses how closely the model's responses resemble those of a human. Faithfulness measures the extent to which the model adheres to user instructions. Factuality evaluates the level of content that is not grounded in factual information. The interactive demo was originally developed for MiniCPM-Duplex. Users engage in voice-based conversations with an AI assistant. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions are facilitated by Google's cloud ASR and TTS APIs. The authors conducted 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions with each model. Three participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree, assessed the dialogue histories. The evaluation criteria included responsiveness, human-likeness, faithfulness, factuality, and overall experience. For each criterion, participants were asked to rank the dialogues generated by MiniCPM-Duo and MiniCPM-Duplex. Standard benchmarks include CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag. The LLM evaluation platform used is UltraEval. The dataset was constructed from Duplex-UltraChat, which structures conversations in a time-division format. Transition sentences are added to enhance the interactive experience. The authors adapted Duplex-UltraChat into a standard turn-based format. The authors append the <1> token to each user's content since all queries require a response. The authors use ChatGPT to generate the non-query text to simulate non-awakening interaction. The prompt for generating non-query text is described in Appendix A.1.

Procedures And Architectures
DUO processes inputs and outputs cyclically. In each cycle, the output channel generates new tokens autoregressively. The input channel prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. According to the predicted tokens, the model decides whether a query is addressed or ignored. A new input token is received at time step t1 while the model generates output autoregressively. This establishes a new input channel. The model generates tokens autoregressively while simultaneously processing the input tokens. The tokens generated by the input and output channels after t1 do not attend to each other. This preserves language modeling in each channel. The attention mask is modified to accommodate the token dependency. Upon processing the input tokens, the output channel persists in generating tokens rather than terminating immediately. This output channel is maintained until the model responds to the new query or the output sequence is completed. State tokens indicate the status of the user's query. The model predicts α tokens to complete the query in each processing cycle. State token <1> denotes that the input is a user query. The original output channel is suspended, and the input channel seamlessly transitions to become the new output channel. State token <2> denotes that the new input is no-query text. The model continues to respond to the original query, and the input channel is disregarded. Otherwise, the key-value cache of the predicted would be disregarded and the next processing cycle goes on. DUO differs from MiniCPM-Duplex, which processes the input and generates output sequentially. MiniCPM-Duplex splits and mixes the input and output in a time slice format. MiniCPM-Duplex needs a lot of computing power to retrain the model. DUO processes the input and output simultaneously by optimizing the decoding strategy. DUO functions as a channel-division multiplexing system. The data format remains largely unchanged, with only the addition of some state tokens. DUO preserves the ability of the original model. DUO is capable of handling non-awakening interactions, an aspect that MiniCPM-Duplex does not address. DUO can be efficiently implemented using Flex-Attention. Flex-Attention facilitates non-standard attention mechanisms. The operations are all accomplished through the management of the key-value cache. DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. DUO processes the input and output channel in each time slice. The model generates output concurrently while the key-value cache of input is prefilled. The next tokens of input are predicted.

summary.title: Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive MIMO for Hybrid Precoding
summary.authors: Hongji Huang, Yiwei Song, Jie Yang, Guan Gui, and Fumiyuki Adachi
summary.field_subfield: Wireless communications / signal processing (mmWave massive MIMO)
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses hybrid precoding for millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which are promising for 5G because they exploit underutilized ultra-high-frequency spectrum and offer orders-of-magnitude pathloss enhancement. Existing hybrid precoding schemes, however, suffer from high computational complexity and fail to fully exploit the spatial information of mmWave channels, largely because they rely on conventional mathematical tools such as singular value decomposition (SVD) and geometric mean decomposition (GMD). To overcome these limitations, the authors propose a deep-learning-enabled framework in which the selection of the hybrid precoder is treated as a mapping relation learned by a deep neural network (DNN). The DNN is constructed as an autoencoder: the input layer captures features of the input data, hidden layers process the encoding operation, a noise layer mixes distortion, and the output layer generates expected output signals. The network uses the rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation in the input and hidden layers, and a special activation that enforces the power constraint in the output layer. To simplify the mapping, the authors adopt the GMD method to decompose the channel matrix, reformulating the received signal so that the precoder can be trained. summary.title: Physics Frontiers: Bridging Theory and Experiment — Spectro-temporal study of atoll source GX 9+9 observed with AstroSat
summary.authors: Sree Bhattacherjee, Arbind Pradhan, Biplob Sarkar
summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics — X-ray binary / high-energy astrophysics
summary.executive_summary: This work presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) and atoll source GX 9+9, using archival data from the Indian multi-wavelength observatory AstroSat. The authors combined data from the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) obtained during a single observation on 25 July 2020 (Obs. ID A09_018T01_9000003774). The source was detected in the soft/banana state, producing a disk-dominated energy spectrum across 0.7–25 keV. The authors performed flux-resolved spectral analysis by dividing the data into three flux levels (FL1, FL2, FL3), each spanning a narrow count-rate range, and fit the combined spectra with the model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) using XSPEC. They estimated source characteristics, including the inner-disk radius (~16.57 km), unabsorbed flux, and inner-disk temperature, and compared these with previously reported values. In the timing analysis, they used only the LAXPC data due to its high timing resolution and searched for quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and broad-band noise (BBN) features via a multi-Lorentzian power density spectrum (PDS) fit. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected, but a BBN-like feature was found centered near ~0.1 Hz. They then modeled the energy-dependent temporal properties of the fractional rms and phase lag using the propagative model formalized by Garg et al., finding that variations in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering (with a phase lag) explain the observed variability. The best-fit reduced χ² was ~0.80 for this model. The authors conclude that the source is transitioning toward a softer state, as indicated by a slight decrease in the Comptonization temperature (kTe) and an increase in the disk temperature (Tin) with rising flux. They note that the study is constrained by poor data quality and the limited availability of a single observation, emphasizing the need for further multi-epoch observations. The paper bridges observational data with theoretical models to interpret the radiative origin of the variability in a poorly studied atoll source.

They note that the study is constrained by poor data quality and the limited availability of a single observation, emphasizing the need for further multi-epoch observations. The paper bridges observational data with theoretical models to interpret the radiative origin of the variability in a poorly studied atoll source.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron-star low-mass X-ray binary identified during the Galactic center sounding rocket mission. It is an established atoll source that traces a 'C'-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram. Atoll sources exhibit two primary states: the hard/island state and the soft/banana state. The soft/banana state is further classified into upper and lower banana states. In the hard state, Comptonization dominates, while thermal disk emission dominates in soft spectra. Atoll sources show significant spectral changes over durations ranging from days to weeks. The rate of accreting mass is believed to increase from island to upper banana state. GX 9+9 is often detected in a luminous soft state with a ~220 mCrab X-ray flux in the 2–20 keV band. Spectral modeling is emphasized but often has geometric and locational ambiguities. The source is not a well-studied object, motivating new observational and modeling efforts.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to characterize the spectro-temporal properties of GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. The authors seek to compare the constancy between spectral and temporal analyses. They intend to estimate source characteristics such as inner-disk radius, flux, and inner-disk temperature. They hypothesize that the source is in the soft/banana state based on the hardness-intensity diagram. They hypothesize that spectral parameter variations with rising flux indicate a transition toward a softer state. They hypothesize that the observed broad-band noise variability originates from variations in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. They predict that the energy-dependent temporal modeling will reveal a phase lag consistent with the propagative model.

Methodological Details
The study used a single AstroSat archival observation of GX 9+9 taken on 25 July 2020. The observation was analyzed using the LAXPC and SXT instruments of AstroSat. SXT and LAXPC data were used for spectral analysis, while only LAXPC data was used for timing analysis. LAXPC counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains from 2018 onwards, so only LAXPC 20 data was used. LAXPC operates over a wide energy band from 3 to 80 keV. Good time interval data free from the South Atlantic Anomaly and Earth occultation was used to extract scientific level-2 data. The LAXPC software pipeline version Oct. 13, 2022 was used to extract scientific products. SXT works in the low energy range of 0.3 to 8.0 keV. The SXT data was processed through the AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b pipeline to generate cleaned level-2 event files. The SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold of 40 counts/sec during the observation. An annular zone with an outer radius of 13 arcmin and an inner radius of 2 arcmin was used to limit counts below the pileup limit. A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for the background uncertainty estimation. The SXT gain fit was applied with a slope of 1 and a free offset parameter. Both LAXPC and SXT spectra were optimally grouped using the ftool ftgrouppha. The spectral analysis was performed within the energy range of 0.7 to 25 keV. The spectral fitting was performed using the XSPEC package of HEASOFT version 6.31.1. The source flux was divided into three flux levels: FL1 (450–570 counts/s), FL2 (570–650 counts/s), and FL3 (650–770 counts/s). The parametric errors were estimated at the 90% level of confidence. The source distance was considered as 10 kpc for the inner-disk radius calculation. The disk inclination angle was considered as 60 degrees. The color-correction factor k was taken as 1.7.

Procedures And Architectures
The best-fit model was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), with the thermal Comptonization model ThComp used. A cross-calibration component 'const' was incorporated to calibrate the different instruments. The LAXPC 20 spectra were used as the base spectra, with its constant fixed at 1. The SXT constant was left free for the calibration. The ThComp model was an improved version of the nThComp model. The energy range was extended with 1000 log bins using 'energies 0.01 500 1000 log' for the ThComp convolution model. The covering fraction parameter of ThComp indicates the amount of seed photons that will be Comptonized. The optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain the other parameters. Edge models were required at energy 2.4 keV to obtain a better fit. The inner-disk radius was calculated using the relation Rin = k2 (Ndbb /cosθ) 1/2 * D10. The total unabsorbed flux was estimated using the XSPEC model 'cflux' in the extended energy range of 0.01–100 keV. The timing analysis used a power density spectrum (PDS) plot to detect variability. The multi-lorentzian approach was used to the PDS to check for variability in different flux levels. The PDS was generated for the full flux in the energy range of 3–20 keV and a frequency range of 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz. The rms and time lag spectra were obtained using the LAXPC subroutine 'laxpc_find_freqlag' at the centroid frequency νo. The characteristic frequency νc was obtained using the relation νc = √(νo² + HWHM). The energy-dependent temporal modeling was fit in the rms and phase lag spectra using the model formalized by Garg et al. The model assumes a truncated disk and a hot electron plasma (corona) between the inner radius and ISCO. The best-fit model was the variation in kTin and fs with some time delay (phase lag) with respect to fs. The time lag was calculated using the relation time lag = phase lag / 2πf, where f is the peak/central frequency.

The source was in the soft/banana state at the time of observation based on the form of the HID. The average inner-disk radius was estimated to be ~16.57±1.29 km. The total unabsorbed flux in FL1, FL2, and FL3 was ~5.94×10⁻⁹, 6.51×10⁻⁹, and 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻², respectively. The maximum flux reached 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻², comparable to 7.8×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² reported by [12]. The unabsorbed flux increased from FL1 to FL3. The inner-disk radius was relatively consistent with the previously reported value of 27±4 km by Iaria et al. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in the timing analysis. The characteristic frequency νc was ~0.1 Hz. The half width at half maximum (HWHM) was approximately 0.09 Hz. The rms at ~0.1 Hz was increasing as the energy was increasing, whereas the phase lag was showing a decreasing trend with energy. The slight decrease in kTe and increase in Tin across the FLs indicate a transition toward a softer state. The fractional scattering and change in inner-disk temperature are the causes of the obtained broad-band noise variability.

The best-fit model was comparable to the one employed by Chatterjee et al. [16]. The ThComp model was an improved version of the nThComp model. The edge models were required at energy 2.4 keV to obtain a better fit.

Ethical Considerations
The study used archival AstroSat data, which is publicly available and does not require ethical approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the HID of the source using the AstroSat data, with a binning time of 32s. Each color in Figure 1 represents the different flux levels as indicated in the plot. Figure 2 shows the best-fit spectrum of FL1, FL2, and FL3 from top to bottom, in the energy range 0.7-25 keV. The red and black points in Figure 2 represent the SXT and LAXPC 20 data, respectively. Figure 3 (left) shows the PDS fit, and Figure 3 (right) shows the energy dependent temporal modelling of fractional rms and phase lag. Table 1 displays the best-fit parameters of spectral analysis and energy-dependent temporal modeling. The best-fit parameters include NH, kTe, fs, Tin, Ndbb, Rin, and χ²/dof for each flux level.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the spectro-temporal characterization of the poorly studied atoll source GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. 2. The strongest evidence is the best-fit reduced χ² of ~0.80 for the energy-dependent temporal model, supporting the variability interpretation. 3. The future path is further multi-epoch observations to improve the understanding of the source and validate the variability interpretation.

summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.field_subfield: Organic synthesis / continuous flow photochemistry
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalysed radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition (dimerization) of electron-rich alkenes, namely vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to give cyclobutane dimers. The authors merge homogeneous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial continuous flow platform to address limitations of prior batch methods, which required cryogenic temperatures, excessive reaction times, and higher catalyst loadings. Using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (10), the target carbazole host material 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB, 1) was synthesized in 82% isolated yield under batch conditions, but in up to 93% yield under optimized continuous flow conditions at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst, and 450 nm irradiation. Flow conditions also enabled greatly reduced catalyst loadings (down to 0.1 mol% at 10 mmol scale, giving 79% yield) and shorter reaction times. The scope was expanded to brominated, chloro-, methoxy-, hydroxy-, and aryl-substituted vinyl carbazoles, as well as styrenes, including the natural lignan magnosalin (4) on a 10 mmol scale (40% yield). The work demonstrates that continuous flow improves yields, reduces catalyst loading, and shortens reaction times relative to batch chemistry, providing scalable routes to functional cyclobutane materials and natural products. The study is notable for using a commercial off-the-shelf flow platform and for mechanistic probes of reversibility and background oxidation. However, several details are limited: the catalyst structure is not fully specified, reaction times for some substrates (e.g., 5 days for 12a in batch) are reported qualitatively, and the bibliography is absent, so top_influential_citations must be set to "". Data/code and ethics fields are also unreported and set to "". The paper is a synthetic methodology report rather than a computational or data-driven study, so reproducibility rests on the described conditions and yields rather than deposited datasets.

The dimerization is reversible and sensitive to oxygen, as evidenced by yield loss at low flow rates and carbazole byproduct formation.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalysed radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition (dimerization) of electron-rich alkenes, namely vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to give cyclobutane dimers. The authors merge homogeneous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with a commercial continuous flow platform to address limitations of prior batch methods, which required cryogenic temperatures, excessive reaction times, and higher catalyst loadings. Using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (10), the target carbazole host material 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB, 1) was synthesized in 82% isolated yield under batch conditions, but in up to 93% yield under optimized continuous flow conditions at 0.5 mL.min⁻¹ (τ = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst, and 450 nm irradiation. Flow conditions also enabled greatly reduced catalyst loadings (down to 0.1 mol% at 10 mmol scale, giving 79% yield) and shorter reaction times. The scope was expanded to brominated, chloro-, methoxy-, hydroxy-, and aryl-substituted vinyl carbazoles, as well as styrenes, including the natural lignan magnosalin (4) on a 10 mmol scale (40% yield). The work demonstrates that continuous flow improves yields, reduces catalyst loading, and shortens reaction times relative to batch chemistry, providing scalable routes to functional cyclobutane materials and natural products. The study is notable for using a commercial off-the-shelf flow platform and for mechanistic probes of reversibility and background oxidation. However, several details are limited: the catalyst structure is not fully specified, reaction times for some substrates (e.g., 5 days for 12a in batch) are reported qualitatively, and the bibliography is absent, so top_influential_citations must be set to "". Data/code and ethics fields are also unreported and set to "". The paper is a synthetic methodology report rather than a computational or data-driven study, so reproducibility rests on the described conditions and yields rather than deposited datasets.

Research Context
Cyclobutane dimers are valuable functional materials and natural products. Electron-rich alkenes dimerize via radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition. Vinyl carbazole is a precursor to the electrophosphorescence host t-DCzCB. Styrenes such as E-asarone are precursors to the lignan magnosalin. Organophotoredox catalysis offers advantages over metal-based catalysts. Prior organophotoredox dimerizations had practical limitations. Continuous flow improves irradiation and conversion in photoredox reactions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks whether continuous flow improves organophotoredox dimerization. The hypothesis is that flow gives higher yields and shorter times. The hypothesis is that flow allows lower catalyst loadings. The hypothesis is that flow enables functionalized and natural product synthesis. The predicted outcome is that flow outperforms batch across substrates.

Methodological Details
The study compares continuous flow versus batch conditions. A commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform was used. The pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst is denoted 10. The target carbazole host material is t-DCzCB (1). Batch synthesis used 3 mol% catalyst under Nicewicz conditions. Batch synthesis gave 82% isolated yield of t-DCzCB. Batch required deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended times. Yields were analyzed by HPLC using p-terphenyl as internal standard. HPLC required calibration of 2 and 1. Full HPLC details are in the supporting information. The reaction was run at 1.00 mmol of 2 at 0.4 M in acetone. Optimal flow conditions: 0.5 mL.min⁻¹, τ = 20 min, 2 mol%, 450 nm. Optimal continuous flow yield was 93% at 1 mol% catalyst. Substrates were vinyl carbazoles 12a-24a, made by the Obora method. Vinyl carbazoles were made in moderate to good yields. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) was isolated in very low yields. Natural product magnosalin (4) was the styrene lignan target.

Procedures And Architectures
The mechanism is radical cation formation, cycloaddition, and reduction. The cyclobutyl radical cation is reduced to the dimer. Irradiation was performed at 450 nm. An alternative wavelength of 405 nm was tested. An alternative wavelength of 420 nm was tested. The reaction did not proceed without catalyst. The reaction did not proceed without irradiation. Flow rate was lowered from 5 to 2 mL.min⁻¹ to test reversibility. A 10 mmol scale run used 0.1 mol% catalyst. Substrates were made by Suzuki coupling and vinylation. Brominated products were made via Suzuki coupling of 13b. Borylation used bis(pinacolato)diboron to make 26. An electron relay anthracene was added to the styrene solution. Diethylaniline was used as an electron relay for styrene 29. E-asarone dimerization used anthracene as an electron relay. The lignan magnosalin was made on a 10 mmol scale.

Key Results
Optimal flow yield of t-DCzCB was 93% at 1 mol% catalyst. A 4.5 mol% catalyst loading gave 90% yield. Lowering flow to 2 mL.min⁻¹ reduced yield to 79%. A 10 mmol scale run at 0.1 mol% gave 79% yield. Reducing flow to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ dropped yield to 53%. Carbazole formed as a byproduct at low flow rate. 405 nm and 420 nm gave comparable yields to 450 nm. The reaction failed without catalyst or light. Batch dimerization of 12a gave 48% yield. Flow dimerization of 12a gave 64% yield in 50 min. Batch dimerization of 13a gave 31% yield. Flow dimerization of 13a gave 71% yield. Flow dimerization of 16a gave 65% yield. Batch slightly outperformed flow for 17a. Flow gave 61% for 18b and 45% for 19b. Flow gave 25% for the bis-enol ether 21b. Flow gave 65% for the fluoroarylated cyclobutane 22b. Flow gave 57% for the tetra-alkyl dimer 23b. Flow gave 50% for the bisarylated cyclobutane 24b. Flow gave 44% for the styrene dimer 28. Flow gave 22% for pellucidin A (29). Flow gave 40% for magnosalin (4) on 10 mmol scale. Suzuki coupling of 13b gave cyclobutane 25 in 75% yield. Borylation gave 26 in 36% yield. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) gave no cyclobutane product.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Flow improves yields and reduces catalyst loading versus batch. Lower flow rates indicate possible reversibility of the dimerization. Carbazole byproduct arises from background oxygen oxidation. The mechanism requires both catalyst and light. Flow enables functionalized carbazole dimers. Flow enables scalable synthesis of the lignan magnosalin. The protocol is general, robust, and scalable. Flow reduces reaction times versus batch.

Contradictions And Limitations
Batch slightly outperformed flow for substrate 17a. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave no cyclobutane product. The catalyst structure is not fully specified in the text. Reaction times for some substrates are reported qualitatively. Solubility at 0.4 M was challenging, requiring 0.2 M. The exact flow platform model is not specified.

Claims
Continuous flow improves organophotoredox dimerization yields, reduces catalyst loading, and shortens reaction times versus batch. Optimal flow yield of t-DCzCB was 93% at 1 mol% catalyst. A 10 mmol scale run at 0.1 mol% gave 79% yield. Flow gave 71% for 13b versus 31% batch. Flow gave 64% for 12b versus 48% batch. The protocol is general, robust, and scalable. Batch slightly outperformed flow for substrate 17a. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave no cyclobutane product. The protocol enables scalable synthesis of functional materials. The protocol enables scalable synthesis of the lignan magnosalin.
The dimerization is reversible and sensitive to oxygen, as evidenced by yield loss at low flow rates and carbazole byproduct formation. Lowering flow to 2 mL.min⁻¹ reduced yield to 79%. Reducing flow to 0.1 mL.min⁻¹ dropped yield to 53%. Carbazole formed as a byproduct at low flow rate. The reaction failed without catalyst or light. 405 nm and 420 nm gave comparable yields to 450 nm. Optimized flow conditions minimize reversibility and oxygen exposure.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The reaction failed without catalyst. The reaction failed without irradiation. Alternative wavelengths gave comparable yields. A 10 mmol scale run at 0.1 mol% gave 79% yield.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 is the optimization study of the continuous flow synthesis. Scheme 1 shows cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products. Scheme 2 shows the radical cation [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism. Scheme 3 shows the merged organophotoredox and flow protocol. Scheme 4 shows the batch versus flow comparison for t-DCzCB. Scheme 5 shows the substrate scope of brominated carbazoles. Scheme 6 shows the synthetic potential of bromocyclobutane products. Scheme 7 shows the styrene and lignan dimerizations.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a continuous flow organophotoredox dimerization protocol. 2. The strongest evidence is the 93% flow yield versus 82% batch yield for t-DCzCB. 3. The future path is scalable synthesis of functional materials and natural products.

summary.title: Spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes
summary.authors: Lina Zhang, Qiyuan Pan, Yun Soo Myung, De-Cheng Zou
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: black hole scalarization in alternative gravity
summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen regular black holes, a phenomenon in which tachyonic instability induced by nonminimal scalar coupling endows an initially hairless black hole with scalar hair without altering weak-field predictions. The authors introduce an Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics framework coupled to a scalar field and examine two coupling forms: quadratic (1−αϕ²) and exponential (e−αϕ²). They demonstrate that the tachyonic instability of Bardeen black holes triggers the formation of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs), which appear in infinite branches indexed by n = 0, 1, 2, .... The n = 0 branch emerges once the coupling parameter α exceeds a threshold αn=0(g) that coincides with the numerically determined instability threshold αth(g). Using a typical nonextremal configuration with M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, they obtain αth(g) = 12.712 and construct the n = 0 branch for both coupling forms. A central and novel finding is that the n = 0 branch is stable against radial (l = 0) perturbations for both couplings, even though the scalar potentials exhibit small negative regions near the horizon. This stability is independent of the magnetic charge g, as verified across g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250. The authors interpret the n = 0 branch as an end point of the Bardeen black hole, making it a viable candidate for observational implications. They also note that the bifurcation point αn=0(g) increases as g decreases, meaning tachyonic instability becomes harder to realize for smaller magnetic charges. The computational workflow proceeds from detecting tachyonic instability, to predicting bifurcation points, to obtaining the n = 0 branch, and finally to performing the stability analysis. The paper contributes to the broader literature on scalarized black holes in scalar-tensor and scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, as well as in Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theories with quadratic and exponential couplings. While the study is theoretically motivated and numerically grounded, it does not report observational data, experimental validation, or demographic information, and it omits details such as the numerical solver, grid resolution, and random seeds. These omissions are noted as limitations. The paper is significant for connecting regular black hole solutions to scalarization dynamics and for establishing the stability of the fundamental scalarized branch, thereby providing a foundation for further observational studies.

claims.description: The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings.
The instability threshold αth(g) coincides with the bifurcation point αn=0(g) for the n = 0 branch.
The bifurcation point αn=0(g) increases as g decreases, making tachyonic instability harder to realize for smaller magnetic charges.
Infinite branches of SCBHs appear from infinite scalar modes.

While the study is theoretically motivated and numerically grounded, it does not report observational data, experimental validation, or demographic information, and it omits details such as the numerical solver, grid resolution, and random seeds. These omissions are noted as limitations. The paper is significant for connecting regular black hole solutions to scalarization dynamics and for establishing the stability of the fundamental scalarized branch, thereby providing a foundation for further observational studies.

Research Context
Spontaneous scalarization imparts scalar hair to black holes without changing weak-field predictions. The phenomenon arises from tachyonic instability due to nonminimal scalar coupling. Black hole scalarization has been widely studied, including rotation and spin-induced cases. Scalarized black holes are entropically favorable and their n = 0 branches are stable. Scalarization has also been explored in scalar-Gauss-Bonnet and other alternative gravity theories. Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theories with quadratic and exponential couplings have been considered. Regular black holes avoid singularities via nonlinear electromagnetic sources. Bardeen proposed the first regular black hole solution free of singularities. The physical source of Bardeen black holes was initially unclear. Nonlinear electromagnetic sources were proposed to explain the matter content.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper studies spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes via two scalar couplings. The central question is whether tachyonic instability triggers scalarized charged black holes. The authors hypothesize infinite branches of SCBHs indexed by n = 0, 1, 2, .... The n = 0 branch should appear for α ≥ αn=0(g), the instability threshold. The authors predict the n = 0 branch is stable against radial perturbations. Stability would make the n = 0 branch usable for observational implications. The instability threshold αth(g) is expected to coincide with αn=0(g). The authors predict the bifurcation point increases as g decreases. The authors predict other branches (n ≠ 0) are unstable against radial perturbations. The authors predict exponential coupling does not affect the stability of SCBHs.

Methodological Details
The framework is Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics coupled with a scalar field. The action includes scalar curvature, scalar kinetic term, and coupling to nonlinear electrodynamics. The nonlinear electrodynamics Lagrangian depends on the magnetic charge parameter g. The parameter s is defined as the ratio of magnetic charge to mass. The Bardeen solution is obtained by setting the scalar field to zero. The metric function f(r) defines the Bardeen black hole geometry. The magnetic field strength is expressed via the field tensor Fµν. The energy-momentum tensor violates the strong energy condition at the center. Two coupling forms are chosen: quadratic and exponential. The quadratic coupling is 1−αϕ² with parameter α. The exponential coupling is e−αϕ². The linearized equation for the perturbed scalar δϕ is derived from the Klein-Gordon equation. The scalar potential V(r) is expressed in terms of f(r) and coupling parameters. The s-mode (l = 0) is used to assess the instability. The authors use M = 0.5 and g = 0.2 as a typical nonextremal configuration. The outer horizon radius is r+ = 0.935 for the typical configuration. The separation of variables ansatz is used for the scalar field. The tortoise coordinate r∗ is defined via an integral of 1/f(r). The instability bound is α ≥ αth(g). The thresholds are αth(g) = 17.338, 12.712, 7.251 for g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250. The scalar cloud solution yields discrete values αn(g) for n = 0, 1, 2, .... The number n denotes the zero crossings of ϕ(r). The metric ansatz for SCBHs includes N(r), δ(r), ϕ(r), and Aφ. The near-horizon expansion coefficients are determined by matching conditions. The asymptotic solution incorporates the ADM mass M and scalar charge Qs. The radial perturbation ansatz introduces H0, H1, and δϕ perturbations. The control parameter ε is much less than 1. The Schrödinger-type equation for scalar perturbations is derived. The potential VSCBH(r) is expressed with the background fields. The numerical solution imposes ingoing and outgoing wave boundary conditions.

Procedures And Architectures
The action is varied with respect to gµν, ϕ, and Aµ to obtain field equations. The three field equations are for the metric, scalar field, and gauge field. The Bardeen solution is obtained by solving the field equations with ϕ = 0. The tachyonic instability is analyzed via the linearized scalar equation. The potential V(r) is evaluated as a function of r and α. The negative region of the potential signals instability. The instability threshold is read from the crossing of Ω curves with the α-axis. The scalar cloud solution is solved with u(r) = rϕ(r) and ω = 0. The asymptotically normalizable condition yields discrete αn(g) values. The SCBH metric ansatz is substituted into the Maxwell equation. The vector potential solution Aφ = −g cos θ is obtained. The three equations for δ(r), m(r), ϕ(r) are derived from Eqs. (3)–(4). The near-horizon coefficients m1, δ1, ϕ1 are determined by matching. The matching incorporates the ADM mass M and scalar charge Qs. The n = 0 branch is constructed numerically for M = 0.5 and g = 0.2. The radial perturbation ansatz is introduced around the SCBHs. The l = 0 mode is focused, neglecting higher angular momentum modes. The scalar potential VSCBH(r) is derived for the perturbed system. The stability is determined by solving the equation numerically. The boundary conditions are vanishing ϕ1 at the horizon and infinity. The exponential version of the equation is solved with redeﬁned scalar field. The computational workflow detects instability, predicts bifurcations, and analyzes stability.

Key Results
Infinite branches of SCBHs appear with magnetic charge g. The n = 0 branch appears for α ≥ αn=0(g) with both couplings. The instability thresholds are αth(g) = 17.338, 12.712, 7.251 for g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250. The instability threshold coincides with αn=0(g). summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek, Ivan Saika-Voivod, Styliani Consta
summary.field_subfield: Physical chemistry / molecular simulation of aqueous nanodroplets
summary.executive_summary: This study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with an analytical reference model to investigate how ions are distributed within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets. The authors simulate Na+ ions in water clusters ranging from 100 to 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. Their central finding is that in supercooled droplets, a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water forms and expels Na+ ions to a denser, more disordered subsurface region. This contrasts sharply with room-temperature behavior, where the ion distribution is nearly uniform. The authors introduce a reference analytical model that treats the droplet as a charged dielectric sphere and predicts an electrostatic confinement effect, where the ion experiences a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. This model agrees with simulations at room temperature but not at supercooling, where the heterogeneous solvent structure dominates. The work is motivated by applications in atmospheric and man-made aerosols, spray-based ionization methods in native mass spectrometry, and the use of droplets as micro-reactors for chemical synthesis. The authors anticipate that their findings will serve as a starting point for understanding supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecular conformations. The study highlights the importance of solvent structure in determining ion location and chemical reactivity, and it identifies gaps in the understanding of supercooled systems, which are notoriously challenging to equilibrate. The authors note that their results are consistent with previous computational studies for clusters at room or elevated temperatures, while extending the understanding to supercooled conditions. The study also discusses the implications for ion mobility-mass spectrometry data interpretation and the physics of jets, and it identifies future directions for research on the structure of low-temperature droplets containing unstructured peptides and complexes of ions.

Ion distribution in droplets is key to aerosol reactivity. Supercooled clusters have fascinated scientists for decades. Most computational studies focus on room or elevated temperatures. Supercooled clusters are challenging to equilibrate. Low-density cores emerge in supercooled water clusters. The distribution of multiple ions at supercooling is unknown.

Research Question And Hypothesis
How do ions distribute in supercooled nanodroplets? Does the low-density core differentiate ion distribution? Can an analytical model explain ion location? Is the effect electrostatic confinement? When is the effect more evident?

Methodological Details
Simulations used molecular dynamics in GROMACS. Water modeled with TIP4P/2005 potential. Na+ used OPLS-AA parameters. Temperatures were 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. System sizes ranged from 100 to 1100 molecules. Systems placed in periodic cubic boxes. Canonical ensemble with Nosé-Hoover thermostat. Thermostat time constant was 0.1 ps. Time step was 2 fs. Cutoff length was L/2. Cluster sizes from 100 to 1100 water molecules. Diameters ranged from 1.8 nm to 4.0 nm. Two simulations run for equilibration checks. Equilibration estimated from convergence. Tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) computed. Voronoi volumes used for density. Data for qT(r) and d5(r) from Ref. 31.

Procedures And Architectures
Energy is sum of electrostatic and surface. Harmonic potential centered at COM. Spring constant K(ε) defined. Maximum K at ε = 2.73. Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution used. Expectation value of r2 derived. EC more pronounced at low temperature. Rayleigh instability discussed. Simulation time 10-100 ns range. Diffusion coefficient ~10^-9 m2/s. Ion placed at surface for most runs. Ion placed at center for two runs. Conjugate-gradient energy minimization. Equilibration for N=776 after 400 ns. Relaxation time ratio τ1100/τ776 ≈ 2. Multiple ions start near COM. Cut off qT(r) at minimum at 1.6 nm. NPB equation for reference model. Surface charge density σ defined.

Key Results
Low-density core forms at supercooling. High density subsurface surrounds core. Na+ expelled to subsurface at low T. Room temperature distribution nearly uniform. Ion resides in highest density environment. Peak within 0.1 nm of subsurface peak. Surface layer ~0.3 nm thick. Multiple ions expelled from core. Two peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. Lower peak at 0.52 nm for one ion. Outer peak at ~1.5 nm. λPB ≈ 1.2 nm for 776 molecules. λPB ≈ 1.3 nm for 1100 molecules. λPB ≈ 0.8 with dielectric 75. EC evident for charge ±3e. Rayleigh limit defines stability. Model agrees with Voth et al. for N=100. N=100 does not form tetrahedral core. Na+ lies one or two layers in. Low tetrahedral structure near COM.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Heterogeneous solvent drives ion distribution. Dielectric constant increases with density. Surface does not provide good solvation. Layering affects small droplets. EC more pronounced at low temperature. Model extends to peptides and complexes. Implications for mass spectrometry. Relevance to atmospheric chemistry. Future study on conical deformation. Model fails at supercooling. Shape fluctuations affect decay. λPB interpreted qualitatively. N=100 lacks tetrahedral core. Small clusters have shape fluctuations. Noisy statistics for r < 0.2 nm. Sampling challenge in confined systems. Simulation time limits. Ion size effects not included. Hydrophobic effects not included.

Supercooled nanodroplets expel ions to the subsurface due to low-density core. Low-density core forms. Ions expelled to subsurface. Ion resides in high density. Peak near subsurface. Room temperature uniform. Model fails at supercooling. N=100 no core. Relevance to mass spectrometry. Future research starting point. Atmospheric chemistry relevance.
Electrostatic confinement explains ion location at room temperature. Harmonic potential at COM. Model agrees at room temperature. Spring constant maximum at 2.73. Model fails at supercooling. Data taken from Ref. 30 and 31. Details in SI. SI contains additional data. Figures S2 and S3 in SI.

Two simulations for equilibration. Convergence after 400 ns. Relaxation time ratio. Multiple starting positions. Cut off qT(r) at minimum. Qualitative interpretation of λPB.

No ethics reported.

Fig. 1 plots spring constant. Fig. 2 shows peptide distribution. Fig. 3 shows density profiles. Fig. 4 shows N=776 behavior. Fig. 5 shows multiple ions. Table 1 shows system sizes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution. 2. The strongest evidence. 3. The future path.

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / Materials Chemistry for Energy Storage
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study on aqueous electrolyte properties and battery application
summary.executive_summary: This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors address the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which suffer from safety issues, high cost, and reliance on thermally unstable LiPF6 salt. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they are limited by the narrow electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. To overcome this, researchers have explored super-concentrated electrolytes, including the 'Water-in-Salt' (WISE) concept, which widens the ESW by reducing water activity through high ion concentrations. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems, such as LiTFSI, exhibit severe toxicity and high cost, limiting their practical application. In contrast, acetate salts like CH3COOK and CH3COONa are cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available, making them attractive alternatives. The authors prepared a series of electrolytes with constant CH3COOK concentration (20 mol kg⁻¹) and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹), then systematically characterized their thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties. The most concentrated solution (7N20K, i.e., 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK with 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COONa) emerged as the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability, exhibiting a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and a stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. As a proof of concept, the authors demonstrated the use of this electrolyte in sodium-ion batteries using a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserted and de-inserted Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE with a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low activation energy for charge transfer (0.12 eV) highlighted the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings support the feasibility of designing electrode interfaces for alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the WISE approach, offering a promising pathway toward sustainable energy storage technologies.

claims.description: Highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes offer a promising, safe, and cost-effective alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries.
The 7N20K electrolyte exhibits optimal transport and electrochemical stability properties.
The carbon-coated NASICON electrode demonstrates excellent performance in sodium-ion batteries.

Organic electrolytes have low flashpoints and high viscosities. LiPF6 salt degrades in moisture, producing corrosive HF. Aqueous electrolytes are limited by water's narrow stability window. The ESW can be kinetically extended only to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. High concentration widens the ESW by reducing water activity. Fluorinated salts enable wide ESW but raise toxicity and cost concerns. LiTFSI exhibits severe toxicity and chronic aquatic effects. Acetate salts are cost-effective, soluble, and available alternatives. NASICON materials are ideal electrodes for concentrated environments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question concerns the physicochemical properties of binary acetate electrolytes. The authors hypothesize that adding NaAc improves electrochemical stability. The most concentrated solution is expected to balance transport and stability. The hypothesis is that 7N20K offers optimal conductivity and stability. The authors predict good performance in sodium-ion batteries. The hypothesis includes favorable interfacial kinetics. The authors expect the WISE approach to enable alkaline-ion batteries.

Methodological Details
The study used high-purity acetate salts from Alfa Aesar. Milli-Q water with defined resistivity was used as solvent. Four electrolytes were prepared with varying NaAc concentrations. Titanium butoxide served as the titanium source. Lithium acetate dihydrate and glucose were used as Li and C sources. The mixture was stirred at 55°C for 4 hours. The temperature was raised to 80°C to form a gel. The precursor was dried under vacuum at 100°C. Calcination was performed at 800°C for 6 hours under argon. The ramp rate was set to 5°C per minute. The current increased to 0.5, 1, 5, and 10 C. The current was reduced to 0.1 C for the last 10 cycles. 1C corresponds to 136 mA g⁻¹. EIS measurements were conducted from 20 to 70°C. The CLTP synthesis used a glucose carbon precursor. The LTP synthesis omitted glucose. The XRD patterns showed phase purity without secondary phases. The crystal structure is rhombohedral NASICON type (R-3c). The peak positions were the same in both samples. The carbon content did not affect the crystal structure. The ionic conductivity followed VTF behavior. The ionic conductivity decreased with increasing concentration. The viscosity followed Arrhenius behavior. The viscosity increased with concentration. The viscosity trend did not vary linearly. The acetate salts are structure-making salts. None of the samples showed a decrease in viscosity. The samples behaved like Newtonian fluids. The molar conductivities were plotted against fluidity. The electrolytes were classified as quasi-ideal. The most concentrated solution followed Kohlrausch's law. The molar conductivity at infinite dilution was 52.90 ohm⁻¹ cm² mol⁻¹. The Kohlrausch law calls for complete salt dissociation. The LSV profiles were measured vs SHE. A threshold of 0.1 mA cm⁻² was used for decomposition potentials. The procedure may lead to overestimated decomposition limits. The procedure is highly reproducible. The cathodic stability increased with concentration. The anodic ESW expansion was not as significant. The impedance spectra showed a depressed semicircle. The straight line relates to the Warburg element. The Arrhenius plot showed low activation energy. The low activation energy proved good interfacial kinetics. The diffusion coefficient was calculated via a formula. The number of mobile ions was evaluated to be 1.7. The concentration of mobile ions was 12930 mol m⁻³. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was around 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹. The aqueous electrolyte improved ion diffusion. The low activation energy for diffusion was 0.48 eV.

Key Results
The glass transition temperature increased with salt concentration. The Tg values are reported in Table 2. The Tg transition reflects the shift from salt-in-water to water-in-salt. summary.title: From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving
summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu
summary.field_subfield: Robotics / Autonomous Driving
summary.executive_summary: Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically customizes autonomous-driving policies to match natural-language user commands without relying on prior driving data. The authors argue that current AVs suffer from a uniform driving style, which is a safety and experience problem, and that existing methods either depend on predefined styles requiring expert input or use data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that struggle with data availability, metric alignment, and generalization. The core innovation is a Style-Customized Reward Function that bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, enabled by large language models (LLMs) and a Driving Style Database. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences by comparing generated policies against natural driving behavior on a reserved test set. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to select relevant style rewards, generates new reward functions when no match exists, and trains new policies via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), replacing existing policies when the new ones perform better. Experiments used the HighD dataset with a car-following scenario, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base model, and temperature 0.3. In human-in-the-loop comparisons against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM), Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of events, with 18.8% ties and only 9.2% preference for IDM. The framework demonstrates strong accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, and includes a fuzzy memory function for recalling similar commands. Code and demo are available online. The paper positions itself as the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies aligned with natural language commands, and outlines future work including expanding to more complex scenarios and adding a Feedback and Reflection module.
