documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Words2Wheels is a framework that automatically customizes autonomous-driving policies to match natural-language user commands without relying on prior driving data. The authors argue that current AVs suffer from a uniform driving style, which is a safety and experience problem, and that existing methods either depend on predefined styles requiring expert input or use data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that struggle with data availability, metric alignment, and generalization. The core innovation is a Style-Customized Reward Function that bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, enabled by large language models (LLMs) and a Driving Style Database. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences by comparing generated policies against natural driving behavior on a reserved test set. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to select relevant style rewards, generates new reward functions when no match exists, and trains new policies via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), replacing existing policies when the new ones perform better. Experiments used the HighD dataset with a car-following scenario, GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base model, and temperature 0.3. In human-in-the-loop comparisons against the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM), Words2Wheels was preferred in 72% of events, with 18.8% ties and only 9.2% preference for IDM. The framework demonstrates strong accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, and includes a fuzzy memory function for recalling similar commands. Code and demo are available online. The paper positions itself as the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies aligned with natural language commands, and outlines future work including expanding to more complex scenarios and adding a Feedback and Reflection module.

Research Context
Autonomous driving has advanced with foundation models improving interactivity and user experience. A key criticism is the uniform driving style of current autonomous vehicles. 52.46% of AVs involved in crashes were rear-ended, 1.6 times the rate of conventional vehicles. Early approaches relied heavily on classification or calibration of predefined styles or driving patterns. Data-driven approaches use clustering and IRL to derive driving policies from natural driving behavior data. These methods face challenges in data availability, metric alignment, and generalization. Foundation models process user instructions but fall short at the style level. These approaches raise concerns about reliability and efficiency.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether Words2Wheels can automatically customize driving policies to align with natural language user commands. The hypothesis is that a Style-Customized Reward Function can bridge user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy without prior driving data. The framework leverages LLMs and RAG to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences. Words2Wheels is hypothesized to outperform existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability. The system can generalize to new commands without user behavior data via zero-shot generation. New policies that outperform existing ones can replace them, expanding the style range.

Methodological Details
The study focused on the car-following scenario as the experimental focus. The experiment utilized the HighD dataset collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone. Data extraction and kinematic model were based on FollowNet. 15% of the data was reserved as a test set to ensure objectivity. User commands were categorized into three levels based on directness. Level I commands are direct, Level II are indirect with strong hints, and Level III are indirect with mild hints. The base model was GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature set to 0.3. k was set to 3 in selecting relevant styles and n was set to 2 in Statistical Evaluation. The Driving Style Database was populated with 8 initial styles. Some styles were data-driven reward functions derived using clustering plus IRL. Others were human-designed reward functions based on prior methodologies. Style Policies are stored as pre-trained neural networks. Analytical data can be saved in JSON format. Metrics include speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing, and time headway. The Statistical Evaluation module uses a Chain-of-Thought approach. Human participants were recruited with valid driving licenses. Each participant was presented with 5 user commands and 20 events per command. This resulted in a total of 1,000 tested events. The fuzzy memory function was tested with 3 experimental sets. Each set tested 5 similar inputs to see if the system could recall the corresponding memory.

Procedures And Architectures
The process starts by applying RAG principles where the LLM selects the top k relevant style rewards. This step can be parallelized for efficiency. If a selected Style Reward has matched a semantically similar command, the Style Policy is used directly. If no match is found, the LLM generates m new reward functions based on the most relevant Style Reward. The LLM's generation may involve logic modifications or restructuring. The initially selected Style Reward provides a temporary solution since its policy is already trained. Newly generated reward functions produce new Style Policies via RL, where trainings can be parallelized. Words2Wheels uses Proximal Policy Optimization for training. RL training was run 5 times using different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. Words2Wheels determines if the new policies outperform the temporary one. The data was normalized using the 10th and 90th percentiles of the natural driving behavior. The Statistical Evaluation module prompts the LLM to answer in JSON format. The visualization tool displays clips of car-following behavior from two different models. The models are anonymized as A and B to eliminate bias. Future work will incorporate a Feedback and Reflection module.

Key Results
The aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration. The conservative style maintained a larger gap and relative speed. The aggressive style had a larger time headway. The normal style showed higher jerk. Words2Wheels demonstrated a strong ability to adapt to different driving styles. When the input was 'I'm going to be late for the train,' the generated style exhibited higher speed, acceleration, and jerk. When the input was 'Safety first. I have plenty of time,' the generated style showed greater spacing, time headway, and relative speed. Words2Wheels can generate driving styles that align with user commands rather than simply selecting from existing styles. In 72% of events, participants judged Words2Wheels to be a better match to the user command than IDM. In 18.8% of events, both models were considered equally effective. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events. For Level I commands, retrieval was 100% and analysis was 100%. For Level III commands, retrieval was 90% and generation was 85%. Overall, Words2Wheels performed well in terms of analysis, decision-making, and generation. The system's handling of Level I commands was slightly more accurate than for Level II and III commands. With the exception of one case involving 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased,' all other test cases were successfully recalled. The system demonstrated a strong ability to recognize and match fuzzy inputs to existing memories.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Words2Wheels bridges user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy via a Style-Customized Reward Function. The reward function guides the driving policy to optimize long-term rewards and serves as a policy index. Style Rewards are less complex than user commands or traffic scenarios, enabling efficient retrieval of Style Policy. The framework generalizes to new commands and styles without user behavior data via zero-shot generation. The Driving Style Database enables efficient retrieval and continuous enrichment of driving styles. The Statistical Evaluation module automatically and accurately measures alignment between driving policies and user commands. Words2Wheels is the first framework that automatically customizes style-aware driving policies to align with natural language user commands. The fuzzy memory function enhances the adaptability of the driving models. The system reduces reliance on RL as the database expands. The framework is extensible, allowing for features like fuzzy memory via LLMs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style had a larger time headway, which may contradict expectations. The normal style showed higher jerk, possibly because the LLM did not prioritize these metrics. In a few isolated cases, the LLM's interpretation and processing were off. In Case 19, the LLM misinterpreted the user command 'You are allowing a large gap with the vehicle in front.' In Case 26, the LLM intentionally selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk value as a counterexample. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. The study focused only on the car-following scenario. The Statistical Evaluation module may require refinement for finer tuning. The base model GPT-4o-2024-08-06 may limit generalizability. The temperature was set to 0.3 for more deterministic text generation. The number of initial styles was limited to 4 for better demonstration in some experiments. The fuzzy memory function had one failure case involving 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased.' The study is a preprint version. The paper is a preprint, which may limit its reliability.

Claims
Words2Wheels automatically customizes driving policies to align with natural language user commands without relying on prior driving data. The framework automatically generates customized driving policies based on natural language user commands. The system uses a Style-Customized Reward Function to generate a Style-Customized Driving Policy. The framework leverages LLMs and RAG to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles. The system can generalize to new commands without user behavior data. In a few isolated cases, the LLM's interpretation and processing were off. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. Words2Wheels offers a novel solution for customized AV driving behavior. The framework improves user experience in autonomous vehicles through style customization. The fuzzy memory function enhances the adaptability of the driving models.
Words2Wheels outperforms existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability. In 72% of events, participants judged Words2Wheels to be a better match to the user command than IDM. Words2Wheels can generate driving styles that align with user commands rather than simply selecting from existing styles. Words2Wheels demonstrated a strong ability to adapt to different driving styles. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events, but 18.8% were ties. The aggressive style had a larger time headway, which may not align with expectations. The framework reduces reliance on RL as the database expands. The system is extensible, allowing for features like fuzzy memory via LLMs.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo are available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/. Experimental records are available at https://bit.ly/4giYhB7. The HighD dataset was used for the experiments.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
RL training was run 5 times using different seeds, selecting the Style Policy with the highest reward. Each command was run 5 times and the outcomes were averaged. Results from 5 repeated runs were averaged in the generation capability experiment. The data was normalized using the 10th and 90th percentiles of the natural driving behavior. The models were anonymized as A and B to eliminate bias.

Ethical Considerations
The models were anonymized as A and B to eliminate bias. We recruited 10 volunteers with valid driving license. The study is a preprint version.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the workflow of Words2Wheels, where a natural language command is matched with a style from the database. Fig. 2 shows the Driving Style Database, which stores Style Rewards, Style Policies, and their statistics. Fig. 3 shows an example of automated Style Policy generation. Fig. 4 shows a simplified example of the Statistical Evaluation module. Fig. 5 shows the comparison of customized policies over style-aware metrics. Fig. 6 shows the evaluation of generated policies when no aligned styles are provided. Fig. 7 shows the user interface of the tool for comparing driving style alignment. TABLE I categorizes user commands into three levels based on directness. TABLE II summarizes human preferences on driving style alignment. TABLE III presents case studies across all command levels. TABLE IV summarizes the system's ability to recall associated driving styles.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Words2Wheels framework that automatically customizes driving policies to align with natural language user commands. 2. The strongest evidence is the 72% preference rate in human-in-the-loop comparisons against IDM. 3. The future path is expanding the framework to more complex driving scenarios and adding a Feedback and Reflection module.

The previous 1 cm² cuvette system accommodated up to 50 droplets but suffered from thermal lag due to the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, limiting parallel cuvette setups to 5–10 and producing several-degree differences. The Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer enabled constant-rate cooling down to −0.5 °C/min, reducing well-to-well variability (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) and overall dispersion by 36% relative to the generic freezer. The authors acknowledge that droplet stability was insufficient when the system was transferred between laboratories, with static electricity causing coalescence. Executive Summary

The central aim is to expand the earlier proof-of-concept system toward higher throughput and accuracy while improving temperature uniformity. Three functional advantages are targeted: (a) increased screening efficiency with fewer manipulation steps, (b) increased measurement accuracy through larger sample sizes, and (c) increased uniformity of temperature distribution via a controlled-rate freezer. The authors describe three components: automated droplet generation using a Biomek 3000 liquid-handling robot, adaptation of the freeze-float assay to a controlled, uniform cooling system, and a semi-automated droplet-detection program. The previous 1 cm² cuvette system accommodated up to 50 droplets but suffered from thermal lag due to the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, limiting parallel cuvette setups to 5–10 and producing several-degree differences. To overcome this, the authors adopted a 96-deep-well plate format and later a 48 cryovial format, generating up to ~3800 uniform 1 µL droplets. Monodispersity was quantified at 9.2% polydispersity, and the authors concluded that more than 30 droplets are sufficient for a reliable freezing temperature. The Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer enabled constant-rate cooling down to −0.5 °C/min, reducing well-to-well variability (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) and overall dispersion by 36% relative to the generic freezer. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C versus −12.3 °C for INA-free droplets, compared with −7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer. The authors acknowledge that droplet stability was insufficient when the system was transferred between laboratories, with static electricity causing coalescence. This work advances ice-nucleation screening toward the scale and reproducibility of high-throughput screening in multi-well plates, while noting that full automation integration remains incomplete.

Research Context
High-throughput screening of biochemical assays is well-established but ice-nucleation measurement has lagged. The prior freeze-float system was a proof-of-concept limited by thermal lag in silicone oil. Low thermal conductivity of silicone oil prevented scaling the cuvette footprint. Droplet diameter strongly affects homogeneous freezing temperature, so monodispersity matters. Stochastic nucleation produces inherent freezing-temperature distributions even for identical droplets.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the freeze-float platform can be scaled to higher throughput and accuracy. The authors hypothesize that automated droplet generation will enable larger, uniform sample sizes. The authors hypothesize that a controlled-rate freezer will improve temperature uniformity. The authors hypothesize that uniform droplets will limit freezing-temperature dispersion to within ±0.09 °C. The authors predict that controlled-rate cooling will better differentiate INA-containing from INA-free droplets.

Methodological Details
The study builds on a prior freeze-float proof-of-concept using a 1 cm² cuvette. The prior cuvette system accommodated up to 50 droplets at once. The prior system was limited to 5–10 parallel cuvettes. The 96-deep-well plate format was tested for compatibility with the Biomek 3000. The same silicone oil buoyant layer with 1% silicone surfactant and HFE-7500 cushion was used. Droplets were generated with the Biomek 3000 at 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The robotic arm generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once. Monodispersity was assessed with 60 fluorescein-dyed 1 µL droplets in a 12-well plate. Fluorescent images were acquired with the ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, CA). Droplet diameters were measured with the Matlab program Droplet_Dispersion.m (Source Code S1). Polydispersity was defined as the standard deviation of radii divided by the mean radius. The measured polydispersity was 9.2%. The mean droplet radius was 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. The standard deviation of radii was 2.86×10⁻⁵. Static electricity was removed with the Auto-set Ion Pump (#19500, Charles Water, MA). Wet filter paper was placed below the plate to minimize static accumulation. The sample contained 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein. The freezing temperature confidence interval was estimated with n ≈ (2k CI/s)². The value k = 1.96 corresponds to 95% confidence. The authors concluded that more than 30 droplets are sufficient. The 48 cryovial format was adopted for higher throughput. The throughput was increased by a factor of 38 relative to the cuvette. The Asymptote VIA Freeze controlled-rate freezer was used for constant-rate cooling. The freezer accommodated up to 48×1 mL cryovials in a metal holder. Each cryovial contained 50 µL HFE-7500 cushion, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 20 aqueous droplets. The INA-free droplets were marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. The controlled-rate freezer provided cooling precision down to −0.5 °C/min. A custom glass lid enabled automated image recording with a generic digital camera. The freezing temperature of droplets was hypothesized to be a random nucleation process. The 96-deep-well freezing temperatures were compared using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The generic freezer was operated at a constant temperature of −28 °C. The Asymptote freezer used linear cooling at −0.25 °C/min.

Procedures And Architectures
The freeze-float assay used a buoyant silicone oil layer over an HFE-7500 cushion. INA-containing droplets were colored with yellow fluorescein dye. INA-free droplets were marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. Droplet diameters were measured with an automated Matlab circle-detection program. The polydispersity was computed as the standard deviation of radii divided by the mean radius. The freezing-temperature dispersion was expected to be no more than ±0.09 °C. The HFE-7500 cushion was placed at the bottom to avoid plastic-wall contact. The ion pump removed static electricity that could cause droplet coalescence. The freeze-float validation used a commodity freezer from the previous publication. Freezing and floating behavior were recorded with the Biomek 3000 system. The KStest.ipynb script compared cumulative freezing-temperature distributions. The script computed a p-value via the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The 96-deep-well system showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature. The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The Asymptote freezer showed a p-value of 0.83 in well-to-well freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer had a standard deviation of 0.73 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer improved INA detection versus the commodity freezer. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C in the Asymptote freezer. INA-free droplets did not freeze until −12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer. The commodity freezer mean freezing temperature was −7.5 ± 0.97 °C. Linear cooling reduced the cell-to-cell thermal delay p-value to 0.31. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories. The detection threshold of the INA concentration was investigated.

Key Results
The 96-deep-well plate was compatible with the Biomek 3000. The robotic arm generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once. The measured droplet polydispersity was 9.2%. The mean droplet radius was 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. The standard deviation of radii was 2.86×10⁻⁵. The INA droplets showed freezing behavior consistent with the previous report. The 96-deep-well system showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature. Linear cooling reduced the 96-deep-well p-value to 0.31. The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The mean freezing time between cells was 47.4 and 50.6 min. The Asymptote freezer accommodated up to 48×1 mL cryovials. The Asymptote freezer provided cooling precision down to −0.5 °C/min. The Asymptote freezer reduced well-to-well variability to p = 0.83. The Asymptote freezer had a standard deviation of 0.73 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C in the Asymptote freezer. INA-free droplets did not freeze until −12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer. The commodity freezer mean freezing temperature was −7.5 ± 0.97 °C. The controlled-rate freezer provided better INA detection than the commodity freezer. The 48 cryovial format yielded 1920 droplets. The throughput was increased by a factor of 38 relative to the cuvette. The controlled-rate freezer improved the cell-to-cell thermal delay p-value to 0.31. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The uniform droplets limited freezing-temperature dispersion to within ±0.09 °C. The 9.2% polydispersity indicated sufficiently uniform droplet volumes. The controlled-rate freezer reduced well-to-well variability to p = 0.83. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer improved INA detection versus the commodity freezer. The higher sample size improved measurement accuracy. The higher throughput enabled more efficient screening. The system can be implemented into a high-throughput freeze-float platform. The freezing behavior was consistent with the previous report. The stochastic nucleation model explains the observed freezing distributions. The linear cooling rate is important for heterogeneous nucleation measurement. The controlled-rate freezer better differentiates INA-containing droplets. The reduced dispersion strengthens the reliability of the freezing temperature.

Contradictions And Limitations
The 96-deep-well system showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature. Linear cooling reduced the 96-deep-well p-value to 0.31. The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The mean freezing time between cells was 47.4 and 50.6 min. Linear cooling significantly increased the range of freezing time. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories. It was not successful to combine the droplet generation system across transfers. The full automation integration remains incomplete. The detection threshold of the INA concentration was investigated but not fully reported. The sample size was small (30 droplets per sample). The 96-deep-well system had a larger thermal gradient than the Asymptote freezer. The Asymptote freezer had a smaller thermal gradient than the 96-deep-well system. The 96-deep-well system had a larger dispersion than the Asymptote freezer. The Asymptote freezer had a smaller dispersion than the 96-deep-well system. The commodity freezer had a larger dispersion than the Asymptote freezer. The Asymptote freezer had a smaller dispersion than the commodity freezer. The freezing-temperature threshold was not explicitly reported. The sample size was small (30 droplets per sample). The random nucleation process explains the observed freezing distributions. The stochastic model explains the observed freezing distributions.

Claims
The freeze-float ice-nucleation platform can be scaled to high throughput via automated droplet generation and a controlled-rate freezer. The 96-deep-well plate was compatible with the Biomek 3000. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer improved INA detection versus the commodity freezer. The system can be implemented into a high-throughput freeze-float platform. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories. It was not successful to combine the droplet generation system across transfers. The full automation integration remains incomplete. The higher throughput enables more efficient screening. The higher sample size improves measurement accuracy. The higher uniformity improves reproducibility. The platform advances ice-nucleation screening toward HTS scale. The platform supports the stochastic nucleation model.

The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The mean freezing time between cells was 47.4 and 50.6 min. Linear cooling significantly increased the range of freezing time. The Asymptote freezer reduced well-to-well variability to p = 0.83. The Asymptote freezer had a standard deviation of 0.73 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer narrowed the freezing-temperature distribution. The higher sample size improved measurement accuracy. The higher throughput enabled more efficient screening. The system can be implemented into a high-throughput freeze-float platform. The freezing behavior was consistent with the previous report. The stochastic nucleation model explains the observed freezing distributions. The linear cooling rate is important for heterogeneous nucleation measurement. The improved uniformity supports the stochastic nucleation model. The controlled-rate freezer better differentiates INA-containing droplets. Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows the 96-deep-well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000. Figure 1C shows the 60 fluorescein-dyed 1 µL droplets in a 12-well plate. Figure 1 D-E shows the droplet dispersion analysis. Figure 2 shows the droplet freezing and floating behavior in the commodity freezer. Figure 3 shows the 96-deep-well freezing temperature distribution. Figure 4 shows the INA-containing versus INA-free droplets in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 shows the Asymptote freezer well-to-well freezing temperature distribution. Figure 6 shows the overall dispersion comparison. The freezing temperatures of 1 mg/mL Snomax droplets were measured over time.

1. The core contribution is a high-throughput, semi-automated freeze-float ice-nucleation platform. 2. The strongest evidence is the 36% reduction in overall dispersion with the controlled-rate freezer. 3. The future path is full automation integration and detection-threshold characterization.

summary.title: Tuning the Dielectric Response in a NC Material through Nanoparticle Morphology
summary.authors: Archita Adluri; Brett Henderson; Irina Paci
summary.field_subfield: Computational materials science / condensed matter physics
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates how the morphology of molecular-scale silver nanoparticle (mNP) inclusions affects the dielectric response of a magnesium oxide (MgO) nanocomposite matrix. The motivation stems from the growing demand for high-κ dielectric materials as traditional single-phase materials like Si/SiO₂ reach their limits in energy storage and device miniaturization. The authors use the Modern Theory of Polarization combined with Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) to model the polarization of silver inclusions in MgO, systematically varying nanoparticle size, shape, and orientation relative to an applied electric field. Their previous work had modeled a spherical Ag₈ inclusion and found significant interfacial effects, prompting this follow-up study to explore the effects of inclusion distribution and shape on dielectric capacity. The key finding is that at mNP scales below 30 atoms, the size, shape, and orientation of the inclusion greatly alter how inclusion electrons behave and affect atomic-scale polarization. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms, considering both rod-like and disk-like inclusions, with alignment either parallel or perpendicular to the external field. The study reveals that asymmetric inclusions can bring on dielectric enhancements even larger than expected based on volume ratios, with multi-layer disks exhibiting more than 70% enhancement over the matrix permittivity. The authors also address a technical challenge: currents calculated using the modern theory of polarization with periodic boundary conditions can experience box edge jumps due to matrix distortion during simulations, and they outline an approach for addressing these issues in CPMD calculations. The research provides important insights for designing smaller and more precise dielectric materials, emphasizing that the nature of induced fields depends on electron dynamics as metal atoms polarize, and that increasing atoms aligned to the applied field increases charge density at the interface. The study uses the Quantum Espresso code with LDA functional, norm-conserving pseudopotentials for Mg, and ultra-soft pseudopotentials for O and Ag, with total energy convergence criteria increased from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁸. Models were built using Avogadro software, and the matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the edge of the inclusion in each direction to prevent conduction into periodic images. The authors note that future work would expand into other matrix materials such as SiO₂ and HfO₂, and simulate other transition metal inclusions like Cu, Co, and Fe. The study acknowledges that %loading is not the only factor, as aggregation and separation are very important, and that direction effects add complexity to crystal structures. The research contributes to understanding quantum materials behavior as materials get smaller and more precise, with implications for transistors, high-density charge storage super-capacitors, and emerging quantum computing technologies.

claims.description: Molecular-scale silver inclusions in MgO matrix increase local dielectric capacity depending on shape, size, and orientation to the external field.
Asymmetric inclusions bring on dielectric enhancements even larger than expected based on volume ratios.
The induced fields at the matrix-inclusion interface arise from the polarization of mNPs and depend on electron dynamics.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates how the morphology of molecular-scale silver nanoparticle (mNP) inclusions affects the dielectric response of a magnesium oxide (MgO) nanocomposite matrix. The motivation stems from the growing demand for high-κ dielectric materials as traditional single-phase materials like Si/SiO₂ reach their limits in energy storage and device miniaturization. The authors use the Modern Theory of Polarization combined with Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) to model the polarization of silver inclusions in MgO, systematically varying nanoparticle size, shape, and orientation relative to an applied electric field. Their previous work had modeled a spherical Ag₈ inclusion and found significant interfacial effects, prompting this follow-up study to explore the effects of inclusion distribution and shape on dielectric capacity. The key finding is that at mNP scales below 30 atoms, the size, shape, and orientation of the inclusion greatly alter how inclusion electrons behave and affect atomic-scale polarization. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms, considering both rod-like and disk-like inclusions, with alignment either parallel or perpendicular to the external field. The study reveals that asymmetric inclusions can bring on dielectric enhancements even larger than expected based on volume ratios, with multi-layer disks exhibiting more than 70% enhancement over the matrix permittivity. The authors also address a technical challenge: currents calculated using the modern theory of polarization with periodic boundary conditions can experience box edge jumps due to matrix distortion during simulations, and they outline an approach for addressing these issues in CPMD calculations. The research provides important insights for designing smaller and more precise dielectric materials, emphasizing that the nature of induced fields depends on electron dynamics as metal atoms polarize, and that increasing atoms aligned to the applied field increases charge density at the interface. The study uses the Quantum Espresso code with LDA functional, norm-conserving pseudopotentials for Mg, and ultra-soft pseudopotentials for O and Ag, with total energy convergence criteria increased from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁸. Models were built using Avogadro software, and the matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the edge of the inclusion in each direction to prevent conduction into periodic images. The authors note that future work would expand into other matrix materials such as SiO₂ and HfO₂, and simulate other transition metal inclusions like Cu, Co, and Fe. The study acknowledges that %loading is not the only factor, as aggregation and separation are very important, and that direction effects add complexity to crystal structures. The research contributes to understanding quantum materials behavior as materials get smaller and more precise, with implications for transistors, high-density charge storage super-capacitors, and emerging quantum computing technologies.

Research Context
The demand for new high-κ dielectric materials is increasing as energy storage and processing power demands reach limits. Traditional single-phase materials like Si/SiO₂ face significant current leakage and tunnelling effects at few-nanometer sizes. Nanocomposite materials combining dielectric matrices with high-κ inclusions offer tunable dielectric and mechanical properties. The aim is to selectively modify the permittivity (dielectric constant κ) and therefore the charge capacity of materials. Previous work found significant interfacial effects between the NC and matrix producing greater than expected polarization response. Molecular nanoparticles bridge the gap between single-atom dopants and traditional nanoparticles while avoiding low percolation thresholds. Theoretical approaches have been developed but several challenges remain in treating quantum polarization of mixed materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study explores how the distribution and shape of mNP inclusions affect the dielectric capacity of a metal-oxide material. The hypothesis is that at mNP scales below 30 atoms, the size, shape, and orientation greatly alter inclusion electron behavior. The authors predict that asymmetric inclusions bring on dielectric enhancements even larger than expected based on volume ratios. The study hypothesizes that rod-like and disk-like structures further enhance the dielectric response through volume ratios and local field enhancements. The authors predict that increasing atoms aligned to the applied field increases charge density at the interface. The study hypothesizes that disk-shaped mNPs suffer from severe screening rings that interact with neighboring inclusions. The authors predict that perpendicular polarization shows a much larger depolarization field that never decays to bulk values.

Methodological Details
The NC systems were based on a magnesium oxide matrix with an array of silver mNP inclusions. MgO is a well researched high-κ metal-oxide gate dielectric with a bulk dielectric constant of 8-9.8 and bandgap of 7.8 eV. Models were built using the Avogadro software. Three rod-like inclusions and five disk-like inclusions were considered. Inclusions were built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice but allowed to optimize in the CPMD simulation. The matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the edge of the inclusion in each direction. Electronic structure calculations used the CPMD methodology implemented in the Quantum Espresso code version 6.0 and 6.6. Calculations used a plane wave-basis set built using LDA functional. Mg atoms used Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials. O and Ag used Rappe-Rabe-Kaxiras-Joannopoulos ultra-soft pseudopotentials from MaterialsCloud. The total energy convergence criteria was increased from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁸ with a force threshold of 10⁻⁴. A wavefunction cutoff of 50-60Ry and charge density cutoff of 560Ry were used. All calculations were done with periodic boundary conditions and the Brillouin zone sampled at the Γ point. Electron masses were kept at 300 a.u then increased to 450 after initial damped minimizations. A thermostat was not applied nor were temperatures controlled. Test runs using thermostats between 200 and 600K were performed with negligible temperature effects. Polarization was calculated using a static 0.001 a.u uniform field applied along the z-axis. The %loading ratios of inclusions to matrix were kept between 3-5%.

Procedures And Architectures
The CPMD method is used in the Quantum Espresso code with structural relaxation and polarization as major stages. Initial electron minimization used Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization followed by damped dynamics steps. The low frequency dielectric constant is calculated according to the equation ε r = 1 + 4π(P ε damped -P ε relax )/ε field. The reference polarization is that of the cell without an applied field. The electronic and ionic polarization is calculated using damped dynamics showing mainly ionic polarization. The values calculated for ε r are not true dielectric constants as surface charge and edge effects are not taken into account. The explicit particle-like electrons in CPMD will occasionally polarize into the neighboring image cell. The reported polarization then shifts in value equal to nxboxlength due to quantum of polarization effects. The Born effective charge tensor is used to examine electronic polarization effects in the composite. In a bulk single material, the static charges are nominal valence charge with +2 for oxygen and -2 for magnesium. Significant changes in charge distribution arise from the influence of mNP electrons particularly under applied field. Forces were normalized to the bulk matrix to highlight the effect of the NP. The electronic polarization and BECs were calculated in the clamped-ion step of the procedure. The fully-relaxed static polarization was calculated by releasing ionic clamps and allowing full relaxation. The mathematical corrections for polarization jumps during post-processing are shown in Figure 6.

Key Results
The inclusion of silver atoms within the MgO matrix distorted the local structure extending to nearest neighbors. The distortion of the crystal structure only extended to around 3 angstroms from the edge of the mNP. The calculated bandgap is generally expected to be significantly lower than the corresponding experimental material. Much of the density of states in the vicinity of the Fermi level arises from NP states. Our previous work observed an ≈ 30% increase in ε r with an ≈ 4% mNP volume ratio in the Ag 8 case. The data indicate that asymmetric inclusions bring on a dielectric enhancement even larger than expected based on volume ratios. The multi-layer disks exhibit more than 70% enhancement in ε r over the matrix permittivity. Enhancement of the polarization field is seen in the matrix in regions adjacent to the NP poles. In the equatorial region a depolarization arises where the effective ionic charge is less than in the absence of the external field. For the Rod-shaped inclusions, polarization along the z-axis results in a greater increase in polarization from the bulk at 9.23. Disk nanoparticles show similar effects with an exponential increase in ε compared to their rod counterparts. Disk442 is twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223 yet has a polarization increase of more than twice. The 2-Dimensional nanoparticles show a decrease in polarization when compared to the bulk in both directions. The forces contributing to increased or decreased permittivity are mainly due to forces felt by interface atoms. When oriented parallel to the applied field the reach of induced field is further physically and also stronger. For perpendicular polarization, the BEC converges to +2,-2 values of matrix in a very short distance. A significant increase in silver d-electron polarization occurs as they couple to the oxygen pband.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study demonstrates that molecular scale metal inclusions increase local dielectric capacity depending on shape, size, and orientation. The nature of the induced field depends on electron dynamics as the metal atom polarizes. Increasing atoms aligned to the applied field increases charge density in the interface. The same is true for the inverse when inclusions are not aligned with the applied field. Disk shaped mNPs suffer from severe screening rings that interact with neighboring inclusions. The induced fields at the matrix-inclusion interface arise from the polarization of mNPs. The study provides a way to understand quantum materials behavior as materials get smaller and more precise. The research contributes to understanding how polarization of molecular-scale inclusions affects induced fields on matrix dielectrics.

Contradictions And Limitations
The calculated values are not true dielectric constants as surface charge and edge effects are not taken into account. summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.field_subfield: Organic Chemistry / Total Synthesis of Marine Natural Products
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the first enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a complex marine natural product from the Xestospongia sea sponges, completed in 30 steps. The authors' central innovation is a new catalytic, highly enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. This single carbon–carbon bond-forming step efficiently constructed the chiral bicyclic (AC) core in near-perfect enantio- and diastereoselectivity, concurrently establishing three stereogenic centers including a quaternary carbon stereocenter, and proved highly scalable. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were probed using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which revealed the crucial substrate/catalyst interactions in the enantio-determining step. Following construction of the bicyclic core, the total synthesis of madangamine E was completed with key steps including a mild one-pot oxidation–lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metatheses to install the two macrocyclic rings. The authors emphasize that this work elegantly demonstrates the enabling power and scope of organocatalytic desymmetrization reactions, converting relatively simple achiral starting materials into high-value stereochemically-rich products. The introduction situates the work within the broader context of natural product synthesis, noting the prominent role that natural products are forecast to play in the future of medicinal chemistry. The madangamine family is characterized by an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system possessing two nitrogen atoms, with three rings constituting a diazatricyclic core (ABC rings) common to all family members, plus the macrocyclic E ring. The authors reasoned that via judicious application of an enantioselective desymmetrization reaction, they would be able to install all the ensuing stereochemical information from this single chirality-inducing step. The results and discussion section details the development of the key reaction, beginning with inspiration from the group's previously reported enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition to α,β-unsaturated esters using bifunctional primary amine thiourea organocatalysts. The computational study revealed that the kinetically preferred transition structure is stabilized because it adopts a conformation that benefits from several hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties, consistent with a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism. The conclusion reiterates that the early application of the organocatalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction enabled the construction of the bicyclic madangamine core with exquisite selectivity and introduces a new method for the construction of stereogenic quaternary carbon centres from β,β'-dialkyl-substituted nitroolefins. These results demonstrate the utility of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reactions in the synthesis of high-value saturated molecular scaffolds and highlight their potential for the rapid and atom-economical generation of stereochemical complexity in target molecule synthesis.

Research Context
The madangamine family is isolated from marine sea sponges of the Xestospongia genus. The family is characterized by an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system possessing two nitrogen atoms. Three rings constitute a diazatricyclic core (ABC rings) common to all family members. The macrocyclic E ring is common to all family members except madangamine F. The D ring differs in each and every madangamine. Natural products are forecast to play a prominent role in the future of medicinal chemistry. Efficient routes enabling rapid generation of complexity are of high importance. Numerous reported strategies exist for polycyclic core fragments of the madangamines. Only two total syntheses and a single formal synthesis of madangamine A exist.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors envisioned developing highly enantio- and diastereoselective organocatalytic desymmetrization reactions for natural product synthesis. The AC bicyclic motif was recognized as well-suited to construction from a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction. The rigid scaffold would allow remaining structural features to be elaborated with high stereochemical fidelity. The authors hypothesized that all stereochemical information could be installed from a single chirality-inducing desymmetrization step. The key disconnection relied on a desymmetrization of prochiral cyclohexanone 6 to access ketone 5 in isomerically pure form. The authors predicted that Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst would provide an efficient reaction profile for the challenging nitroolefin. The authors hypothesized that the reaction would proceed via a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism with hydrogen bonding. The authors predicted that the enantio-determining step would be irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining. The authors hypothesized that the kinetically preferred transition structure would be stabilized by hydrogen bonding interactions.

Methodological Details
The study reports a 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E. The target is madangamine E (1), a member of the madangamine natural product family. The model substrate was methyl-substituted nitroolefin 7, constructed in 3 steps from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal. An oxidative radical nitration was employed to construct nitroolefin 7 in 3 steps. A range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts was investigated. Catalysts included trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds. Reactions were run in dichloromethane at 20 mol% loading with benzoic acid as a co-catalyst. Most tested catalysts (9a-9d, 9g-9k) did not provide cyclised product 8 but gave complex product mixtures. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f gave the desired bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. The stereochemical configuration of 8 was established by single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. A simplified bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e yielded 8 in 51% yield as a single diastereoisomer in 96% ee. DFT calculations were used to investigate the intramolecular Michael addition of nitroolefin 7. A conformational search identified 16 possible transition structures for the key C-C bond forming step. The starting material 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal (10) was used to access nitroolefin 17. Tosylation of the reductive amination product gave tosyl amide 11. Oxidative cleavage, Henry reaction, and dehydration gave β-substituted nitroolefin 13 in 72% yield over 3 steps. The butenyl chain was installed by Michael addition of an organo-zinc-copper complex (Denmark) in 90% yield. The organo-zinc-copper Michael addition proved highly scalable at 17 g scale. Selenoxide elimination chemistry installed the nitroolefin in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z = 3.8:1. The selenoxide elimination efficiency depended strongly on the solvent mixture, with Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1, 0.033M) optimal. Treatment of 17E with 20 mol% catalyst 9f and 20 mol% benzoic acid gave bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield. The desymmetrization of 17E gave near-perfect enantio- and diastereoselectivity (>99% ee, single diastereomer, >5g scale). The stereochemical configuration of 18 was determined through single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis of the oxidised enone S10. The ketone 20 was elaborated by adapting Garg's three-step strategy developed in the synthesis of the akuammiline natural products. Nicolaou's IBX-NMO-mediated oxidation proved optimal for dehydrogenation of ketone 20 to afford enone 21. Epoxidation of 21 with hydrogen peroxide and aqueous NaOH in MeOH introduced oxygenation at C3 in high yield. The Wittig homologation using (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS gave aldehyde 23 in 86% yield with rigorous quench. Sequential reduction and partial amine deprotection gave diol 24 in 77% yield over 2 steps. Reductive amination with oct-7-en-1-al provided aminodiol 4 in 79% yield over 2 steps. The B ring was constructed by oxidative lactamization using Iwabuchi's oxidation conditions with AZADO, copper chloride, 2,2'-bipyridine, and DMAP. The oxidative lactamization afforded the tricyclic enone 25 in good yield. The D ring was closed by RCM with Grubbs 1st generation catalyst in CH2Cl2 at 40 ºC to give tetracyclic enone 26 in 82% yield. Treatment of 26 with palladium on carbon under a ~1 bar hydrogen atmosphere gave saturated ketone 3. Ketone 3 reacted with non-basic, yet highly nucleophilic organocerium reagents in high yield. Ishihara's triorganozincate reagents afforded tertiary alcohol 27 in high yields (70-78%) in a highly reproducible manner. The tosyl protecting group was exchanged for a hexenoate side chain in good yield to afford RCM precursor S8. Early elimination of tertiary alcohol 27 gave the Z-configured skipped diene 28 in 90% yield with 4.3:1 Z-selectivity. RCM precursor 29 was treated with Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with co-catalytic p-benzoquinone to afford diamide 30 in 71% yield. A final double amide reduction using excess LiAlH4 in Et2O afforded synthetic madangamine E (1) in 72% yield. All analytical data were consistent with that reported by Chida and Sato and by the isolation team of Andersen. Detailed synthetic procedures and computational methods are provided in the Supporting Information.

The key reaction is a desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. The key stereoselectivity-determining step is the C-C bond forming intramolecular Michael addition. TS1 amounts to a computed 99% ee in excellent agreement with the experimental enantioselectivity (99% ee). The Michael addition is highly exergonic (ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹) and furnishes an iminium-nitronate species Int4. The C-C bond formation through TS1 is irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining. TS1 is stabilized because it adopts a conformation that benefits from several hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The mechanism is consistent with a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism. The difference in mechanism between nitroolefin and ester is the result of the pKa difference between the nitronate and enolate. The formation of dihydrooxazine oxide intermediate IV was studied but this pathway is unfavorable with a higher energy barrier than TS2. The cyclobutane intermediate V can be formed from Int4 but is energetically unstable and can easily reopen with a low energy barrier. All analytical data were consistent with that reported by Chida and Sato and by the isolation team of Andersen. The attempted application of Amat's Wittig reaction was unsuccessful, indicating that the strategy is not universally applicable. All attempts to form the macrocyclic E ring via RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation. The results demonstrate the utility of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reactions in the synthesis of high-value saturated molecular scaffolds. The results highlight their potential for the rapid and atom-economical generation of stereochemical complexity in target molecule synthesis. The transformation introduces a new method for the construction of stereogenic quaternary carbon centres from β,β'-dialkyl-substituted nitroolefins.
The DFT calculations rationalize the origins of enantioselectivity in the desymmetrization reaction. TS1 emerged as the most energetically favorable transition structure by ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ compared to the second-lowest-energy transition structure. TS1 amounts to a computed 99% ee in excellent agreement with the experimental enantioselectivity (99% ee). The kinetically preferred TS is stabilized because it adopts a conformation that benefits from several hydrogen bonding interactions. The mechanism is consistent with a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism. The formation of dihydrooxazine oxide intermediate IV was studied but this pathway is unfavorable with a higher energy barrier than TS2. The cyclobutane intermediate V can be formed from Int4 but is energetically unstable and can easily reopen with a low energy barrier. The C-C bond formation through TS1 is irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining. The difference in mechanism between nitroolefin and ester is the result of the pKa difference between the nitronate and enolate. The spatial organisation of reacting alkenes should guide future macrocyclization campaigns employing this strategy.

Data And Code Availability
Detailed synthetic procedures and computational methods are provided in the Supporting Information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The desymmetrization of 17E gave near-perfect enantio- and diastereoselectivity (>99% ee, single diastereomer, >5g scale). The tertiary alcohol 27 could be afforded in high yields (70-78%) in a highly reproducible manner. The attempted application of Amat's Wittig reaction was unsuccessful, indicating that the strategy is not universally applicable. The formation of dihydrooxazine oxide intermediate IV was studied but this pathway is unfavorable with a higher energy barrier than TS2. The cyclobutane intermediate V can be formed from Int4 but is energetically unstable and can easily reopen with a low energy barrier.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system of the madangamine family. Figure 1B shows the two total syntheses and a single formal synthesis of madangamine A. Figure 1C shows the retrosynthetic analysis of the pentacyclic skeleton. Figure 2A shows the enantioselective desymmetrising intramolecular Michael addition to α,β-unsaturated esters. Figure 2B shows the catalytic cycle summarized in the study. Figure 2C shows the DFT-computed reaction pathway. Figure 3 shows the DFT-computed transition structures. Figure 4A shows the restructured route to access nitroolefin 17. Figure 4B shows the key organocatalytic enantioselective desymmetrization.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the new catalytic, highly enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. 2. The strongest evidence is the near-perfect enantio- and diastereoselectivity (>99% ee, single diastereomer, >5g scale) of the desymmetrization of 17E, corroborated by DFT (computed 99% ee). 3. The future path is guided by the profound effect that the spatial organisation of reacting alkenes had on the outcome of the RCM reaction, which should guide future macrocyclization campaigns.

summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from high-throughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler
summary.field_subfield: Catalysis / Materials informatics (heterogeneous catalysis)
summary.executive_summary: Heterogeneous catalyst design is difficult because the number of good catalysts is very small relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials, and because the full catalytic progression cannot be explicitly modelled by first-principles methods. The authors address this gap by applying the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical data set for the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. Using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 three-component catalyst compositions were synthesized and tested across temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC. The reactivity measured by HTE (yield of oxygenates) was used as the target, while temperature and ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom properties were offered as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD analysis identified temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity as the key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenates acrolein and acrylic acid. The resulting SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes associated with high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements. Applying the rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts, including a five-component material (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium and tantalum) achieving an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC, which is more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. These results demonstrate the potential of the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to identify generalizable, interpretable rules describing exceptional catalytic performance and to hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.

claims.description: The SGD approach can identify interpretable, chemically meaningful rules associated with exceptional catalytic performance.
The SG rules can guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Heterogeneous catalyst design is difficult because the number of good catalysts is very small relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials, and because the full catalytic progression cannot be explicitly modelled by first-principles methods. The authors address this gap by applying the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical data set for the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. Using high-throughput experimentation (HTE), 120 three-component catalyst compositions were synthesized and tested across temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC. The reactivity measured by HTE (yield of oxygenates) was used as the target, while temperature and ten composition-dependent physicochemical parameters derived from density-functional-theory (DFT) free-atom properties were offered as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD analysis identified temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity as the key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenates acrolein and acrylic acid. The resulting SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes associated with high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements. Applying the rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts, including a five-component material (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus, tellurium and tantalum) achieving an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC, which is more than twice as large as any observation in the training data set. These results demonstrate the potential of the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to identify generalizable, interpretable rules describing exceptional catalytic performance and to hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis involves complex surface reaction networks and dynamic restructuring. First-principles modelling of the full catalytic progression is impractical. High-throughput experimentation tests many materials but cannot decide the next promising ones. Good catalysts are rare relative to the practically infinite number of possible materials. Detailed characterization of each tested material is typically not feasible. Catalytic mechanisms vary with materials and conditions, causing unbalanced performance distributions. Global models minimize average prediction error and may miss the most interesting materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks how to identify key physicochemical parameters and constraints associated with high performance. The central hypothesis is that the SGD local approach can identify rules associated with high performance. The authors predict that temperature, phosphorus content and electronegativity are key parameters. The authors predict that the SG rules can guide the design of more complex catalysts. The authors predict that the SG rules can hint at materials more performant than those in training.

Methodological Details
The study investigated selective partial oxidation of light alkanes to value-added products. The reaction system studied propylene selective oxidation on SiO2-supported catalysts. The catalysts were three-component compositions containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. The catalysts were prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support. Several reaction temperatures between 200 and 400 ºC were examined at each composition. Reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors. The reaction feed included Ar, H2O, N2, O2 and propylene at specified molar rates. The same mass of catalyst was used so that contact time was kept fixed. The target was the yield of oxygenates, defined as acrolein plus acrylic acid over propylene fed. Eleven descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis. The candidate parameters were derived from DFT-PBEsol and FHI-aims calculations. The per-element free-atom properties were converted into system-specific properties by composition-weighted averaging. The oxygen content was not included because it is not known from the formulation. The target distribution was highly skewed, with most observations being low performance. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set was 4.83%. Only 41 measurements out of 1220 had oxygenate yields above 20%. The maximum oxygenates yield value was 26.85%. The selected SG contained only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. The average yield of oxygenates in the selected SG was 24.15%.

Procedures And Architectures
The SGD approach starts with the generation of a pool of propositions. For continuous parameters, the propositions are inequalities constraining their values. SGD identifies selectors formed by propositions connected with the AND connector. The selectors select subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of the target values. The approach maximizes a quality function measuring how outstanding specific subselections are. The quality function includes a coverage term controlling the subgroup size. The quality function includes the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence. The divergence favors subgroups with unusual target values compared to the majority. The divergence favors distributions contained in narrower value ranges. The key parameters were temperature, phosphorus content and composition-weighted electronegativity. The temperature rule highlighted intermediate temperatures within the tested range. The phosphorus rule showed that a relatively high phosphorus content is needed. The electronegativity rule limited the range of Ru contents. Ru is needed for propylene conversion but too much leads to combustion products. The rules were validated with a cross-validation study using 90% of the data. The rules were validated by excluding data points with oxygenate yields lower than 3%. Four-component materials were designed by fixing phosphorus content to 0.60 and Ru content to 0.05. The VÇ elements considered were niobium, tantalum, chromium, molybdenum, tin, antimony and tellurium. The VÇ elements had atomic radii of 1.40 to 1.45 Å. The atomic radius of tungsten is 1.45 Å. The VÇ elements were constrained to have a maximum atomic radius difference of 0.10 Å. The five-component materials fixed VÇ as tellurium and evaluated V^ as molybdenum, niobium, tantalum and antimony. The four-and five-component HTE data contained 746 data points. The selected SG for the four-and five-component data had a cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence of 0.355. The selected SG contained 18 data points, approximately 2.4% of the data set. The rules for the four-and five-component data constrained temperature, electron affinity and electron affinity. The electronegativity and electron affinity are related by VY = V^ + V^.

Key Results
The selected SG had the highest cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence of 0.693. The selected SG contained only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. The average yield of oxygenates in the selected SG was 24.15%. The average yield in the SG was five times higher than the average on the whole data set. The SG was described by rules on three descriptive parameters. The temperature rule constrained the temperature to 280 to 300 ºC. The phosphorus rule required a phosphorus content higher than 0.55. The electronegativity rule constrained the value to 3.910 to 4.002 eV. The ranges of variation of the minimum and maximum thresholds were 3.882 to 3.910 eV and 3.989 to 4.031. The SG rules were not strongly affected by variations on the data used for their derivation. The highest yield of oxygenates achieved for each four-component composition is shown by the colors. The catalyst achieving the highest yield of oxygenates was 60.19% at 400 ºC. The highest-yield catalyst contained 0.35 molar fraction of tellurium as VÇ element. The VY value for the highest-yield five-component catalyst was 3.947 eV. The five-component catalyst achieved an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC. The five-component catalyst contained tantalum as V^ element. The oxygenate yields for the four-and five-component catalysts were up to twice as large as those obtained with three-component materials. The highest three-component yield was 26.85%. The four-and five-component catalysts achieved the highest yields at higher temperatures than the three-component systems. The SG rule on the reaction temperature derived from the three-component data is not transferable to the four-component ones. The SG rules correctly describe the experimental trend for the four-component materials. The materials based on niobium, chromium, molybdenum, tin, lead and antimony achieve the highest oxygenate yields at relative lower contents. The agreement between the SG rule and the measured oxygenate yield is reasonable despite higher complexity. The identified four-and five-component catalysts are significantly more complex than the training data set. The SG rules hinted at materials significantly more performant than any observation used in training.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The SG rules reflect the specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance. The approach identifies a local behavior associated with exceptional performance. The local modelling approach is suitable for the search of exceptional materials. The structures and functions of exceptional materials are hardly modelled explicitly by theory. The composition-weighted electronegativity, phosphorus content and temperature are key parameters. The SG rules rationalize a local reactivity pattern associated with exceptional catalytic performance. The SG rules guide the design of more complex catalysts. The five-component material is captured by the SG rules. The SG rules can identify generalizable rules describing exceptional performance. The SG rules can hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training.

Contradictions And Limitations
The SG rules might not identify exceptional materials for arbitrary ruthenium content. The SG rules might not identify exceptional materials for VÇ and V^ elements with significantly different radii. Different mechanisms may operate on these materials which could also lead to exceptional performance. The SGD analysis might need to be performed including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space. The SG rule on the reaction temperature is not transferable to the four-component materials. The analysis was focused on low ruthenium contents and on elements compatible with tungsten. The atomic structures of all the tested catalysts are not known in detail. The oxygen content is not included in the material's characterization. The detailed preparation, characterization and reactivity analysis of the catalysts is discussed in a separate contribution. The study only provides details on the propylene selective oxidation reaction. The SG rules are expected to describe outstanding materials whose performance is governed by the same processes.

Claims
The SGD approach can identify interpretable, chemically meaningful rules associated with exceptional catalytic performance. The SG rules were described by rules on three descriptive parameters. The SG rules correctly describe the experimental trend for the four-component materials. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data used for their derivation. The SG rules reflect the specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance. The SG rule on the reaction temperature is not transferable to the four-component materials. It is unclear if the SG rules can identify exceptional materials for arbitrary ruthenium content. The SG rules guide the design of more complex catalysts. The SG rules can hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training. The local modelling approach is suitable for the search of exceptional materials.
The SG rules can guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements. The five-component material is captured by the SG rules. The highest-yield five-component catalyst achieved an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC. The oxygenate yields for the four-and five-component catalysts were up to twice as large as those obtained with three-component materials. The agreement between the SG rule and the measured oxygenate yield is reasonable despite higher complexity. The SG rule on the reaction temperature is not transferable to the four-component materials. The analysis was focused on low ruthenium contents and on elements compatible with tungsten. The SG rules can hint at materials significantly more performant than those used in training. The SG rules demonstrate the potential of the SGD-HTE-&theory approach to identify generalizable rules. The SGD analysis might need to be performed including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and values for the elemental properties used in the work are available in the electronic supporting information. Further SGD details are available in the electronic supporting information. The detailed preparation, characterization and reactivity analysis of the catalysts is discussed in a separate contribution. The detailed description of the approach and of the Jensen-Shanon divergence are available in the electronic supporting information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar SG rules are obtained when the training is performed with randomly-selected 90% of the data points. Similar SG rules are obtained when the data points presenting yield of oxygenates lower than 3% are excluded from training. The SG rules constraining the VY parameter to an intermediate range are always observed when only 90% of the data is used for training. The ranges of variation of the minimum and maximum thresholds were 3.882 to 3.910 eV and 3.989 to 4.031. The ranges of variation of the thresholds are similar to the thresholds shown in Fig. 2F. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data used for their derivation.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1A shows the SGD approach selecting subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of the target values. Fig. 1B shows the materials based on ruthenium combined with tungsten and phosphorus. Fig. 1C shows the most interesting compositions displaying both considerable activity and selectivity. Fig. 2A and B show the propylene conversion vs. oxygenates selectivity profiles and the distribution of yield of oxygenates. Fig. 2C shows the SG described by rules on three descriptive parameters. Fig. 2D shows the rule on the phosphorus content. Fig. 2F shows the rule on the composition-averaged electronegativity. Fig. 3B shows the ternary diagram of the composition-averaged electronegativity. Fig. 4A shows the catalyst map of the composition-averaged electronegativity for the selected VÇ. Fig. 4C and D show the oxygenate yields for the four-and five-component materials. Fig. 5A and B show the distribution of the yield of oxygenates in the four-and five-component data set. Fig. 5C shows the rules describing the SG for the four-and five-component data. Fig. 5D, E and F show the rules constraining the values of temperature, electron affinity and electron affinity. Fig. S3 shows the SGs providing near-optimal quality-function values. Fig. S4 shows the temperatures at which the four-and five-component materials achieve the highest yields. Fig. S5A shows that Ru is needed to achieve propylene conversion. Fig. S5B shows that too much Ru leads to undesired combustion products.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the application of the SGD approach to identify interpretable rules associated with exceptional catalytic performance. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of a five-component catalyst achieving an oxygenate yield of 59.60% at 400 ºC. 3. The future path is to perform the SGD analysis including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space.

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang, Jiawen Zhou, Yiheng Zhang, Weiya Zhu, Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Organic photothermal materials / radical chemistry / solar-driven water evaporation
summary.executive_summary: Open-shell organic radicals are usually unstable in air because of unsatisfied valency, which has limited their use as photothermal materials. This work introduces aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs), a class of neutral conjugated nitrogen-oxide radicals that lack steric hindrance protecting groups yet remain thermodynamically and kinetically stable in air. The authors prepared a series of star-shaped ANARs by demethylating phenolic hydroxyl precursors followed by air oxidation, yielding four compounds: TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8. Characterization by cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, photoluminescence quantum yield measurements, electron spin resonance, and IR thermography established that these radicals are electrochemically reversible, highly air-stable, and possess high spin concentration. The central finding is that high spin concentration drives strongly enhanced nonradiative decay and suppressed radiative decay, which translates into excellent photothermal conversion. The best performer, TPA-TPA-O6, shows broadband absorption extending to 2000 nm, rapid temperature rise under an 808 nm laser, and outstanding stability over ten on/off cycles. In an interfacial solar evaporation system based on polyurethane foam loaded with TPA-TPA-O6, the material achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun, among the top values for pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The material also demonstrated negligible photobleaching and effective seawater desalination. The study positions stable high-spin radicals as a promising, low-cost, and reproducible strategy for solar energy conversion and identifies future directions in organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

claims.description: Aromatic nitric acid radicals are air-stable open-shell radicals suitable for photothermal conversion.
High spin concentration enhances nonradiative decay and photothermal conversion efficiency.
TPA-TPA-O6 achieves top-tier solar-driven water evaporation among pure organic materials.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
