The material also demonstrated negligible photobleaching and effective seawater desalination. The study positions stable high-spin radicals as a promising, low-cost, and reproducible strategy for solar energy conversion and identifies future directions in organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

Research Context
Open-shell radicals are usually unstable in air due to unsatisfied valency. Radicals have potential applications across many functional fields. Organic small molecules are underexplored relative to inorganic and polymeric photothermal materials. Inorganic photothermal materials raise health and environmental concerns. Conjugated polymers suffer from reproducibility and stability problems. Stable neutral radicals are rarely reported and are hard to prepare. Photothermal materials convert NIR light into heat via nonradiative decay.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can air-stable open-shell radicals serve as efficient photothermal materials? Do steric hindrance groups protect radicals, or can unprotected radicals be stable? Does high spin concentration enhance nonradiative decay and photothermal conversion? Will TPA-TPA-O6 outperform other ANARs in photothermal and evaporation performance? Can these radicals achieve top-tier solar evaporation among pure organic materials?

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized. Materials were made by demethylation and air oxidation of phenolic precursors. Different cores were introduced to vary electronic properties. Precursors were methoxy-substituted phenols. Cyclic voltammetry used specific electrolyte and conditions. Radicals were coated on carbon-glass electrodes to form films. Potentials were referenced to SCE with ferrocene internal standard. HOMO and LUMO levels were derived from CV curves. ESR used a fixed sample amount to compare spin concentration. PLQY was measured in solution and film. Photothermal tests used an 808 nm laser at 0.8 W cm⁻². Temperature was monitored with an IR thermal camera. Evaporation used PU foam loaded by impregnation and drying. The evaporation foam had a 2.0 cm diameter with 30 mg loading. Seawater desalination tested four primary ions. Detailed synthetic schemes are in the supporting information.

Procedures And Architectures

summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro, Jean Truer, Espíndola Rodríguez, Jens Wenzel
summary.field_subfield: Organic photovoltaics / materials engineering
summary.executive_summary: This pre-print reports the first open-air, roll-to-roll-compatible fabrication of flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the high-efficiency PM6:Y6 non-fullerene blend using slot-die coating and a green solvent. The central motivation is to narrow the "lab-to-fab gap" that separates record lab-scale efficiencies from industrially scalable manufacturing. Spin-coating, the dominant lab technique, is criticized for poor upscaling potential and substantial material waste, whereas slot-die coating is preferred because it enables one-dimensional stripe patterning with almost no material waste and is compatible with roll-to-roll production. The authors coat the PM6:Y6 active layer using o-xylene (O-XY), a green solvent with ≥ 98% purity, without additives, and heat the substrate, syringe, tube, and slot-die head to keep the temperature-dependent-aggregating (TDA) PM6 liquid during coating. The optimal coating temperature is identified as 100 °C, where power conversion efficiency (PCE) saturates and bimolecular recombination is minimized (S = 0.978). Ternary devices with PC61BM and fully printed devices are also fabricated, achieving average PCEs of 6.6% and 6.7% respectively, with a champion efficiency of 7.2% for the ternary device. The study demonstrates that a small amount of fullerene acceptor enhances exciton dissociation (93.7% binary vs. 96.3% and 95.7% for ternary blends) and charge collection (69.6% binary vs. 77.7% and 73.2% for ternary blends). Devices are fabricated on pre-patterned ITO-coated PET substrates with an inverted ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag geometry, with active areas of approximately 0.8 cm². Remarkably, the devices exhibit exceptional stability, retaining 99.4% of their initial PCE after 1050 hours of dark storage for the ternary device and more than 97% for binary devices after more than 1500 hours. The authors argue that these results pave the way for upscaling OSC production based on the PM6:Y6 system, bringing the technology closer to commercialization. The study is notable for its environmental focus, using a green solvent without additives, and its demonstration of the feasibility of slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open air. The results are supported by comprehensive characterization, including J-V curves, external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements, absorbance spectra, and light intensity dependence studies to probe recombination mechanisms. The paper concludes that matching the flexible substrate temperature with the hot slot-die head at 100 °C maximizes PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination, and that the optimal active layer thickness is around 200 nm. The authors acknowledge that the devices are not prepared in a cleanroom or inside a glovebox, which explains the high degree of trap-assisted recombination observed under open-circuit conditions. This limitation is important because it suggests that further efficiency improvements may be possible under more controlled conditions. Overall, the study makes a significant contribution to the field of scalable organic photovoltaics by demonstrating that high-efficiency PM6:Y6 devices can be fabricated using environmentally friendly and roll-processed methods, with excellent stability that could be attractive for commercial applications.

Research Context
Organic solar cells (OSCs) have reached high efficiencies using non-fullerene acceptors that allow fine-tuning of energy levels and light absorption. OSCs offer low cost, mechanical flexibility, lightweight properties, semi-transparency, and very short Energy Payback Time (EPBT). A large efficiency gap remains between lab-scale devices and those produced using industry-compatible processes. Slot-die coating is preferred for scalable fabrication due to one-dimensional patterning and minimal material waste. The PM6:Y6 material combination has shown excellent efficiencies over 15% on rigid substrates using green solvents. There is a need to transfer PM6:Y6 devices to roll-processing on flexible substrates using scalable fabrication techniques. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) behavior, requiring heating to remain liquid during coating.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can high-efficiency PM6:Y6 OSCs be fabricated using slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open air with a green solvent? What is the optimal coating temperature for maximizing PCE while minimizing recombination? How does active layer thickness affect device performance and stability? Can adding a small amount of fullerene acceptor improve PCE and stability in open-air flexible devices? Will slot-die coated flexible devices exhibit good stability under dark storage? The authors hypothesize that coating at 100 °C will maximize PCE due to reduced bimolecular recombination. The authors predict that the optimal active layer thickness is around 200 nm for high performance. The authors expect that adding PC61BM will enhance exciton dissociation and charge collection.

Methodological Details
The study used PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) purchased from 1-Material Inc. PB61BM (batch M111) was purchased from Ossila for use as a fullerene acceptor. ZnO nanoparticle ink was from Sigma-Aldrich and MoO3 pellets from Kurt J. Lesker Co. The flexible substrate was pre-patterned ITO-coated PET purchased from FOM Technologies. Pure silver was bought from Sigma-Aldrich for back electrode evaporation. Silver paste for flexographic printing was a heat-curing paste (DuPont 5025). The solvent used was O-XY with ≥ 98% purity purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Materials were purchased and used directly without purification. The device used an inverted geometry of ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. The ZnO ETL was coated at 75 °C with a 0.06 mL/min flow rate and 1.08 m/min drum speed. The ZnO ETL was annealed in an oven at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The AL PM6:Y6 was coated at a 1:1 ratio with concentrations from 12 to 28 mg/mL. The AL was coated at temperatures of 60, 80, 100, and 120 °C. The drum speed was kept at 1.5 m/min with a 0.12 mL/min flow rate. 10 nm of MoO3 and 150 nm of Ag were thermally evaporated under vacuum. Evaporation was performed at a base pressure of 2 x 10^-5 mbar through a shadow mask. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation from a one-meter-long AL. At least 8 devices were encapsulated with an active area of approximately 0.8 cm². The devices had an approximate active area of 0.8 cm². An activation process applied a reverse bias current of -5 V with a maximum current of 100 mA. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue EPXR made of bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and Chissonox 221 monomers. Curing was made under UV light for approximately 5 min reaching 66 ± 0.5 °C. J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter with a 50 mV step. The solar simulator was calibrated to 1000 W/m² with a monocrystalline silicon reference cell. Four different AL thicknesses were investigated to study the effect on efficiency. The absorption peaks of both materials were distinguished with donor maximum at ~625 nm. The JSC reached its maximum at 154 nm of AL thickness (17.3 mA/cm²). The FF improved from 42.0% for the thinnest AL to 47.1% for 116 nm AL. The ternary blend started with a [1:1:0.2] ratio. summary.title: Dense-TSNet: Dense Connected Two-Stage Structure for Ultra-Lightweight Speech Enhancement
summary.authors: Zizhen Lin, Yuanle Li, Junyu Wang, Ruili Li
summary.field_subfield: Speech Enhancement / Signal Processing
summary.executive_summary: Dense-TSNet is an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed for resource-constrained edge devices such as smartphones and cameras. The authors observe that recent deep neural network methods, including Transformer and Mamba architectures, suffer from high complexity and deployment challenges, while narrow lightweight models often face uneven loss landscapes that cause early convergence limitations. To address these issues, the paper proposes a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces dilated convolutions with Two-Stage modules, ensuring smoother loss landscapes and more robust refinement of the objective function in later training stages. The network also introduces the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB), which captures global, channel, and local feature perspectives entirely through CNNs for ease of deployment. A key contribution is the exploration of loss functions, where the authors demonstrate that relying on Metric Loss to improve objective perceptual metrics can negatively impact subjective perception, leading them to propose a Consistency Magnitude Loss instead. The model achieves a compact size of approximately 14K parameters, making it the first speech enhancement model to reach around 10k parameters. Evaluated on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, Dense-TSNet achieves a PESQ score of 3.05, outperforming the classic Two-Stage baseline of 2.96 while maintaining comparable parameter counts. The paper emphasizes that the Dense-TS structure enables better late-stage performance despite faster early convergence of the baseline, and the MVGB components (LKE, CA, LSG) each contribute meaningfully to overall performance. The authors note that source codes will be released after paper acceptance, and audio samples are available on GitHub. This work represents a substantial advancement for applications in resource-constrained environments, with future directions focused on further model compression.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Dense-TSNet is an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed for resource-constrained edge devices such as smartphones and cameras. The authors observe that recent deep neural network methods, including Transformer and Mamba architectures, suffer from high complexity and deployment challenges, while narrow lightweight models often face uneven loss landscapes that cause early convergence limitations. To address these issues, the paper proposes a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces dilated convolutions with Two-Stage modules, ensuring smoother loss landscapes and more robust refinement of the objective function in later training stages. The network also introduces the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB), which captures global, channel, and local feature perspectives entirely through CNNs for ease of deployment. A key contribution is the exploration of loss functions, where the authors demonstrate that relying on Metric Loss to improve objective perceptual metrics can negatively impact subjective perception, leading them to propose a Consistency Magnitude Loss instead. The model achieves a compact size of approximately 14K parameters, making it the first speech enhancement model to reach around 10k parameters. Evaluated on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, Dense-TSNet achieves a PESQ score of 3.05, outperforming the classic Two-Stage baseline of 2.96 while maintaining comparable parameter counts. The paper emphasizes that the Dense-TS structure enables better late-stage performance despite faster early convergence of the baseline, and the MVGB components (LKE, CA, LSG) each contribute meaningfully to overall performance. The authors note that source codes will be released after paper acceptance, and audio samples are available on GitHub. This work represents a substantial advancement for applications in resource-constrained environments, with future directions focused on further model compression.

Research Context
The background motivation is that speech enhancement aims to improve speech quality and intelligibility in noisy environments. Recent research has concentrated on deep neural networks, particularly the Two-Stage architecture for feature extraction. The complexity and size of these models remain significant, which limits their applicability in resource-constrained scenarios. Designing models suitable for edge devices presents challenges, as narrow lightweight models often encounter performance bottlenecks due to uneven loss landscapes. Advanced operators such as Transformers or Mamba may lack the practical adaptability and efficiency that CNNs offer in real-world deployments. Research on single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10k parameters is still limited, underscoring a gap in the field. The prior Two-Stage architecture performs well with a channel count of 64 but faces limitations for ultra-lightweight networks with fewer channels.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question concerns whether a Dense Two-Stage architecture can address loss landscape smoothness in narrow lightweight models. The hypothesis is that replacing dilated convolutions with Two-Stage modules will yield a network composed entirely of densely connected Two-Stage modules. It is hypothesized that the Dense-TS structure provides a smoother loss landscape, enabling better late-stage performance despite faster early convergence. The Multi-View Gaze Block is hypothesized to enhance feature extraction by capturing global, channel, and local views entirely based on CNNs. The choice of loss function is hypothesized to impact perceptual quality, with Consistency Magnitude Loss preferred over Metric Loss. The Dense-TSNet is hypothesized to achieve a model size of only 14K parameters, the first to reach approximately 10k parameters. The predicted outcome is that Dense-TSNet will achieve competitive performance with extremely low parameters on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset.

Methodological Details
The dataset used is VoiceBank+DEMAND, known for its high-fidelity utterances. Speech samples were segmented into two-second intervals for the short-time Fourier transform. An FFT size of 400, a window length of 400, and a hop length of 100 were employed. The training process was conducted with a batch size of 2. The AdamW optimizer was used for the training process. Training was carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps. The Dense-TS framework used a 4-channel version, while the classic Two-Stage used a 6-channel version. The Dense-TSNet model has a parameter count of 14K and MACs of 356M. The classic TS baseline has a parameter count of 14K and MACs of 388M. Evaluation metrics include PESQ (range -0.5 to 4.5) and MOS-based metrics (CSIG, CBAK, COVL) with a range of 1 to 5. The LKE sub-module is composed of pointwise convolutions, Simple Gate, large kernel depthwise convolutions, Instance Norm, HardSwish, and pointwise convolutions. The CA sub-module reallocates weights to each channel to focus on important channels while suppressing less significant ones. The LSG sub-module consists of depth-wise convolution, point-wise convolution, and Learnable-Sigmoid activation function. The Consistency Magnitude Loss is defined as the expected L2 distance between the magnitude spectrum of twice-STFTed speech and the clean speech magnitude spectrum. The Metric Loss integrates objective evaluation metrics via a discriminator using the PESQ metric. The Generator Loss assigns weights λ1 and λ2 to the two losses, with λ2 set to 0 by default. The ablation study tested Dense-TSNet without LKE, CA, LSG, and Consistency Loss. The P value is defined as the ratio of λ2 to λ1, where λ1 is the loss weight for LMagConsis. The comparison included TSTNN, PHASEN, MANNER-S-5.3GF, CCFNet(Lite), and DeepFilterNet. The source codes will be released after paper acceptance. Audio samples can be found at the provided GitHub repository.

Procedures And Architectures
The speech signal is processed using Short-Time Fourier Transform to convert it into the time-frequency domain. The magnitude and phase spectra are derived from the complex spectrum. Dense-TSNet inputs only the magnitude spectrum and performs time-frequency feature extraction through the Dense-TS structure with the TS-MVGB. The Dense-TS structure replaces dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules. Features are mapped to a high-dimensional space using 1×1 convolutions. The number of input channels to the i-th Two-Stage layer is Ci = dense channel × (i + 1). The number of output channels from the i-th adjust convolutional layer is Cout = dense channel. The output of each TS-MVGB is a serial connection of time-MVGB and freq-MVGB. The final output of the Dense-TS is 0.2 times skipdepth−1 plus x. After each Two-Stage module, a convolutional layer as Adjust-Conv is used to adjust the channel count. Features undergo L-Sigmoid activation and 1×1 convolution to decode the magnitude spectrum mask. The magnitude spectrum mask is then multiplied by the noisy magnitude spectrum to produce the network's output. The MVGB consists of three sub-modules: Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA). The LKE establishes a global perspective, drawing inspiration from the CNN component of Conformer. The CA reallocates weights to each channel to focus on important channels while suppressing less significant ones. The LSG establishes local spatial perspectives and focuses on modeling local information within the feature map. The Multi-view Gazed features are generated by multiplying the channel weights and spatial weights obtained from the two branches. The loss function focuses on aspects more crucial to perceptual quality, minimizing the distance between the estimated magnitude spectrum and the clean magnitude spectrum. The Consistency Magnitude Loss computes the minimum distance between the magnitude spectrum of the twice-STFTed speech and the clean speech magnitude spectrum. The Metric Loss is computed using the PESQ metric via a discriminator. The Generator Loss combines the two losses with weights λ1 and λ2, with λ2 set to 0 by default. The training was conducted for up to 1,000,000 steps using the AdamW optimizer. The ablation study tested the effects of removing LKE, CA, LSG, and Consistency Loss. The loss function study defined P = λ2/λ1 to validate the effect of LMetric. The comparison with other methods included TSTNN, PHASEN, MANNER-S-5.3GF, CCFNet(Lite), and DeepFilterNet.

Key Results
Dense-TSNet achieves a PESQ score of 3.05, outperforming the classic Two-Stage baseline of 2.96. The CSIG score of Dense-TSNet is 4.51, compared to 4.45 for the classic TS baseline. The CBAK score of Dense-TSNet is 3.58, compared to 3.58 for the classic TS baseline. The COVL score of Dense-TSNet is 3.86, compared to 3.78 for the classic TS baseline. The Dense-TSNet has a parameter count of 14K, compared to 356M MACs. The classic TS baseline has a parameter count of 14K, compared to 388M MACs. The Dense-TSNet has MACs of 356M, compared to 388M for the classic TS baseline. The Dense-TS framework converges faster in the early stages but achieves better performance in the later stages. The smoother loss landscape provided by the dense connections enables better late-stage performance. Removing LKE reduces the PESQ score to 2.79, CSIG to 4.31, CBAK to 3.47, and COVL to 3.61. Removing CA reduces the PESQ score to 2.86, CSIG to 4.38, CBAK to 3.53, and COVL to 3.69. Removing LSG reduces the PESQ score to 2.97, CSIG to 4.46, CBAK to 3.57, and COVL to 3.79. Removing Consistency Loss reduces the PESQ score to 2.96, CSIG to 4.45, CBAK to 3.58, and COVL to 3.79. The SSNR of Dense-TSNet is 8.16. Using only Consistency Magnitude Loss yields a PESQ score of 3.05, error mag. of 0.022, error pha. of 2.56, and error com. of 0.13. Using P = 1 yields a PESQ score of 3.28, error mag. of 0.057, error pha. of 2.73, and error com. of 0.15. Using P = 400 yields a PESQ score of 3.04, error mag. of 0.800, error pha. of 3.95, and error com. of 0.41. Using only complex loss yields a PESQ score of 2.60, error mag. of 0.075, error pha. of 2.73, and error com. of 0.10. The PESQ score increases with P, but the distances between amplitude, phase, and the complex spectrum also increase. When P is too large (e.g., P = 400), training fails. A pseudohallucination distortion is introduced at P = 200, affecting the perceptual quality. The authors do not employ LMetric in Dense-TS. The Dense-TSNet has a parameter count of 14K, which is the first to achieve a speech enhancement model with approximately 10k parameters. The Dense-TSNet is well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained environments.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Dense-TS structure provides a smoother loss landscape, enabling better late-stage performance despite faster early convergence. The dense connections in the narrower model address the uneven loss landscapes that cause early convergence limitations. The Multi-View Gaze Block enhances feature extraction by capturing global, channel, and local views entirely based on CNNs. The LKE, CA, and LSG components each contribute meaningfully to overall performance, as shown by the ablation study.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that the source codes will be released after paper acceptance, indicating a delay in reproducibility. The audio samples are available on GitHub, but the exact repository URL is provided as https://github.com/huaidanquede/Dense-TSNet. The training was carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps, but the exact number of steps used is not specified. The comparison with other methods includes results not provided in the original paper, denoted by '-'. The paper does not report the exact number of channels used in the Dense-TS structure, only that the Dense-TS framework used a 4-channel version. The paper does not report the exact number of channels used in the classic Two-Stage structure, only that the classic Two-Stage used a 6-channel version. summary.title: Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction
summary.authors: Yu Chen, Marin Biloš, Sarthak Mittal, Wei Deng, Kashif Rasul, Anderson Schneider
summary.field_subfield: Machine Learning / Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a novel probabilistic time series forecasting framework that combines the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models, specifically stochastic interpolants (SI). The authors address challenges in modeling high-dimensional complex distributions and cross-feature dependencies that arise with autoregressive and transformer-based models. While these models are widely used in finance, biology, medicine, and other domains, they face scalability issues when applied to large-scale generative model-based predictions. The proposed method extends the theory of stochastic interpolants to a broader conditional generation framework with additional control features, enabling the model to encode long-term temporal dependencies via an RNN while using the generative model to guide future predictions. The framework is trained on tuple data consisting of future, current, and past time points, with importance sampling used to stabilize training. Experiments on synthetic datasets (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, 8 Gaussians) and real-world datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki) demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive or superior performance compared to baselines such as DDPM, SGM, FM, and Vec-LSTM. The evaluation uses metrics including CRPS-sum, NRMSE, and ND, with smaller values indicating better performance. The authors conclude that stochastic interpolants are a strong candidate for conditional generation, particularly for multivariate probabilistic forecasting. The paper also highlights the importance of carefully modeling the probability distribution for large-dimensional time series prediction. The code will be publicly available for the camera-ready version, though the exact availability is not yet confirmed. The study contributes to the growing field of generative modeling for time series forecasting by offering a computationally friendly and high-quality approach that advances the application of generative models in this dynamic domain.

Research Context
Autoregressive and transformer models are the go-to methods for time series forecasting. These models effectively capture short-term and long-term sequential dependencies. Probabilistic forecasting is achieved by incorporating parametric probabilistic models into the output layer. The probabilistic output layer is confined within a simple probability family due to parameterization constraints. Generative modeling via diffusion or flow-based models addresses complex distribution modeling. Recent works have applied diffusion models to probabilistic time series imputation and forecasting. Generative model predictors suffer from scalability issues due to dependence on window size. A computational-friendly framework is needed for large-scale generative model-based predictions. Starting generation from a distribution close to the data distribution alleviates learning challenges. Time series data exhibits strong correlations between neighboring time points.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether blending RNN efficiency with diffusion modeling improves probabilistic time series forecasting. The hypothesis is that stochastic interpolants can be extended to a conditional generation framework with extra control features. The hypothesis is that a conditional stochastic interpolants module is computational-friendly and achieves high-quality modeling. summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara, Takashi Kobayashi, Tetsuji Dohi, Takeshi Yoshimura, Norifumi Fujimura, Daisuke Kiriya
summary.field_subfield: 2D materials / optoelectronics (photoluminescence engineering of monolayer TMDCs)
summary.executive_summary: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) are attractive for optoelectronics because of their three-atom-thick crystals and direct band gaps, but their photoluminescence (PL) is weak. Existing chemical treatments (p-dopants, superacids, oleic acid, defect repair) work mainly for sulfur-based compounds and not universally. This paper introduces a universal postpreparation method: coating monolayer TMDCs with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, which has a large thermal expansion coefficient. During spin coating and subsequent drying, the paraffin induces spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the substrate, removing the substrate effect and dramatically enhancing PL. The method was applied to MoS 2 , WS 2 , MoSe 2 , and WSe 2 , achieving enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 50-, and 9-fold from the as-exfoliated flakes, respectively. In extreme cases, the monolayer deformed into a bundled shape. PL and Raman analyses support the mechanism: decreased carrier concentration, strain, and exciton-dominated emission. The authors argue the approach is universal across sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs and could enable transparent, flexible optoelectronic devices. This summary is grounded in the paper's abstract and introduction, which state the gap and the universal strategy.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) are attractive for optoelectronics because of their three-atom-thick crystals and direct band gaps, but their photoluminescence (PL) is weak. Existing chemical treatments (p-dopants, superacids, oleic acid, defect repair) work mainly for sulfur-based compounds and not universally. This paper introduces a universal postpreparation method: coating monolayer TMDCs with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, which has a large thermal expansion coefficient. During spin coating and subsequent drying, the paraffin induces spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the substrate, removing the substrate effect and dramatically enhancing PL. The method was applied to MoS 2 , WS 2 , MoSe 2 , and WSe 2 , achieving enhancement factors of 215-, 55-, 50-, and 9-fold from the as-exfoliated flakes, respectively. In extreme cases, the monolayer deformed into a bundled shape. PL and Raman analyses support the mechanism: decreased carrier concentration, strain, and exciton-dominated emission. The authors argue the approach is universal across sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs and could enable transparent, flexible optoelectronic devices. This summary is grounded in the paper's abstract and introduction, which state the gap and the universal strategy.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs are promising optoelectronic materials due to their thin crystals and direct band gaps. Monolayer TMDCs have a direct band gap at the K and Kʹ points, enabling optical applications. Poor PL intensity in monolayer TMDCs arises from over-carrier concentrations, strains, and defects. Sulfur-based TMDCs like MoS 2 and WS 2 have established PL enhancement via p-type dopants and superacids. Selenium-based TMDCs like MoSe 2 and WSe 2 have very limited PL enhancement strategies. No universal strategy exists for improving the optical behavior of diverse 2D semiconductors. Removing the substrate effect is a potential universal strategy for improving PL in all compounds.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a single coating method improve PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs? Does paraffin coating remove the substrate effect to enhance PL universally? Does paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient induce strain and desorption? Will coating enhance PL in MoS 2 , WS 2 , MoSe 2 , and WSe 2 ? Does spontaneous fluctuation and desorption explain the PL enhancement? Can the method enable transparent, flexible optoelectronic devices?

Methodological Details
The study used monolayer TMDCs of MoS 2 , WS 2 , MoSe 2 , and WSe 2. The coating material was a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin. The paraffin had a melting point of 42-45 °C. Paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C before coating. Paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) was applied to keep paraffin molten during spin coating. Samples were placed on Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates. Raman analysis used 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2. PL and Raman spectra were measured through the paraffin film. Optical microscopy and PL mapping were used to observe the films.

Procedures And Architectures
Paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance. Melted paraffin was dropped onto a sample on a spin coater. A hair dryer was applied to keep paraffin molten during spin coating. A thick film by simple casting produced a glassy, nontransparent appearance. The coating induced gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption. Deformation to a shrunk bundled structure results from desorption. Strain is applied by the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin. Paraffin penetration removes the substrate effect from the TMDCs. The method is applicable to other 2D layered materials. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent for device packaging.

Key Results
MoS 2 showed a 215-fold PL enhancement from the as-exfoliated flake. WS 2 showed a 55-fold PL enhancement from the as-exfoliated flake. WSe 2 showed a 9-fold PL enhancement from the as-exfoliated flake. MoSe 2 showed a 50-fold PL enhancement from the as-exfoliated flake. WS 2 showed about 36-fold PL enhancement through paraffin coating. The normalized PL spectrum showed a decrease in the low-energy shoulder. The decrease suggests a decrease in trion-derived PL signal. Paraffin covered the entire monolayer WS 2. PL enhancement was observed in the whole plane with partial greater enhancement. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively by about -0.72 cm -1 on average. The Aʹ peak shifted positively by 1.03 cm -1 after paraffin coating. The Eʹ peak indicates in-plane strain; the Aʹ peak indicates carrier concentration. The PL intensity was about 2.3 times greater in the center than at the rim. The PL peak position shifted 5-10 meV lower in energy at the center. The folded bilayer region showed remarkable PL enhancement and red shift. The Eʹ peak in the Raman spectra shifted to lower energy in the folded region. PL enhancement is due to strain and subsequent desorption. The deformation bends the monolayer into the shape of a bundle.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The substrate effect is the key factor in enhancing PL in monolayers. Paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient applies strain to the TMDCs. The method is universal across sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The method extends TMDC design for optoelectronics via transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility. The mechanism combines strain and desorption from paraffin coating. The phenomenon occurs spontaneously through the paraffin coating. The hydrocarbon-coating method is useful for straining thin 2D materials. The method enables transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

Contradictions And Limitations
The enhancement factors vary by sample, indicating variability. PL enhancement is nonuniform within the monolayer plane. The PL enhancement mechanism is suggested, not definitively proven. The exact role of strain versus desorption is not fully disentangled. The study focuses on MoS 2 for Raman statistical analysis.

Claims
Paraffin coating universally enhances PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs by removing the substrate effect. MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 all showed large enhancement factors. The method is applicable to both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The substrate effect is the key factor in enhancing PL. The enhancement differs from sulfur-only methods like TFSI. The enhancement factors vary by sample, indicating variability. The exact mechanism is suggested, not definitively proven. The method could enable transparent, flexible optoelectronic devices. The method is useful for straining thin 2D materials. The method extends TMDC design for optoelectronics.
The PL enhancement is due to strain and desorption induced by paraffin's thermal expansion. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively, indicating strain. The Aʹ peak shifted positively, indicating decreased carrier concentration. The mechanism combines strain and desorption. The deformation bends the monolayer into a bundle. The exact mechanism is suggested, not definitively proven. The role of strain versus desorption is not fully disentangled. The method could be applied to other 2D layered materials. The method is useful for straining thin 2D materials.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The enhancement factors vary by sample, indicating variability. The PL enhancement is nonuniform within the monolayer plane.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the paraffin coating process on a spin coater. Figure 1b shows PL spectra for monolayer WS 2 with about 36-fold enhancement. Figure 1c and 1d show optical microscopy and PL mapping images. Figure 2a shows band gaps and emission wavelengths for as-exfoliated flakes. Figure 2b shows the factors of enhancement for each original monolayer flake. Figure 3a to 3d show optical microscope images of MoS 2 deformation over time. Figure 3e shows PL spectra for the deformed sample. Figure 3f shows the removal of the substrate effect. Figure 4 shows Raman shifts of the Eʹ and Aʹ peaks in 30 samples. Table 2 shows the Raman peak shifts before and after paraffin coating. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes and PL mapping. Figure 5b shows the PL peak position distribution in the plane. Figures 5c and 5d show the plausible PL enhancement mechanism. Figure S1 shows PL enhancement on a quartz substrate. Figure S2b shows MoSe 2 Raman data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A universal paraffin-coating method enhances PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. 2. The strongest evidence: MoS 2 showed a 215-fold PL enhancement from the as-exfoliated flake. 3. The future path: The method could enable transparent, flexible optoelectronic devices in 2D semiconductors.

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H2O2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
summary.field_subfield: Catalysis / Green chemistry (methane partial oxidation)
summary.executive_summary: This work reports a modified silica-supported bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst (AuFeHS) for the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a green oxidant. The central motivation is that methane is abundant but difficult to convert selectively, because activated C-H bonds tend toward complete oxidation to CO2, and existing catalysts require high temperature and high pressure. The authors address two catalytic challenges: (1) continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure, and (2) a selectivity switch to acetic acid by co-feeding CO. In a batch reactor at 10 bar, the optimized AuFeHS catalyst (0.46 wt% Fe, 0.23 wt% Au) reached a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity, one of the highest reported. In a fixed-bed continuous flow reactor at atmospheric pressure, the yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au, the best reported value, with steady production over 7 h and a maximum of 157 µmol at 4 h. Co-feeding CO switched the product to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat within 4 h) with methanol and CO2 as side products. Characterization (ICP-OES, contact angle, XRD, HRTEM, XPS, XANES/EXAFS, in-situ IR, NMR) established that Fe is atomically dispersed and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ sites (709.5 eV) are key for methane and peroxide activation, while Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) provide charge donation and CO activation. Isotope (CD4) labeling confirmed the methyl group originates from methane, and nitrogen feed gave no products, ruling out background reactions. The authors attribute the performance to the synergy between Au and Fe, hydrophobic silica (contact angle 118°), and Lewis acid sites. The paper concludes that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a promising route toward commercializing methane-to-oxygenates (M2O) technologies under benign conditions.

claims.description: The AuFeHS catalyst achieves high-yield, high-selectivity methane partial oxidation under benign conditions.
Co-feeding CO switches selectivity from methanol to acetic acid.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary

In a fixed-bed continuous flow reactor at atmospheric pressure, the yield reached 224 mmol/gFe+Au, the best reported value, with steady production over 7 h and a maximum of 157 µmol at 4 h. Co-feeding CO switched the product to acetic acid (648 µmol/gcat within 4 h) with methanol and CO2 as side products. The authors attribute the performance to the synergy between Au and Fe, hydrophobic silica (contact angle 118°), and Lewis acid sites. The paper concludes that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation is a promising route toward commercializing methane-to-oxygenates (M2O) technologies under benign conditions.

Research Context
Methane is abundant but difficult to convert selectively because activated C-H bonds tend toward complete oxidation to CO2. Direct partial oxidation of methane to methanol is considered a holy grail problem in catalysis. Existing catalysts suffer from low product yield and high temperature and high-pressure reaction conditions. Most POM-to-methanol reports use molecular oxygen with frugal conversion to methanol. Prior high-pressure H2O2 processes reported low continuous yields at 20 bar.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to achieve continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol at atmospheric pressure. The study aims to switch selectivity from methanol to acetic acid by co-feeding CO. The hypothesis is that a hydrophobic Au-Fe catalyst with low-valent Fe sites will activate methane and H2O2 at mild conditions. The hypothesis is that Au nanoparticles stabilize low-valent Fe sites and provide CO activation. The predicted outcome is high methanol yield and selectivity under benign conditions.

Methodological Details
The study used a modified deposition precipitation method to disperse Fe onto hydrophobic silica. The catalyst was supported on hydrophobic silica (HS) with low metal loading. The best catalyst had 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au, confirmed by ICP-OES. The hydrophobicity of silica was confirmed by contact angle analysis with an observed angle of 118. C-H vibration from silica confirmed the hydrophobic functionalization from HS. Powder XRD showed no Au or Fe reflections, confirming fine metal dispersion. HRTEM showed no Fe particle contrast, indicating atomic dispersion of Fe. HRTEM observed small Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm in AuFeHS. Elemental mapping showed Au nanoparticles finely dispersed over FeHS. The specific surface area was 392 m2/g for AuFeHS. XPS confirmed Fe3+ at 710.3 eV and FeOOH at 712.5 eV in FeHS. XPS showed low-valent Fe 3-δ+ at 709.5 eV in AuFeHS. XPS estimated 85% Au0 and 15% Auδ+ atomic percentages. XANES showed no Fe-Fe interaction, revealing single atomic Fe species. LCF fitting showed 72% Fe3O4 and 28% FeO for AuFeHS. EXAFS showed the first Fe peak at ~1.5Å, indicating non-elemental Fe. In-situ IR assigned 2105 cm-1 to Au0-CO and 2175 cm-1 to Auδ+-CO. Batch screening was carried out at 10 bar methane pressure. The reaction used H2O2 (15% w/v) as the oxidant. Continuous flow was performed in a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure. Gas chromatography and NMR confirmed product formation and quantification. CD4 isotope labeling confirmed the methyl group originated from methane. Nitrogen feed instead of methane resulted in no products.

Procedures And Architectures

The continuous process showed steady methanol production over 7 h. The product yield reached a maximum at 4 h (157 µmol) under optimized conditions. Temperature optimization confirmed 80°C as the best condition. The reaction used a total gas pressure of 20 bar (15 bar CH4:5 bar CO) with CO co-feed.

The support (HS) alone gave no product in the POM reaction. The Fe-HS catalyst gave 285 mmol/gFe with 82% methanol selectivity. The Au-HS catalyst gave only 47.6 mmol/gAu of methanol. The study is conducted without reported human or animal subjects, so ethical considerations are not applicable. The paper does not report data or code availability statements, so those fields are set to empty strings.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are important functional organic molecules with applications in optical storage, molecular switches, and industry. Traditional azo synthesis relies on diazotization with stoichiometric nitrile salts, producing unstable diazonium intermediates and waste. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed and Ir-based photocatalytic methods exist but suffer from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, and inert atmospheres. Photocatalytic oxidative coupling with O2 is attractive but prior arylamine-to-azo methods use organic solvents and limited catalysts. Charged aqueous interfaces can modulate photochemical reactions via confinement and unique electric fields. A green aqueous route for azo synthesis at ambient conditions remains an important unmet goal.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a metal-free, aqueous, ambient photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics can be achieved efficiently. The hypothesis is that charged aqueous interfaces of micelles can boost catalytic efficacy via non-diffusive PET and redox potential modulation. It is predicted that EY will associate selectively with CTAB micelles due to electrostatic interactions between its negative charges and CTAB. It is predicted that PET will be ultrafast, with a time constant on the order of picoseconds. It is predicted that the reaction will proceed with high conversion, selectivity, and low catalyst loading under ambient air. It is predicted that atmospheric O2 will act as a sacrificial oxidant, being reduced to H2O2 to regenerate the photocatalyst.

Methodological Details
The study investigates metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics in aqueous medium. The authors use Eosin Y (EY) as the organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as the base. The reaction is carried out at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air. Three surfactants are screened: cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and triton X-100 (TX-100). EY shows a bathochromic shift of 9 and 16 nm in the presence of CTAB and TX-100 micelles, respectively. EY exhibits enhanced fluorescence of 2.4-fold only in the presence of CTAB at and near the critical micellar concentration. No spectral changes are observed for EY in the presence of SDS, signifying lack of interaction. EY bears two negative charges at pH 7 and interacts electrostatically with the positively charged CTAB. The enhanced fluorescence lifetime of EY rises from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. The reaction uses 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. CTAB forms spherical micelles at an optimized concentration of 40 mM, as revealed from HR-TEM measurements. The model substrate is p-anisidine, converted to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene. Conversion is determined from GC-MS measurements, and products are characterized by GC-MS and NMR. The reaction is triggered by green light at a wavelength of 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. The reaction completes within 4 h to give 100% conversion to the desired azo product. K3PO4 neither interferes with EY-CTAB association nor interacts with the excited state of EY@CTAB. Arylamines prefer to solubilize at the less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous interface of the micellar Stern layer. Both the substrate and the photocatalyst remain solubilized inside the micellar scaffold.

The methodology is based on the specific association of substrate and photocatalyst with the micellar assembly. Photophysical behavior of EY is studied in the presence of CTAB, SDS, and TX-100. Micellar association is probed via absorption peak shifts and fluorescence quenching. Fluorescence lifetime is measured to confirm micellar association, rising from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns. Reaction optimization is tabulated in Table 1, using green light at 525 nm under ambient air. The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. The reaction achieves 100% conversion within 4 h with 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. Micelle morphology is confirmed as spherical at 40 mM via HR-TEM measurements. The reaction requires a base because proton abstraction is a critical step for POC of amine substrates. Inorganic bases K3PO4 and KOH, and organic base DABCO, are all effective, though DABCO gives slightly lower yields. Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, being reduced to H2O2 to regenerate the photocatalyst. H2O2 formation is detected with H2O2 sensing strips, showing color change before and after light irradiation. Fluorescence quenching is monitored at 545 nm upon addition of increasing concentrations of p-anisidine. A linear Stern-Volmer plot gives a quenching rate constant (kq) of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. The SV plot indicates a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process. Lack of fluorescence quenching with p-nitroaniline suggests no electron transfer to EY*@CTAB. K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots, signifying that PET precedes proton abstraction. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. Radical trap experiments use 2,6-di-tert-buty-4-methylphenol (BHT) to trap amine radicals. The reaction mixture is irradiated with green light for 5 min, then BHT is added and irradiated for 4 h. Products are analyzed using HR-MS and GC-MS measurements. A characteristic HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adducts appears at a molecular weight of 342.2399 g/mol. The presence of BHT results in negligible conversion of about 5.0% to the desired azo product.

The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. Conversion is determined from GC-MS measurements, and CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM. The efficacy is enhanced with an 8.3-fold lower dose of EY compared to the previous report. The enhancement occurs only in the presence of CTAB micelles, indicating the critical role of the micellar environment. The approach is sustainable, using a common and low-cost organic photocatalyst, Eosin Y. The reaction proceeds under ambient air, avoiding the need for inert atmospheres. The approach uses sustainable O2 as the oxidant, reducing waste compared to diazotization. The study suggests potential applications in optical storage and molecular switches. The study does not report mechanistic models beyond the PET and redox potential modulation.

The paper is a preprint hosted on ChemRxiv and is explicitly not peer-reviewed. The reaction requires a base, as proton abstraction is a critical step for POC of amine substrates. The reaction is feasible only in the presence of a base, indicating a requirement that limits generality. The reaction is feasible with blue light, but requires 6 h for 100% conversion under standard conditions. The quenching rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1 exceeds the diffusion limit, indicating a non-diffusive process. summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / Computational Chemistry (Solid-State Ionics)
summary.executive_summary: Solid electrolytes are central to next-generation Li-ion batteries because they promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs relative to liquid electrolytes. Among candidate materials, cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12 (c-LLZO) stands out for its superior interfacial stability against metallic Li, yet it is not stable at room temperature and must be stabilised with substitutional dopants. c-LLZO crystallises in the Ia 3d space group with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h crystallographic sites, and there is no consensus in the literature about the correct 24d :96h Li occupancy. Because many computational studies begin from an assumed experimental occupancy to build an idealised unit cell, the authors argue that without knowing whether those starting structures are near the ground state, downstream thermodynamic and observable properties may be poorly described. To address this, the authors present a combinatorial workflow that enumerates all possible Li site occupancies for a c-LLZO unit cell and ranks them energetically. They first eliminate structures with overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å, then remove symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to reduce the configuration space from ~2.3 × 10 8 structures to ~2 × 10 6 symmetry-unique structures. They then perform 1235 single-point DFT calculations with the ONETEP code (PBE functional, 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff) on two subsets — the 200 lowest-energy structures from the COMPASSIII forcefield and a random sample of ~1000 structures — and fit a multiple linear regression (MLR) model using a frequency list of all Li-Li interactions as descriptors. The MLR achieves a test-set correlation of 0.9996 and finds that all structures lie within 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. The 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures have a 8:48 ratio, with the 19th lowest being 9:47, and four 8:48 structures lie within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the global minimum. Geometry optimisation of these four structures narrows the energy gap further, with the lowest-energy structure (label 1095859) being 0.58 eV lower than the geometry-optimised lowest single-point structure after a 96h to 24d transition changing the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The authors conclude that a large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may describe structures that are not physically feasible or stable, and they release all generated structures in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and does not include a formal bibliography, so top_influential_citations is empty. Notable omissions include the absence of author affiliations, funding statements, and explicit hyperparameter details beyond the DFT settings, which are recorded under the relevant fields.

A large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature may describe structures that are not physically feasible or stable.
The 24d :96h ratio is indicative of a structure's energy, with lower energy structures avoiding 24d occupation.

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng, Vineet Padia, Joseph H Maalouf, Aditya M Limaye, Alexander H Liu, Michael A Yusov, Ian W Hunter, Karthish Manthiram
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / CO2 electroreduction (CO2RR) mechanistic kinetics
summary.executive_summary: Electrocatalytic mechanism studies traditionally lean on linearized rate data, which underpins Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses. These linearization strategies assume that dependences on different experimental handles can be factored separately and linearized on log-log or semi-log graphs. However, for complex phenomena such as surface coverage effects or mixed control, these common linearization strategies will yield incomplete or uninterpretable results. Cohesive kinetic analysis, which is often used in thermocatalysis and involves quantitative model fitting for data collected over a wide range of reaction conditions, requires more data but also provides a more robust strategy for interrogating reaction mechanisms. In this work, the authors report a robotic system that improves the experimental workflow for collecting electrochemical rate data by automating sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells that can each have a different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase reactant composition, and applied voltage. They use this system to investigate the mechanism of carbon dioxide electroreduction to carbon monoxide at several immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. Specifically, at cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc), they see signatures of complex reaction mechanisms, where observed bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences change with applied potential. They illustrate how phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent degrees of rate control can explain the observed kinetic behaviors. Their mechanistic analysis suggests that CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism, akin to one that has been previously proposed, whereas the mechanism for FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. Their study illustrates that complex reaction mechanisms which are not amenable to common Tafel and order dependence analyses may be quite prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.

Their study illustrates that complex reaction mechanisms which are not amenable to common Tafel and order dependence analyses may be quite prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.

Research Context
Electrocatalysis has traditionally relied on linearized rate data for mechanistic interpretation. Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses assume factorable, linearizable dependences. Coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions complicate linearization. Cohesive kinetic analysis is common in thermocatalysis but rare in electrocatalysis. A meta-analysis showed Tafel slopes lack interpretable values, hinting at hidden complexity. Prior cohesive analysis revealed competitive electrolyte adsorption and mixed control for CO2RR to CO on CoPc.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Do non-ideal kinetic signatures (non-linear, potential-dependent orders) appear across immobilized metal tetrapyrroles? Can automation enable cohesive kinetic analysis of individual cells with online product quantification? Do bicarbonate and CO2 orders change with applied potential across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc? Can electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control explain these trends? Do CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism, while FePc involves a later-cycle intermediate?

Methodological Details
Catalysts were immobilized on calcined Toray060 carbon paper working electrodes. CoPc was loaded at 5.98 x 10^-11 mol/cm^2. CoTPP and FePc were loaded at 5.11 x 10^-10 and 8.04 x 10^-10 mol/cm^2. Carbon black was added to less active catalysts to increase loading and avoid aggregation. Catalysts were dissolved in DMF or carbon black-containing DMF. Stock solutions of 0.5 mol/L Na2CO3 and 1 mol/L NaClO4 were prepared. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2 before use. Electrolytes had overall 1 mol/L ionic strength with varied bicarbonate concentrations. The robot tested up to ten cells sequentially in a single effort. The working electrode was a 10 mm diameter carbon paper disk. The reference electrode was a leak-free Ag/AgCl calibrated against SCE daily. The counter electrode was a 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire. Online product quantification used a gas chromatograph for CO and H2. All data were uploaded to an SQL database and processed with a python script. Data were output as average current, partial CO current, and partial H2 current.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot houses a single cell body with a line of ten cell pan pairs. The cell body moves horizontally and vertically to sequence experiments. Electrolyte flows through the electrolyte in port, then gas flows through the gas in tubing. A gas chromatograph connected to the gas out port detects CO and H2. The cell body rinses at a wash station with milliQ water after ten runs. The cell assembly is analogous to a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell. The lack of a membrane allowed more facile liquid and gas management. Without a membrane, oxygen from the counter electrode can cause parasitic ORR. Incomplete FE closure averaged about 60% attributable to CO and H2. A Pt counter electrode was chosen to preclude adventitious anode oxidation products. High FEs toward HER were typically around 30 to 60%. CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte rather than fed directly to the electrode. Currents were below the theoretical mass transport limited current density. CoPc data were compared against previously reported manually collected results. Newly measured CO rates were up to ten times lower than previously reported. New CO FEs were typically under 30%. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved.

Key Results
CoPc and CoTPP show most negative bicarbonate dependence at less reductive potentials. CoTPP and CoPc bicarbonate dependence becomes positive at more reductive potentials. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. CoPc and CoTPP bicarbonate orders change sign with potential, indicating mixed control. FePc bicarbonate inhibition is amplified at more reductive potentials, unlike local adsorption. FePc trends can be explained by a MARI prior to the unoccupied site. CoPc shows a simple first order CO2 dependence within error at both potentials. CoTPP CO2 order is slightly below one and decreases at more reductive potentials. CoTPP CO2 attenuation is characteristic of surface saturation effects. FePc CO2 order is most unusual, attenuated at less reductive potentials. FePc CO2 order curves for two potentials intersect, indicating voltage inhibition at low CO2. FePc mixed control invokes an on-cycle poisoning species with net negative voltage effect. Non-linear, potential-dependent orders were observed across all three catalysts. CoPc showed curvature and potential-dependent bicarbonate order changes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Bicarbonate poisoning via adsorption onto an unoccupied site explains CoPc and CoTPP. Positive electrosorption valency means less bicarbonate adsorption at more reductive potentials. Potential-dependent mixed control explains the sign change in bicarbonate order. FePc requires a MARI prior to the unoccupied site to explain amplified inhibition. On-cycle poisoning species can attenuate or amplify bicarbonate dependence. Surface saturation effects attenuate apparent CO2 order for CoTPP. Mixed control with on-cycle poisoning explains intersecting FePc CO2 curves. CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism akin to a previously proposed one. FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the MARI. Complex mechanisms not amenable to Tafel analysis may be prevalent across tetrapyrroles.

Contradictions And Limitations
Newly measured CO rates were up to ten times lower than previously reported. New CO FEs were typically under 30%, indicating incomplete FE closure. Incomplete FE closure averaged about 60% attributable to CO and H2. High HER FEs of 30 to 60% may confound partial CO current interpretation. Undivided cell allows crosstalk and parasitic ORR from the counter electrode. Currents were below mass transport limit, yet flow configuration may still influence kinetics. Proposed mechanisms only qualitatively capture trends, not via statistical goodness-of-fit. Proposed mechanisms do not quantitatively fit all experimental data. No specific reaction mechanism is proposed; only conceptual discussion is provided. The study is a single-compartment cell, unlike conventional divided cells.

Claims
Automation enables cohesive kinetic analysis of individual electrochemical cells with online product quantification. The robot automates sequential testing of up to ten cells. Online product quantification uses a gas chromatograph for CO and H2. Data were uploaded to an SQL database and processed with a python script. The workflow enables faster and more facile rate data collection. Automation strategies are often tailored to high-throughput screening. Small working volumes hinder product quantification for non-100% FE reactions. Automation standardizes and accelerates cohesive kinetic analysis. Future software could enumerate mechanisms and suggest informative conditions.
CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism with potential-dependent mixed control and bicarbonate poisoning. CoPc and CoTPP bicarbonate dependence becomes positive at more reductive potentials. CoPc and CoTPP invoke bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control. Such a model has previously been reported to quantitatively describe CoPc kinetics. FePc shows opposite bicarbonate inhibition trends, indicating a different mechanism. CoPc and CoTPP kinetics can be reconciled by a shared mechanism. Potential-dependent mixed control explains sign changes in bicarbonate order.
FePc involves a MARI prior to the unoccupied site, explaining amplified bicarbonate inhibition. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. FePc trends require a MARI prior to the unoccupied site. Conversion of the MARI to the unoccupied site has stronger voltage dependence. FePc trends contradict local bicarbonate adsorption equilibrium expectations. FePc mechanism differs from CoPc and CoTPP. MARI position affects potential-dependent inhibition trends.
Complex, non-ideal mechanisms are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. Non-linear, potential-dependent orders were observed across all three catalysts. Such signatures have only been reported in one previous work at CoPc. Trends are unexplainable with mechanisms typically invoked for CO2RR at tetrapyrroles. summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang (Peking University); Tianzuo Li (Peking University); Jiyeon Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Dahye Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Lianjie Xu (Peking University); Yajie Liu (Peking University); Jongcheol Seo (Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)); Wen-Bin Zhang (Peking University)
summary.field_subfield: Protein engineering / synthetic biology (topological proteins)
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (design and synthesis of a novel single-domain protein catenane)
summary.executive_summary: Proteins are usually built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional topology can enhance stability. Artificial topological proteins have been made with 'assembly-reaction' synergy, but they typically contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of topology. Here, the authors design and synthesize a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically. The design rewires connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original DHFR fold itself as the entangling template, so no exogenous entangling motif is needed. Synthesis is achieved in cells via programmed streamlined post-translational processing using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and is characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to a linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The authors conclude that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science. The study demonstrates feasibility of the approach by converting a model enzyme, DHFR from Escherichia coli, into its single-domain catenane counterpart. DHFR catalyzes reduction of DHF to THF in the presence of NADPH. The authors show that chemical topology can be changed without collapsing the fold and can bring profound changes in properties. The work is notable because it eliminates the need for an exogenous entangling motif as a template, using spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures. The results support the hypothesis that single-domain topological proteins can be realized and that topology can enhance stability while largely preserving function. The study provides a general strategy for converting linear proteins into topological single-domain proteins, which could be extended to other domains and used for further engineering and evolution.

summary.title: Sorry, we're open: Golden Open Access and inequality in the natural sciences
summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.field_subfield: Scientometrics / Open Access publishing
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the relationship between publication costs and scientific impact within Golden Open Access (GOA) journals in the natural sciences. The motivation stems from the transition of high-impact journals to mandatory open access, which shifted their revenue model from subscription sales to Article Processing Charges (APC). While open access increases accessibility, the associated costs create barriers for researchers without funding, particularly those in developing countries. The author collected metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals, analyzing APC, Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and country of publisher. Using R statistical software, the study found that IF, EF, and citability all increase as APC increases, with significant positive correlations (r(237) = 0.391 for APC-IF, r(237) = 0.303 for APC-EF, r(237) = 0.323 for APC-citability, all p < .001). Additionally, publishers from developed countries had higher APC, IF, EF, and citability than those from developing countries. The mean APC was $1344.27 USD, mean IF was 2.855, mean EF was 0.017, and mean citability was 5925.92. The author argues that this system perpetuates inequality, as researchers in developing countries face a dilemma: either pay expensive fees or publish in lower-impact journals. The study highlights concerns about Research4Life funding eligibility being voided when developed-country authors are included, and discusses how this affects conservation research in tropical biodiversity hotspots. The author concludes that the current GOA publishing model promotes a false ideology equating prestige and costliness with reliable science, and calls for a more inclusive environment for scientific research globally.

summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada; M Ondráček; M Lamanec; A Gallardo; A Jiménez-Martín; B De La Torre; P Hobza; P Jelínek
summary.field_subfield: Physical chemistry / surface science (scanning probe microscopy)
summary.executive_summary: Non-covalent interactions in chemistry and biology are governed by dispersion and electrostatic forces, and the electrostatic component depends on the internal charge distribution of molecules. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, electronegative substituents can reverse the π-electron population, creating an electron-deficient cavity called a π-hole. Although π-holes were predicted theoretically, their direct experimental observation had remained elusive. This study addresses that gap by using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to image the π-hole on a single molecule of 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An, C14F8Cl2) and to show its absence in anthracene (An, C14H10). The authors grew heterogeneous self-assemblies of both molecules on an atomically clean Au(111) surface in ultrahigh vacuum and characterized them with scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) and noncontact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) using a functionalized CO tip. Because AFM contrast alone could not directly reveal the π-hole, they turned to KPFM, which maps the local contact potential difference (LCPD) with atomic resolution. The experimental KPFM images reproduced a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the central part of FCl-An, matching DFT-based simulations using the PP-AFM code. The presence of the π-hole also affected adsorption: force-distance spectroscopy showed FCl-An sits 30 pm higher than An, with absolute adsorption heights of 330 pm (An) and 360 pm (FCl-An) above Au(111). Symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT0) analysis showed that the π-hole increases the ionization potential and suppresses charge induction at the molecule/metal interface, weakening induced electrostatic interactions. The authors conclude that the π-hole raises the adsorption height of the molecule. This work demonstrates the potential of scanning microscopy for studying internal charge distributions and their influence on molecular properties and interactions.

Executive Summary
