The authors conclude that the π-hole raises the adsorption height of the molecule. This work demonstrates the potential of scanning microscopy for studying internal charge distributions and their influence on molecular properties and interactions.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions underpin many chemical and biological processes. Dispersion is attractive and directionless; electrostatics are directional. Electrostatic interactions depend on internal molecular charge distribution. π-holes were predicted theoretically but lacked direct experimental proof. π-holes can strongly affect intermolecular stacking interactions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can the π-hole be directly visualized on a single molecule? Is KPFM suitable for real-space observation of π-holes? Does the π-hole influence adsorption on metallic surfaces? Does the π-hole raise the adsorption height of the molecule? Predicted outcome: FCl-An shows π-hole contrast while An does not.

Methodological Details
Two molecular species were studied. Experiments were performed at cryogenic temperature. A commercial STM/nc-AFM microscope was used. Pt/Ir tips were sharpened by focused ion beam. Tips were cleaned by gentle indentation. The qPlus sensor had specific resonant properties. nc-AFM operated in frequency modulation mode. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by sputtering and annealing. Images were processed with WSxM software. Molecules were deposited simultaneously via Knudsen cells. Deposition lasted 15 seconds. STM was acquired in constant current mode. nc-AFM and KPFM were captured in constant height mode. KPFM used a CO-functionalized tip. Each data point took about 3 seconds. Each parabola contained 600 points. The bias range was (-150, 400) mV. DFT calculations used FHI-AIMS code. The PBE GGA functional was employed. The Au(111) slab had 4 atomic layers. The surface supercell was 6×6. The supramolecular cell was √39×√39. vdW correction used Tkatchenko-Scheffler method. Forces were optimized below 2 meV/Å. MP2/cc-pVTZ was used for molecular orbitals. SAPT0 used the PSI4 program. The SAPT0 cluster had 38 gold atoms. The CO tip quadrupole was -0.2 e/Å². The CO lateral spring constant was 0.25 N/m.

Procedures And Architectures
Orbitals were compared between An and FCl-An. Orbitals in An were localized at the carbon skeleton. Orbitals in FCl-An extended to halogen substituents. Self-assembly grew by simultaneous sublimation. STM revealed ordered molecular islands. Islands contained alternating molecular species. nc-AFM distinguished two molecular species. The assembly had a rhombic periodic structure. The unit cell contained one An and two FCl-An. Arrangement was dictated by electrostatic interactions. An alone did not form self-organized structures. KPFM maps the local contact potential difference. LCPD magnitude depends on tip-sample distance. Contrast depends on tip-sample distance. Shorter distance enhances submolecular contrast. Tip relaxations cause LCPD deviations. Height was chosen near Δf minima. Δf* images lacked submolecular resolution. KPFM simulations used PP-AFM code. Simulations reproduced the bow-tie pattern. The bow-tie matched electrostatic potential. Adsorption heights were measured by force-distance spectroscopy. The height difference was 30 pm. Adsorption heights were 330 and 360 pm. DFT adsorption heights were 325 and S1 pm. Molecules were physisorbed. Induction energy was larger for An. The π-hole increased ionization potential. The π-hole suppressed charge density induction.

Key Results
π-hole was confirmed in FCl-An. π-hole was absent in anthracene. Orbitals in An were localized at the carbon skeleton. Orbitals in FCl-An extended to halogen substituents. The assembly had a rhombic structure. The unit cell had one An and two FCl-An. An alone did not self-organize. AFM did not directly reveal the π-hole. KPFM mapped the charge distribution. Contrast depended on tip-sample distance. Shorter distance enhanced submolecular contrast. Tip relaxations caused LCPD deviations. Height was chosen near Δf minima. Simulations matched experimental KPFM images. Simulations reproduced the bow-tie pattern. The bow-tie was in the central part of FCl-An. The bow-tie matched electrostatic potential. The π-hole affected adsorption height. Submolecular contrast emerged on FCl-An. The height difference was 30 pm. Adsorption heights were 330 and 360 pm. DFT adsorption heights were 325 and S1 pm. Molecules were physisorbed. Induction energy was larger for An. The π-hole increased ionization potential. The π-hole suppressed charge density induction. The π-hole weakened induced electrostatic interactions. The π-hole increased adsorption height.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole was directly observed for the first time. KPFM resolved the π-hole on a single molecule. The observation confirmed theoretical predictions. The bow-tie pattern indicated heterogeneous charge. The pattern matched electrostatic potential. The π-hole influenced adsorption. The π-hole increased ionization potential. The π-hole inhibited charge density induction. The π-hole weakened induced electrostatic interactions. The π-hole increased adsorption height. Scanning microscopy studies internal charge distribution. Charge distribution affects molecular properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
AFM did not directly reveal the π-hole. AFM contrast was affected by topographic effects. Tip-sample distance affected KPFM contrast. Tip relaxations caused artifacts. Height was chosen to avoid tip relaxation. Δf* images lacked submolecular resolution. The bias range was limited. The cluster model gave similar results. DFT and SAPT0 gave similar results. The SAPT0 cluster had 38 gold atoms. The CO tip quadrupole was assumed. The CO lateral spring constant was 0.25 N/m. The height difference was 30 pm. Adsorption heights were 330 and 360 pm. DFT adsorption heights were 325 and S1 pm.

Claims
The π-hole can be directly visualized on a single molecule using KPFM. The π-hole was confirmed in FCl-An. The π-hole was absent in anthracene. KPFM resolved the π-hole on a single molecule. The observation confirmed theoretical predictions. The bow-tie pattern indicated heterogeneous charge. AFM did not directly reveal the π-hole. AFM contrast was affected by topographic effects. The π-hole influenced adsorption. The π-hole increased ionization potential. The π-hole inhibited charge density induction. The π-hole weakened induced electrostatic interactions. The π-hole increased adsorption height.
The π-hole affects the adsorption of molecules on metallic surfaces. The π-hole influenced adsorption. Submolecular contrast emerged on FCl-An. The height difference was 30 pm. Adsorption heights were 330 and 360 pm. DFT adsorption heights were 325 and S1 pm. The height difference was small. The cluster model gave similar results. The π-hole increased ionization potential. The π-hole inhibited charge density induction. The π-hole weakened induced electrostatic interactions. The π-hole increased adsorption height.

Data And Code Availability
The data was collected at constant height. The bias range was (-150, 400) mV.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The cluster model gave similar results. DFT and SAPT0 gave similar results. The SAPT0 cluster had 38 gold atoms. The CO tip quadrupole was assumed. The CO lateral spring constant was 0.25 N/m. The height difference was 30 pm. Adsorption heights were 330 and 360 pm. DFT adsorption heights were 325 and S1 pm.

Ethical Considerations
The experiments were conducted in ultrahigh vacuum.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 showed quadrupole moments. Fig. 2a showed molecular self-assembly. Fig. 2b showed nc-AFM images. Fig. 2c showed the rhombic structure. Fig. 2d showed electrostatic interactions. Fig. S1 showed occupied orbitals. Fig. S2 showed An deposition. Fig. 3a showed electrostatic potential. Fig. 3c,f showed simulated KPFM images. Fig. 4a showed Δf-z spectroscopy. Fig. 4b,c showed induced electron density. Table S2 showed adsorption energies. Table S3 showed SAPT0 energy decomposition.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution. 2. The strongest evidence. 3. The future path.

summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.field_subfield: Materials informatics / machine learning force fields for battery interphases
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology + candidate-generation study (ChemRxiv preprint, not peer-reviewed)
summary.executive_summary: The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials, combining organic and inorganic components, and it allows a battery to function by protecting electrode materials from unwanted side reactions. The authors note that key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered, limiting the development of next-generation batteries. Existing methods are inadequate: pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers, and even the fastest useful DFT methods are much too slow to study the time and length scales of the SEI. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X that yield improved barrier heights struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. The authors therefore use a combination of classical sampling and a novel machine learning model to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy, to be used in future machine learning applications and compared to experimental results. They describe a model and sampling procedure that describes the interaction of these materials and thus permits the ranking of candidate SEI structures. The model is a multitask-trained QRNN (a machine learning force field) trained on multiple levels of theory, including GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and a SPICE organic-chemistry subset. They used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation, enhanced reaction sampling using Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) on the QRNN potential energy surface, and a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space via multitask training. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrodinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics and reaction templates applied at intervals. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, giving a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. They defined four sets of candidates with different levels of added Li: 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. Having produced a series of unique initial geometries, they annealed them using their reactive QRNN model with NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each, and ranked each set of candidates by calculating the mean potential energy of each structure over an MD trajectory of 20 ps length at ambient conditions of 300 K and 1 atm. The difficulty of characterizing the SEI system experimentally is a strong motivation for this work, but also an obstacle to validation, because experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. Instead, they validated their model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. They generated the first plausible ranking of SEI candidate structures, along with analysis of hypotheses related to SEI composition. They refer to the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) as predicted by wB97X-D3BJ output head as their "best" candidate. They performed statistical analysis of the bonding in SEI candidate structures by recalculating the Lewis structure of the entire system based on the atomic positions after reactive MD, then tabulating the counts of various bond types versus the total system energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. They have demonstrated that multitask training with a QRNN model, combined with sampling of relevant chemical systems, allows a machine learning force field to model the complex reactions characteristic of an SEI. They constructed SEI candidates using only a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF6 in EC, and suggest that the full power of this technique will come from comparing multiple formulations. Future work should include the application of other model architectures, including Nequip and MACE as well as architectures which allow the use of atomic partial charges such as CHGNet. They note that MLFFs offer a powerful opportunity to understand SEI materials, but only if we are willing to tolerate working in an environment where theoretical and experimental references are currently limited and the probability of being proven wrong by future events is high.

claims.description: A multitask-trained reactive MLFF can model the complex redox reactions characteristic of an SEI.
Adding a general organic chemistry dataset shapes the latent space without heavy cost on model capacity.
P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable SEI structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones.

Research Context
The SEI is a vital but poorly-understood class of materials combining organic and inorganic components. An SEI allows a battery to function by protecting electrode materials from unwanted side reactions. Key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered, limiting the development of next-generation batteries. An SEI is a complex chemical structure that forms over large length and time scales, and involves conductors, insulators, and redox reactions; no existing method is fully applicable to the task of simulating such a system. Pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers. Even the fastest useful DFT methods are much too slow to study the time and length scales of the SEI. Hybrid functionals such as wB97X that yield improved barrier heights struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. MLFFs promise to allow atomistic simulation with the accuracy and wide applicability of DFT, but with the fast sampling of classical force fields. Multitask learning lets us train MLFFs to both pure and hybrid DFT labels simultaneously. MLFFs can already predict properties of Li metal and of organic liquids.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal is to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy for future ML applications and comparison to experiments. The authors hypothesize that a multitask-trained reactive MLFF can model the complex redox reactions characteristic of an SEI. They hypothesize that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones. They predict that adding a general organic chemistry dataset shapes latent space without heavy cost on model capacity. They predict that GFN1-xTB is the most suitable reference for generating charge labels for SEI training sets. They predict that the full power of the technique will come from comparing multiple electrolyte formulations. They predict that stable dynamics are achievable despite extreme conditions, which is often not the case for MLFFs. They predict that the dataset can be efficiently extended with a wider variety of reaction data.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the SEI in lithium-ion batteries, using a single electrolyte formulation of 1M LiPF6 in EC. The reference level of theory for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD. The reference level of theory for periodic systems is PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis. A random subset of non-periodic systems was labeled with PBE-D3 to improve information exchange between output heads. Periodic systems were not labeled with wB97X-D3BJ due to its great expense. Unlike previous QRNN models, theirs did not use GFN2-xTB atomic partial charge labels or DFT dipole labels. They tested reference atomic partial charges from GFN1-xTB, GFN2-xTB, and GFN0-xTB. They used multiple rounds of active learning for data generation to increase accuracy. They used enhanced reaction sampling using AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface. They added a general organic chemistry dataset, SPICE, using elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P. Adding SPICE data caused only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. They doubled the width of the hidden layers to increase model capacity as they added more disparate data. They used a higher-priority dataset of periodic and cluster surface reaction subset, sampled half per batch (as in rehearsal). They applied decoupled weight norms with the norms not included in the optimizer. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrodinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, giving a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. Each system runs with a unique random seed for packing and for MD, ensuring the sampling of many configurations. They defined four sets of candidates with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box. They annealed initial geometries using reactive QRNN NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each. They ranked candidates by mean potential energy over a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K and 1 atm. Because each set of candidates has the same number of atoms of each element, the system energies are directly comparable.

Procedures And Architectures
The model is a multitask-trained QRNN (machine learning force field) trained on multiple levels of theory. The loss function consists of energy and atomic force mean squared error for each level of theory in each training batch, plus charge mean squared error. Charges are not separated into different output heads, with all levels of theory using consistent charge labels. They had four output levels of theory: GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and SPICE wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPPD. The first and last output heads were only used to shape the latent space during training, not for prediction on SEI systems. They used the Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay. They used a learning rate of 2e-3 for the final model. They used only 1% of the data as the validation set, selected uniformly at random. They used hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 for all elements. Their batch size was 64. A high weight decay of 3e-3 per batch was helpful but reduced reaction barrier heights, so they used 1e-3 for the final model. The final model was an exponential moving average of training parameters, averaging every 10 batches with alpha = 0.001. They used NPT ensemble for 1 ns to obtain equilibrated density for liquid systems. For solid-liquid interfaces, they started from a BCC lattice of lithium with an initial spacing of 2 Å. No constraints were applied to the lithium slab; the lithium was allowed to participate fully in the dynamics. They added lithium oxide, lithium carbonate, lithium fluoride, and lithium hydroxide to the training set. They sampled non-equilibrium geometries by adding Gaussian noise to the Cartesian coordinates of the original geometries. They used Quantum Espresso with PBE functional, D3 dispersion correction, and a plane wave energy cutoff of 40 Ry. They used a 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk supercells and a 3x3x1 k-point mesh for surface supercells. For NEB with periodic systems, they used lithium surfaces with 54 atoms topped with a single EC molecule. They extracted clusters within 3-6 Angstroms from reacting atoms for non-periodic labeling with wB97X-D3BJ. They chose a radius around each central atom from a uniform distribution from 3.0 to 5.2 Å, plus a 1.2 Å buffer for hydrogen atoms. They did not use DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries as training inputs.

Key Results
The authors produced the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. They validated their model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers. They could not compare density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus against experimental values because such experiments do not exist for any SEI composition. They refer to the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) as predicted by wB97X-D3BJ output head as their "best" candidate. They performed statistical analysis of bonding by recalculating the Lewis structure of the entire system based on atomic positions after reactive MD. They tabulated the counts of various bond types versus the total system energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable structures. The QRNN models gave stable dynamics despite the extreme conditions applied, which is often not the case for MLFFs. Adding SPICE data did not increase PBE-head validation RMSE on the battery datasets. The most stable SEI candidate for each formulation could allow calculation of Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties. The authors note that this is the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF or any method of comparable accuracy.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The latent space of these MLFF models contains unused capacity that can be applied to broadening chemical applicability. They recommend the use of a supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry to shape the latent space via multitask training as part of future MLFF works. The result implies that the greatly increased scope of the data did not impose a heavy cost on model capacity. The finding that GFN1-xTB achieves the best compromise between accuracy and convergence across isolated and periodic systems supports its use for charge labels. The association of P-F and Li-O bonds with stability suggests these bonds stabilize the SEI. The association of C-O and Li-F bonds with instability suggests these bonds destabilize the SEI. The ability to model complex redox reactions implies MLFFs can handle systems previously out of reach. summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires (NOVA School of Science and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Chemoinformatics / Computational Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a Python graphical user interface (GUI) built on the RDKit chemoinformatics toolkit that allows users without programming skills to calculate molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations of molecular structures. The application is grounded in the QSPR/QSAR methodology, which relies on molecular descriptors as core inputs, and addresses a gap in accessible, teaching-oriented software for chemoinformatics. The GUI is constructed using tkinter, the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk GUI toolkit, and employs various widgets including buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, and a scrollbar, all controlled by the grid geometry manager. Users can select input and output files through native look-and-feel dialog windows implemented with the tkinter.filedialog module, and a log file is created to register successful processing and failures for each molecule. The software generates 3D molecular models using the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule with the MMFF94 force field variant and a maximum of 5000 iterations, with options to remove metals, keep the largest fragment, or neutralize the molecule, and to add hydrogen atoms. For descriptor calculation, the interface provides access to several 3D descriptors available in the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module, including RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA, as well as the exact molecular weight. Beyond descriptors, GUIDEMOL implements direct 3D representations of molecular structures through electrostatic potential grids or voxel encoding. The electrostatic potential at each grid cube is computed from partial atomic charges (Gasteiger or MMFF) using a Coulombic formula, while voxelization encodes atomic properties such as atomic number, partial charge, or contributions to molecular refractivity and logP using the Wildman-Crippen approach with a Gaussian decay function. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license and is available on GitHub, allowing both commercial and non-commercial use and easy extension for other descriptors or tasks. A command-line interface (CLI) is also provided for the calculation of electrostatic potential and voxel grids, enabling batch processing without the GUI. The paper notes that some descriptor values may differ across runs or operating systems due to numerical sensitivity, and highlights the potential for these 3D representations to be processed by deep learning neural networks, including convolutional neural networks, for larger datasets. Overall, GUIDEMOL serves as a minimalist interface to routine chemoinformatics tasks, facilitating access to well-established descriptors and 3D representations for scientists and students in chemistry, biology, and material science education.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Molecular diagnostics / clinical genomics (SARS-CoV-2 detection and surveillance)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the limitations of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis and surveillance. Although RT-PCR is the gold standard and claims to detect about 5 copies of virus, only 47-59% of true positive cases were identified, likely due to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations spanning primer binding sites. The authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based method comprising 343 pairs of specific primers that simultaneously amplify hundreds of targets across the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. The assay produces clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, enabling direct identification of positives by electrophoresis. The method was validated using plasmids containing the S and N genes spiked into human cDNA, with copy numbers precisely determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) using a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. The two plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy, and library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies. The full SARS-CoV-2 genome was amplified from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive nasopharyngeal swab specimens, which were previously diagnosed positive by RT-PCR, with viral loads ranging from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. These genomes were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq, revealing a correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number. The mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms, and only mutations detected by both methods were reported. The study also developed a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamer-adapters to detect SARS-CoV-2 and potentially novel or emerging isolates with modest sequencing depth. The panel was demonstrated to specifically amplify the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome, with 0% of sequencing reads aligned to other human coronaviruses such as MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, and CoV HKU1. The method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA while requiring approximately 0.6M of total reads per library. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. This work provides a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for detection and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2, with implications for diagnostics, surveillance, and phylogenetic studies.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the limitations of reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis and surveillance. Although RT-PCR is the gold standard and claims to detect about 5 copies of virus, only 47-59% of true positive cases were identified, likely due to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations spanning primer binding sites. The authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based method comprising 343 pairs of specific primers that simultaneously amplify hundreds of targets across the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. The assay produces clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, enabling direct identification of positives by electrophoresis. The method was validated using plasmids containing the S and N genes spiked into human cDNA, with copy numbers precisely determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) using a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. The two plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy, and library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies. The full SARS-CoV-2 genome was amplified from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive nasopharyngeal swab specimens, which were previously diagnosed positive by RT-PCR, with viral loads ranging from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. These genomes were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq, revealing a correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number. The mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms, and only mutations detected by both methods were reported. The study also developed a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamer-adapters to detect SARS-CoV-2 and potentially novel or emerging isolates with modest sequencing depth. The panel was demonstrated to specifically amplify the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome, with 0% of sequencing reads aligned to other human coronaviruses such as MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, and CoV HKU1. The method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA while requiring approximately 0.6M of total reads per library. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. This work provides a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for detection and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2, with implications for diagnostics, surveillance, and phylogenetic studies.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis due to its ease of use and high sensitivity. RT-PCR claims to detect about 5 copies of virus, but only 47-59% of true positive cases were identified. Low detection rates are attributed to low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations spanning primer binding sites. Multiplex PCR has been shown to detect other pathogens with high coverage, specificity, and sensitivity. Full-length viral genome sequencing through NGS is essential for surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 evolution.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether multiplex PCR can improve sensitivity over RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection. The hypothesis is that multiplex PCR, by simultaneously targeting and amplifying hundreds of targets, has significantly higher sensitivity than RT-PCR. The hypothesis is that multiplex PCR may detect nucleotide fragments resulting from degraded viral genomes and tolerate genomic variations. The hypothesis is that the mathematical model can predict the limit of detection for both RT-PCR and multiplex PCR. The predicted outcome is that the multiplex PCR panel can detect SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers, down to 0.29 copies when both primer pools are used.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted by researchers from Paragon Genomics Inc, Stanford University, and Children's Hospital Los Angeles. The multiplex PCR method comprised 343 pairs of specific primers. The SARS-CoV-2 genome size used for modeling was 29,903bp (NC_045512.2). The RT-PCR amplicon lengths reported are around 78-158bp, and 100bp was chosen for modeling. The assumed RT-PCR efficiency was 99% for mathematical modeling. The first multiplex PCR panel consisted of 172 pairs of primers with an average amplicon length of 99bp. The average gap between adjacent amplicons was 76±10bp. The assumed multiplex PCR efficiency was 6% for single-strand cDNA amplification. The second primer pool consisted of 171 primer pairs overlapping with the first pool. The two overlapping pools provide full coverage of the entire viral genome. Two plasmids containing the S and N genes were used to validate the multiplex PCR method. The plasmids were spiked into cDNA generated from human total RNA to simulate real clinical samples. The copy number of each plasmid was determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) with a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. The plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy. The 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens were previously diagnosed positive by RT-PCR. The viral load ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. The genomes were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform. The metagenomic method used random hexamer-adapters to amplify DNA or cDNA targets. Paragon Genomics' background removal reagent was used to remove non-specific amplification products. Paragon Genomics' reverse transcription reagents were used to convert RNA into cDNA.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow involved multiplex PCR products being further amplified in a secondary PCR, during which sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers are added. The PCR products were first analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize potential positives. The library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. Quantification of peaks demonstrated a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids. The yield of the libraries started to saturate when the copy number reached 1,700. The recovered reads were within a range of about 20-fold relative depth with about 1.4 to 2.8 plasmids. When detecting down to 1.4 copies of plasmids, only the reads from one amplicon were about 100-fold lower than the average. Approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids, 77% with 2.8 copies, and 37% with 0.6 copies. About 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. 98-99% of the genomes were covered at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies of virus at an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. CleanPlex libraries are usually sequenced at about 1,000 paired-end reads. At least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X with 150,000 total reads. 86% of the genome was covered at 100X with 100,000 total reads. Even at 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X. The mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms, and only mutations detected by both methods were reported. Mutations with frequencies (%AF) > 60% were considered to be empirically true. Only mutations with %AF ≥ 20% were considered to eliminate noise from PCR amplification and sequencing. The metagenomic method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA. The metagenomic method required approximately 0.6M of total reads per library. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA.

Key Results
The mathematical model estimated that RT-PCR assays could only detect 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability. The predicted probability of RT-PCR assays to detect one copy of SARS-CoV-2 is only 26%. The mathematical model estimated that the SARS-CoV-2 panel can detect 1.15 copies of the virus at 95% probability. Using both primer pools would lead to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. Quantification of peaks demonstrated a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids. The theoretical calculation gives a 66% probability to sample 1.1 copies, and a 12% chance to detect them based on a multiplex PCR efficiency of 6%. In practice, the experimentally observed probability to detect 1.1 copies was significantly higher at 56%. About 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. 98-99% of the genomes were covered at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies of virus at an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. At least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X with 150,000 total reads. 86% of the genome was covered at 100X with 100,000 total reads. Even at 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. All 13 strains contained at least one mutation that has been reported to be associated with SARS-CoV-2 virulence. 16% of the recovered bases, or 13% of the recovered reads, were within the viral N and S genes. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered. Only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified. The method was optimized so that 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered. 0% of the obtained sequencing reads from each of the 13 samples were aligned to the genome sequence of any of the above viral species.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The multiplex PCR method is more sensitive than RT-PCR and tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2. The experimental probability to detect 1.1 copies was higher than the theoretical prediction, suggesting the efficiency of multiplex PCR is actually higher than the previously estimated 6%. The LOD is independent of the viral genome size, remaining 4.8 copies at 95% probability for genomes of 4 to 100kb. The high specificity argues strongly that the panel could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus. The metagenomic method achieved superior coverage given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. Increasing sequencing depth alone might not improve the coverage of the targeted regions further. The multiplex PCR method can be tailored to simultaneously address multiple questions of interest within various epidemiological settings.

Contradictions And Limitations
Since no UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification, intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification. The 20% cutoff was selected based on the mutation profile from sequencing the synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA controls from Twist Bioscience. Some true intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% might be missed. The occurrence of noise may be exacerbated by low viral copy inputs in the multiplex PCR, or low read depth per amplicon in sequencing. It is still necessary to verify and validate the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and the other coronaviruses and respiratory viruses by this metagenomic method. The coverage was lower than expected for one genome, which might have been caused by the poor sample quality resulting from processing or handling the viral RNA or library.

Claims
The multiplex PCR method is more sensitive than RT-PCR and can detect SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers. The mathematical model estimated that the SARS-CoV-2 panel can detect 1.15 copies of the virus at 95% probability. Using both primer pools would lead to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. The theoretical calculation gives a 66% probability to sample 1.1 copies, and a 12% chance to detect them based on a multiplex PCR efficiency of 6%. The experimental probability to detect 1.1 copies was significantly higher at 56%, suggesting the efficiency of multiplex PCR is actually higher than the previously estimated 6%. The multiplex PCR method can be tailored to simultaneously address multiple questions of interest within various epidemiological settings. The method can be used for the detection of new and ever-evolving viral strains.
The multiplex PCR method can be used for full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 and detection of mutations. The full SARS-CoV-2 genome was amplified from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens. The mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms, and only mutations detected by both methods were reported. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. Since no UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification, intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification. The occurrence of noise may be exacerbated by low viral copy inputs in the multiplex PCR, or low read depth per amplicon in sequencing. The method can be used for the surveillance of SARS-CoV-2's evolution and for the containment of community spread. The method can be used for phylogenetic studies through genome sequence analysis.
The multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method can detect SARS-CoV-2 and potentially novel or emerging isolates with modest sequencing depth. The method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA. The method required approximately 0.6M of total reads per library. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. It is still necessary to verify and validate the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and the other coronaviruses and respiratory viruses by this metagenomic method. Increasing sequencing depth alone might not improve the coverage of the targeted regions further. The method can be used for the identification of novel pathogens with a moderate sequencing depth. The method can be used for the detection of highly mutated viruses that would otherwise not be amplified by the predesigned primer pairs.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the mathematical model of RT-PCR detection. Figure 1B shows the panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers. Figure 1C shows the mathematical model of multiplex-PCR-based detection method. Figure 2A shows the library peaks of expected sizes obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. Figure 2B shows the wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids. Figure 2C shows the experimentally observed probability to detect 1.1 copies was significantly higher at 56%. Figure 2D shows the recovered reads were within a range of about 20-fold relative depth with about 1.4 to 2.8 plasmids. Figure 2E shows approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids, 77% with 2.8 copies, and 37% with 0.6 copies. Figure 3A shows about 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. Figure 3B shows at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X with 50,000 total reads per library. Figure 3C shows the superior uniformity of the number of amplicons amplified in the multiplex PCR reaction. Figure 3D shows the log10 distance of the number of each amplicon to the mean number of all amplicons in the library. Figure 3E shows the majority of the mutations identified in these 13 SARS-CoV-2 genomes clustered around 7 loci. Figure 4A shows 16% of the recovered bases, or 13% of the recovered reads, were within the viral N and S genes. Figure 4B shows 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered. Figure 4C shows the base coverage was significantly higher for SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial targets than for human targets. Figure 4D shows the human exonic regions were preferentially amplified. Figure 4E shows the long gaps and lack of coverage in very large repetitive regions were observed in human chromosomes. Figure 4F shows the gaps in SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial regions were significantly shorter. Figure 4G shows 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered. Supplemental Table 2 shows the viral load ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL. Supplemental Table 3 shows the mutations identified in these 13 SARS-CoV-2 genomes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for the detection and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration that the full SARS-CoV-2 genome was amplified from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens. 3. The future path is to expand the panel to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus.

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime; Galina Lebedev; Jackline Abo-Nassar; Sally Marzouk; Moshe Inbar; Murad Ghanim; Radi Aly
summary.field_subfield: Entomology / Plant-Integrated Pest Management (phytoecdysteroid bioactivity)
summary.executive_summary: This preprint investigates whether crude leaf and stem extracts of the Lamiaceae plant Ajuga iva can serve as a green, plant-derived pest-control agent against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The authors build on their prior identification and quantification of three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) and two clerodanes in Israeli-grown A. iva (Taha-Salaime et al. 2019), hypothesizing that these compounds, which interfere with insect molting and metamorphosis, could reduce larval damage. Using a diet-based bioassay, they smeared mature castor bean leaves with aqueous A. iva crude extract and exposed first- and third-instar S. littoralis larvae to three concentrations (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl). Results showed a clear dose-dependent effect: first-instar mortality rose from 5% (control) to 25%, 65%, and 85% at the three concentrations, while third-instar larvae exhibited reduced larval weight gain (LWG), reduced relative growth rate (RGR), and reduced survival. Critically, larvae fed first on control leaves and then on treated leaves (and vice versa) still suffered reduced RGR and mortality, indicating a direct effect on the gut rather than merely a nutritional effect. Histological analysis of the larval gut revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filaments, consistent with gut epithelial deterioration and apoptosis. Pupation was also disrupted, with larvae unable to reach the threshold weight for pupation. The authors note that a purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (250 µg/µl) reproduced much of the effect, while a low-concentration commercial standard mixture (100 ppm each) had no significant effect, underscoring the importance of concentration. They conclude that A. iva phytoecdysteroids may be useful in integrated pest management programs while reducing risks to human health and the environment. The study is notable for using a fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture as a mechanistic control, for testing both feeding orders to isolate direct gut effects, and for combining bioassay with confocal histology. Limitations include the high cost of commercial standards, the difficulty of calibrating clerodane fractionation, and the absence of clerodane-specific assays. The paper is a bioRxiv preprint posted March 13, 2020, and is not yet peer-reviewed.

claims.description: Crude A. iva leaf extract significantly reduces the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner.
Phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut, causing histological damage.
The phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for pest management while reducing risks to human health and the environment.

Using a diet-based bioassay, they smeared mature castor bean leaves with aqueous A. iva crude extract and exposed first- and third-instar S. littoralis larvae to three concentrations (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl). Critically, larvae fed first on control leaves and then on treated leaves (and vice versa) still suffered reduced RGR and mortality, indicating a direct effect on the gut rather than merely a nutritional effect. Histological analysis of the larval gut revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filaments, consistent with gut epithelial deterioration and apoptosis. Pupation was also disrupted, with larvae unable to reach the threshold weight for pupation. The authors note that a purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (250 µg/µl) reproduced much of the effect, while a low-concentration commercial standard mixture (100 ppm each) had no significant effect, underscoring the importance of concentration. They conclude that A. iva phytoecdysteroids may be useful in integrated pest management programs while reducing risks to human health and the environment. The study is notable for using a fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture as a mechanistic control, for testing both feeding orders to isolate direct gut effects, and for combining bioassay with confocal histology. Limitations include the high cost of commercial standards, the difficulty of calibrating clerodane fractionation, and the absence of clerodane-specific assays. The paper is a bioRxiv preprint posted March 13, 2020, and is not yet peer-reviewed.

Research Context
Insects cause severe damage to numerous crops and their control relies on pesticides. Green control is becoming increasingly popular due to concerns about the negative impacts of pesticides on the environment. The African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis is considered one of the most serious pests of cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals and orchard trees. Many organic insecticides have been derived from plant sources, and some, such as alkaloids, terpenoids, phenols and steroids, exhibit very high toxicity against a variety of agricultural pests. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroids that are analogs of the steroid hormones that control molting and metamorphosis in arthropods. Phytoecdysteroids may cause abnormal larval development, feeding deterrence and ultimately, death. Ecdysone, a natural molting hormone of insects derived from enzymatic modification of cholesterol by p450 enzymes, controls developmental events by changing the levels of other ecdysteroids. The ecdysone receptor is a nuclear receptor (a ligand-activated transcription factor) that binds to and is activated by ecdysteroids. Discovery of the same molecules (phytoecdysteroids) in several plant species suggests that they may be effective against insect herbivores by acting as antifeedants and/or disrupting the insects' endogenous endocrine levels. Kubo (1997) reported that an extract of Ajuga remota containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone, added to the diet of Bombyx mori, inhibited ecdysis, resulting in larval retention of the exuvial head capsule and the insect's death. An extract of 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone from A. iva showed high activity against Oligonychus perseae. Clerodanes (diterpenoids) are a large group of C20 terpene compounds derived from geranylgeranyl diphosphate and biosynthesized through the deoxyxylulose phosphate pathway in the cytoplasm. Clerodin was originally isolated from Clerodendrum infortunatum L. (Lamiaceae), and has potential as a natural pesticide due to its insect antifeedant and repellent activities. We previously identified and quantified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids and two clerodanes in A. iva growing in Israel. We hypothesized that crude extract of A. iva leaves that includes the three phytoecdysteroids, which specifically interfere by controlling molting, might be a promising pest-control agent.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether crude A. iva leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae, with the hypothesis that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes reduce larval damage. The authors hypothesized that crude extract of A. iva leaves that includes the three phytoecdysteroids, which specifically interfere by controlling molting, might be a promising pest-control agent. A key question is whether phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae. A key question is whether phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut. The predicted outcome is that A. iva crude extract reduces S. littoralis larval development and survival in a dose-dependent manner. The predicted outcome is that phytoecdysteroids interfere with developmental stages, especially during metamorphosis. The predicted outcome is that the effect on pupation is a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance effected by internal levels of ecdysone. The predicted outcome is that larvae fed on phytoecdysteroid-treated leaves cannot develop and survive. The predicted outcome is that exogenous application of ecdysteroids is lethal to larvae and toxic to midgut epithelial cells. The predicted outcome is that reduced growth rate reflects another possible mode of action of phytoecdysteroids. The predicted outcome is that abnormal gut development leads to reduced LWG, leading to mortality. The predicted outcome is that the phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for pest management while reducing risks to human health and the environment.

Methodological Details
Plant material was collected from fresh A. iva plants growing in Israel after blooming (July-November). Young and mature leaves and stems were oven-dried at 55 °C for 3-4 days, then homogenized to a fine powder. The African cotton leafworm colony was reared on castor bean leaves in Murad Ghanim's laboratory, Department of Entomology, Agricultural Research Organization. First and third instars of S. littoralis larvae were used for the bioassays. Leaf and stem powder (24 g) was soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH, sealed and homogenized with shaking (2500 rpm) for 1 h. The extract was centrifuged (112 g) for 10 min, filtered and concentrated under vacuum. The final filtered methanol solution was analyzed by liquid chromatography-time of flight-mass spectrometry (LC-TOF-MS). For purification, leaf and stem powder (100 g) was soaked in 300 ml methanol and homogenized. The filtered extract was vacuum-concentrated and treated with H2O to give 30% aqueous methanol. LC-TOF-MS analysis was used to identify and confirm the presence of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes in three concentrations (50, 100 and 250 µg/µl). Extracts (1 µl) were injected into an Agilent 1290 Infinity Series liquid chromatograph coupled with an Agilent 1290 Infinity DAD and Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) was used to separate the components into well-defined spots. The crude leaf extract, the pure isolated compounds (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A and cyasterone) and a commercial ecdysterone sample were applied to silica gel GF-254 plates (0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm). Mature castor bean leaves were smeared with aqueous A. iva crude leaf extract (1:10) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg), then dried in a chemical hood for 2 h. Control leaves were smeared with double-distilled water (ddH2O) and Tween 20. Larvae were exposed to three concentrations of crude leaf extract (50, 100 and 250 µg/µl), one concentration per treatment. Larvae were allowed to feed for 3 days in a climate-controlled room at 25 °C. Larval mortality was compared to that of controls using a t-test, with significance determined by t-test. For third instars, 1 or 10 larvae were fed on 1 treated castor bean leaf for 4 or 8 days at 25 °C. Four different treatments were tested, including a fractionated mixture of three phytoecdysteroids from A. iva leaf extract. Relative growth rate (RGR) was calculated as (ln W2 -ln W1)/ (t2 -t1), where W1 and W2 are weights at times t1 and t2. RGRs were compared using a mixed-model ANOVA (repeated measures ANOVA until day 4 and two-way ANOVA from day 4 to the end). Survival rates were analyzed using a Friedman test, since the data for larval survival did not follow a normal distribution. Data for larval weight gain (LWG) are the result of 10 replicates (10 larvae in each replicate). Comparisons of LWG were assessed using a repeated measures ANOVA. Statistical significance was reported at p < 0.05. Error bars in all graphs represent the standard error of the mean (SEM). All statistical analyses were performed with IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows. Larvae fed on treated and control leaves were tested after 7 days of treatment for gut morphology. Guts were dissected in phosphate buffered saline (1X PBS), then fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1X PBS for 30 min. Guts were washed in 0.1% Triton X-100 for 30 min, then incubated in 0.1% phalloidin in PBST for 30 min. Guts were mounted whole in 0.1% DAPI in hybridization buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 0.9 M NaCl, 0.01% w/v sodium dodecyl sulfate, 30% v/v formamide). Changes in actin fibers and nuclei were visualized under a Leica confocal microscope (Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81). Data in the first-instar experiment represent the results of 11 replicates (10 larvae/replicate).

Procedures And Architectures
A. iva crude extracts were prepared according to the recently published procedure (Taha-Salaime et al. 2019). The crude leaf extract was dried in a chemical hood; 1.2 g dried extract powder was dissolved in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 (0.5 mg/ml) for the 250 µg/µl concentration. 0.83 ml of the high concentration (250 µg/µl) extract was dissolved in 3 ml ddH2O to obtain the 100 µg/µl concentration. 0.67 ml of the 100 µg/µl solution was dissolved in 3 ml ddH2O to obtain the 50 µg/µl concentration. A. iva crude leaf extract was subjected to flash chromatography on a silica gel (TLC), yielding three individual isolated compounds. The retention factor (Rf) values of the phytoecdysteroid spots were similar to those of the respective commercial ecdysteroids. The effect of A. iva crude leaf extract and purified phytoecdysteroid mixture on larval gut was examined using DAPI and phalloidin staining. Phalloidin is an actin-specific marker that binds to the interface between adjacent actin monomers in the F-actin polymer. DAPI stains the nuclei. Changes in actin fibers and nuclei were visualized under a Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope. The fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture was tested at 250 µg/µl, corresponding to a maximum of 100 ppm each of the three commercial standards. The crude leaf extract and phytoecdysteroid fraction treatments corresponded to 250,000 ppm. S. littoralis larvae were fed on castor bean leaf treated with 100 ppm of the mixture for 8 days. No significant effect of the mixture on S. littoralis larvae was seen. Tanaka (1995) reported altered epidermal sensitivity to 20-hydroxyecdysone at 300 ppm ecdysone, higher than the standard concentration used in our study. Kubo (1993) conducted an artificial diet-feeding assay with the wheat aphid Schizaphis graminum, showing ajugasterone C was 10-fold more potent as a feeding deterrent than 20-hydroxyecdysone. The omission of clerodane fractionation was due to the difficulty involved in calibrating the protocol for fractionation and the high cost of commercial clerodane standards. We only used a few commercial standards because they are very expensive and are not feasible as a control treatment. The larvae were exposed to three concentrations of crude leaf extract (50, 100 and 250 µg/µl) for 4 days. More freshly treated leaves were provided after 4 days of feeding to avoid feeding on decayed leaves. Pupation was evaluated for an additional 15 days.

Key Results
None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days for the highest concentration and 10 days for the other concentrations (Fig. 3b). When larvae were first fed on control leaves and then on treated leaves, RGR was affected after day 5 (F3.16, 18 =7.310, p < 0.001), with no surviving larvae (X2 3 = 9.282, p = 0.021). The same result was obtained when the order of the treatments was reversed (Fig. 4c, d). When larvae were first fed on treated leaves and then on control leaves, a significant decrease in RGR was obtained on days 2-4 (p = 0.034, 0.02 and 0.001 for 50, 100 and 250 µg/µl). Castor bean leaves treated with 250 µg/µl of the mixture of the three fractionated and purified phytoecdysteroids significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001). Few larvae survived on the leaves treated with purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (X2 3 = 11.305, p = 0.04). Larvae feeding on 250 µg/µl A. iva crude leaf extract for 8 days had smaller nuclei with an abnormal shape (Fig. 6d-f). In guts from larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract or 250 µg/µl of the three phytoecdysteroids, the actin filaments were smaller and their amount reduced (Fig. 6d-i). Larvae fed 250 µg/µl of crude leaf extract or 250 µg/µl of its phytoecdysteroid fraction for 8 days were unable to complete their development and pupate after 15 days (Fig. 7). The dying larvae had short limbs, small heads, decreased weight and only stomach and chest pupated, considered nonpupation. None of them completed their development to adult moths.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results support the hypothesis that A. iva crude extract reduces S. littoralis development and survival across all larval stages, including pupation. The dose-dependent effect indicates that A. iva crude leaf extract was most effective at the highest concentration applied. The effect on pupation is a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance effected by internal levels of ecdysone. The larvae did not reach the threshold weight for pupation and they died because they could not complete their life cycle. The gut epithelium showed massive deterioration, destruction of the microvilli of the columnar cells, and formation of vacuoles. The histological observations support the notion that the effect on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance. The reduced growth rate suggests that larvae are adversely affected by ingestion of the crude leaf extract and of the mixture of three phytoecdysteroids. Disruptions in gut morphology and disappearance of microfilament structures in actin could be a consequence of the phytoecdysteroid titers in A. iva crude leaf extract. The fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture reproduced much of the crude extract effect, supporting a phytoecdysteroid mode of action. The low-concentration commercial standard mixture had no significant effect, underscoring the importance of concentration. The results suggest that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for pest management while reducing risks to human health and the environment. The results are in agreement with previous studies suggesting that insect herbivores cannot develop and survive when fed on phytoecdysteroid-treated leaves.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is a bioRxiv preprint posted March 13, 2020, and is not yet certified by peer review. The authors did not fractionate clerodanes from A. iva crude leaf extract due to the difficulty involved in calibrating the protocol for fractionation and the high cost of commercial clerodane standards. The low-concentration commercial standard mixture (100 ppm each) had no significant effect, which may contradict the crude extract effect at 250,000 ppm. The omission of clerodane-specific assays limits the ability to attribute effects to clerodanes versus phytoecdysteroids. The study used only first and third instars, omitting other developmental stages. The study used only castor bean leaves as the feeding substrate, which may limit generalizability.

Claims
Crude A. iva leaf extract significantly reduces the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae in a dose-dependent manner. First instar mortality increased to 25, 65, 85% at 50, 100 and 250 µg/µl. Third instar LWG was significantly reduced (p < 0.001). The extract was most effective at the highest concentration applied. Larval survival was significantly reduced after 11 days (p = 0.038). The low-concentration commercial standard mixture had no significant effect. The results suggest that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for pest management. The results may reduce the risks to human health and the environment. The results are in agreement with previous studies on phytoecdysteroid-treated leaves.
Phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut, causing histological damage. Larvae fed on control leaves and then treated leaves still had reduced RGR. The actin filaments were smaller and their amount reduced (Fig. 6d-i). The gut epithelium showed massive deterioration and formation of vacuoles. The histological observations support the notion that the effect on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance.  The results suggest that phytoecdysteroids may affect insects by interfering with their developmental stages. The results support the use of A. iva extracts in IPM programs.
The phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for pest management while reducing risks to human health and the environment. The results suggest that phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes of A. iva may be useful for pest management. The results may reduce the risks to human health and the environment. Ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals because their structure is quite different from mammalian steroids. The study is a bioRxiv preprint and is not yet certified by peer review. The results may provide a green alternative to synthetic insecticides. The results may support the development of new pest-control agents.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture reproduced much of the crude extract effect, supporting a phytoecdysteroid mode of action. The low-concentration commercial standard mixture had no significant effect, which may contradict the crude extract effect.

Ethical Considerations
The study used S. littoralis larvae, which are agricultural pests, not vertebrates. The study used castor bean leaves as the feeding substrate, which may limit generalizability.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the Rf values of the phytoecdysteroid spots were similar to those of the respective commercial ecdysteroids. Fig. 2a shows first instar mortality (25, 65, 85%) at 50, 100 and 250 µg/µl, compared to the control (5%). Fig. 2b shows third instar LWG was significantly reduced (p < 0.001). Fig. 3a shows larval RGR was significantly decreased (p < 0.001) compared to the control diet. Fig. 3b shows third instar larval survival was significantly reduced after 11 days (p = 0.038). Fig. 4a shows RGR was affected after day 5 (p < 0.001), with no surviving larvae (p = 0.021). Fig. 5a shows castor bean leaves treated with 250 µg/µl of the phytoecdysteroid mixture significantly reduced RGR (p = 0.001). Fig. 6d-f shows larvae fed on 250 µg/µl A. iva crude leaf extract for 8 days had smaller nuclei with an abnormal shape. Fig. 6d-i shows the actin filaments were smaller and their amount reduced in treated larvae. Fig. 7 shows larvae fed 250 µg/µl of crude leaf extract or 250 µg/µl of its phytoecdysteroid fraction were unable to pupate after 15 days.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that crude A. iva leaf extract and its fractionated phytoecdysteroids significantly reduce the development and survival of S. littoralis larvae. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-dependent increase in first-instar mortality (25, 65, 85%) and the histological gut damage showing reduced actin filaments and abnormally shaped nuclei. 3. The future path is the development of A. iva-based phytoecdysteroid formulations for integrated pest management, pending further fractionation and dose-response studies.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular biology / Translation biology
summary.executive_summary: Ribosomes are evolutionarily conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes that function as two separate subunits across all kingdoms of life. During translation initiation, the small (30S) and large (50S) subunits assemble into the mature ribosome, which translates messenger RNA. When a ribosome reaches a stop codon, release factors drive termination and peptide release, and recycling factors dissociate the subunits for reuse. A tethered ribosome, Ribo-T, in which the two subunits are covalently linked into a single entity, was recently described in Escherichia coli. A hybrid ribosomal RNA combining both small and large subunit rRNA sequences was engineered, and the resulting ribosome was shown to be functional and to sustain cell growth. Here, Fabret and Namy investigated the translational properties of Ribo-T, analyzing its behavior in -1 and +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. They used the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain with and without the poRibo-T2 vector carrying the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA, and the pCL99 dual reporter system (lacZ-luc fusion) to quantify translational efficiency. Previous work reported slower doubling times (107 min for Ribo-T versus 35 min for wild-type) and a protein synthesis rate of 50% that of wild-type ribosomes, attributed to slower Ribo-T biogenesis rather than impaired activity. The authors' central hypotheses were that covalent attachment of the subunits would impair the ribosome's ability to correctly initiate and terminate translation, and that it would alter frameshifting behavior. Their data indicate that covalent attachment modifies ribosome properties, altering its ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly. Specifically, Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift independently of the Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence for -1 frameshifting (13-14% for IS911, 33% for IS3, 43-45% for dnaX), but are strongly impaired for +1 frameshifting (2% versus 33% for wild-type). They use the SD sequence much less efficiently during translation initiation, and terminate translation less efficiently at stop codons (0.07% versus 0.013% for UAG, 0.26% versus 0.11% for UGA, 0.04% versus 0.01% for UAA). The authors propose that the SD-acceptor stem (ASD) sequence orientation is modified in Ribo-T ribosomes due to helix 44 (H44) tethering, preventing normal SD usage during initiation and elongation. These results highlight the greater-than-expected flexibility of ribosomes and raise the question of whether tethered ribosomes would be efficient in eukaryotes, which use a different translation initiation mechanism not involving SD-ASD interaction.

Ribo-T ribosomes use the SD sequence much less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes during translation initiation.
Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes at stop codons, promoting stop codon readthrough.

documents.judge_context:
