Executive Summary
This study addresses a long-standing paradox in cancer biology: while surgical removal of a primary tumor (PT) is often feared to accelerate residual disease, numerous case studies document spontaneous postoperative regression of metastases. The authors argue that this regression reflects the loss of pro-metastatic factors secreted by the primary tumor, and they present, for the first time, an animal model capable of empirically testing this hypothesis. Using a highly metastatic triple-negative breast cancer cell line (MDA-MB-231 HM) engineered to express a sensitive luciferase reporter, they tracked early micro-metastases in immunodeficient BALB/c nu/nu mice. Excision of the primary tumor produced dramatic regression of the smallest metastases (up to a 100-fold decrease in bioluminescent signal within 24 hours) but not of larger metastases, and regression was abolished by sham surgery. In vitro, tumor-conditioned medium enhanced cancer cell viability, adhesion, and endothelial tube formation, indicating that secreted factors support survival and growth. To identify the specific mediators, the authors combined a human cytokine array with unbiased mass spectrometry proteomics, converging on four candidate factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors with monoclonal antibodies completely blocked metastatic progression even in the presence of the primary tumor. The clinical relevance was assessed using the public TCGA provisional dataset, where high protein levels of these four factors correlated with poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The authors interpret these findings as evidence that the primary tumor secretome is a vital driver of early micro-metastatic survival, and that the perioperative window offers an opportunity to control minimal residual disease. They acknowledge limitations, including testing only four factors, the use of a xenograft rather than syngeneic models, and the unknown prevalence of spontaneous regression in patients. The study's key innovation is the sensitive luciferase reporter enabling detection of early-stage metastases and their regression into latent foci, which would be undetectable with lower-sensitivity methods. If generalized, these findings could inform novel prophylactic and therapeutic strategies targeting primary tumor-secreted factors during and after surgery.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment. Surgical removal has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease. Alternatively, regression may result from elimination of inhibitory signaling from the primary tumor. Numerous case studies report spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis. Such regression has been most commonly reported for lung metastases. Several mechanisms have been suggested, including surgical trauma and elimination of stimulating factors. Postulated mechanisms have not been empirically tested, as no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. The presence of a primary tumor is a systemic disease with continuous crosstalk to distant organs. The primary tumor secretes numerous factors that promote its growth and induce a pre-metastatic niche. Nonetheless, the presence of a primary tumor is generally believed to be primarily metastasis-inhibitory.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether primary tumor-secreted factors drive early micro-metastatic survival and regression upon excision. The authors hypothesize that removal of the primary tumor and its secreted factors induces regression of early-stage metastases. Regression is predicted to be specific to early metastatic stages, as larger metastases may be self-sufficient. Specific pro-metastatic factors are hypothesized to mediate regression when blocked in vivo. The authors predict that these factors correlate with poor survival in patients. The surgical-trauma hypothesis predicts no regression without excision, which is the predicted null outcome. The pre-metastatic niche theory predicts that secreted factors promote distant organ colonization.

Methodological Details
The cancer model used a highly metastatic triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma cell line, MDA-MB-231 HM. Cells were transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5g/L D-glucose and 110mg/L sodium pyruvate. Mice were eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice housed under SPF conditions. Mice were injected with 2×10^5 cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging following i.p. injection of 150 mg/kg D-luciferin. Excision occurred once metastatic foci reached 10^6 photons/s, with an average primary tumor size of 80mm^3. Follow-up imaging continued for 50 days post-excision, and animals were euthanized 10 min following luciferin injection. Tumor cell-conditioned medium was produced by incubating ~80% confluent cells with serum-free medium for 24 h. CM was collected from ~30 million cells and filtered through a 0.45μm strainer. CM was concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to a final volume of 100 μl/mouse. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with CM or SM and implanted i.p. The secretome released by minipumps was estimated to be ~1/8 of in vivo production. Adhesion studies used the IncuCyte system with imaging in 20 min intervals for 8 hours. Apoptosis studies used AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD staining analyzed by flow cytometry. Tube formation assays seeded HUVEC reconstituted in CM or SM on Cultrex BME. Human cytokine analysis used a Proteome Profiler Array (ARY022) comparing 102 soluble proteins. Mass spectrometry used UHPLC (Easy-nLC1000) and Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer. Proteomics analysis used MaxQuant with Label-free quantification and an FDR of 0.01. Enrichment analysis used Gene Ontology annotations with an FDR threshold of 0.02. Neutralizing antibodies targeted CXCL8/IL-8, Serpin E1/PAI-1, PDGF-AA, and MIF. Antibodies were injected at 1μg each/mouse once a day for two days. Lung sections (6 μm) were stained for Hematoxylin and Eosin. Patient outcome analysis used the public TCGA provisional dataset via cBioPortal. Survival analysis used Kaplan Meier Analysis with hazard ratio calculated in R software. Statistical analysis used ANOVA with significance level of 0.05 and Fisher's PLSD contrasts.

Procedures And Architectures
Primary tumor resection was performed under 2% isoflurane anesthesia with a small incision. The incision avoided injuring the peritoneal cavity, and the skin was immediately sutured. Sham surgery involved an identical incision but left the primary tumor untouched. For in vivo supplementation, CM was implanted immediately following tumor excision. Animals were randomly assigned to experimental conditions. Cancer cells were seeded in either SM or CM for adhesion and apoptosis studies. The cytokine array compared CM with plasma from tumor-bearing, post-excision, and control mice. Proteins were digested overnight with LysC/Trypsin mix and sequencing-grade modified Trypsin. Peptides were separated by reverse-phase chromatography with a 140 min linear gradient. MS analysis used a top10 method fragmenting the 10 most abundant peaks by HCD. MS/MS spectra were referenced to the Uniprot human proteome by the Andromeda search engine. Statistical analysis used two-sided tests with paired or unpaired student's t-test. The cocktail of antibodies was injected 24 h prior to tumor excision at an early metastatic stage. The early metastatic stage was defined by chest bioluminescence below 10^6 p/s. The model relies on the sensitive luciferase reporter to detect early-stage micro-metastases. The study design distinguishes surgical-procedure effects from tumor-mass removal effects. The four-factor blockade was designed to mimic the effect of primary tumor removal. The cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Factors evident in non-tumor or post-excision plasma were excluded from candidates. The proteomic analysis identified 2,600 proteins, 359 annotated as extracellular factors. Pathway enrichment identified apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation.

Key Results
Excision of the primary tumor caused a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal of up to 100-fold within 24 h. The decrease was statistically significant with p<0.0001 following tumor excision. Metastases regressed into latent foci with no signal increase for 50 days post-excision. Microscopic malignant foci were evident on day 1 and 50 days later, confirmed by H&E staining. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases, with p<0.000. Metastases regressed following excision but continued to increase in sham surgery mice, p<0.05. Tumor-conditioned medium enhanced viability with p<0.001 compared to serum-free medium. Tumor-conditioned medium enhanced adhesion with p<0.01 compared to serum-free medium. Tumor-conditioned medium induced tube formation with p<0.0001 compared to serum-free medium. Mice treated with tumor-conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression than serum-free medium, p<0.005. The cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Four candidate factors were identified: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. Mass spectrometry identified 2,600 proteins, 359 annotated as extracellular factors. Antibody neutralization of the four factors completely blocked metastatic progression, p<0.0001. No difference in regression was evident between groups on post-excision day-1. High protein levels of the four factors correlated with poor survival, hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05. The patient cohort was a lung adenocarcinoma cohort from the TCGA provisional dataset. The survival analysis used relative protein levels in RPPA assay. The four factors were validated in CM using ELISA. Larger micrometastases showed lower or no regression, potentially due to self-sufficiency.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings indicate a crucial supportive role for the tumor secretome in survival and progression of distant metastatic foci. The four factors act through multiple mechanisms affecting both malignant cells and their microenvironment. The study provides an opportunity to empirically study metastatic regression into latent foci. The findings may explain the rare but validated clinical phenomenon of spontaneous regression. The perioperative period could be exploited to control minimal residual disease. Identifying critical factors via biopsy may enable individually tailored neutralizing antibody combinations. Such treatment could counteract the metastasis-promoting effects of surgery. The perioperative period presents a window of opportunity for high-impact interventions. The four factors promote angiogenesis and/or suppress tumor apoptosis. IL-8 is a pro-angiogenic and pro-inflammatory chemokine promoting EMT and invasion. SerpinE1 promotes metastases by increasing thrombosis and inducing anti-apoptotic activities. PDGFaa acts as a survival factor, inhibiting apoptosis and increasing vessel density. MIF initiates the NF-κB signaling cascade and promotes MMPs activity. The findings suggest that established larger metastatic foci may be self-sufficient. The sensitive luciferase reporter enabled detection of regression that would be missed at lower sensitivity. The results support the systemic disease model with continuous crosstalk between PT and distant organs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study contradicts the prevailing belief that the primary tumor is primarily metastasis-inhibitory. The regression is specific to early micro-metastases, not larger metastases, limiting generalizability. Only four key secreted factors were tested, though many others may be involved. The study used a xenograft model rather than syngeneic lines, limiting generalizability. The prevalence of post-operative regression in cancer patients is currently unknown. The amount of secretome released by minipumps was estimated, not measured directly. The study acknowledges that the phenomenon may be overlooked due to low detection sensitivity. The four-factor blockade may not fully replicate the complete removal of all secreted factors. The in vitro effects were observed in MDA-MB-231 HM cells specifically. The clinical correlation was based on a public provisional dataset, which may have limitations.

Claims
Primary tumor-secreted factors drive early micro-metastatic survival and regression upon excision. Excision caused a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal of up to 100-fold. Tumor-conditioned medium enhanced viability, adhesion, and tube formation. Antibody neutralization of four factors completely blocked metastatic progression. High protein levels correlated with poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients. Regression was less prominent in larger metastases, suggesting self-sufficiency. Sham surgery did not elicit regression, ruling out surgical trauma as a mechanism. Only four factors were tested, though many others may be involved. The perioperative period could be exploited to control minimal residual disease. Individually tailored neutralizing antibody combinations may be developed. The findings may explain spontaneous regression following PT excision.
The four identified factors (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) promote metastasis through multiple mechanisms. All four factors promote angiogenesis and/or suppress tumor apoptosis. IL-8 promotes EMT and invasion of tumor cells. SerpinE1 increases thrombosis and induces anti-apoptotic activities. MIF initiates the NF-κB signaling cascade. The factors may act through shared and distinct pathways, complicating targeting. Other secreted factors are likely also involved in supporting metastatic progression. Targeting these factors could tilt the balance toward eradication of metastases. Syngeneic lines should be studied to identify other or common mediating factors.
The sensitive luciferase reporter enables detection of early-stage metastases and their regression. The sensitive reporter enabled detection of metastases that would not occur at advanced stages. Microscopic malignant foci were evident on day 1 and 50 days later. The model enabled study of early-stage micro-metastases. The phenomenon may be overlooked due to low detection sensitivity in other models. Larger micrometastases showed lower or no regression, limiting the model's scope. The model provides an opportunity to explore mediating mechanisms. The approach may be applicable to other animal models.

Data And Code Availability
The study used public datasets (TCGA provisional dataset via cBioPortal). Proteomics data analysis used MaxQuant and Perseus software. The String database and Cytoscape software were used for network analysis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study distinguished surgical-procedure effects from tumor-mass removal effects via sham surgery. Antibody neutralization was tested versus IgG control. The four-factor blockade was designed to test combined effects. The cytokine array and proteomics provided complementary approaches. The in vitro effects were validated in MDA-MB-231 HM cells. The clinical correlation was based on a public provisional dataset.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees. Mice were housed under SPF conditions on a 12 h dark/light cycle. Surgical procedures were performed under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. The incision avoided injuring the peritoneal cavity to minimize harm. Animals were euthanized 10 min following luciferin injection at the endpoint.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B showed a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal following tumor excision. Figure 1E showed regression was less prominent in larger metastases. Figure 1F showed regression following excision but not in sham surgery. Figure 2A showed enhanced viability with tumor-conditioned medium. Figure 2B showed enhanced adhesion with tumor-conditioned medium. Figure 2C showed induced tube formation with tumor-conditioned medium. Figure 2D showed 10-fold less regression with tumor-conditioned medium. Figure 3A showed pathways involved in early stages of metastasis. Figure 3B showed antibody neutralization completely blocked metastatic progression. Figure 3C showed no difference in regression on post-excision day-1. Figure 3D showed high protein levels associated with lower survival. Table S1 listed factors excluded from candidates. Figure 2 showed tumor-secreted factors affecting malignant cells and microenvironment.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that primary tumor-secreted factors drive early micro-metastatic survival and that their neutralization arrests metastatic progression. 2. The strongest evidence is the complete blockade of metastatic progression by antibody neutralization of four factors, p<0.0001. 3. The future path involves developing individually tailored neutralizing antibody combinations during the perioperative period.

summary.title: Activation of Macrophages by CpG DNA and LPS: an FTIR Spectroscopic Study
summary.authors: Emrulla Spahiu, Senol Dogan, Jörg Schnauß, Mayda Gursel, Feride Severcan
summary.field_subfield: Analytical/biophysical chemistry applied to immunology
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (spectroscopic investigation of macrophage activation)
summary.executive_summary: This study applies Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy to monitor the global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The authors state that "Whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to global molecular changes in cells that are detected by FTIR spectroscopy is currently unknown," framing the central knowledge gap. Using ATR-FTIR, they avoided the water-absorption limitation of conventional IR by employing a diamond-ZnSe crystal and direct sample deposition, requiring only a small amount of sample. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduced the dimensionality of the spectral data, with PC-1 accounting for 83% of variability and PC-2 for 11%, enabling identification of the sources of variation. Detailed peak analysis revealed that CpG DNA and LPS increase total nucleic acid concentration from the early periods post-activation, with DNA synthesis following RNA synthesis. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ (ribose vibration) was shown to indicate the activation state of macrophages in early periods post-treatment, allowing detection as early as 10 minutes. Protein concentration increased rapidly initially and leveled off two hours post-activation, as reflected by the amide I (1639 cm⁻¹) and amide II (1540 cm⁻¹) peaks. Both activated groups increased the concentration of fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol, pointing to a shared synthesis pathway and de novo lipogenesis. The study concludes that FTIR spectroscopy can serve as an independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of murine macrophages. The authors emphasize that this technique provides a broad view of the relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, proteins, and other metabolites that are not readily accessible by other techniques, contrasting with the trending omics techniques that yield precise quantitative data on specific molecules. The experimental design used four time points (10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h) to evaluate the kinetics of induced effects, with five replicates per group. The findings align with prior gene expression studies showing that LPS induces up to 263 genes and that CpG DNA induces short-lived immune activation regulated by synchronized inducers and suppressors. This work demonstrates the utility of FTIR as a non-destructive, rapid, and high-throughput tool for studying cellular responses to stimulatory motifs, which can foster the design of oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) for therapeutic uses. The study contributes to understanding the rules governing cellular responses to stimulatory motifs, bridging the gap between bulk analysis and targeted molecular profiling.

summary.authors: Rosa M Mcguire, Kenji T Hayashi, Xinyi Yan, Marcel Caritá Vaz, Damla Cino Glu, Madeline C Cowen, Alejandra Martínez-Blancas, Lauren L Sullivan, Sheila Vazquez-Morales, Gaurav S Kandlikar
summary.field_subfield: Ecology and Evolutionary Biology (EEB) education and open-source software
summary.executive_summary: EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package and website that provides interactive Shiny apps simulating fundamental ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB) models, addressing a barrier to integrating theory and empirical work in the life sciences. The authors argue that mathematical models and their analytical solutions can seem foreign to empirically trained researchers, and that equation-heavy papers are cited less often and quantitative instructors receive worse student evaluations. Interactive tools, however, have been shown to increase student interest and understanding of quantitative concepts. EcoEvoApps addresses this gap by offering 11 interactive apps, functions to run models through the R console, and vignettes for customization and direct simulation. The package is freely available online via shinyapps.io or locally from the R console, and a core set of nine apps is available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The authors illustrate use cases at the level of an individual seeking familiarity with a model and in large undergraduate classroom settings. In classroom evaluations, 51 students at UCLA used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition, rating the apps on a 1-7 scale; an overwhelming majority (40/51) reported the apps were moderately to very helpful for learning the models as a whole. Similar surveys at the University of Missouri found substantial gains in student confidence, especially among higher-interest students. The authors note that EcoEvoApps is entirely open-source and written in R, distinguishing it from other interactive EEB education resources, and plan to incorporate evolutionary biology and population genetics models in future releases. The paper is a software/methods paper with classroom evaluation, providing preliminary evidence that shiny apps are useful tools for teaching quantitative models.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
EcoEvoApps is an open-source R package and website that provides interactive Shiny apps simulating fundamental ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB) models, addressing a barrier to integrating theory and empirical work in the life sciences. The authors argue that mathematical models and their analytical solutions can seem foreign to empirically trained researchers, and that equation-heavy papers are cited less often and quantitative instructors receive worse student evaluations. Interactive tools, however, have been shown to increase student interest and understanding of quantitative concepts. EcoEvoApps addresses this gap by offering 11 interactive apps, functions to run models through the R console, and vignettes for customization and direct simulation. The package is freely available online via shinyapps.io or locally from the R console, and a core set of nine apps is available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The authors illustrate use cases at the level of an individual seeking familiarity with a model and in large undergraduate classroom settings. In classroom evaluations, 51 students at UCLA used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition, rating the apps on a 1-7 scale; an overwhelming majority (40/51) reported the apps were moderately to very helpful for learning the models as a whole. Similar surveys at the University of Missouri found substantial gains in student confidence, especially among higher-interest students. The authors note that EcoEvoApps is entirely open-source and written in R, distinguishing it from other interactive EEB education resources, and plan to incorporate evolutionary biology and population genetics models in future releases. The paper is a software/methods paper with classroom evaluation, providing preliminary evidence that shiny apps are useful tools for teaching quantitative models.

Research Context
Integrating theory with observations and experiments is a fundamental driver of progress across the life sciences, including EEB. Research that synthesizes data with mathematical models can enable generalization, promote conceptual understanding, and inform policies. There is widespread agreement that more synergism between empiricists and theoreticians can yield fruitful insights. The language of mathematical models may seem foreign to those trained empirically, limiting integration. Equation-heavy papers tend to be cited less often, and quantitative instructors receive worse student evaluations. Calls for quantitative training focus primarily on statistical models or programming, with few advances in the pedagogy of theoretical models. Interactive tools that let users explore model structure and outcomes help increase student interest and understanding. Establishing a platform for interactive simulations of EEB models could facilitate communication between theoretical and empirical researchers. Theoretical models remain intimidating for many empirical researchers due to limited quantitative training in traditional curricula. Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions but can give easier access to theoretical insights.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central aim is to describe EcoEvoApps, an open-source R package and website providing interactive apps that simulate fundamental EEB models. The package should serve as a bridge to help users become familiar with coding and implementing theoretical models. The apps should help communicate and learn insights from theoretical models at both individual and classroom levels. The authors hypothesize that interactive apps will help students understand models as a whole and specific concepts like carrying capacity and coexistence. The authors expect that using interactive apps will lead to substantial gains in student confidence, especially among higher-interest students. The authors predict that EcoEvoApps will grow as a collaborative and inclusive effort, incorporating evolutionary biology and population genetics models. The authors anticipate building on the current collection with future releases of the package. The authors expect the interactive apps to be the primary avenue through which most users interact with the package. The authors plan to continue adding new apps and translating existing apps internally and via community contributions. The authors envision the package to grow as a collaborative and inclusive effort with community contributions.

Methodological Details
The study describes the first release of EcoEvoApps, an open-source R package (ecoevoapps) and website. The package is available at https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io and provides freely available interactive apps simulating fundamental EEB models. The package includes functions to directly run models through the R console, serving as a bridge to coding and implementing models. The authors chose models for the first release by surveying syllabi for undergraduate ecology courses and commonly-used textbooks. The first release includes 11 interactive apps, which the authors expect to be the primary avenue for most users. Some apps implement one specific model, while others present several closely related models. A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, and Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The apps are freely available online on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers or can be launched locally from the R console. The package provides functions with the prefix shiny_ that launch the apps from the R console. The package includes a vignette with instructions for customizing and deploying an app instance. The package includes model-specific vignettes with instructions for simulating model dynamics directly through R. The authors surveyed syllabi from undergraduate ecology courses and textbooks such as Gotelli (2008) and Begon and Townsend (2020). The UCLA classroom evaluation surveyed 51 students who used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition. The learning activity included short (~15 minutes) video lectures followed by a worksheet navigating guided exploration. Students rated on a scale of 1-7 the degree to which the apps helped them understand the model as a whole. The authors conducted similar surveys of students in a General Ecology course at the University of Missouri. The authors tracked individual students' interest and confidence in models before and after the activity. The classroom surveys were reviewed by the UCLA and MU Institutional Review Boards and determined to be exempt studies. The authors invite community contributions to writing new apps, adding features, translating apps, or contributing teaching plans. Author contributions were documented, with GSK coordinating and overseeing the project. The authors plan to prioritize incorporating evolutionary biology and population genetics models in future releases.

Procedures And Architectures
The shiny apps use functions in the ecoevoapps package to simulate and visualize model dynamics. Simulations are conducted by functions with the prefix run_, which take parameter values and other relevant information. For example, run_predprey_model() requires a vector of parameter values, initial population sizes, and time steps. The run_ functions return a dataframe of population sizes for each species over the specified time series. The package includes plotting functions prefixed plot_ that take the object returned by the corresponding run_ function. The plot_ functions return a ggplot2 object. The outputs in Fig. 1 can be generated using ecoevoapps functions. Users familiar with R can use these functions to conduct visualizations or analyses beyond those presented in the apps. The package can serve as a gateway for users to implement and manipulate mathematical models at the command line. The app includes three other tabs that incorporate logistic growth in the prey, type II functional response, or both. The app is available online at https://ecoevoapps.shinyapps.io/predator_prey_dynamics/ or can be deployed with shiny_predprey(). The complete list of functions for simulating and plotting model dynamics is provided in Table 1. Key Results
The first release of EcoEvoApps includes 11 interactive apps, which the authors expect to be the primary avenue for most users. A core set of nine apps are available in English, Spanish, and Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The paradox of enrichment can be visualized with the predator-prey model app by altering the prey carrying capacity (K). Low values of prey carrying capacity result in a stationary equilibrium or stable oscillations. High values of prey carrying capacity result in unstable oscillations that ultimately limit the system's persistence. Careful exploration of the parameter K can reveal the logic behind Rosenzweig (1971)'s conclusion about persistence. At K = 200, dampened oscillations arise when the predator isocline intersects the prey isocline to the right of the hump. At K = 500, unstable oscillations arise when the predator isocline intersects the prey isocline to the left of the hump. The study surveyed 51 students at UCLA who used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition. summary.field_subfield: Cell biology / Lymphangiogenesis signaling
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the intracellular signaling of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor, CTGF) in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor, but its roles in lymphangiogenesis remained unclear. Using primary cultured LECs, the authors found that CCN2 upregulated lymphatic endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, but not at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 significantly increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001) without affecting total ERK, and this effect was partially mediated by integrin av, since knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Although CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth, it enhanced the interaction between ERK and dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), which dephosphorylates ERK; knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels. In vivo Matrigel plug assays showed that exogenous CCN2 increased the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels and induced phospho-ERK-positive and DUSP6-positive LECs. These results suggest that CCN2-related lymphangiogenesis is regulated by DUSP6, which enables negative modulation of ERK-signaling. The study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding CCN2 signaling in lymphangiogenesis and identifies integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets for lymphatic diseases such as oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

CCN2 enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6, which negatively modulates ERK-signaling.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo via Matrigel plug assay.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the intracellular signaling of cellular communication network factor 2 (CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor, CTGF) in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor, but its roles in lymphangiogenesis remained unclear. Using primary cultured LECs, the authors found that CCN2 upregulated lymphatic endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4/Vegfr3) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, but not at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 significantly increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001) without affecting total ERK, and this effect was partially mediated by integrin av, since knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Although CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth, it enhanced the interaction between ERK and dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6), which dephosphorylates ERK; knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels. In vivo Matrigel plug assays showed that exogenous CCN2 increased the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels and induced phospho-ERK-positive and DUSP6-positive LECs. These results suggest that CCN2-related lymphangiogenesis is regulated by DUSP6, which enables negative modulation of ERK-signaling. The study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding CCN2 signaling in lymphangiogenesis and identifies integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 as potential therapeutic targets for lymphatic diseases such as oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

Research Context
CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein and a well-known angiogenic factor. CCN2 contains four structural domains including the TSP domain. CCN2 activates MAPKs such as p38 MAPK, ERK, and JNK. CCN2 interacts with integrins via its TSP and C-terminal domains. CCN2 is closely associated with lymphangiogenesis in fibrous diseases. CCN2 signaling in LECs in lymphangiogenic signaling has not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether CCN2 regulates lymphangiogenesis in LECs. The authors hypothesized that CCN2 activates ERK signaling in LECs. The authors hypothesized that CCN2-mediated ERK activation involves integrins. The authors hypothesized that CCN2 enhances ERK-DUSP6 interaction. The authors hypothesized that DUSP6 negatively modulates ERK-signaling. The authors predicted that CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo.

Methodological Details
Primary LECs were derived from C57BL/6 mice. LECs were cultured in EGM2 medium at 37°C with 5% CO2. Cells up to 6 passages were used in in vitro experiments. LECs were stimulated with 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100 or 200 ng/mL of CCN2. Gene expression was analyzed by quantitative RT-PCR. Phospho-RTKs were analyzed using a phospho-RTK array. Integrin mRNAs were examined in primary LECs treated with CCN2. Integrins and DUSP6 were suppressed by siRNA. siRNAs were designed using siDirect ver.2. Protein expression was analyzed by Western blot. Total protein was incubated with receptor-spotted membrane for RTK array. Immunoprecipitation used anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6 antibodies. Male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice were used for in vivo assays. Mice were euthanized at day 7 after injection. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism version 8. Statistical significance was set at a p-value of less than 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
Cell proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining. Cells were plated at 2 × 10^4 cells per well. Absorbance at 590 nm was measured using the SPARK 10M plate reader. Cell proliferation was expressed as the ratio to the absorbance at 0 h. Total RNA was prepared using the Purelink RNA purification Kit. cDNA was prepared from 1 μg of total RNA. Quantitative RT-PCR used TB Green Premix ExTaq II. LECs were pre-cultured with FBS-free medium for 24 h. Protein samples of 5-20 µg were separated with SDS-PAGE. The membrane was blocked in Blocking-one for 30 min. Primary antibodies were incubated at 4°C overnight. Secondary antibodies were incubated for 2 h. Signals were quantified using ImageQuant TL 8.1 software. Growth factor reduced Matrigel was mixed with recombinant rat CCN2. 450 µL of Matrigel and 8.33 µg of CCN2 were injected. Sections 4 µm thick were deparaffinized and stained with HE. Confocal microscopy used the LSM710 microscope. All experiments were performed more than three times.

Key Results
CCN2 upregulated Lyve1, Pdpn and Prox1 in a dose-dependent manner. At 200 ng/mL, marker expression dramatically decreased. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd and Flt4 but not Kdr. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged by CCN2. EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation were increased by CCN2. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2 (p<0.001). Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2. Itgav, Itga9 and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs. Knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Knockdown of integrin a9 slightly increased phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1 (p=0.05). Dusp6 was predominant among DUSPs in LECs. DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001 at 15 min). Phospho-ERK was increased at 15 min and up to 4 h. Phospho-ERK-positive LECs were detected in CCN2 plugs. DUSP6-positive LECs were detected in CCN2 plugs. The number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased by CCN2. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression were increased in CCN2 gel (p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av in LECs. CCN2 enhances the binding between ERK and DUSP6. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERK-signaling. DUSP6 suppresses excessive activation of ERK. Integrin av, ERK and DUSP6 may be therapeutic targets of OSCC. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 has not been analyzed.

Contradictions And Limitations
CCN2 weakly suppressed LEC proliferation in vitro. CCN2 enhanced lymphangiogenesis in vivo Matrigel assays. The discrepancy may be due to effects of ECM and MMP. The results between these assays may not be comparable. Integrin b1 loss was not compensated by integrins b2 and b3. Integrin a5 is increased by suppression of integrin b1. The interaction between CCN2 and integrin a5 has not been reported. The exact number of mice per group is not specified. The study used only C57BL/6 mice.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av in LECs. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased by CCN2. Knockdown of integrin av reduced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Itgav, Itga9 and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed. Knockdown of integrin a9 slightly increased phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was increased by suppression of integrin b1. Integrin av is a key mediator of CCN2 signaling. Integrin av may be a therapeutic target.
CCN2 enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6, which negatively modulates ERK-signaling. DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK, enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001). DUSP6 is highly expressed in LECs. CCN2 slightly decreased LEC growth. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 has not been analyzed. DUSP6 suppresses excessive activation of ERK. DUSP6 may be a therapeutic target.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo via Matrigel plug assay. The number of Podoplanin-positive vessels was increased. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 expression were increased (p<0.05). Tubular structures were observed in CCN2 gels. The discrepancy may be due to effects of ECM and MMP. The results between these assays may not be comparable. CCN2 positively modulated lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 may be relevant to OSCC progression.

Data And Code Availability
Primers are listed in Table S1. siRNA sequences are listed in Table S2. Antibodies are listed in Table S3. Supplementary figures are provided (Fig. S1-S4).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
All experiments were performed more than three times. The RTK assay was performed with n=2. Knockdown of integrin av reduced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). Knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001). Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK (p=0.05).

Ethical Considerations
All experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee. Experiments complied with relevant laws and institutional guidelines. Approval number was 2008024.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1A showed dose-dependent upregulation of Lyve1, Pdpn and Prox1. Fig. 1B showed increased Vegfc, Vegfd and Flt4. Fig. 2A showed increased phospho-ERK by CCN2. Fig. 3B showed reduced phospho-ERK by integrin av knockdown. Fig. 4A showed weak growth inhibition by CCN2. Fig. 5B showed DUSP6 co-precipitated with ERK. Fig. 6A showed blood vessels in CCN2 plugs. Fig. 7A showed phospho-ERK in CCN2 gel.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of CCN2-ERK-DUSP6 signaling in LECs. 2. The strongest evidence is the integrin av knockdown reducing phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). 3. The future path is analyzing FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 relationships.

summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay, Rebecca E Hewett, Noa T Smith, Tammy L Waters, John S Scandrett
summary.field_subfield: Molecular diagnostics / apicultural disease surveillance (environmental DNA)
summary.type_of_paper: Methodological study (novel sampling method + validated qPCR assay)
summary.executive_summary: American Foulbrood (AFB) is a devastating disease of honeybees caused by the spores of the Gram-positive bacterium Paenibacillus larvae, which infects larvae during development and can remain infectious for over 30 years. Diagnosis traditionally relies on the beekeeper's subjective visual inspection of capped brood cells using a 'roping' field test, an activity that is labour-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to missing disease, particularly with ERIC II strains that exhibit reduced clinical symptoms. The increase in hive numbers and densities in New Zealand, combined with a rise in less-skilled beekeepers, has led to an increase in the percentage of hives reported as infected from 0.21% in 2015 to 0.46% in 2021. While qPCR is the preferred diagnostic tool due to its speed and lower contamination risk, most applications have used it only for rapid confirmation of culture isolates rather than exploiting the quantitative data, which is important because low levels of AFB are often not clinically relevant. This study introduces the Foster method, a novel environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling method using colony entrance swabs together with a commercially available dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) for P. larvae. The authors evaluated and compared the levels of P. larvae among nurse bees, swabs from the entire baseboard, and entrance swabs across three cohorts of hives sampled from quarantine apiaries in multiple regions of New Zealand. The AFBduo assay demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, detecting down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction, with high amplification efficiency (ftsZ = 94%, 16S = 96%) and excellent linearity over 7 orders of magnitude (r = 0.998). The DNA extraction method from bees generated high purity DNA with OD260/280 measurements of between 1.8 and 1.9. Across the cohorts, 45 hives were sampled up to 6 times in the first cohort, 23 hives in the second, and pooled swab trials were conducted in the third. Statistical analyses using a binary logistic regression model and analysis of variance indicated a strong relationship between increasing spore levels and clinical signs (p = 0.00), with a spore quantity of 565,000 or more revealing a 95% probability of clinical signs being present. The study demonstrated that entrance swabs could clearly differentiate clinically infected hives from non-infected ones, even before visual symptoms were apparent, as shown by Hive 11 which developed clinical signs two weeks after sampling. The levels of P. larvae on whole baseboard and entrance swabs were similar, showing that dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard was not required. The authors also demonstrated the potential for the same DNA sample to be used to test for other bee pathogens such as Nosema ceranae, and for biosecurity surveillance for unwanted hive pests such as tracheal mites, tropilaelap mites, and small hive beetle. The Foster method is a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing that provides clinically significant information as to the AFB status of the hive.

claims.description: The Foster method, using colony entrance swabs combined with a dual-target qPCR assay, can detect clinically significant AFB levels rapidly and non-invasively, even before visual symptoms are apparent.
The AFBduo assay provides high analytical sensitivity and specificity, with the single copy ftsZ gene used for quantification purposes.
The DNA extraction method from bees generates high purity DNA, and the use of 10 bees permits easier and more convenient handling for DNA extraction.

The Foster method is a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing that provides clinically significant information as to the AFB status of the hive.

Research Context
AFB is one of the most destructive diseases in honeybees caused by spores of the Gram-positive bacteria Paenibacillus larvae. The spores are extremely hardy, resistant to heat and chemical treatments, and can remain infectious for over 30 years. Diagnosis is centred on the beekeeper's skill in recognising clinical symptoms, which is a highly subjective and time-consuming activity. Previous testing methods have relied on sampling that necessitates dismantling the hive and/or requires multiple visits to retrieve passive samples. The increase in hive numbers and densities combined with newer, less-skilled beekeepers has led to an increase in the percentage of hives reported as infected from 0.21% in 2015 to 0.46% in 2021. Clinical signs can vary based on the AFB genotype present, with ERIC II strains exhibiting reduced clinical symptoms. Confirmation of AFB has traditionally been performed by culture, which is a variable process and may take up to a week for results. Most molecular publications have relied on conventional PCR or SYBR Green-based qPCR and the sole use of the 16S gene due to its high sensitivity as a multicopy target. This sensitivity can be at the expense of specificity, as evidenced by the initial design and subsequent re-evaluation/re-design of qPCR primers to improve specificity. Low levels of AFB are often not clinically relevant, and such hives may never develop clinical symptoms. Many microbiological qPCR tests now routinely utilise two independent targets to enhance both sensitivity and specificity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a rapid, non-invasive colony entrance swab sampling method combined with a dual-target qPCR assay can detect clinically significant AFB levels. The study hypothesises that swabs from the hive entrance can detect relevant levels of P. larvae without the need to dismantle and disrupt the hive. The study hypothesises that quantification of P. larvae spore levels can identify hives with clinically significant infections, even before visual symptoms are apparent. The study hypothesises that the quantification data can be used to establish a threshold spore level that predicts the likelihood of clinical signs being present. The study hypothesises that the same DNA sample can be used to test for other bee pathogens and for biosecurity surveillance of unwanted hive pests. The predicted outcome is that entrance spore levels will correlate strongly with clinical disease likelihood, supporting the use of a single-copy ftsZ gene for quantification. The predicted outcome is that the Foster method will be a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing.

Methodological Details
Samples were collected from five quarantine apiaries around New Zealand in the East Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa and South Canterbury regions. Multiple hives were sampled two-monthly from late 2018 to early 2020, in addition to samples from visually clinical hives and neighbouring hives. Samples included nurse bees, swabs from the hive entrance and swabs from over the entire baseboard. Bees were collected from the brood frames using 50 mL sterile containers and frozen to euthanise the bees. Sterile foam-tipped swabs (Puritan) were moistened in sterile water before swabbing either the whole baseboard or just through and across the hive entrance for three to five seconds. Instructions were provided to participating beekeepers to rotate the swabs during collection to ensure all swab surfaces could collect hive material. Swab heads were snapped off into a 2 mL microcentrifuge tube, capped and sent to the laboratory with the bee samples at ambient temperature by overnight courier. Bee samples were frozen at -20°C and swabs were stored at ambient temperature until DNA extraction was performed. Genomic DNA extraction was performed from each sample containing 10 bees using the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit. The kit is a column-based kit in conjunction with beadbeating, using 3 mL DXL lysis buffer added to 10 bees in a 5 mL tube. The lysis buffer contained a mixture of 0.5 mm (~2.4 g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica (~1 g) beadbeating beads (BioSpec Products, Bartlesville, USA). The bees were homogenised in a Mini Beadbeater 16 instrument (BioSpec Products, Bartlesville, USA) for 3 minutes. Tubes were incubated at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. 1 mL of the homogenate was transferred to a 2 mL microcentrifuge tube and centrifuged at 15,000 x g for 5 minutes. 500 µL of supernatant was transferred to a new microcentrifuge tube containing 450 µL AD buffer and mixed well. The solution was applied to a nucleic acid binding column from the kit in two passes and centrifuged through before successive washing steps and elution in 100 µL elution buffer. A similar process was used for swabs, which were placed in screwcap 2 mL tubes with 0.5mm zirconia silica beads (~0.8g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica beads (0.3g). 800 µL DXL buffer was added to each swab tube and the swab material homogenised in the Mini Beadbeater 16 for 3 minutes. For pooled applications, individual swabs were added to 500 µL DXL buffer and vortexed for 10 seconds to dislodge cells and bacteria off the swab. 60 µL of each swab eluate (up to twelve swabs) was added to a 2 mL beadbeating tube and processed as for single swabs. A synthetic DNA standard (gBlock, IDT, Singapore) was utilised that incorporated both amplicon sequences (available on request). The synthesised 153 bp standard was resuspended in TE buffer, pH8, quantified in nanograms per µL on a DS-11 FX microvolume spectrophotometer (DeNovix, Wilmington, USA). The copy number was calculated using the equation: Copies = ng * Avogadro's constant copies/mole length of standard x 660 g/mole x 1x10 9 ng/g. Quantification standards were generated from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL (Svec et al., 2015). For all dilutions, the diluent was a pooled DNA sample extracted from bees free of P. larvae. The standards and their resulting Cq's (supplementary S1) were used to convert the Cq's to spore levels using the amplification efficiency of the single copy ftsZ gene, the y-intercept, and the formula: Spores per swab or 10 bees = 10 (Cq ftzZ-39/-3.48) x 50. Statistical analysis was performed after imputing data points by regression analysis of the other paired data, for two clinical hives resulting in a total of 26 data points with paired clinical data. A binary logistic regression model was performed in Minitab (Minitab®, State College, PA, USA) to identify the relationship between spore numbers at the entrance and clinical disease likelihood. Analysis of variance was calculated to confirm the correlation between increased entrance spores and the clinical signs of AFB. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant.

Procedures And Architectures
The AFBduo assay is a commercially available multiplex qPCR assay for P. larvae (Hall et al., 2021) using a dual-target approach. The assay uses hydrolysis probe (TaqMan®) qPCR assays that permit quantification of each target by selected fluorescent wavelengths. The assay allows the use of an internal control in an additional detection channel for confirmation of suitable quality DNA present in the reaction. The assay targets the 16S gene and the single copy ftsZ gene, with the ftsZ gene used for quantification purposes. The standard curve was prepared with a quantified synthetic template diluted in AFB-negative bee DNA. The AFBduo assay demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, with both target reactions able to reliably detect down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction. The reaction targets amplified with high efficiency in the multiplex (ftsZ = 94% and efficiency for 16S = 96%). The targets showed excellent linearity over the 7 orders of magnitude (r = 0.998). The 16S target typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier (i.e. lower Cq's) than the ftsZ target as expected, due to the multiple copies of the 16S sequence per AFB bacterium. The DNA extraction method from bees generated high purity DNA as shown by OD260/280 measurements of between 1.8 and 1.9. Extracted DNA samples serially diluted in elution buffer showed the expected increase in Cq's with decreasing concentration, indicating no inhibitors were present. DNA yields from swabs were too low to be measured on the spectrophotometer, however internal control Cq's for serial dilutions indicated the DNA was of suitable quality. The AFBduo assay provided high confidence in the results due to the integrated internal control and detection of two markers for AFB. The variability in Cq difference between the two markers among samples indicated the 16S copy number possibly varied among AFB isolates and thus could not be relied on for quantification. The use of the single copy ftsZ gene was used for quantification purposes using a standard curve prepared with a quantified synthetic template. The binary logistic regression model and analysis of variance (Supplementary figure 4) indicated the strong relationship between the increasing spore levels and clinical signs (p = 0.00). A spore quantity of 565,000 or more revealed a 95% probability of clinical signs being present in the hive. The levels of both P. larvae and internal control DNA seen on the swabs taken from the whole baseboard or just the entrance area were similar (Table 4). This showed dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard was not required to detect the higher levels of P. larvae in clinically infected colonies. The spore levels were the highest in the bees from the brood nest area of the hive. The use of 10 bees permitted easier and more convenient handling for DNA extraction compared to up to 100 bees per sample for culturing. The same DNA sample can be used to test for other bee pathogens such as Nosema ceranae, which has been detected through the use of hive debris and qPCR. The use of the sampling technique combined with an appropriate qPCR assay could provide rapid detection of any incursion to countries such as New Zealand. The Foster method is a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing that provides clinically significant information as to the AFB status of the hive.

Key Results
The AFBduo assay demonstrated high analytical sensitivity, with both target reactions able to reliably detect down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction. The reaction targets amplified with high efficiency in the multiplex (ftsZ = 94% and efficiency for 16S = 96%). The targets showed excellent linearity over the 7 orders of magnitude (r = 0.998). The 16S target typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier (i.e. lower Cq's) than the ftsZ target as expected, due to the multiple copies of the 16S sequence per AFB bacterium. The DNA extraction method from bees generated high purity DNA as shown by OD260/280 measurements of between 1.8 and 1.9. Extracted DNA samples serially diluted in elution buffer showed the expected increase in Cq's with decreasing concentration, indicating no inhibitors were present. In the first cohort of quarantine beehives from multiple regions in NZ, 45 hives were sampled up to 6 times during the 2018-2019/20 seasons. Among these hives, 8 were found to have clinical signs of AFB ('roping' larval remains) during sampling while another 6 were presumed to have AFB. In a second cohort of hives from one beekeeper, 23 hives were tested in a quarantine apiary using bee and hive entrance swab samples. Four of these hives showed clinical signs of AFB, and most hives showed no or low levels of P. larvae, while those with clinical AFB demonstrated much higher P. larvae spore levels. In a third cohort, swab eluates were pooled into groups of eight and later twelve, and even in the pools of twelve hive samples, single hives with higher levels of AFB could be clearly detected. This showed dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard was not required to detect the higher levels of P. larvae in clinically infected colonies. The spore levels were the highest in the bees from the brood nest area of the hive. The use of 10 bees permitted easier and more convenient handling for DNA extraction compared to up to 100 bees per sample for culturing.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The AFBduo assay provided high confidence in the results due to the integrated internal control and detection of two markers for AFB. As expected, the 16S marker had higher analytical sensitivity (amplifying 3-5 cycles earlier) due to the multi-copy nature of this marker (Dingman, 2017). The variability in Cq difference between the two markers among samples indicated the 16S copy number possibly varied among AFB isolates and thus could not be relied on for quantification (Dahllof et al., 2000). This variability in copy number for diagnostic targets has been noted in other diagnostic qPCR assays for AFB (Rossi et al., 2018; Dainat et al., 2018). The use of the single copy ftsZ gene was used for quantification purposes using a standard curve prepared with a quantified synthetic template diluted in AFB-negative bee DNA. The ability to sample the hive through the entrance removed the need to dismantle and disrupt the hive as with the first two sample types (bees and whole baseboard swabbing). This showed dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard was not required to detect the higher levels of P. larvae in clinically infected colonies. While spore levels varied among clinically affected hives, they were still easily differentiated from the very low or undetectable spore levels in non-infected hives. Some of the hives showed increasing levels at each testing point before clinical signs were observed in the respective hive and the hive destroyed (Table 1), demonstrating the ability of qPCR to find infected hives that may have pre-clinical infections. The quantification provides an important risk element of the hive as to whether visual signs are likely present at the time of sampling or likely to demonstrate these clinical signs in the near future. The same DNA sample can be used to test for other bee pathogens such as Nosema ceranae, which has been detected through the use of hive debris and qPCR (Copley et al., 2012). Another application could be for biosecurity surveillance for unwanted hive pests such as tracheal mites (Acarapis woodi), tropilaelap mites or small hive beetle (Aethina tumida). The use of the sampling technique combined with an appropriate qPCR assay could provide rapid detection of any incursion to countries such as New Zealand by providing faster sampling of hives than dismantling hives. All the methods published to date have required either dismantling the hive to sample from the baseboard or repeated visits to the hive to insert and remove sampling sheets. In contrast, the rapid sampling method described here, named the Foster method, is a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing. The Foster method provides clinically significant information as to the AFB status of the hive, even before visual symptoms are apparent.

The variability in Cq difference between the two markers among samples indicated the 16S copy number possibly varied among AFB isolates and thus could not be relied on for quantification (Dahllof et al., 2000). The hiveware was new (< 2 weeks old at time of sampling) for both these hives, and the colonies were newly established from an unknowingly infected parent colony, so there had not been enough time for spores to be deposited around the hive entrance surfaces. While most hives without clinical signs of AFB had low or undetectable levels of P. larvae DNA detected, one hive without visual signs of AFB (Hive 11) showed levels similar to two other hives with clinical AFB signs. Statistical analysis was performed after imputing data points by regression analysis of the other paired data, for two clinical hives (due to spore numbers being skewed lower by the new hiveware baseboards at time of sampling) resulting in a total of 26 data points with paired clinical data. The use of 10 bees permitted easier and more convenient handling for DNA extraction, but this may reduce the sensitivity of detection compared to up to 100 bees per sample for culturing. DNA yields from swabs were too low to be measured on the spectrophotometer, however internal control Cq's for serial dilutions as for the bees, indicated the DNA was similarly of suitable quality. The quantification standards were generated from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL, but the lower limit of detection may not be clinically relevant for all hives. Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the progression of P. larvae levels in three of the colonies, where the resulting Cq data has been converted to spores per 10 bee or swab sample processed. 1. summary.title: Stem Cell Microarrays for Assessing Growth Factor Signaling in Engineered Glycan Microenvironments
summary.authors: Glycan Microenvironments (University of California San Diego); Austen L Michalak (University of California San Diego); Greg W Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kelsey A Trieger (University of California San Diego); Kamil Godula (University of California San Diego)
summary.field_subfield: Chemical Biology / Biomaterials for Regenerative Medicine
summary.executive_summary: This study introduces a stem cell microarray platform that integrates glycosaminoglycan (GAG) polysaccharides into a polyacrylamide hydrogel to directly measure their contributions to growth factor (GF) signaling in cells. The motivation stems from the essential regulatory role of extracellular glycans, such as heparan sulfate (HS), in establishing gradients of morphogens and forming active signaling complexes at the cell surface, yet their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make structure-function relationships difficult to establish. Recent advances in synthetic, recombinant, and chemoenzymatic technologies now enable the production of well-defined GAG structures, creating an opportunity to systematically analyze both GF binding and signaling. The platform arrays HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels to generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding FGF2 and influencing embryonic stem cell (ESC) signaling. The selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity is defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. The study uses murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1 -/-), which lack cell surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs like FGF2, to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs. The MAPK pathway activation in response to FGF2 is quantified via immunofluorescence for phosphorylated ERK1/2 (pERK) and total ERK1/2 (ERK). Key findings include the demonstration that covalently linked heparin provides superior FGF2 binding capacity (~5-to 10-fold higher signal) compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin, and that heparin arrays remain stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours under cellular culture conditions. The study confirms that NHS-crosslinking enhances the stability of GAG displays without altering protein binding specificity, and that Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin show significant increases in ERK1/2 phosphorylation. This platform offers a convenient tool to systematically analyze the biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling and to accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

Executive Summary

The platform arrays HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels to generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding FGF2 and influencing embryonic stem cell (ESC) signaling. The selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity is defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. The study uses murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1 -/-), which lack cell surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs like FGF2, to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs. The MAPK pathway activation in response to FGF2 is quantified via immunofluorescence for phosphorylated ERK1/2 (pERK) and total ERK1/2 (ERK). Key findings include the demonstration that covalently linked heparin provides superior FGF2 binding capacity (~5-to 10-fold higher signal) compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin, and that heparin arrays remain stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours under cellular culture conditions. This platform offers a convenient tool to systematically analyze the biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling and to accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications.

Research Context
Extracellular glycans like GAGs are essential regulators of growth factor signaling. GAGs harbor binding sites for growth factors and establish signaling gradients. GAGs promote formation of active signaling complexes at the cell surface. GAGs are pursued as biologically active components for regenerative biomaterials. Structural complexity hinders structure-function analysis of GAGs. HS polysaccharides are essential regulators of GF signaling. HS comprise chains of alternating residues with sequential modifications. Recent advances enable production of well-defined GAG structures. Arrays of HS structures are used to profile HS-binding protein specificity. Multiplexed on-array analysis of HS-dependent signaling could streamline biomaterial discovery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether GAGs can be arrayed to measure their contributions to GF signaling. The hypothesis is that GAG polysaccharides conjugated to adhesion proteins can be introduced into hydrogels to measure signaling. The platform should enable analysis of both GF binding and signaling in response to GAGs. The hypothesis is that FGF2 binding and activity are defined by the chemical composition of HS. The hypothesis is that Ext1 -/-ESCs isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling. The hypothesis is that covalent crosslinking enhances GAG retention without altering binding specificity. The hypothesis is that immobilized GAGs can facilitate GF-mediated activation of signaling events. The predicted outcome is that well-defined GAG structures enable systematic structure-function analysis.

Methodological Details
The study used murine embryonic stem cells lacking Exostosin 1 expression. Ext1 -/-ESCs lack cell surface HS structures and cannot engage HS-dependent GFs. The cell model was chosen to isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling. Several surface passivation strategies were screened for array construction. A thin poly(acrylamide) hydrogel deposited on glass best supported ESC growth. The hydrogel method followed a protocol by Brafman et al. Gelatin was loaded into the hydrogel in its dehydrated form. Gelatin was spotted at a concentration of 500 µg/mL in PBS. Best ESC growth was observed over 6 days in culture. Heparin (12 kDa) was used as a model HS glycan. Heparin concentrations ranged from 50 to 750 µg/mL. Heparin was crosslinked via carboxylic acid groups activated as NHS esters. Heparin was activated with EDC in HEPES buffer at pH 7.4. The coupling reagent EDC was used at 4°C for 18 hours. Purification was performed by size exclusion on a PD10 column. Low levels of crosslinking were targeted at ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain. A panel of CS, DS, and HA GAGs was arrayed. Heparin was chemically treated to remove 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates. N-desulfated heparin had amino groups capped as acetamides. The array was probed with FGF2, CS56, and HABP. FGF2 was labeled with AlexaFluor 647. Slides were washed for 3 hours prior to staining. Cells were seeded at an intermediary density of 40,000 cells/cm². Cells were grown for 24 hours in embryonic culture media with LIF and FBS. The last 24 hours were carried out under serum-free conditions. Oct4 was used as an embryonic marker. Nestin was used as a neural differentiation marker. Cells were stimulated with FGF2 at 0.5 ng/mL for 15 min at 37°C. MAPK activity was quantified using antibodies against Erk1/2 and pErk1/2. A microarrays scanner was used to detect fluorescence. Image J analysis was used to confirm co-localization of pERK and ERK signals. Soluble heparin (s-Hep, 5 µg/mL) was used as a positive control.

The platform integrates GAG-protein conjugates into a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray. The goal was to analyze the activity of extracellular glycans in growth factor signaling. The platform enables rapid development and optimization of functional glycomaterials. GAGs harbor binding sites for a range of growth factors and morphogens. summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length on Six-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
summary.field_subfield: Cardiovascular medicine / interventional cardiology
summary.executive_summary: This prospective single-center cohort study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length influences angiographic and clinical outcomes after successful drug-eluting stent (DES)–based percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in the DES era. A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients treated with DES between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (<30 mm, n=76). Six-month angiographic outcomes were assessed by quantitative coronary angiography, and two-year clinical outcomes were evaluated through face-to-face interviews, medical record review, and telephone contact. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6–12 months, and the primary clinical endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as the composite of total death, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), and revascularization including PCI and coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). Baseline characteristics were similar between groups except that prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. In-hospital complications were comparable except for a higher incidence of significant intimal dissection in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes were similar between groups, including binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12), in-stent restenosis (33.3% vs. 26.6%, p=0.42), and late loss (0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm, p=0.13). Over two years, hard clinical endpoints were comparable: total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), MI (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71), and MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13). However, repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05), predominantly driven by target vessel revascularization (TVR, 16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR; 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006). The authors conclude that, despite successful DES-based PCI, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, though this did not translate into differences in mortality, cardiac death, or MACE. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized, single-center, prospective registry design, small sample size, incomplete follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration. These findings suggest that while long CTO lesions carry a higher revascularization burden, the overall safety profile and long-term hard clinical outcomes remain comparable to short CTO lesions, underscoring the need for larger, longer-term studies to draw definitive conclusions.

Research Context
CTO PCI outcomes depend on baseline lesion characteristics and clinical risk factors. Long coronary artery lesions are a worse prognostic factor after PCI. CTO procedural success remains lower than non-CTO despite device advances. Lesion length predicts MACE and restenosis in non-CTO DES treatment. CTO clinical and angiographic outcomes remain worse than non-CTO disease. No definitive answers exist regarding CTO outcomes by lesion length in the DES era.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question concerns the impact of CTO lesion length on outcomes. The study hypothesized that adverse outcomes would be more frequent in long CTO lesions. Long CTO lesions carry worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI and PCI. Newer generation DES use was more common in the short CTO group. The predicted outcome was higher repeat PCI and TVR in long CTO lesions. The predicted outcome was worse angiographic outcomes at six months.

Methodological Details
The study enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients treated with DES. Patients were treated between November 2004 and October 2010. The study was conducted at Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul. Patients were divided into long and short CTO groups by lesion length. The long CTO group included 159 patients with lesion length ≥30mm. The short CTO group included 76 patients with lesion length <30mm. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board. All patients provided informed consent to participate. CTO was defined by TIMI flow grade 0 and duration ≥3 months. Only de novo lesions were included; in-stent restenosis was excluded. Loading doses of clopidogrel and aspirin were administered pre-procedure. Maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy included aspirin and clopidogrel. Clopidogrel was encouraged to continue for at least one year. Cilostazol use depended on physician discretion. PCI procedures followed current guidelines using standard techniques. Atheroablative devices were not utilized in the procedures. Simple balloon pre-dilation was mostly performed. All PCI was performed using drug-eluting stents. DES type was decided by the operator during procedures. Procedural success required diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. QCA parameters were measured before, after, and at 6 months. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included ISR, DS, MLD, and LL. Two-year follow-up used interviews, records, and telephone contact. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE. MACE included total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. Deaths were considered cardiac unless non-cardiac death was confirmed. Continuous variables were analyzed with Student's t-test. Categorical variables were analyzed with χ2 or Fisher's exact test. Logistic regression adjusted for multiple risk factors. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using SPSS 20.

Procedures And Architectures
QCA measurement was performed at the study hospital. Follow-up angiography was obtained in 99 of 159 long CTO patients. Follow-up angiography was obtained in 45 of 76 short CTO patients. The logistic regression model estimated risk of repeat PCI and TVR. Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI. Long CTO was an independent predictor for TVR. The study used Table 1 for baseline characteristics. The study used Table 2 for complications. The study used Table 3 for clinical outcomes. The study used Table 4 for predictors. Baseline characteristics were similar except prior PCI frequency. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. In-hospital complications were similar except intimal dissection. Total death was 3.1% vs. 5.2% between groups. Cardiac death was 1.2% vs. 2.6% between groups. MI was 1.8% vs. 2.6% between groups. MACE was 21.3% vs. 13.1% between groups. Long CTO lesions carry a higher revascularization burden. The higher TVR did not translate into critical hard endpoints. This pattern was reported previously from the j-Cypher Registry.
