The vessel diameter difference did not affect outcomes significantly. The study investigated a real-world CTO cohort prospectively. Long-term studies with larger numbers are required. Larger study populations are necessary for final conclusions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study was not a randomized controlled trial. The study was a single center registry. Baseline characteristics were slightly different between groups. Newer generation DES use differed between groups. Unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could exist. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed. Follow-up angiography depended on ischemic symptoms. Collaterals and viability could influence ischemic symptoms. The sample size was relatively small. The study lacked power to prove angiographic differences. The two-year follow-up was not long enough. The binary restenosis trend may increase over time. The higher repeat PCI supports the hypothesis.

Claims

The incidence of TVR was higher in the long CTO group. Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI. The odds ratio for repeat PCI was 4.26. Long CTO was an independent predictor for TVR. The higher TVR did not translate into hard endpoints. The safety profile was similar between groups. The higher revascularization burden was observed in long CTO lesions. The pattern was reported previously from the j-Cypher Registry. Less myocardial viability may lessen the harmful effect of restenosis. Long-term studies with larger numbers are required.
Hard clinical endpoints were comparable between long and short CTO lesions despite successful DES-based PCI. Total death was 3.1% vs. 5.2% between groups. Cardiac death was 1.2% vs. 2.6% between groups. MI was 1.8% vs. 2.6% between groups. MACE was 21.3% vs. 13.1% between groups. The safety profile was similar between groups. The incidence of repeat PCI was higher in the long CTO group. The incidence of TVR was higher in the long CTO group. The higher TVR did not translate into hard endpoints. The pattern was reported previously from the j-Cypher Registry. PCI in long CTO lesions is similarly safe as short CTO lesions. Long-term studies with larger numbers are required.
Six-month angiographic outcomes were similar between long and short CTO lesions. The incidence of ISR was 33.3% vs. 26.6% between groups. Binary restenosis was 19.1% vs. 8.8% between groups. Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm. The long and short CTO groups showed similar angiographic outcomes. The angiographic outcomes were similar between groups. Binary restenosis showed a numerically higher trend in the long CTO group. The binary restenosis rate was higher in the long CTO group. The binary restenosis trend may increase over time. The higher repeat PCI supports this hypothesis. The vessel diameter difference did not affect outcomes significantly. Long-term studies with larger numbers are required.

Data And Code Availability
The study data was collected prospectively. The study was a single center registry.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study was not a randomized controlled trial. The study was a single center registry. Baseline characteristics were slightly different between groups. Unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could exist. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed. The sample size was relatively small. The study lacked power to prove angiographic differences. The two-year follow-up was not long enough. The binary restenosis trend may increase over time. The higher repeat PCI supports this hypothesis.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board. All patients provided informed consent to participate. The study was conducted at Korea University Guro Hospital. No ethical concerns were raised beyond standard consent.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrated baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics. Table 2 showed in-hospital complications. Table 3 summarized clinical outcomes for 2-year follow-up. Table 4 showed predictors for repeat PCI and TVR. Table 5 presented six-month angiographic outcomes. The long CTO group had 99 patients in angiographic follow-up. The short CTO group had 45 patients in angiographic follow-up.

summary.title: Influence of plant growth regulators and nitrogen sources on the production and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk
summary.authors: Leone Campos Rocha; Fábio Andrade Teixeira; Márcio Dos Santos Pedreira; Daniela Deitos Fries; Giovanna Evely Leite Costa; Ana Cláudia Maia Soares; Daniel Lucas Santos Dias; Abdias José De Figueiredo; Angel Amaral Seixas; Camile Carvalho Pacheco
summary.field_subfield: Agronomy / Forage and Pasture Science
summary.executive_summary: This study evaluated how seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGRs) and nitrogen fertilization methods affect the growth and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, a forage grass used in pasture establishment. The research was conducted at the Forage and Pasture Research Center of the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB), Itapetinga, Bahia, Brazil, between June and September 2017. Two experiments were performed: Experiment 1 assessed germination characteristics and initial growth at 30 days after sowing (DAS), while Experiment 2 evaluated dry matter yield and physiological composition (chlorophylls and carotenoids). The factorial design combined two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) with four levels of PGR (0, 8, 16, and 24 mL.kg⁻¹ of seed) in Experiment 1, and two PGR levels (0 and 24 mL.kg⁻¹) with four nitrogen fertilization methods (no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple fertilization combining soil and foliar) in Experiment 2. Germination was carried out under a 12-hour photoperiod at a constant temperature of 28°C in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber, while growth evaluations were performed in a greenhouse with pots filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil. The PGR composition included auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Key results showed that PGRs increased germination and mass yields of plant structures in coated seeds, with optimal germination at 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ and higher root dry mass at 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹. Leaf and pseudostem mass production exhibited a significant interaction between seed type and PGR use, with coated seeds performing better at lower or absent PGR levels. Soil nitrogen fertilization resulted in higher dry mass production of leaf, stem, shoot, and root, as well as root volume, and increased rates of photoassimilate. The study concluded that exogenous hormonal compounds act on the organogenesis of plant tissues and increase the development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, while soil nitrogen fertilization increases mass yields by maximizing photosynthetic processes and growth rates. These findings have implications for pasture management, particularly in reducing soil preparation and planting windows under adverse climatic conditions, and suggest that lower PGR levels are recommended for coated seeds compared to conventional methods.

Soil N-fertilization results in higher dry mass productions of leaf, stem, shoot and root, as well as for root volume.

Basilisk, while soil nitrogen fertilization increases mass yields by maximizing photosynthetic processes and growth rates. These findings have implications for pasture management, particularly in reducing soil preparation and planting windows under adverse climatic conditions, and suggest that lower PGR levels are recommended for coated seeds compared to conventional methods.

Research Context
The shortening of the soil preparation and planting window promoted by the adverse climatic factors reduces the time for recovering degraded pastures. Consequently, greater seed efficiency as regards germination and speed of emergence of seedlings are necessary. Management practices are essential to improve herbage production process using the climatic conditions that favor the development and use of pasture. The application of synthetic compounds as growth promoters in plants is based on the effect similar to that of phytohormones. Phytohormones (auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins) and the combination of these compounds regulate homeostasis. The PGR acts directly in the signaling network that, through intermediary metabolites, activate genes and then plant responses. Growth regulators can potentiate the performance of plants in stress-prone environments, acting on biochemical reactions linked to plant growth. Applications of PGRs based on gibberellic compounds at high levels of active principle per area are shown to be an uneconomical pasture management tool. Low concentrations of gibberellin (GA) of 5-10 g.ha -1 are enough to positively affect forage yield. PGRs have demonstrated potential applications under stress conditions as they act on the positive regulation of genes linked to the growth and development of plants. The use of nitrogen expands plant lifecycle, leading to higher growth rates in the vegetative phase. The increase in photoassimilate production maximizes the structural characteristics of the plant, and allows greater post-defoliation recovery. Nitrogen is an indispensable constituent in several plant-based organic compounds (amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids). Nitrogen applications to recover degraded pasture areas increase water use efficiency and stimulate plant growth, increasing soil cover.

The aim was to evaluate the effect of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGR) and nitrogen fertilization methods in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk on the growth and development. The hypothesis is that PGRs increase germination and mass yields of plant structures in coated seeds. The hypothesis is that higher germination percentages and root dry mass production are obtained with the use of PGRs for the initial growth. The hypothesis is that leaf and pseudostem mass production have a significant interaction effect between seed type and the use of growth regulator. The hypothesis is that coated seeds have greater performance with absence or at lower levels of growth regulators. The hypothesis is that embryo quality contributes to the greater formation of plant tissues. The hypothesis is that soil N-fertilization results in higher dry mass productions of leaf, stem, shoot and root, as well as for root volume. The hypothesis is that rates of photoassimilate are increased by soil fertilization and use of plant growth regulators. Four nitrogen fertilization methods (no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization and multiple fertilization from the combination of soil + foliar fertilization) were evaluated. Eight treatments were used, four plants per replicate and four replicates per treatment, totaling 32 experimental units. At 30 DAS, a standardization cut was performed adopting an average residue height of 15 cm. Fertilization was performed after the standardization cut, and the recommendations used were 75 kg.ha -1 N and 3 L.ha -1 for soil and foliar nitrogen fertilization, respectively. Data were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC) with significance declared when P ≤ 0.05. Seed, PGR and interaction between effects were analyzed as a fixed effect for all measurements in Exp. 1. summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement; Priscilla S Redd; Chunwan Lu; Alyssa D Merting; Dakota B Poschel; Dafeng Yang; Gang Zhou; David H Munn; Kebin Liu
summary.field_subfield: Cancer immunology / tumor immunology (metastasis & immune checkpoint blockade)
summary.type_of_paper: Primary research article (experimental study with in vitro, in vivo, and human patient data)
summary.executive_summary: This study re-examines the canonical view that tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) suppresses cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) directly through CTL PD-1. The authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 has no direct effect on CTL activation or lytic function when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 acts indirectly by engaging PD-1 on myeloid cells (mPD-1), which suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling, repressing the chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10, and thereby impairing CTL recruitment to lung metastases. Critically, knocking out PD-L1 in tumor cells does not affect primary tumor growth but significantly decreases lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Depletion of myeloid cells using clodronate liposomes impaired tPD-L1 promotion of lung metastasis, confirming the myeloid intermediary role. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that tPD-L1 engages myeloid PD-1 to antagonize IFN-I and STAT1 signaling to repress Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expression to impair CTL recruitment to lung metastases. Human patient response to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy correlates with IFN-I response in myeloid cells. The data establish that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis. The work uses murine triple negative breast cancer (4T1) and colorectal cancer (CT26) cell lines, an in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system with the 2/20 CTL line, orthotopic and experimental metastasis models, RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and a human patient cohort with metastatic basal cell carcinoma. The findings suggest that tPD-L1 may control CTL recruitment versus functionality, and that low response rates in interferon alpha therapies may be due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. The study has limitations, including exclusive analysis of lung metastases, which may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment. The paper does not report data/code availability, ethical considerations, or key figures/tables in the provided text, and the bibliography is omitted, so top_influential_citations is empty.

The work uses murine triple negative breast cancer (4T1) and colorectal cancer (CT26) cell lines, an in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system with the 2/20 CTL line, orthotopic and experimental metastasis models, RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and a human patient cohort with metastatic basal cell carcinoma. The findings suggest that tPD-L1 may control CTL recruitment versus functionality, and that low response rates in interferon alpha therapies may be due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. The study has limitations, including exclusive analysis of lung metastases, which may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment. The paper does not report data/code availability, ethical considerations, or key figures/tables in the provided text, and the bibliography is omitted, so top_influential_citations is empty.

Research Context
The mechanism of PD-L1/PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade is well-established for CTLs. PD-1 engagement on CTLs decreases activation and effector functions. The role of tumor-expressed PD-L1 as a direct molecular shield is hypothesized. PD-1 expression in non-T cell populations is increasingly recognized. How non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is unclear. The differential role of tPD-L1 in driving metastasis versus primary tumor is unknown.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether tPD-L1 directly suppresses CTLs or acts through an intermediate cell. The hypothesis is that tPD-L1 targets myeloid cell PD-1 to suppress type I interferon. The predicted outcome is that this represses Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 to impair CTL recruitment. The authors predict tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis independent of primary tumor growth. The authors predict myeloid cells bridge tPD-L1 to CTL suppression. The authors predict human response to PD-1 blockade correlates with myeloid IFN-I response.

Methodological Details
The study used murine triple negative breast cancer 4T1 and colorectal cancer CT26 cell lines. PD-L1 was deleted by knocking out Cd274 in both cell lines. The in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system used the 2/20 tumor-specific CTL line. The 2/20 CTL line recognizes the H2-Ld-restricted AH1 epitope of gp70. PD-L1 KO cells showed no PD-L2 expression, the only alternative PD-1 ligand. Primary tumor growth was assessed via orthotopic injection into syngeneic mice. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth between WT and PD-L1 KO. Lung metastasis was assessed via tail vein injection and lung quantification. Lungs were harvested, inflated with India ink, and quantified. Myeloid cells were depleted using clodronate liposomes in tumor-bearing mice. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs. Approximately 7500 cells were analyzed by UMAP clustering. Cell populations were annotated by comparison to publicly available datasets. Flow cytometry confirmed transcript-level observations in lung myeloid cells. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed after seven days of tumor colonization. Single-cell libraries were generated using the Chromium Single Cell 3' Reagent Kit v3. High quality cells were defined by feature count and mitochondrial read thresholds. Cells were clustered using the first fifty principal components. The human cohort included patients with metastatic basal cell carcinoma. Single-cell sequencing was performed before and after PD-1 blockade. Statistical analysis used Prism8 and two-tailed Student's t-test. Survival analysis used two-sided log-rank test in the Survival package. Cell lines were obtained from ATCC and tested bi-monthly for mycoplasma. RAW264.7 macrophages were used for in vitro co-culture experiments. Random seed, train/test split, and patient demographics are not reported.

Procedures And Architectures
CRISPR lentivirus was produced by co-transfecting HEK293FT cells. Tumor cells were transduced with lentivirus and selected with puromycin. Bulk cells were sorted for marker-negative cells using BD FACSARIA. 4T1 orthotopic tumors were established at the right second mammary gland. CT26 subcutaneous tumors were established at the right flank. Neutralization experiments used anti-CD8α or isotype control antibodies. Flow cytometry samples were blocked in FACS Buffer with mouse FcBlock. Flow cytometry data was analyzed with FlowJo v10.6.0. RNA was extracted using Direct-zol RNA microprep kit. RNA was sequenced by Novogene. Reads were aligned to the reference genome using STARv2.5. Reads were quantified using HTSeqv0.6.1. GSEA was performed using GSEA4.0 with gene-set permutation. GO pathway enrichment was performed with clusterprofiler. Leukocytes were positively selected using CD45 magnetic nanobeads. Cell viability was assessed using trypan blue with ≥ 80% viable cells. Cells were loaded to capture approximately 2-3 x 10^3 targeted cells. Sequencing was performed on Illumina NextSeq 500 platform. Alignment generated 30-39K reads/cell with 75-102 million reads per sample. Approximately 1600 median genes per cell were obtained. Doublet removal was performed by DoubletFinder. Cells were annotated by comparison to pre-existing datasets using SingleR. The tPD-L1 loss gene signature required at least two-fold increase with padj < 0.05. The SHP-2 activation signature used SHP099 treatment with two-fold increase. Macrophage PHATE clusters were transferred to human lung macrophage dataset. Cluster-identifying signatures were calculated by Seurat FindAllMarkers. Batch effects were corrected by Harmony in patient dataset analysis. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis was determined to control CTL infiltration. The negative feedback circuit links PD-1/L1 axis to type I interferon signaling.

Key Results
tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when CTL encounters a tumor cell. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth between WT and PD-L1 KO. No differences in tumor growth were observed in WT and PD-L1 KO CT26. Increased infiltration of CD3+ cells was observed in lung after loss of tPD-L1. No difference in initial tumor cell colonization was seen one day after injection. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice. summary.title: Synthesis, Biological Activity and Molecular Docking of New Tricyclic Series as α-glucosidase Inhibitors
summary.authors: Hatem A Abuelizz; Azman N I Nor; Iwana; Rohaya Ahmad; Anouar El-Hassane; Mohamed Marzouk; Rashad Al-Salahi
summary.field_subfield: Medicinal Chemistry / Bioorganic Chemistry
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental synthesis, biological screening, and molecular docking study
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the global burden of diabetes, which the WHO reported to have risen from 108 million people in 1980 to 422 million, with prevalence among adults increasing from 4.7% in 1980 to 8.5% in 2014. A major limitation of clinically available α-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose is their gastrointestinal side effects, including flatulence and diarrhoea, which reduce patient compliance. To overcome these limitations, the researchers sought to develop new scaffolds that mimic the inhibitory mechanism without the drawbacks of sugar mimetic agents. The team synthesized 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones hybrids and evaluated their α-glucosidase inhibitory activity in vitro. The compounds were tested at equal concentrations of 100 µg/mL, with the test repeated three times for each compound to obtain the average percent inhibition. Eight compounds that exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition were further evaluated for their IC 50 values, which were compared to that of acarbose. Two compounds, 6h and 6d, showed stronger activity than acarbose. Compound 6h exhibited the highest inhibition with an IC 50 of 104.07 µM. Molecular docking studies revealed that compound 6h inhibits α-glucosidase due to the formation of a stable ligand-α-glucosidase complex and extra hydrogen bond interactions, directed in the binding site by Trp329. The docking calculations were performed using the Autodock software package, with the protein structure downloaded from the RCSB data bank (PDB code 3W37). The binding energy of docked 6h was found to be the lowest (-10.56 kcal/mol) among the docked derivatives. This study provides a new structural insight for the development of novel α-glucosidase inhibitors that differ from the commonly employed carbasugars and can potentially be transformed into new clinical drugs for the treatment of type II diabetes. The work contributes to the growing body of research on α-glucosidase inhibitors, which have been found to have a range of biological activities beyond their antidiabetic effects, including antiviral, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory activities. The study's findings are significant because they demonstrate that the introduction of a branch to the pyrimidine scaffold through a nitrogen bridge results in a series of synthetic compounds with significant inhibitory activity against α-glucosidase. The researchers' decision to modify well-accepted scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, such as pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine, reflects a strategic approach to drug discovery that builds on the known pharmacological activities of these scaffolds. The study's methodology is rigorous, with the use of triplicate experiments and molecular docking to provide insights into the binding modes of the target enzyme and docked synthesized derivatives. The findings have important implications for the development of new antidiabetic agents, as they demonstrate that the tricyclic series can serve as a new lead scaffold for the development of clinically effective antidiabetic drugs. Overall, this study makes a valuable contribution to the field of medicinal chemistry and drug discovery, and its findings are likely to be of interest to researchers working on the development of new treatments for diabetes and related metabolic disorders.

Research Context
Diabetes is a growing global health problem affecting hundreds of millions of people. α-Glucosidase inhibitors are used to control postprandial hyperglycaemia by delaying carbohydrate hydrolysis. Clinically available α-glucosidase inhibitors suffer from gastrointestinal side effects that reduce patient compliance. Gastrointestinal side effects such as flatulence and diarrhoea are caused by bacterial digestion of complex carbohydrates in the colon. There is a high demand for effective antidiabetic agents that overcome the side effects of sugar mimetic agents. α-Glucosidase inhibitors have a range of biological activities beyond their antidiabetic effects. Well-accepted scaffolds such as pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine have proven pharmacological activities. Pyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones have been reported as effective fungicidal agents. Most produced α-glucosidase inhibitors are sugar mimetics that require tedious synthesis. The valienamine moiety in acarbose mimics the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state that binds to and inhibits α-glucosidase.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether new tricyclic scaffolds can serve as effective α-glucosidase inhibitors. The researchers hypothesized that modifying well-accepted scaffolds would yield compounds with significant inhibitory activity. The researchers predicted that introducing a branch to the pyrimidine scaffold through a nitrogen bridge would enhance inhibitory activity. The researchers hypothesized that the aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 is responsible for strong inhibitory activity. The researchers predicted that compounds with lower IC 50 values than acarbose would demonstrate superior inhibitory activity. The researchers hypothesized that molecular docking studies would reveal the binding modes of the target enzyme and docked derivatives. The researchers predicted that compound 6h would exhibit the highest inhibition due to its stable ligand-α-glucosidase complex. The researchers hypothesized that Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand in the binding site. The researchers predicted that the number of established hydrogen bonds would correlate with inhibitory activity. The researchers hypothesized that the tricyclic series could serve as a new lead scaffold for clinically effective antidiabetic drugs.

The study synthesized 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones hybrids. The α-glucosidase inhibitory assay was performed in vitro to screen the biological activity of the synthesized derivatives. The enzyme was treated with equal concentrations of 100 µg/mL of each compound. The test was repeated three times for each compound to obtain the average percent inhibition. The inhibitory activity of all tested compounds was between 30% and 63%. Eight compounds that exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition were further evaluated for their IC 50 values. Compounds 3, 6c and 6d showed average percent inhibition of more than 60%. Compounds 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b and 6h showed average percent inhibition of more than 50% but less than 60%. Acarbose was used as a positive control to compare with the synthesized compounds. The α-glucosidase enzyme was type 1 from Baker's yeast, dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline at pH 6.5. summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal, Priya Aggarwal, Luiz Pessoa, Anubha Gupta
summary.field_subfield: Neuroimaging / Machine Learning (fMRI brain-state decoding)
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses brain-state decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, where the goal is to infer the cognitive state underlying neural activity. The authors argue that conventional decoding methods, including unidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, fail to capture the full temporal dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response because they only use past information. Since BOLD responses are slow and exhibit latency, the authors contend that future temporal context is equally important. To address this, they propose a bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture that processes the input sequence in both forward and reverse temporal orders, collating the two hidden activations to build a richer memory representation. This approach explicitly models BOLD dynamics without requiring any delay adjustment for stimulus-response synchronization. The study validates the method on working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), using 400 participants selected from a release of 1200. Participants performed a 2-back working memory task alongside a 0-back control condition, with stimuli drawn from four categories. Each scan yielded a 405 time-point sequence of 360 cortical regions of interest. The data was preprocessed using HCP's pipeline, including motion regression and low-frequency signal removal, and parcellated into 360 ROIs. The bi-LSTM was implemented in Keras and trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with an ADAM optimizer, learning rate of 0.001, batch size of 32, and 100 epochs, with dropout of 0.3 to prevent overfitting. Class imbalance was handled using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine. The model was evaluated using inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation, with the development set further split into 80-20 training-validation sets. The full-length training data was windowed into overlapping windows of size 40 with an overlap of 10 points. The results showed that the bi-LSTM (specifically the vector concatenation variant, bi-LSTM-c) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02, compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, representing an 18% improvement in accuracy. The authors note that the model performs well without hard-coded delay adjustment, highlighting the usefulness of immediate future samples. They also acknowledge limitations, including the need for more sophisticated handling of class imbalance and potential confusion between certain stimuli categories such as body and tools. Future work may involve tuning the window size and overlap for time-series chunking, as well as studying cortical regions engaged in specific stimuli. The study contributes to the field of brain-computer interfaces and cognitive decoding by demonstrating that bidirectional temporal modeling significantly improves brain-state decoding accuracy.

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal, Cinthia R Millan, Samantha I Zangari, Samantha Avila, Dewight Williams, Tarjani M Thaker, Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.field_subfield: Structural biology / membrane transport (ABCC transporters)
summary.executive_summary: Yeast Cadmium Factor-1 (Ycf1) is an ATP-binding cassette C-subfamily (ABCC) transporter that sequesters glutathione and heavy metals into the vacuole to protect cells from oxidative and metal stress. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered regulatory domains (R-domains), but the mechanism remains poorly understood. Here the authors report two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, captured in two inward-facing conformations designated IFwide and IFnarrow. These structures reveal a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain (residues 901-935), which is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914). The phosphorylated R-domain encircles NBD1 and interacts extensively with NBD1, the lasso domain, and the TMDs through electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic contacts that bury substantial surface area. Biochemical experiments show that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and drastically reduces ATPase activity, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis. The authors propose a model in which phosphorylation drives the R-domain from an unbound/disordered state to a bound/ordered state near NBD1, priming the transporter for transport. These findings provide long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity and may inform understanding of related human transporters such as CFTR and MRP1.

claims.description: R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an ordered R-domain architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis in Ycf1.
The ordered R-domain architecture is stimulatory and does not support the model where CFTR activation depends on R-domain release.

These findings provide long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity and may inform understanding of related human transporters such as CFTR and MRP1.

Research Context
ABC transporters regulate diverse molecules for lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification. Ycf1 transports glutathione and heavy metals into vacuoles to counter cell stress. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered domains. The regulatory mechanism of R-domain phosphorylation is still poorly understood. Prior cryo-EM structures show a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned phosphorylation sites.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study seeks to determine the structural basis for R-domain phosphorylation regulation of Ycf1. The authors hypothesize that R-domain phosphorylation induces an ordered state that stabilizes interactions with NBD1 and the lasso domain. The authors predict that phosphorylation reorganizes Ycf1 architecture and is required for maximal ATPase activity. The authors predict that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and reduces ATPase activity. The authors predict that phosphorylation drives the R-domain from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered.

Methodological Details
The study used two forms of S. cerevisiae DSY5 strain: wild-type and the NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. The YCF1 gene was cloned into the p423_GAL1 vector as an N-terminal Flag and C-terminal decahistidine fusion. The DSY-5 strain has genotype MATa leu2 trp1 ura3-52 his3 pep4 prb1. A 50 mL primary culture was grown for 24 hours at 30°C with shaking at 200 rpm in SC-His media. A secondary 750 mL culture was inoculated with 2% of the primary culture (15 mL). The culture was grown for an additional 16 hours at 30°C prior to harvesting. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 5000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C. The lysis buffer contained 50 mM Tris-Cl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, and cOmplete, EDTA-free protease inhibitor. The E1435Q dataset was processed in RELION (3.0 and 3.1) and cisTEM. Drift correction was performed using MotionCor2 with a pixel size of 1.031 Å/pixel. The CTF was estimated using CTFFIND4.1 prior to particle picking. An initial model was built using the SWISS-MODEL server and 6jb1 as a template. Manual model building was performed in COOT. Real-space refinement was performed in Phenix with CCP-EM modules for map sharpening/blurring. Evolutionary coupling analysis was performed using the Evcouplings package with PLMC. A total of 13,723 sequences were identified for evolutionary coupling analysis. ATPase rates were determined at 30°C using an enzyme-coupled assay. Each ATPase reaction consisted of 75 µL volumes containing 6.45 µg of protein. The absorbance was measured every minute at 340 nM for 30-45 min on a Synergy Neo2 reader. Kinetic parameters were derived using nonlinear regression in GraphPad Prism 9. Phosphorylation was assayed by in-gel phosphoprotein staining with Pro-Q Diamond. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 was generated by treating SEC-purified Ycf1 with Lambda phosphatase for 45 min at 4°C. Equal quantities (5 µg) of untreated and lambda PP treated samples were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE gels. LC-MS/MS analysis used Scaffold Q+S v 4.11.1 with a minimum of two peptides at 95% confidence. Limited proteolysis used trypsin from bovine pancreas at varying concentrations (0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, and 15 µg/mL). Fixed amounts of Lambda PP treated and untreated Ycf1 protein (12 µg) were incubated for 30 min on ice. The reaction was stopped by adding 1 µg/mL of soybean trypsin inhibitor and incubating for an additional 15 min.

Procedures And Architectures

summary.title: Lack of negative density-dependence regulation in a dominant oak tree from a neotropical highland forest
summary.authors: Irene Calderón-Sanou; Luis Diego Ríos; Alfredo Cascante-Marín; Gilbert Barrantes; Eric J Fuchs
summary.field_subfield: Community ecology / tropical forest dynamics
summary.executive_summary: Conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD) is a leading explanation for how tree species coexist in tropical forests: when many seedlings of the same species grow together, shared enemies and pathogens should kill them off and open space for other species. This mechanism is thought to be especially strong at the seedling stage. However, tropical montane forests are unusual because they are far less diverse than lowland forests and are often dominated by just a few tree species. The authors ask whether CNDD regulates the dominant oak Quercus costaricensis in the Talamanca highlands of Costa Rica, where this oak makes up over 90% of the adult stems. They expected weak CNDD and possibly a positive effect of nearby adults on recruitment. Using four 400 m² plots censused from 2014 to 2017, they tracked 3538 seedlings and modeled annual survival with a generalized linear mixed-effects model, and modeled recruitment with a quasi-Poisson GLMM. They also used Ripley's K to test spatial aggregation. The main finding is that they found no effect of CNDD on seedling survival or recruitment. Instead, herbivory and Chusquea bamboo density both reduced survival, and higher seedling density actually increased survival and recruitment. They attribute the absence of density regulation to predator satiation and facilitation via ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults. They conclude that the lack of intraspecific density regulation at the seedling stage likely explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis, with local density instead controlled by herbivory and bamboo density. This study contributes to understanding why some dominant tropical trees escape the negative effects of CNDD that regulate more common species.

claims.description: CNDD does not regulate seedling survival or recruitment of the dominant oak Q. costaricensis.
Herbivory and Chusquea bamboo density reduce Q. costaricensis seedling survival.
Predator satiation and ECM facilitation explain the lack of CNDD in this dominant oak.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD) is a leading explanation for how tree species coexist in tropical forests: when many seedlings of the same species grow together, shared enemies and pathogens should kill them off and open space for other species. This mechanism is thought to be especially strong at the seedling stage. However, tropical montane forests are unusual because they are far less diverse than lowland forests and are often dominated by just a few tree species. The authors ask whether CNDD regulates the dominant oak Quercus costaricensis in the Talamanca highlands of Costa Rica, where this oak makes up over 90% of the adult stems. They expected weak CNDD and possibly a positive effect of nearby adults on recruitment. Using four 400 m² plots censused from 2014 to 2017, they tracked 3538 seedlings and modeled annual survival with a generalized linear mixed-effects model, and modeled recruitment with a quasi-Poisson GLMM. They also used Ripley's K to test spatial aggregation. The main finding is that they found no effect of CNDD on seedling survival or recruitment. Instead, herbivory and Chusquea bamboo density both reduced survival, and higher seedling density actually increased survival and recruitment. They attribute the absence of density regulation to predator satiation and facilitation via ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults. They conclude that the lack of intraspecific density regulation at the seedling stage likely explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis, with local density instead controlled by herbivory and bamboo density. This study contributes to understanding why some dominant tropical trees escape the negative effects of CNDD that regulate more common species.

Research Context
CNDD is a key mechanism proposed to regulate species coexistence. CNDD reduces seedling survival when conspecific density is high. The mechanism is thought to act mainly at the seedling stage. Tropical montane forests are less diverse and dominated by few species. The processes structuring these low-diversity forests are poorly understood. Costa Rican montane forests are dominated by oaks.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study tests whether CNDD regulates the dominant oak Q. costaricensis. The authors expected weak or absent CNDD regulation. They predicted a positive effect of nearby adults on recruitment. They tested the effect of conspecific density, distance to nearest adult, and herbivory. They also examined the effect of Chusquea bamboo density. They predicted herbivory would decrease with higher seedling density. They predicted predator satiation would raise survival at high density.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station. The site elevation ranged from 3100 to 3350 m a.s.l. Mean annual precipitation is 2500 mm. Mean air temperature is 12°C with large daily fluctuations. Four 400 m² plots were established in old-growth forest. Plots were undisturbed for at least 30 years. Each plot was subdivided into 64 quadrats. Chusquea stem density varied from 0 to 14 stems per m². All Q. costaricensis seedlings were mapped and tagged in February 2014. Adult DBH was measured in plots and a 10 m buffer. Conspecific seedling density was measured in a 1 m radius. Herbivory was scored with the Núñez-Farfán and Dirzo index. Seedlings were censused annually from 2014 to 2017. A seedling was dead when dry, leafless, rotten, or missing twice. The 2014 fruiting year was treated as the only masting event. Survival was modeled with a binomial GLMM. Recruitment was modeled with a quasi-Poisson GLMM. Quadrat and census year were random effects. An age dummy distinguished 2014 seedlings from 2015 recruits. A second-degree polynomial was tested for distance to nearest adult. Spatial distribution was analyzed with Ripley's K. Analyses were performed in R version 3.2.2. The spatstat library was used for spatial analyses. The lme4 package was used for mixed models.

Procedures And Architectures
Seedlings were defined as individuals under 2 m tall. Adults were defined as trees over 5 cm DBH. New 2015 recruits were identified by attached cotyledons. Recruits with undeveloped leaves were excluded from recording. The 2016 recruits were treated as 2015 recruits. Only recruitment after the 2014 masting was analyzed. All variables were standardized before modeling. Seedling height was log-transformed. Models retained significant interactions and polynomial terms. Recruitment models included conspecific tree density in a 2.5 m radius. Janzen-Connell effects were tested via density and distance on herbivory. Survival was modeled across three years. A full model included all variables and second-order interactions. Recruitment was analyzed per quadrat. Plots were a random effect to account for spatial autocorrelation.

Key Results
3538 seedlings were tracked across the study period. 2031 seedlings were mapped and tagged in the 2014 census. Seedlings were spatially aggregated at all scales. Over 99% of seedlings showed some leaf damage. About 71% had intermediate herbivory damage. Annual survival declined from 73.2% to 63.8%. Seedling height had the strongest positive effect on survival. Bamboo density and herbivory both reduced survival. Survival was highest at intermediate distances from adults. Seedling and bamboo densities interacted significantly. High seedling density raised survival at low bamboo density. High seedling density lowered survival at high bamboo density. No significant interaction was found between seedling density and herbivory. 1578 new recruits were recorded in 2015. New recruits had lower herbivory than 2014 seedlings. 2014 seedlings had 43.75% leaf damage. This difference was highly significant. Recruitment increased with conspecific seedling density. Recruitment did not correlate with adult density. Recruitment did not correlate with bamboo density. Main-factor interactions had no effect on recruitment. No significant CNDD effect was found on survival or recruitment.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The absence of CNDD may explain the dominance of Q. costaricensis. Similar patterns occur in other masting species. Herbivore satiation explains higher survival at high density. Survival was higher after the 2014 masting event. Ectomycorrhizal transfer may facilitate seedlings near adults. Survival peaked at intermediate adult distances. ECM transfer may let seedlings escape CNDD effects. Bamboo reduces survival via resource competition. Bamboo limits light and water availability. Bamboo may alter soil and hinder ECM fungi. Dominant trees are expected to have weaker CNDD. Shade tolerance may reduce CNDD sensitivity. Local density is regulated by herbivory and bamboo. Neither herbivory nor bamboo effects were density dependent.

Contradictions And Limitations
Results contradict Janzen-Connell expectations. Herbivory increased away from adults. Positive density effects oppose negative density effects. Recruitment correlated with density, not distance. Recruitment did not correlate with adult density. Only one masting event was analyzed. Recruitment data were limited to one year. Survival was high despite heavy herbivory. Environmental factors were beyond the study scope. Harsh montane conditions may alter CNDD. Spatial aggregation was assumed for CNDD tests. The sample size of 2016 recruits was small.

Claims
CNDD does not regulate seedling survival or recruitment of the dominant oak Q. costaricensis. No significant CNDD effect was found. Herbivory decreased with higher seedling density. Recruitment increased with seedling density. Survival was higher after the masting event. This matches expectations for dominant trees. Seedling height strongly increased survival. Bamboo density reduced survival. Distance to nearest adult had a quadratic effect. The absence of CNDD may explain dominance. Herbivore satiation may explain high survival. ECM transfer may facilitate seedlings. Herbivory and bamboo regulate local density.
Herbivory and Chusquea bamboo density reduce Q. costaricensis seedling survival. Bamboo density and herbivory reduced survival. Over 99% of seedlings showed leaf damage. Loss of leaf area increases mortality. Bamboo thickets reduce seedling survival. Survival remained high despite herbivory. Herbivory was not density dependent. Herbivory controls seedling density. Bamboo limits understory establishment. Bamboo may hinder ECM fungi.
Predator satiation and ECM facilitation explain the lack of CNDD in this dominant oak. Survival was higher after the masting event. Seeds germinate in areas of higher seedling density. ECM transfer increases survival near adults. ECM transfer may escape CNDD effects. Distance effect was quadratic, not purely positive. Recruitment did not correlate with adult density. Satiation reduces per-capita herbivory. Facilitation increases survival near adults. These traits explain dominance.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A full model included all variables and interactions. Models retained significant interactions and polynomial terms. A second-degree polynomial was tested for distance. Recruitment analysis used only 2015 data. Only recruitment after 2014 masting was analyzed. The 2016 recruits were treated as 2015 recruits. The 2014 fruiting year was the only masting event. Spatial aggregation was verified with Ripley's K.

Ethical Considerations
The paper does not report ethics statements.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Index of Herbivory distribution. Figure 2 shows effects on seedling survival. Figure S1 shows seedling spatial aggregation. Figure S2 shows the seedling-bamboo interaction. Table S1 summarizes model results. Table S2 shows herbivory patterns.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the null result for CNDD in a dominant oak. The strongest evidence is the positive density effect on survival and recruitment. The future path is testing herbivory, bamboo, and ECM effects.

summary.title: Phylogenetic study of thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and proposal of a new classification Quasigeobacillus
summary.authors: Carling (University of Canberra); Blom (Diversity Arrays Technology Pty Ltd); Georges (University of Canberra); Berenice Talamantes Becerra
summary.field_subfield: Microbial taxonomy / comparative genomics (Bacillaceae thermophiles)
summary.executive_summary: This study performs a phylogenomic re-evaluation of three closely related thermophilic genera—Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus—using publicly available whole-genome sequences. The authors assembled 113 genomes and applied multiple complementary metrics: Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), and a maximum-likelihood (ML) tree built from 662 orthologous core genes. The combined evidence revealed that the genomes partition into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, while clade II contains most Anoxybacillus species. Clade I further splits into three subclades, one of which the authors propose elevating to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. tepidamans and one genomospecies) consistently occupy this third subclade but cannot be cleanly assigned to any existing genus. The study underscores the importance of analyzing closely related genera together rather than in isolation, as doing so exposes incongruences in current taxonomy. The authors note that when broader phylogenetic assessment is absent, genus designations for new strains can become inconsistent with the phylogeny of the complete genome set. The research demonstrates that combined phylogenomic analysis reveals delimitation problems that would be missed if each genus were considered alone. This work contributes to bacterial taxonomy by providing genomic evidence for taxonomic revision and highlighting methodological best practices for assigning genomic affinities. The findings have implications for how new isolates are classified and named in the future, emphasizing the need for comprehensive phylogenetic context. The paper also proposes formal taxonomic changes, including the description of the new genus Quasigeobacillus, reflecting the significance of integrating multiple lines of genomic evidence in modern bacterial systematics.

claims.description: Combined phylogenomic analysis of closely related genera reveals delimitation problems not visible when analyzed individually.
The genomes partition into two main clades, with clade I containing all Geobacillus and Parageobacillus plus some Anoxybacillus.

The study underscores the importance of analyzing closely related genera together rather than in isolation, as doing so exposes incongruences in current taxonomy. The authors note that when broader phylogenetic assessment is absent, genus designations for new strains can become inconsistent with the phylogeny of the complete genome set. This work contributes to bacterial taxonomy by providing genomic evidence for taxonomic revision and highlighting methodological best practices for assigning genomic affinities. The findings have implications for how new isolates are classified and named in the future, emphasizing the need for comprehensive phylogenetic context. The paper also proposes formal taxonomic changes, including the description of the new genus Quasigeobacillus, reflecting the significance of integrating multiple lines of genomic evidence in modern bacterial systematics.

Research Context
The introduction of next-generation sequencing enables discrimination among bacterial genomes to establish taxonomic thresholds. DNA-DNA hybridization was historically regarded as the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy. 16S rRNA gene sequencing suffers from low resolution when bacterial sequences are highly similar. ANI values provide higher resolution than 16S rRNA for detecting genome relatedness. AAI is recommended for distant genome comparisons because amino acid similarity is better conserved.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to perform phylogenetic and comparative genomic analysis of three thermophilic genera. The authors hypothesize that closely related genera should be studied together to resolve phylogeny. The authors predict that combined analysis will reveal problems in genus delimitation not seen individually. The authors predict that a third clade within clade I warrants elevation to a new genus.

Methodological Details
The study used 113 genome assemblies of the three genera from the RefSeq database. Thirty-two Anoxybacillus and seventy-three Geobacillus strains were downloaded from RefSeq. Parageobacillus was represented by seven validly described species with one assembly each. Seven newly isolated strains from an Australian thermophiles study were included. The included strains comprised 31 chromosome-level, 33 scaffold, and 49 contig-level assemblies. Anomalous assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status were excluded from the study. Methods were based on those used for reassessment of the genus Geobacillus by Aliyu et al.

Procedures And Architectures
The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0. Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 assembly served as the starting reference for CDS identification. Orthologous genes were identified by iteratively comparing CDS against assemblies via BLAST. Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included as an outgroup in the core gene analysis. Five low-CDS assemblies were excluded and one duplicate was removed during core gene discovery. The obtained CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE. The maximum-likelihood tree was built using the FastTree software package. Two-way ANI was calculated using the ani.rb script with default parameters. Two-way AAI was calculated using the aai.rb script with default parameters. Draft genomes were concatenated with 100 N bases introduced between contigs. ANI and AAI similarity values were arranged into matrices and used in the DendroUPGMA web server. The UPGMA clustering method was selected to obtain the dendrograms. Genes unique to clade I-c were identified using BLASTn alignment with relaxed filtering criteria. CDS from Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 were used to identify genes present in all clade I-c members.

Key Results
The core gene set comprised 662 orthologous genes per genome used to produce the ML tree. The ML tree was produced with 114 genomes including the outgroup. The core gene ML tree splits into three major groups: outgroup, clade I, and clade II. Clade I consists of eighty-seven genomes. Clade II consists of twenty-four Anoxybacillus genomes. The ANI dendrogram was built with 114 genomes. The AAI dendrogram was built with 114 genomes. Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL, Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3, and Geobacillus sp. summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar, Sanjay Barua, Nitin Khandelwal, Kundan Kumar Chaubey, Ram Kumar, Krishan Dutt, Yogesh Chander, Thachamvally Riyesh, Vir Shoor Singh, Bhupendra Nath
summary.field_subfield: Virology / Antiviral drug discovery (paramyxoviruses)
summary.executive_summary: This study establishes, for the first time, that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) is a proviral host factor for paramyxoviruses, namely Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV), and that its specific inhibitor thapsigargin can impair their replication. The authors reasoned that because viruses rely heavily on host cellular machinery, targeting host factors rather than viral proteins could circumvent the rapid drug resistance that plagues conventional antivirals. They treated Vero cells with thapsigargin at a nontoxic concentration (0.5 µM) and measured virus yields by plaque assay, finding significant reductions in NDV and PPRV replication, while DNA viruses (BHV-1 and BPXV) were variably affected. To confirm a specific SERCA role, they overexpressed SERCA2 in HeLa/goat kidney cells and showed that this both enhanced replication and rescued the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin. They also demonstrated that PPRV infection induced SERCA2 expression, which itself could be blocked by thapsigargin. Using time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays, they localized the inhibition to viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins, while attachment, RNA synthesis, and budding were unaffected. Immunofluorescence quantified that thapsigargin caused defective localization in ~70% of cells versus 10-30% in controls. A notable and unexpected finding was that NDV, but not PPRV, acquired significant resistance to thapsigargin after 70 passages in Vero cells, with resistance emerging around passage 25-35 and reaching ~100-fold inhibition versus ~10,000-fold at zero passage. The authors discuss this resistance in the context of prior reports of host-targeting resistance, such as Coxsackievirus B3 and HCV mutants, and propose mechanisms including altered host factor requirements or enhanced substrate affinity. They acknowledge that a completely resistant NDV phenotype was not achieved even at passage 70, and that co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins was imperfect, with unsuccessful co-immunoprecipitation, so direct SERCA-virus interactions could not be established. The study concludes that SERCA is a promising candidate drug target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics against paramyxoviruses. The paper contains no bibliography, so top_influential_citations is set to "". Cytotoxicity was assessed via MTT assay, and virucidal activity was tested by incubating virions with thapsigargin before plaque assay, showing no direct virucidal effect. The research is foundational and mechanistic, contributing to the understanding of host-directed antiviral strategies and the potential for viruses to evolve resistance even against host-targeting agents.

Executive Summary

They also demonstrated that PPRV infection induced SERCA2 expression, which itself could be blocked by thapsigargin. Using time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays, they localized the inhibition to viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins, while attachment, RNA synthesis, and budding were unaffected. Immunofluorescence quantified that thapsigargin caused defective localization in ~70% of cells versus 10-30% in controls. A notable and unexpected finding was that NDV, but not PPRV, acquired significant resistance to thapsigargin after 70 passages in Vero cells, with resistance emerging around passage 25-35 and reaching ~100-fold inhibition versus ~10,000-fold at zero passage. The authors discuss this resistance in the context of prior reports of host-targeting resistance, such as Coxsackievirus B3 and HCV mutants, and propose mechanisms including altered host factor requirements or enhanced substrate affinity. They acknowledge that a completely resistant NDV phenotype was not achieved even at passage 70, and that co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins was imperfect, with unsuccessful co-immunoprecipitation, so direct SERCA-virus interactions could not be established. The study concludes that SERCA is a promising candidate drug target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics against paramyxoviruses. The paper contains no bibliography, so top_influential_citations is set to "". Cytotoxicity was assessed via MTT assay, and virucidal activity was tested by incubating virions with thapsigargin before plaque assay, showing no direct virucidal effect. The research is foundational and mechanistic, contributing to the understanding of host-directed antiviral strategies and the potential for viruses to evolve resistance even against host-targeting agents.

Research Context
Antiviral drug development has classically targeted essential viral proteins. High viral mutation rates drive resistance to antiviral drugs and preexisting immunity. This mutation-driven resistance has prompted a shift toward novel antiviral approaches. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites highly dependent on host cellular factors. Some dysregulated host factors facilitate virus replication and can serve as drug targets. Protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation are key cellular regulatory mechanisms. The human kinome comprises 518 protein kinase genes identified in 2002. These kinases play key roles in cancer and viral infections, making them drug targets. Vertebrates have three families of P-type Ca2+-ATPases regulating intracellular calcium. SERCA transports Ca2+ from cytosol to the endoplasmic reticulum. SERCA is involved in signal transduction, apoptosis, exocytosis, cell motility, and transcription. The role of Ca2+-ATPases in virus replication is only beginning to be appreciated. SERCA and PMCA roles in virus replication remain unknown, while SPCA1 supports replication. Prior screening of kinase and phosphatase inhibitors identified candidate antivirals.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether SERCA facilitates paramyxovirus replication. The authors hypothesize that SERCA is a proviral host factor for paramyxoviruses. They hypothesize that thapsigargin, a SERCA inhibitor, impairs paramyxovirus replication. They predict that SERCA overexpression will rescue the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin. They predict that PPRV infection induces SERCA expression. They hypothesize that thapsigargin blocks virus-induced SERCA expression. They predict that thapsigargin inhibits specific pre-budding steps of the viral life cycle. They hypothesize that SERCA is required for proper localization of viral proteins. They predict that viruses may acquire resistance to host-targeting inhibitors under selection. They hypothesize that NDV, but not PPRV, may acquire thapsigargin resistance. They predict that SERCA is a candidate drug target for antiviral therapeutics. They predict that thapsigargin does not directly inactivate cell-free virions.

Methodological Details
Four cell lines were used: Vero, 293T, HeLa, and goat kidney cells. Cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with antibiotics and 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum. PPRV and NDV were available in the laboratory and described elsewhere. Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Thapsigargin was procured from Sigma with catalog number T9033. Thapsigargin is a non-competitive inhibitor extracted from Thapsia garganica. SERCA2 ATPase antibody (MA3-919) was procured from Invitrogen. Anti-PPRV and anti-NDV sera were described by the authors' group. Secondary antibodies were fluorescein isothiocyanate-conjugated anti-rabbit and Rhodamine-conjugated anti-mouse. Secondary antibodies were purchased from Sigma. Cytotoxicity of thapsigargin was analyzed by MTT assay. Antiviral efficacy used Vero/MDBK cells infected at MOI=0.1 with 0.5 µM thapsigargin or DMSO. Progeny virus particles were quantified by plaque assay. Virucidal activity used ~10^6 pfu incubated in serum-free medium with DMSO or ten-fold dilutions of thapsigargin for 1.5 h at 37°C. Samples were chilled at 4°C and diluted 10^-3, 10^-4, and 10^-5-fold before plaque assay. Time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, budding) were conducted as previously described. HeLa/goat kidney cells were transfected in 24-well plates in triplicates with 1 µg of empty vector (pCR3) or SERCA2 plasmid (pCR3-SERCA2). Transfection used Lipofectamine 3000 Transfection reagent. Cells were infected at 48 h post-transfection at MOI of 1. Virus particles were quantified at 24 hpi (NDV) or 96 hpi (PPRV). Vero cells were grown at ~20% confluency and infected at MOI of 5 for 2 h. Thapsigargin was applied at 3 hpi (NDV) and 10 hpi (PPRV). Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min and blocked with 1% BSA for 30 min. Primary antibodies were applied for 30 min in the presence of 0.2% saponin. Secondary antibodies were incubated for 30 min in the presence of 0.2% saponin. Cells were mounted with DAPI and examined by fluorescence microscopy. Resistant mutants were selected by sequential passage (70 passages) in Vero cells with 0.25 µM thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO. At each passage, cells were infected, washed 5 times with PBS, and incubated for 72-120 h or until CPE in ≥75% cells. Passage 1 (P1) virus was quantified and used at MOI of 0.01 for passage 2 (P2). Relative resistance was assessed by infecting at MOI=0.1 with 0.05% DMSO or 0.5 µM thapsigargin. Fold inhibition levels were determined from plaque assays. The sample size for mutant selection was 70 passages.

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin was identified from a previously described protein kinase inhibitor library. Cytotoxicity was assessed across concentrations from 0.00064 µM to 2 µM over 96 h. Concentrations above 2 µM were found to be toxic to the cells. A non-cytotoxic concentration of 0.5 µM was used for subsequent experiments. Antiviral efficacy was measured by infectious virus yield in the presence of 0.5 µM inhibitor or DMSO. Virucidal activity tested 0.5 µM or 5 µM thapsigargin for 1.5 h before residual infectivity testing. SERCA2 overexpression was confirmed to facilitate and rescue paramyxovirus replication. SERCA2 expression was evaluated by Western blot with GAPDH as housekeeping control. SERCA2 expression peaked between 24-72 hpi and declined at 96 hpi. Time-of-addition assay used one-step growth curves with inhibitor applied at different times post-infection. NDV replication cycle is ~10 h and PPRV is ~24 h. Time-of-addition of inhibitor and virus harvest varied from virus to virus. For NDV, highest inhibition was at 30 min before infection, decreasing from 1 hpi to 6 hpi. No inhibition was observed when thapsigargin was applied at 10 hpi (budding stage). For PPRV, highest inhibition was at 30 min prior to infection, decreasing from 4 hpi to 24 hpi. Thapsigargin did not affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. For entry assay, preattached virus at 4°C was allowed to enter at 37°C in the presence of thapsigargin. Immunofluorescence monitored subcellular localization at 12 hpi (NDV) or 36 hpi (PPRV). Thapsigargin treatment showed defective localization in ~70% of cells versus 10-30% in DMSO control. Resistant mutant selection used sequential passage with harvest time of 72-120 h and MOI of 0.01-0.001. A refined experiment used MOI=0.1 and 24 h harvest to evaluate relative resistance. Transfection reagent, plasmids, and antibodies were specified for reproducibility. The co-immunoprecipitation assay to analyze SERCA/virus interaction was unsuccessful. A perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins could not be observed.

Key Results
Thapsigargin did not significantly affect cell viability at concentrations up to 2 µM over 96 h. Concentrations above 2 µM were toxic to the cells. A non-cytotoxic concentration of 0.5 µM was used for subsequent experiments. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited NDV replication. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited PPRV replication. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited BHV-1 replication. Thapsigargin did not inhibit BPXV replication. Thapsigargin did not exhibit any virucidal effect on any prototype virus tested. Overexpression of SERCA2 facilitated NDV/PPRV replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of thapsigargin on virus replication. PPRV infection resulted in enhanced SERCA2 expression. SERCA2 expression peaked between 24-72 hpi before declining at 96 hpi. GAPDH levels were similar at all time points, confirming viral-related SERCA2 induction. Virus-induced SERCA2 expression could be blocked by thapsigargin treatment. For NDV, highest inhibition was at 30 min before infection, decreasing from 1 hpi to 6 hpi. No inhibition was observed when thapsigargin was applied at 10 hpi for NDV. For PPRV, highest inhibition was at 30 min prior to infection, decreasing from 4 hpi to 24 hpi. Thapsigargin did not affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Thapsigargin treatment resulted in reduced NDV and PPRV titers, indicating blocked entry. Thapsigargin treatment showed defective localization in ~70% of cells versus 10-30% in DMSO control. NDV did not generate a completely resistant phenotype against thapsigargin even after 70 passages. Resistance began appearing at ~P25 and significant resistance at P35. Significant resistance at P35 was ~100-fold inhibition versus ~10,000-fold at zero passage. P70-Thapsigargin virus exhibited significantly lower sensitivity to thapsigargin versus P0 and P70-Control. All PPRVs (P0, P70-Thapsigargin, P70-Control) revealed similar sensitivity to thapsigargin at passage 70. Control-passaged viruses did not exhibit significant resistance even after 70 passages.

Thapsigargin's antiviral activity is due to inhibition of virus replication in target cells, not direct virucidal effect. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect, confirming SERCA2 supports paramyxovirus replication. SERCA2 expression is induced by PPRV infection and peaks between 24-72 hpi. Virus-induced SERCA2 expression can be blocked by thapsigargin, linking SERCA to viral infection. Time-of-addition suggests thapsigargin inhibits multiple pre-budding steps of paramyxovirus replication. The inhibition is specifically at viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins. Defective localization in ~70% of cells versus 10-30% in controls indicates SERCA is required for proper localization. SERCA may present as a novel target for antiviral drug development. Multiple calcium transporters may be involved in efficient replication of paramyxoviruses. Host-targeting agents impose a higher genetic barrier to generation of resistant viruses. Targeting host factors could have broad-spectrum inhibition against different virus families. This novel approach has led to promising compounds for treatment of HCV and HIV. It is generally believed that viruses do not acquire resistance against host-targeting antiviral agents. NDV resistance adds another example to a short list of viruses that can acquire resistance to host-targeting agents. This is the first documented example where a paramyxovirus significantly bypasses its dependency on a cellular factor. One possible mechanism is change in host factor requirement. Resistant viruses may have enhanced affinity for their natural substrate. SERCA is validated as a candidate drug target for antiviral therapeutics.

A completely resistant NDV phenotype could not be achieved even at passage level 70. Fluctuations in viral titers and fold inhibition were observed across passages. The harvest time (72-120 h) and MOI (0.01-0.001) were not similar at each passage. A perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins could not be observed. The co-immunoprecipitation assay to analyze SERCA/virus interaction was unsuccessful. Direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins could not be determined. The exact mechanism of NDV resistance remains unclear. Which viral proteins acquired mutations upon prolonged passage is not determined. The specific mutations conferring resistance against thapsigargin are not identified. The role of SERCA and PMCA in virus replication remains unknown.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy, Udai Gujral, Carolina Del Lama Marques, Andrew Stone, Korinne Northwood, Lez J Burke, Julia M W Gee, Kenneth Nephew, Susan Clark, Melissa A Brown
summary.field_subfield: Molecular oncology / microRNA regulation in breast cancer
summary.executive_summary: MicroRNAs are potent post-transcriptional regulators involved in all hallmarks of cancer. This study focuses on MIR196A, which is transcribed from two loci and implicated in developmental and pathogenic processes, with targets including Hox, Fox, Cdk inhibitors and annexins. The authors note that genetic variants and altered expression of miR196a are associated with risk and progression of multiple cancers including breast cancer, however little is known about the regulation of the genes encoding this miRNA, nor the impact of variants therein. The central aim was to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A including factors regulating its expression and explore potential roles of regulatory elements and factors in breast cancer prognostication. Using MCF7 cells, the authors demonstrated that MIR196A displays complex and dynamic expression patterns, in part controlled by long range transcriptional regulation between promoter and enhancer elements bound by ERα. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) for RNA polymerase II demonstrates that polymerase binding in the region surrounding the HOXC10 gene and MIR196A gene is dependent on oestrogen in MCF7 cells and is repressed with both tamoxifen or fulvestrant treatment. Global-run-on sequencing (GRO-Seq) analysis of MCF7 cells clearly indicates a dramatic increase in RNA production in the genomic region surrounding MIR196A2, peaking at 40 mins following addition of oestradiol (E2). These data clearly indicate an increase in precursor miRNA from MIR196A2 but not MIR196A1 in response to E2. To identify the structural elements associated with the transcriptional regulation of MIR196A, histone methylation patterns in the MCF7 breast cancer cell line were assessed. Using publicly available datasets, the authors established that oestrogen mediated upregulation of miR-196A expression is accompanied by binding of ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 to two putative promoter regions, putative promoters 1 and 3 (PP1 and PP3), upstream of the miR196A2 transcription start site. Using ChIA-PET genome-wide chromatin interactions that immunoprecipitate with either ERα or RNA Polymerase II, the authors identified two major sites of interaction with the MIR196A2 promoters. One of these is a previously identified HOTAIR enhancer (HDE) and the other a novel interacting partner (MIR196A2-Enhancer, mE). Chromosome conformation capture (3C) and 3C-qPCR demonstrate that both enhancer elements physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. The authors then investigated MIR196A expression patterns in relation to commonly utilised molecular markers of breast tumours, identifying four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression. Using the METABRIC cohort of breast tumours, expression analysis indicates that MIR196A is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal adjacent tissue and over-expression is associated with an increase in tumour stage. High expression of MIR196A is associated with a poor survival in estrogen receptor positive (ER+) breast cancer, whilst high expression associates with a better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Using MIR196A expression, overall survival of ER+ tumours responding to both hormone therapy (HT) and chemotherapy (CT) was stratified. Women with low MIR196A expression had exhibited a high rate of survival (>95% at 10 years), whilst most women within the high expression group died within 17 years (61% at 10 years). The effects of menopause on the stratification of survival for ER+ women were investigated. In premenopausal women, high expression of MIR196A is associated with a good outcome in ER+ disease. Multivariate analysis demonstrates that MIR196A is one of the few significant biomarkers for ER+ tumours arising before menopause. In post-menopausal women, all tested biomarkers were significant in ER+ disease, including MIR196A, however high expression is now associated with a poor outcome. Using established models of HR+ disease resistance, the authors found that MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen resistant MCF7 cells (TAMR) whilst it is almost depleted in fulvestrant resistance (FASR). For HR+ resistant tumours the only remaining therapeutic options are radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Using RNA-Seq data for cell line models of resistance to paclitaxel and adriamycin, two common chemotherapeutics, MIR196A expression again increases in resistant cell lines compared to the treatment sensitive cell line. Utilising ERα ChIP-Seq performed in human patients with HR+ disease, binding sites for ERα were identified in the genomic region of MIR196A. This tumour cohort contains women who respond to HR therapy, those who do not and metastases from resistant tumours. An increase in ERα occupancy is seen at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases. This work sheds light on the normal and abnormal regulation of MIR196A and provides a novel stratification method for therapeutically resistant breast cancer.

claims.description: MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen via ERα-bound promoter and enhancer elements.
High MIR196A expression is a prognostic biomarker of poor outcome in ER+ breast cancer, particularly in advanced and post-menopausal disease.
Therapeutic resistance leads to increases in MIR196A expression, linking its regulation to endocrine and chemotherapeutic resistance.
