Research Context
MicroRNAs are potent post-transcriptional regulators involved in all hallmarks of cancer. MIR196A is transcribed from two loci and has been implicated in a wide range of developmental and pathogenic processes. MIR196A is overexpressed in breast tumours, and a SNP within the MIR196A2 gene is associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer. Despite the clear importance on miR-196a in cancer, its transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Several instances of miRNA regulation by enhancers have been described, but this area is very much in its infancy. The expression of MIR196A in breast cancer is both dynamic and complex. This work sheds light on the normal and abnormal regulation of MIR196A and provides a novel stratification method for therapeutically resistant breast cancer.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A including factors regulating its expression and explore potential roles of regulatory elements and factors in breast cancer prognostication. Given that MIR196A expression strongly correlates with expression of HOXC protein coding genes in breast cancer, the authors sought to determine if oestrogen also regulates MIR196A2. Given that MIR196A expression is regulated by oestrogen we hypothesized that its transcription may be controlled by the oestrogen receptor (ER). Given that ERα often binds to distal enhancer elements to exert its function, we examined the hypothesis that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation, mediated by ERα tethered gene looping. Given that MIR196A is regulated by ERα, we investigated its expression patterns in relation to commonly utilised molecular markers of breast tumours. High expression of MIR196A is a biomarker of poor prognosis in ER+ tumours, especially in those patients resistant to therapy. We hypothesise that a consorted effort of multiple enhancers is responsible for the overexpression of these genes in cancer possibly driven by extensive binding and activity of ERα. Future studies should aim to uncover the purpose of increase MIR196A expression and if it is required for development of resistance alone or in combination with other HOXC genes.

Methodological Details
MCF7 cells, for the development of endocrine resistance sub-lines, were obtained from AstraZeneca. MCF7, Tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR), Fulvestrant-resistant (FASR), and oestrogen-deprived (MCF7x) cells were cultured as described. All cell lines were cultured for less than 6 months after authentication by short-tandem repeat (STR) profiling. MCF7 cells were transfected with 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs, 20 ng of pRL-TK and 0.5μL of Lipofectamine 3000. 48 hours post transfection luciferase readings were measured using a DTX-880 luminometer and Dual-Glo Stop and Glo luciferase reporter kit. Cell lysates were prepared using Life Technologies TRIzol reagent and RNA was chloroform extracted and isopropanol precipitated. RNA for miRNA analysis was reverse transcribed using the miScript RT II kit from Qiagen. Assays for all miRNAs were performed with Qiagen's miScript SYBR Green PCR Kit. Expression data for miRNAs was normalised to the snoRNA RNU6b. All qRT-PCRs were performed using the protocols advised by the manufacturers on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000. RNA-Seq on MCF7 cells following oestradiol treatment was performed as described previously by K. Nephew. RNA-Seq from Adriamycin (ADM) and paclitaxel (PTX) resistant MCF7 derived cells was sourced from GSE68815. Expression of HOX genes in human breast cells was sourced from Gascard et al. Accession codes for publically available data were MCF7 ChIP-Seq (GSE14664), GRO-Seq (GSE27463), ChIA-PET (GSE39495), Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq (GSE32222). MCF7 histone ChIP-Seq and breast cell 450K array data was sourced from ENCODE via http://genome.ucsc.edu/ENCODE/downloads.html. ChIP-Seq data was mapped with Bowtie and peaks called by MACS and viewed in the Interactive Genome Viewer (IGV). DNA methylation of breast tumours was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and correlated to the gene expression of MIR196A from the TCGA cohort. METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083. Clustering of Illumina Array and miR-Seq data was performed using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV). Data was mean-centred and hierarchically clustered via Manhattan average-linkage based clustering of both rows and columns. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses were performed using MedCalc for Windows, version 12.7. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and generation of survival curves was done GraphPad Prism. Optimal cutoffs for low and high expression groups were determined using receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curves. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) was adapted from Vakoc 2005, Hagege 2007 and Tan-Wong 2008. Cells were grown to 60-80% confluence and fixed with 1% formaldehyde. Libraries were generated for each cell line using HindIII with control libraries undigested and unligated. GAPDH primers were used to determine the digestion and ligation efficiency of each library. The sample sizes for the cell culture experiments and the specific patient cohort demographics are not reported in the text.

Procedures And Architectures
All PCR products for luciferase reporter assays were ligated into Invitrogen's pCR-Blunt plasmid using T4 DNA Ligase, at 4 0 C overnight. MIR196A enhancers and promoters were digested from pCR-Blunt and cloned into the luciferase reporter plasmid pGL3-Basic. Enhancers were cloned into the BamHI/SalI site whilst promoters were cloned into the multiple cloning site immediately upstream of the luciferase gene. See Supplementary Table1 for primers. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) for RNA polymerase II demonstrates that polymerase binding in the region surrounding the HOXC10 gene and MIR196A gene is dependent on oestrogen in MCF7 cells and is repressed with both tamoxifen or fulvestrant treatment. Global-run-on sequencing (GRO-Seq) is able to measure nascent RNA, assessing changes in transcription with high sensitivity. Analysis of MCF7 GRO-Seq data clearly indicates a dramatic increase in RNA production in the genomic region surrounding MIR196A2, peaking at 40 mins following addition of oestradiol (E2). This increase in RNA production from the HOXC locus was validated with qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq from MCF7 cells following addition of E2. This analysis uncovered putative promoter elements upstream of MIR196A including a shared promoter with HOXC10. Using publically available datasets we established that oestrogen mediated upregulation of miR-196A expression is accompanied by binding of ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 to two putative promoter regions, putative promoters 1 and 3 (PP1 and PP3). Upon cloning of these putative promoter sites into luciferase reporter vectors where PP1 and also PP2; modestly; increases luciferase gene transcription. we examined the hypothesis that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation, mediated by ERα tethered gene looping. Using ChIA-PET genome-wide chromatin interactions that immunoprecipitate with either ERα or RNA Polymerase II, we identified two major sites of interaction with the MIR196A2 promoters. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) digestion of the HOXC genomic locus digests the MIR196A2 region into two fragments. 3C-qPCR demonstrates that both enhancer elements physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. Cloning of these fragments downstream of the putative promoter luciferase reporters clearly demonstrates significant augmentation of transcription for both the PP1 and PP2. Analysis of DNA methylation reveals that this CpG island is mostly methylated in non-malignant MCF10A and cancerous MCF7 cells, whilst unmethylated in human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC). Using established models of HR+ disease resistance we found that MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen resistant MCF7 cells (TAMR) whilst it is almost depleted in fulvestrant resistance (FASR). These expression patterns match changes in DNA methylation to the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters in these same cells. Using RNA-Seq data for cell line models of resistance to paclitaxel and adriamycin, two common chemotherapeutics, MIR196A expression again increases in resistant cell lines compared to the treatment sensitive cell line. Utilising ERα ChIP-Seq performed in human patients with HR+ disease, binding sites for ERα were identified in the genomic region of MIR196A. This tumour cohort contains women who respond to HR therapy, those who do not and metastases from resistant tumours. An increase in ERα occupancy is seen at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases. To explore this hypothesis a high resolution chromatin interaction analysis of this region in breast cancer cells would be required, such as 5C or NG Capture-C, coupled with ERα ChIP-Seq and ChIA-PET.

MIR196A expression highly correlates to HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10. The association between MIR196A expression and HOXC genes is more limited, observed most strongly with HOXC11 and HOXC10, the genes surrounding the MIR196A gene. MIR196A appears to be mostly expressed within the basal stem-cell (BSC) derived cells, whilst much lower in expression of the more differentiated cell types. This analysis identified four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression (Clusters 1-4). Interestingly clusters 1 and 3 show a strong correlation to expression of hormone receptors (HR) and HR cofactors. In contrast, clusters 2 and 4 have significant negative correlation to expression of ERα, PGR, FOXA1 and GATA3, whilst associating with EGFR and HER2. This expression is further defined by the PAM50 intrinsic subtypes where MIR196A is strongly expressed in the HER2 subtype. Expression analysis of this miRNA indicate that it is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal adjacent tissue and over-expression is associated with an increase in tumour stage. High expression of MIR196A is associated with a poor survival in estrogen receptor positive (ER+) breast cancer, whilst high expression associates with a better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors hypothesise that a consorted effort of multiple enhancers is responsible for the overexpression of these genes in cancer possibly driven by extensive binding and activity of ERα. Given the strong correlation in expression of all HOXC genes in breast tumours with MIR196A is in stark contrast to expression in normal tissues. Interestingly, DNA methylation at several sites within the HOXC locus negatively correlates with the expression of this miRNA, supporting the notion of DNA methylation as a repressive epigenetic modification in this context. High expression of MIR196A is a biomarker of poor prognosis in ER+ tumours, especially in those patients resistant to therapy. These data raise the possibility that the pathway to resistance to therapy in ER+ tumours involves the de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements. Given the strong involvement of HOX genes in development, we hypothesise that there is a change in the regulation and expression of these genes through and following menopause. This miRNA is a possible biomarker for the progression of breast tumour to becoming resistant to therapy. Future studies should aim to uncover the purpose of increase MIR196A expression and if it is required for development of resistance alone or in combination with other HOXC genes.

The authors note that whilst we show that PP3 is not able to increase luciferase expression in a luciferase reporter assay, the binding of ERα may be important for the activity of the HOXC10 and MIR196A2 promoters. The association between MIR196A and HOXC genes is not significant in the cell types of the human breast. It is currently unclear how dual-encoded miRs are regulated of which many exist.

summary.title: Maximal abelian extension of a modular curve unramified outside cusps
summary.authors: Takao Yamazaki and Yifan Yang
summary.field_subfield: Number theory / arithmetic geometry (modular curves, abelian extensions)
summary.type_of_paper: Short research note / proof of a theorem
summary.executive_summary: This note addresses the problem of finding a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the open modular curve Y0(p) over Q, where Y0(p) is X0(p) with its two cusps removed. The background is Mazur's theorem that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np = (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12) is the maximal unramified abelian covering of the whole curve X0(p). The gap is that X0(p) is proper, so its two cusps are ramification points; removing them enlarges the pool of available unramified coverings. The authors prove that the maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) is cyclic of degree 2Np, obtained by adjoining a square root of an explicitly constructed rational function Fh^2 on X2(p). The construction uses generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) Eg, whose transformation and cusp-order properties are recalled and applied. The key result is that Fh^2 is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q whose order at every cusp is odd, so that X'2(p) → X2(p) is a degree-two cover ramified exactly at the cusps, and the composite X'2(p) → X0(p) is geometrically maximal unramified over Y0(p). The proof splits into the case p ≢ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) is a genuine intermediate group) and the case p ≡ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) = Γ1(p) and a triplet construction is used). The note is theoretical, with no numerical experiments, datasets, or code. The main quantitative facts are the degree 2Np, the index [Γ0(p):Γ2(p)] = k = Np, the index [Γ2(p):Γ1(p)] = ℓ = gcd(p−1,12)/2, and the order-2 character machinery. The theoretical implication is that the maximal unramified abelian extension over Y0(p) is a quadratic extension of the Shimura field, controlled by the coinvariants of the generalized Jacobian's torsion.

Executive Summary
This note addresses the problem of finding a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the open modular curve Y0(p) over Q, where Y0(p) is X0(p) with its two cusps removed. The background is Mazur's theorem that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np = (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12) is the maximal unramified abelian covering of the whole curve X0(p). The gap is that X0(p) is proper, so its two cusps are ramification points; removing them enlarges the pool of available unramified coverings. The authors prove that the maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) is cyclic of degree 2Np, obtained by adjoining a square root of an explicitly constructed rational function Fh^2 on X2(p). The construction uses generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) Eg, whose transformation and cusp-order properties are recalled and applied. The key result is that Fh^2 is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q whose order at every cusp is odd, so that X'2(p) → X2(p) is a degree-two cover ramified exactly at the cusps, and the composite X'2(p) → X0(p) is geometrically maximal unramified over Y0(p). The proof splits into the case p ≢ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) is a genuine intermediate group) and the case p ≡ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) = Γ1(p) and a triplet construction is used). The note is theoretical, with no numerical experiments, datasets, or code. The main quantitative facts are the degree 2Np, the index [Γ0(p):Γ2(p)] = k = Np, the index [Γ2(p):Γ1(p)] = ℓ = gcd(p−1,12)/2, and the order-2 character machinery. The theoretical implication is that the maximal unramified abelian extension over Y0(p) is a quadratic extension of the Shimura field, controlled by the coinvariants of the generalized Jacobian's torsion.

Research Context
The setting is the maximal unramified abelian covering of a curve over a number field. The relevant group is the maximal abelian quotient of the étale fundamental group. The geometric part is the kernel of the map to the absolute Galois group. This geometric part is finite, which guarantees a maximal covering exists. Mazur's theorem establishes the maximal unramified covering of X0(p) as the Shimura cover. The Shimura covering has degree Np = (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12). The gap is that X0(p) is proper, so its cusps are ramification points. Removing the cusps enlarges the set of available unramified coverings.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is the degree of the maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p). The hypothesis is that this covering is a cyclic quadratic extension of the Shimura cover. The predicted outcome is that the degree is exactly 2Np, twice the Shimura degree. The predicted structure is a factorization through X2(p) via a degree-two cover. The predicted ramification is exactly at the cusps. The predicted field generator is a square root of an explicit rational function. The predicted tool is generalized Dedekind eta functions. The predicted modular-function property is that Fh^2 has odd order at each cusp.

Methodological Details
The base field is Q and the curves are X0(p) and X1(p) over Q. The base curve Y0(p) is X0(p) with its two cusps 0 and ∞ removed. The analysis requires X to admit a degree one divisor. The generalized Jacobian is defined in the sense of Rosenlicht–Serre. The generalized Jacobian is a semi-abelian variety fitting an exact sequence. The torsion module is defined via Hom from the Tate module to Q/Z(1). The character group LD has rank rD = Σ[x∈D][k(x):k] − 1. The abelian fundamental group is identified with Hom(MµTor(−1), Q/Z). The covering invariants Σ(f) and ΣD(f) are kernels of pull-back maps. The maximal unramified Galois groups are Hom(Σ, Q/Z(1)). Geometric maximality is defined by Σ(f) = JµTor. A maximal covering exists when k is finitely generated over its prime subfield. The prime p is assumed odd, and the main case is p ≥ 5. The construction splits into the case p ≢ 11 mod 12 and p ≡ 11 mod 12. The second case uses Γ2(p) = Γ1(p) and a triplet of integers. The second author's funding is from Taiwan's Ministry of Science and Technology.

Procedures And Architectures
The generalized Dedekind eta function Eg is defined via an infinite product. The Bernoulli polynomial used is B(x) = x^2 − x + 1/6. These functions are also called Siegel functions up to scalars. The transformation Eg+N = E−g = −Eg is a key property. The transformation under Γ0(N) is given by explicit root-of-unity factors. Products of Eg form modular functions on Γ1(N) under congruence conditions. The conditions require Σeg ≡ 0 mod 12, Σgeg ≡ 0 mod 2, Σg^2 eg ≡ 0 mod 2N. The function Fh is a 6th-power root of a product of ℓ eta functions. The indices are k = Np = (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12) and ℓ = gcd(p−1,12)/2. The group Γ2(p) is generated by Γ1(p) and a matrix with g^k in the top-left. The indices satisfy [Γ0(p):Γ2(p)] = k and [Γ2(p):Γ1(p)] = ℓ. Fh^2 is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q. The field Q(X'2(p)) is a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)). The extension is generated by a square root of Fh^2. The character ψ is the order-2 character of SL(2,Z) with explicit values. The character χ is the order-2 character of Γ2(p) when ℓ is even. The group Γ'2(p) is the kernel of ψχ or ψ, and Γ0(p)/Γ'2(p) is cyclic of order 2k. The covering X'2(p) → X2(p) ramifies exactly at each cusp.

Key Results
The main theorem states the maximal covering of Y0(p) is cyclic of degree 2Np. The covering factors as fp ∘ πp with πp of degree two. The restriction to Y0(p) is geometrically maximal unramified. The order of MµTor(−1) is either Np or 2Np. The degree-2Np cover automatically satisfies the maximality condition. The generalized eta function Eg satisfies Eg+N = E−g = −Eg. The functions Fh satisfy Fh = F−h = Fp+h. The sign of Fgkh depends on p mod 4. Fh^2 is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q. The order of Fh^2 at any cusp of X2(p) is odd. The epsilon factor to the sixth power equals ψ(γ). The sum Σ_{j=0}^{ℓ−1} g^{2jk} is ≡ 0 mod p since ℓ > 1. The factor 2p divides S, giving Fh(γτ) = ψ(γ)Fah(τ). The order of Fh^2 at a non-cusp p∤c cusp is 1. The order of Fh^2 at a p|c cusp is odd via a floor-function computation. The congruence reduces to p ≡ 1 mod 2 for the p|c cusps. The field Q is algebraically closed in Q(X'2(p)). The function z(τ) = (η(τ)/η(pτ))^(12/(p−1,12)) is also modular on Γ'2(p). The relation between Fh and z is a product over j. The group Γ'2(p) is normal in Γ0(p) with quotient cyclic of order 2k. For p ≢ 1 mod 8, z transforms by ψ under Γ2(p).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) is a quadratic extension of the Shimura field. The doubling reflects the Z/2Z coinvariants of the generalized Jacobian. The odd cusp orders force ramification exactly at the cusps. The construction realizes the abstract maximal covering concretely. The result extends Mazur's theorem to the cuspidally-open curve. The degree-two cover is unramified outside cusps. The theory links generalized Jacobians to unramified coverings. The eta-function approach provides explicit generators.

Contradictions And Limitations
The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 requires a separate construction. The case p = 2 or 3 is handled trivially via Gm. The existence of a maximal covering needs k finitely generated over its prime subfield. The proof is non-canonical in the splitting of the exact sequence.

Claims
The maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) over Q is cyclic of degree 2Np, a quadratic extension of the Shimura cover. The main theorem asserts degree 2Np. The covering factors through X2(p) via a degree-two map. The order of MµTor(−1) is Np or 2Np. The degree-2Np cover satisfies the maximality condition.  
Generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) produce explicit modular functions whose cusp orders are odd. The eta product Eg+N = E−g = −Eg. The construction requires p ≥ 5. The case p ≡ 11 mod 12 needs a different construction. Odd cusp orders force ramification exactly at cusps. The field is generated by a square root of Fh^2. The eta approach gives explicit generators.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The proof is split by the case p ≢ 11 mod 12 versus p ≡ 11 mod 12. The case p = 2 or 3 is handled via Gm. The odd case ℓ > 1 uses the vanishing sum mod p. The even case uses the character χ of order 2.

Key Figures Tables
The paper contains no figures or tables.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is proving the maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) is cyclic of degree 2Np. 2. The strongest evidence is the odd cusp order of Fh^2 forcing ramification exactly at the cusps. 3. The future path is extending this to other modular curves and level structures.

summary.title: Lusin characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators
summary.authors: Tan Duc Do, Trong Ngoc Nguyen and Truong Xuan Le
summary.field_subfield: Harmonic analysis / operator theory
summary.executive_summary: This paper establishes a Lusin integral characterisation of Hardy spaces Hp_L(R^d) associated with the Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|^2 on its maximal domain in L^2(R^d). The authors consider dimension d ∈ {3, 4, 5, ...} and index p ∈ (0, 1], extending prior work that treated only the endpoint p = 1. The central object is the maximal function MLf(·) = sup_{t>0} |e^{-tL}f(·)|, under which Hp_L is defined as the completion of {f ∈ L^2(R^d) : MLf ∈ L^p(R^d)}. The main theorem (Theorem 1.1) proves that Hp_L equals Hp_S, where Hp_S is built from a Lusin area integral S built from derivatives of the form ∂_j + x_j, which are specific to Hermite operators and were first suggested by Thangavelu. To reach this, the authors introduce intermediate spaces: the maximal space Hp_{L,max}, defined via a grand maximal function f*_L built from the Poisson semigroup Pt = e^{-tL^{1/2}}f; and the atomic space Hp_A built from (p, 2, M)-atoms associated with L. They prove Hp_L ⊂ Hp_{L,max}, then Hp_L = Hp_A ∩ L^2, and finally Hp_L = Hp_S. A second main result (Theorem 1.2) shows the Riesz transforms RL_j = (∂_j + x_j)L^{-1/2} are bounded on Hp_L. The proofs rely on kernel estimates for the heat kernels of T_t and P_t, an atom decomposition of Hp_L, generalized Hölder inequalities, tent space techniques, and Calderón reproducing formulas. The paper is entirely theoretical, with no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational benchmarks. Its contributions are structural: equivalent quasi-norms, atomic decompositions, and boundedness results that parallel classical Hardy space theory but adapted to the Hermite setting.

summary.title: Uniﬁcation of the phonon mode behaviour in semiconductor alloys
summary.authors: O. Pag`es, M. Kassem, A. Chaﬁ, A. Nassour, S. Doyen and A. V. Postnikov
summary.field_subfield: Condensed matter physics / materials science (vibrational spectroscopy of semiconductor alloys)
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/computational study with literature data analysis and ab initio calculations
summary.executive_summary: This paper concludes a series of systematic re-examinations of Raman and infrared (IR) spectra of representative semiconductor alloys, namely In1−xGaxAs (1-bond→1-mode), In1−xGaxP (modified 2-mode) and ZnTe1−xSex (traditionally classified as 2-bond→1-mode). The authors challenge the traditionally admitted classification of phonon mode behaviour, which is based on the virtual crystal approximation (VCA) and the modified-random-element-isodisplacement (MREI) model. They argue that the VCA misses the essence of phonon behaviour in alloys because it treats the alloy at the macroscopic scale as a continuum, whereas the bond force constant K is sensitive to local bond distortions at the mesoscopic scale. The central claim is that ZnTe1−xSex obeys the same phonon mode behaviour as In1−xGaxAs and In1−xGaxP, namely a universal percolation-type behaviour of 1-bond→2-mode. The authors propose a three-oscillator [1 (Zn-Te), 2 (Zn-Se)] version of the percolation model, supported by extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) data and home-made ab initio phonon calculations. The percolation model requires two adjustable parameters per bond, i.e. the frequency of the impurity mode ωimp plus the splitting ∆ between like TO modes in the dilute limit. The ωimp values were estimated by relying on thorough EXAFS measurements of bond length in ZnTeSe, and the shift of an impurity mode with respect to the TO mode in the pure crystal was inferred from the related difference in bond length δ via the TO mode Gr¨uneisen parameter γ in the pure crystal. For the Zn-Te (Zn-Se) bond, δ and γ are 2.480–2.452 Å (2.600–2.643 Å) and 1.4 (1.7), according to refs. 15 and 16, respectively. The (ωimp, ∆) values for the Zn-Te and Zn-Se bonds are (∼189 cm−1, ∼0 cm−1) and (∼195 cm−1, ∼8 cm−1), respectively. The agreement between the TO (thick lines) / LO (thin lines) theoretical curves and the data is rather good, in spite of the simplicity of our model. The authors also provide independent ab initio insight into the TO density of states (TO-DOS) at the zone-center (ZC), that compares directly to the Raman signal, in a fully-relaxed 32-atom supercell at the representative composition x∼0.5. They apply the plane-wave pseudopotential method within the density functional theory and the local density approximation (LDA), and a linear response technique. The ZC TO-DOS obtained per atom for uniformly-damped Zn, Se and Te oscillators (∼10 cm−1) show three equidistant oscillators spaced by ∼10 cm−1, with similar strengths, i.e. a ZnTe-like below two ZnSe-like ones. A slight overall blue-shift of the ZC TO-DOS with respect to the corresponding Raman lineshape (∼20 cm−1) is due to a well-known overbinding in LDA. The authors show that ZnTeSe obeys the 1-bond→2-phonon percolation model, as InGaAs and InGaP do, which leads to unification of the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classification into a single class covered by the percolation model. They emphasize that even those ideally-disordered systems that are the usual SC alloys cannot escape a description of some of their very basic physical properties via a percolation concept. On the practical side, this work reveals that vibrational spectroscopies provide natural insight (non destructive and contactless) into the alloy disorder at the unusual mesoscopic scale, which offers an attractive perspective for the study of the long scale (self-) organization in alloys. The authors acknowledge support from the IFCPAR (N◦3204-1) and the CINES (N◦pli2623).

The central claim is that ZnTe1−xSex obeys the same phonon mode behaviour as In1−xGaxAs and In1−xGaxP, namely a universal percolation-type behaviour of 1-bond→2-mode. For the Zn-Te (Zn-Se) bond, δ and γ are 2.480–2.452 Å (2.600–2.643 Å) and 1.4 (1.7), according to refs. 15 and 16, respectively. The (ωimp, ∆) values for the Zn-Te and Zn-Se bonds are (∼189 cm−1, ∼0 cm−1) and (∼195 cm−1, ∼8 cm−1), respectively. The ZC TO-DOS obtained per atom for uniformly-damped Zn, Se and Te oscillators (∼10 cm−1) show three equidistant oscillators spaced by ∼10 cm−1, with similar strengths, i.e. a ZnTe-like below two ZnSe-like ones. A slight overall blue-shift of the ZC TO-DOS with respect to the corresponding Raman lineshape (∼20 cm−1) is due to a well-known overbinding in LDA. The authors show that ZnTeSe obeys the 1-bond→2-phonon percolation model, as InGaAs and InGaP do, which leads to unification of the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classification into a single class covered by the percolation model. On the practical side, this work reveals that vibrational spectroscopies provide natural insight (non destructive and contactless) into the alloy disorder at the unusual mesoscopic scale, which offers an attractive perspective for the study of the long scale (self-) organization in alloys. The authors acknowledge support from the IFCPAR (N◦3204-1) and the CINES (N◦pli2623).

Research Context
The study concludes a series of systematic re-examinations of the Raman/Infrared spectra of representative semiconductor alloys. The traditionally admitted classification is based on the virtual crystal approximation (VCA). The VCA treats the alloy at the macroscopic scale as a continuum, with each atom A surrounded by four virtual B1−xCx atoms. The physical properties are accordingly averaged, and no singularity is expected in their dependence on x. The key issue regarding mixtures is how to handle the substitutional disorder. A percolation-based approach was developed at the mesoscopic scale, with the central notion being the volume fraction of each constituent. Singularities in the physical properties are expected at the percolation thresholds, at which compositions the minor constituents coalesce into a continuum. The VCA seems sufficient, in first approximation, for ideally-disordered mixtures that are usual semiconductor AB1−xCx alloys. The bond force constant K is sensitive to the bond distortion required to accommodate the mismatch in the A-B and A-C bond lengths. The VCA for K leads to a 1-bond→1-mode TO behaviour, as accounted for by the MREI model. The Elliott et al. criterion within the coherent potential approximation (CPA) predicts type (ii) when the A-B and A-C optical bands overlap in the alloy. The MREI-VCA (experimental) and Elliott-CPA (theoretical) classifications were found to be remarkably consistent, except for InGaP. The apparent anomalies in InGa(As,P) could be explained within a 1-bond→2-mode percolation model. The perspective is a change of paradigm regarding the way to describe phonons in alloys.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigates whether the percolation scheme for InGa(As,P) is fortuitous or reflects a deeper universal reality. The hypothesis is that ZnTeSe obeys the same phonon mode behaviour as InGaAs and InGaP, namely a universal percolation-type behaviour of 1-bond→2-mode. The lattice mismatch in ZnTeSe is similar to that of InGa(As,P), i.e. ∼7%, so that similar lattice distortions can be expected. The hypothesis is that a InGaP-like version of the percolation model should apply to ZnTeSe. The VCA misses the essence of the phonon behaviour in alloys, and the proper understanding of TO phonons requires insight into the topologies of the (B,C)-substituting species. The hypothesis is that the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classification has no raison d'ˆetre, and that all these alloys belong to a single percolation class. The predicted outcome is that ZnTeSe exhibits three equally spaced TO modes in the range 180–200 cm−1, that blue-shift when the Se content increases. The predicted outcome is that the percolation schemes for InGaAs, InGaP and ZnTeSe are analogous, indicating that the traditional classification has no raison d'ˆetre. The predicted outcome is that the percolation schemes are consistent with the MREI-VCA classification, as a matter of regrouping close individual/double TO branches. The predicted outcome is that vibrational spectroscopies provide natural insight into the alloy disorder at the unusual mesoscopic scale.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the bond force constant K in SC alloys, which is sensitive to the bond distortion required to accommodate the mismatch in the A-B and A-C bond lengths. K is routinely probed by Raman and Infrared (IR) spectroscopies, via the frequency of the transverse optical (TO) phonon. The MREI-VCA model requires only one adjustable parameter per bond, i.e. the frequency of the impurity mode ωimp. The MREI-VCA supports a classification of the TO-Raman/IR data in terms of 2-mode (pure 1-bond→1-mode), mixed-mode (2-bond→1-mode) and dominant-plus-minor mixed-modes (modified-2-mode). Representative systems are In1−xGaxAs, ZnTe1−xSex and In1−xGaxP, respectively. The percolation model requires two adjustable parameters per bond, i.e. ωimp plus the splitting ∆ between like TO modes in the dilute limit. The ωimp values were estimated by relying on thorough extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) measurements of bond length in ZnTeSe. The shift of an impurity mode with respect to the TO mode in the pure crystal was inferred from the related difference in bond length δ via the TO mode Gr¨uneisen parameter γ in the pure crystal. For the Zn-Te (Zn-Se) bond, δ and γ are 2.480–2.452 Å (2.600–2.643 Å) and 1.4 (1.7), according to refs. 15 and 16, respectively. The (ωimp, ∆) values for the Zn-Te and Zn-Se bonds are (∼189 cm−1, ∼0 cm−1) and (∼195 cm−1, ∼8 cm−1), respectively. The authors use the generic expression of the Raman cross section given by Eq. (1) in ref. 9, in a form restricted to the second member it gives access to the TO modes; in full it provides the LO modes. The authors use a classical form of the dielectric function, generalized to three harmonic oscillators. The authors take Zn-Se and Zn-Te phonon dampings that scale like in pure crystals, i.e. 3:1, as inferred from the full widths at half maximum of the LO Raman lines. The remaining (CF−H, ϵ∞, TO–LO) values for the pure ZnSe and ZnTe crystals are (−0.56, 5.75, 206–252 cm−1) and (−0.32, 7.20, 176–206 cm−1), respectively. The authors use small dampings for the Zn-Te (1 cm−1) and Zn-Se (3 cm−1) modes, for a clear overview of the whole collection of oscillators. The authors provide independent ab initio insight into the TO density of states (TO-DOS) at the zone-center (ZC), in a fully-relaxed 32-atom supercell at the representative composition x∼0.5. The authors apply the plane-wave pseudopotential method within the density functional theory and the local density approximation (LDA), and a linear response technique. The authors use 64-atom supercells, that are well-converged in size for such purpose. The authors use a supercell containing a single impurity (∼3% imp.) to access ωimp. The authors use a supercell containing two neighbouring substitutional impurities to access ∆. The systematic error due to LDA is thus eliminated, and the theoretical and experimental (ωimp, ∆) values agree within ∼5%. The theoretical and experimental (ωimp, ∆) values for random InGaAs, InGaP and ZnTeSe, and also (Zn,Be)-chalcogenides, agree within ∼5%. The Se and Te atoms are equally distributed over all substituting planes, as expected in a random alloy. The ZC TO-DOS obtained per atom for uniformly-damped Zn, Se and Te oscillators (∼10 cm−1) show three equidistant oscillators spaced by ∼10 cm−1. A slight overall blue-shift of the ZC TO-DOS with respect to the corresponding Raman lineshape (∼20 cm−1) is due to a well-known overbinding in LDA.

Procedures And Architectures
The authors propose a three-oscillator [1 (Zn-Te), 2 (Zn-Se)] version of the percolation model, with a unique TOZn−Te branch below a well-resolved Zn-Se TO double-branch. Bonds are longer (shorter) in environments rich of the shorter (longer) bonds, which reduces (enlarges) the TO frequency. The middle and upper TO branches are due to Zn-Se vibrations in the Se- and Te-rich regions, accordingly labelled as TOSeZn−Se and TOTeZn−Se. The lower set of TO data is attached to the limit (x∼0,1) Zn-Te frequencies at its two ends, indicating an apparent 1-bond→1-mode MREI behaviour for the Zn-Te bond, which comes to ∆Zn−Te ∼0 cm−1. The remaining sets of TO data share quasi-symmetrically on each side of the limit Zn-Se frequencies, indicating a well-resolved 1-bond→2-mode type behaviour for the Zn-Se bond. This was adjusted to ∼8 cm−1 by fitting a rescaled-MREI curve to the data in the continuum regime of the dominant TOSeZn−Se branch at large Se content. The remaining pieces of the Zn-Se double-branch were directly inferred, see Methods. The agreement between the TO (thick lines) / LO (thin lines) theoretical curves and the data is rather good, in spite of the simplicity of our model. Slight discrepancy exists with respect to the TOTeZn−Se branch in the Te-dilute limit, where the mode becomes weak and hard to detect. The authors re-assign the presumed unique TO mode in the Raman/IR spectra of ZnTeSe as the sum of close TOZn−Te and TOSeZn−Se modes. The two modes exhibit antagonist strength variations when the composition changes, and have similar heights at ∼70% Se, consistently with experimental observations. The authors use the percolation picture, in which the alloy is described at the mesoscopic scale as a composite, with the result of different local bond distortions. The percolation schemes for InGaAs, InGaP and ZnTeSe are schematically reproduced in Fig. 4, and there is an obvious analogy between the three schemes. In both InGaAs and InGaP, the impurity modes stay out of the parent TO-LO bands, so that the Ga- and In-related TO-LO bands in the alloy do not overlap. In contrast the Zn-Se and Zn-Te TO-LO bands do overlap in ZnTeSe, which is consistent with the Elliott-CPA classification of InGa(As,P) and ZnTeSe as types (i) and (ii), respectively. The usual terminology of individual modes [(i), Fig. 4a], dominant-plus-minor modes [(iii), Fig. 4b] and mixed-mode [(ii), Fig. 4c] comes out naturally. The authors emphasize that the TO and LO modes behave differently in an alloy, and that the actual 1-bond→2-mode behaviour visible in the TO symmetry is literally rubbed out in the LO symmetry. The authors show that ZnTeSe obeys the 1-bond→2-phonon percolation model, as InGaAs and InGaP do. This leads to unification of the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classification into a single class covered by the percolation model.

Key Results
The data indicate three equally spaced TO modes in the range 180–200 cm−1, that blue-shift when the Se content increases. The (ωimp, ∆) values for the Zn-Te and Zn-Se bonds are (∼189 cm−1, ∼0 cm−1) and (∼195 cm−1, ∼8 cm−1), respectively. The agreement between the TO (thick lines) / LO (thin lines) theoretical curves and the data is rather good, in spite of the simplicity of our model. Slight discrepancy exists with respect to the TOTeZn−Se branch in the Te-dilute limit, where the mode becomes weak and hard to detect. The ZC TO-DOS obtained per atom for uniformly-damped Zn, Se and Te oscillators (∼10 cm−1) show three equidistant oscillators spaced by ∼10 cm−1, with similar strengths. A slight overall blue-shift of the ZC TO-DOS with respect to the corresponding Raman lineshape (∼20 cm−1) is due to a well-known overbinding in LDA. The theoretical and experimental (ωimp, ∆) values for random InGaAs, InGaP and ZnTeSe, and also (Zn,Be)-chalcogenides, agree within ∼5%. The ZC TO-DOS obtained per atom for uniformly-damped Zn, Se and Te oscillators (∼10 cm−1) are displayed in the inset of Fig. 3, together with the supercell. As expected, three equidistant oscillators spaced by ∼10 cm−1, with similar strengths, i.e. a ZnTe-like below two ZnSe-like ones, show up. The two modes exhibit antagonist strength variations when the composition changes, and have similar heights at ∼70% Se, consistently with experimental observations. The LO-TO inverted splitting is large at intermediate composition, and further increases with the Te content, as evidenced by Burlakov et al. (ref. 6). Then it vanishes in the dilute limits, as observed by Yang et al. (ref. 13). There is an obvious analogy between the three schemes, indicating that the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classification has, in fact, no raison d'ˆetre. The percolation schemes are also consistent with the MREI-VCA classification, as a matter of regrouping close individual/double TO branches. The resulting three-mode TO and LO Raman lineshapes are shown in Fig. 3. In a multi-wave system, such as an alloy, the electric field ⃗E is well-known to act as a carrier of coherence, that makes LO modes a complicated issue. The individual LOZn−Te, LOSeZn−Se and LOTeZn−Se modes do ⃗E-couple strongly, with the result that the available oscillator strength is almost fully channelled into a 'giant' LO+ mode at high frequency. This exhibits a model type (ii) behaviour, as is obvious in Fig. 3, certainly the origin of the MREI-VCA classification of ZnTeSe. The authors show that even those ideally-disordered systems that are the usual SC alloys cannot escape a description of some of their very basic physical properties via a percolation concept.

summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang (Peking University Institute of Hematology); Leping Zhang (Peking University People's Hospital); Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.field_subfield: Computational/Bioinformatics Genomics (3D genome analysis of hematological malignancy)
summary.type_of_paper: Primary research: integrative multi-omics study (Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq)
summary.executive_summary: This study integrates 3D genome architecture with transcriptomics to dissect the molecular etiology and prognosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The authors analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T-cell controls using RNA-seq, Hi-C, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq. They found that 3D genome organization at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, together with gene expression profiles, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T-cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome alterations, and after accounting for transcription factor mediation, 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The authors identified 46 translocations in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel, and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. They demonstrated that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions could activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors, including ectopic HOXA cluster expression. Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, but not other HOXA genes, was associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. HOXA13 positivity was an independent predictor of overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. The study suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk subgroup. The findings highlight the roles of 3D genome alterations in the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes, supporting the use of RNA-seq as a biological readout for functional impact. The study also provided subtype-specific insights into ETP versus non-ETP ALL, and explained diverse HOXA expression patterns through 3D genome organizations. The results imply that 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and regulating T-ALL development. The newly identified translocations and enhancer hijacking mechanism may explain how T-ALL-associated transcription factors are ectopically activated and block differentiation at certain T-cell developmental stages. The study identified associations of ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression with poor survival, corresponding to a subtype currently incurable by standard treatments. Overall, the work advances understanding of the 3D genome in leukemia and suggests potential therapeutic targets.

Executive Summary
This study integrates 3D genome architecture with transcriptomics to dissect the molecular etiology and prognosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The authors analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T-cell controls using RNA-seq, Hi-C, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq. They found that 3D genome organization at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, together with gene expression profiles, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T-cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome alterations, and after accounting for transcription factor mediation, 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The authors identified 46 translocations in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel, and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. They demonstrated that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions could activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors, including ectopic HOXA cluster expression. Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, but not other HOXA genes, was associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. HOXA13 positivity was an independent predictor of overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. The study suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk subgroup. The findings highlight the roles of 3D genome alterations in the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes, supporting the use of RNA-seq as a biological readout for functional impact. The study also provided subtype-specific insights into ETP versus non-ETP ALL, and explained diverse HOXA expression patterns through 3D genome organizations. The results imply that 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and regulating T-ALL development. The newly identified translocations and enhancer hijacking mechanism may explain how T-ALL-associated transcription factors are ectopically activated and block differentiation at certain T-cell developmental stages. The study identified associations of ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression with poor survival, corresponding to a subtype currently incurable by standard treatments. Overall, the work advances understanding of the 3D genome in leukemia and suggests potential therapeutic targets.

Research Context
The 3D genome alterations play important roles in tumorigenesis, including hematological malignancies. How 3D genome alterations provide insights into T-ALL patients is largely unknown. 3D genome organization could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL. Translocations are major driving forces for tumorigenesis, especially for leukemia. HOXA-positive T-ALLs represent a homogeneous clinical entity has not been systematically studied. The impact of 3D genome alterations on gene expression in T-ALLs needs investigation. 3D genome alterations could link to the etiology of T-ALL development.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how 3D genome alterations provide insights into T-ALL patients. The hypothesis is that 3D genome organization could classify T-ALL subtypes by differentiation trajectory. The hypothesis is that 3D genome alterations associate with a large fraction of upregulated genes. The hypothesis is that translocations mediate enhancer hijacking and gene fusions activating transcription factors. The hypothesis is that ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with poor outcomes. The hypothesis is that 3D genome alterations play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome. The hypothesis is that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit high-risk T-ALL patients. The hypothesis is that the transcriptome serves as a biological readout for 3D genome alterations. The hypothesis is that T-ALL chromosomal organizations represent frozen stages of T cell development. The hypothesis is that HOXA13 positivity is an independent predictor of overall survival.

Methodological Details
The study analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T cell controls. Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee. ETP status was defined as previously published. Leukemia blast cells were prepared by density-gradient centrifugation of bone marrow samples. CD19-CD14-CD235-CD45+CD7+ cells were further purified by FACS analysis. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from four healthy donors. T cells were purified using the EasySep TM Direct Human T Cell Isolation Kit. RNA-seq libraries were prepared with TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2. Paired-end RNA-seq reads were generated with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. Reads were aligned to the hg19 genome with TopHat (v2.1.0). DESeq2 was applied to identify DEGs with FDR <0.01 and fold change >2. Genes with fewer than 5 reads in 20% of the samples were excluded. ChIP-seq reads were mapped to the hg19 genome with Bowtie2 (v2.3.5). ATAC-seq reads were mapped with Bowtie2 using parameter -X 2000 --no-mixed --no-discordant --no-unal. Aligned reads were filtered for a minimum MAPQ of 20. Signal tracks and peaks were generated by using the -SPMR option in MACS2. FIMO was used to detect the 20 bp CTCF motif from the Homer motif database. Hi-C was performed on one million cells/sample, according to the BL-Hi-C protocol. Raw BL-Hi-C reads were processed by the in-house HiCpipe framework. ChIA-PET2 was used to trim the bridge linkers and HiC-Pro to align reads. Juicer was applied to generate individual or merged Hi-C files. Knight-Ruiz normalized matrices were used in the compartment and TAD analyses. The compartment was calculated with the eigenvector command of Juicer under 100 kb resolution. A or B compartments were defined by the over 70% sample majority rule. TAD boundaries were calculated by the Insulation score method with parameters -is 1000000 -ids 200000 -im mean -nt 0.1. Differential TAD boundaries were defined with a t-test FDR<0.01 and a difference higher than 50% quantile. A TAD was defined when its boundaries were detected in at least two conditions. The domain score was calculated by dividing the intra-TAD interactions with all interactions connected to the TAD. Differential domain scores were calculated with a t-test FDR<0.01 and fold change higher than 70% quantile. Loops were called by HiCCUPS. The differential loop detection method was adapted from Douglas et al. Loops were split into two distance ranges (> or < 150 kb) to minimize potential bias. Differential loops were called within each range (FDR < 0.1) and then combined. The loop anchors were analyzed by GREAT (v3.0.0) using the nearest gene within 100 kb. DAVID 6.8 was used for KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. hic_breakfinder was adapted to detect translocations in 18 T-ALL patient samples. The average depth of patient Hi-C samples is 486 million read pairs and the read length is 150 bp. Hi-C raw data were treated as single ends to refine the breakpoint locations to single base-pair resolution. The exact locations supported by more than 3 chimeric reads were identified as the actual breakpoints. A translocation was considered novel if any breakpoint was not near any known breakpoint within 100 kb. A gene near a breakpoint was considered upregulated if its FPKM was >1- and 2-fold higher than control samples. Hi-C heatmaps and Visual 4C plots were generated by MATLAB code.

Procedures And Architectures
The study integrated analyses of 3D genome alterations and differentially expressed genes. The 3D genome organization was analyzed at compartment, TAD, and loop levels. The gene expression profiles could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL. The PCA and hierarchical clustering showed transcriptome changes consistent with 3D genome structural changes. The T-ALL samples were projected onto the T cell developmental trajectory defined by RNA-seq analysis. The ETP ALL samples were arrested at the immature stage, corresponding to the LMPP to Thy1 stages. The non-ETP samples were arrested at the Thy2 to Thy4 stages. The ETP and non-ETP ALL samples showed 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops. The Pearson's correlation coefficient between gene expression changes and loop strength was 0.685. The genes associated with ETP enhanced loops were enriched in immune response-activating signal transduction. The genes associated with non-ETP enhanced loops were enriched in TCR V(D)J recombination. The RcisTarget was used to predict the key transcription factors controlling upregulated genes. The SOX4, WT1 and TFDP2 potentially regulated approximately 28% of the upregulated genes. The translocation-mediated loops were named and analyzed across the translocated chromosomes. The ends of the translocation-mediated loops tend to anchor at the pre-existing loop anchors and CTCF binding sites. Nearly 78% of the translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to convergently oriented CTCF motifs. The loops may be mediated by the loop extrusion mechanism. The non-ETP ALL was classified into the HOXA, TLX and TAL subtypes. The loop-based hierarchical clustering matched the T-ALL subtypes. The cis mechanism involved translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking in the ETP, TLX and TAL subtypes. The trans mechanism involves translocation-mediated gene fusions. The HOXA cluster contains 11 genes. The HOXA + T-ALLs were separated into the 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between 2 TADs. The 6 enhancer regions were labeled E1 to E12. The ChIP-seq analysis indicated increased interactions may be correlated with gains in the H3K27ac histone mark. The breakpoints were located within the 5' TAD, upstream of the HOXA13 gene. The translocation partner breakpoints lie in the gene bodies of the BCL11B and CDK6 genes. The CTCF binding sites could insulate genes located in the 3' TAD from the influence of the hijacked enhancers. The multivariate analysis showed HOXA13+ status as an independent predictor for overall survival. The HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes. The HOXA11-A13+ cases had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations.

Key Results
The 3D genome organization could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with the corresponding 3D genome structural changes. Approximately 29% (996/3392) of the DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. The genes associated with B-to-A compartment switches were mostly upregulated. The genes associated with A-to-B compartment switches were mostly downregulated. The genes were enriched in pathways such as hematopoietic cell lineage, transcriptional misregulation in cancer and cell cycle. The genes were enriched in pathways such as cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and T cell receptor signaling. The 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The 56% could be directly related to structural alterations. The CDK6 locus exhibited a strong intra-TAD interaction. The MYB, MYCN, BCL11A, SOX4 and WT1 had increased D-scores. The SOX4, WT1 and TFDP2 had structural alterations at all 3 levels. The 46 translocations were identified in 14/18 T-ALL samples. The 34 were novel events and 26 were interchromosomal events. The 47% were located in noncoding regions. The 66% were located in the stable A compartment. The 44 new loops were formed across the translocated chromosomes. The 78% of the translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to convergently oriented CTCF motifs. The 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops were identified in ETP. The Pearson's correlation coefficient was 0.685. The 28% of the upregulated genes were potentially regulated by SOX4, WT1 and TFDP2. The 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups were identified. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between 2 TADs. The 6 enhancer regions were labeled E1 to E12. The 5/7 HOXA+ samples had translocation-mediated fusion events. The HOXA11-A13+ cases had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations. The HOXA13+ status was an independent predictor for overall survival. The TAL+ positivity was associated with better overall survival. The TLX positivity had no association with the outcome.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D genome alterations could link to the etiology of T-ALL development. The transcriptome changes could serve as a biological readout for the functional impact of 3D genome alterations. The chromosomal organizations of T-ALL may represent different frozen stages of T cell development. The translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking or fusion events may drive ectopic transcription factor activation. The hijacked enhancers are from genes normally expressed during T cell development. The ectopic expression blocks normal differentiation. The fusion proteins recruit histone methyltransferase DOT1L to the HOXA locus. The differential HOXA gene expressions were associated with different 3D genome organizations. The increased interactions may be correlated with gains in the H3K27ac histone mark. The translocations mediated new loop formations between the 5' of the HOXA cluster and active enhancers. The CTCF binding sites could insulate genes located in the 3' TAD from the influence of the hijacked enhancers. The 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome. The 3D genome alterations may regulate T-ALL development. The ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with poor survival. The anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this group of patients.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study relied on a small sample size of 18 T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls. The study did not report the random seed, train/test split, or specific demographic details. The study did not report the demographics of the patients. The study did not report the specific statistical methods in detail.

The Supplementary Table 7 showed the patient characteristics.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: The study integrated 3D genome alterations with transcriptomics to dissect the molecular etiology and prognosis of T-ALL. 2. The strongest evidence: The 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. 3. The future path: The study suggested that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit the high-risk T-ALL patients.

summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.field_subfield: Ecotoxicology / Nanotoxicology
summary.executive_summary: This study assessed the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon dioxide) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, and AgNO3) on the hatching of Artemia sp. cysts and on the viability of newly hatched nauplii. The researchers used the brine shrimp Artemia as a model organism because of its ubiquitous distribution, robust nature, and cost-effective culture, making it suitable for toxicological assays. The study employed two complementary endpoints: hatching rate of hydrated cysts and mortality of nauplii in a standard toxicity test. Nanoparticles were characterized using transmission electron microscopy and dynamic light scattering, both in distilled water and salt water, to understand their physicochemical behavior. The hatching experiments were conducted in 25% salt water at 28°C with continuous aeration and light for 24 hours, while the standard toxicity test monitored nauplii viability at intervals up to 48 hours. The results revealed a clear order of toxicity: Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2, with silver and copper oxide being the most toxic. The study found a strong inverse correlation (coefficient of -0.7853) between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching rate could serve as a viable bioassay for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The findings have implications for environmental risk assessment and the development of high-throughput toxicity screening methods for nanomaterials.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study assessed the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon dioxide) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, and AgNO3) on the hatching of Artemia sp. cysts and on the viability of newly hatched nauplii. The researchers used the brine shrimp Artemia as a model organism because of its ubiquitous distribution, robust nature, and cost-effective culture, making it suitable for toxicological assays. The study employed two complementary endpoints: hatching rate of hydrated cysts and mortality of nauplii in a standard toxicity test. Nanoparticles were characterized using transmission electron microscopy and dynamic light scattering, both in distilled water and salt water, to understand their physicochemical behavior. The hatching experiments were conducted in 25% salt water at 28°C with continuous aeration and light for 24 hours, while the standard toxicity test monitored nauplii viability at intervals up to 48 hours. The results revealed a clear order of toxicity: Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2, with silver and copper oxide being the most toxic. The study found a strong inverse correlation (coefficient of -0.7853) between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching rate could serve as a viable bioassay for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The findings have implications for environmental risk assessment and the development of high-throughput toxicity screening methods for nanomaterials.

Research Context
Nanomaterials pose risks to environment and human health due to their unique properties. There is a dearth of information on the impact of nanoscale objects on the environment. The behavior of nanoparticles in various conditions like pH, salinity, and biotic factors is not clearly known. Hazard identification is an important step for risk assessment of nanomaterials. Many ecotoxicology assays have been tested for nanomaterials in bacteria, fishes, copepods, and Daphnia. Few studies have used Artemia sp. for nanomaterial toxicity, and hatching of hydrated cysts has rarely been used as an endpoint.

Research Question And Hypothesis
What is the toxicity order of the tested nanoparticles on Artemia sp. hatching and nauplii viability? Can hatching rate of hydrated cysts serve as a valid endpoint for nanoparticle toxicity assessment? Is there a correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality in nanoparticle suspensions? Can Artemia hatchability test be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity? The predicted outcome was that silver and copper oxide would be the most toxic nanoparticles.

Methodological Details
Six engineered nanoparticles and three soluble salts were tested on Artemia sp. Silicon nanoparticles were supplied by Nanologica AB. Silver nanoparticles were obtained from Colorobbia. Gold nanoparticles were obtained from INMETRO. Copper oxide nanoparticles were from Intrinsiq Materials (UK). Zinc oxide nanoparticles were from Nanogate (Germany). Titanium dioxide particles were synthesized in house using an existing protocol. Nanoparticles were characterized using TEM and DLS. TEM studies used JEOL 2010 TEM at 100KV with 20µ aperture. DLS measurements were conducted using Horiba Nanopartica SZ100. Artemia cysts used were the San Francisco Bay strain. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water under aeration for 45 minutes. Cysts were bleached using 20% sodium hypochlorite solution for 15 minutes. Bleached eggs were washed 6 times with distilled water. Hatching was conducted in 25% salt water at pH 8.0. Temperature was maintained at 28°C for hatching. Nanoparticles were added at concentrations of 100mg/l and 10mg/l. The experiment was repeated six times. Three aliquots of 100µl were taken from each flask. Nauplii viability was counted at intervals of 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. LD50 was calculated using Graphpad software. Nauplii were exposed to concentrations of 100mg/l, 10mg/l, 1mg/l, 0.1mg/l, and 0.01mg/l. DCFDA was used at a concentration of 10µM for oxidative stress testing. Oxidative stress was imaged using Zeiss Axiovert imager. The validity criterion for hatching studies was low mortality in the control. The validity criterion for toxicity tests was mortality below 10% in 24 hr. The correlation test was performed using online software and Microsoft Excel.

Procedures And Architectures
A suspension of SiO2, TiO2, CuO, and ZnO NPs was made at 2mg/ml. The suspension was sonicated at ~30W with a pulse of 50% for 10 minutes. Silver nanoparticles were obtained as a suspension at 4% with PVP as a stabilizing agent. Gold nanoparticles were in water at a concentration of 0.006%. Working dilutions were made in salt water (NaCl). TEM studies applied a 50µg/ml suspension to formvar coated copper grids. About 10 images were taken using GATAN camera. DLS measurements were conducted at 25µg/ml in milliQ water and salt water. Each suspension was analyzed thrice for three days. Hatching was counted after 24 hours for each culture. Number of hatched Artemia (immotile vs. motile), umbrella stage, and unhatched cysts were counted. Hatching rate was expressed as percent of total number of fully hatched Artemia. Nauplii were transferred to six well plates for the toxicity test. Mortality was recorded as cessation of swimming or any movement by nauplii. Oxidative stress was observed using DCFDA which reacts with ROS. The hatching studies were conducted 6 times. Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5. The viability of hatched nauplii was about 97%. The pH of salt water remained around 6.3-6.5 up to 48 hours. Artemia were not fed during the test period. LC50 was calculated for each particle.

Key Results
The order of toxicity was estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The highest toxic effect was seen in silver and copper oxide nanoparticles. The hatching rate dropped to about 29% in silver and copper oxide at 100mg/L. Only 50% of hatched Artemia were motile and viable at 100mg/L. The hatching rate remained lower at 10mg/L of silver nanoparticles. The viability of hatched nauplii was good at 85% at 10mg/L of silver. In copper oxide, hatching rate was low with better viability around 64%. Hatching rate was low in gold, silicon, titanium, copper, and zinc oxide at around 50-60%. Post-hatching mortality was not very high in these nanoparticles. In zinc oxide, hatching rate was high at 60% but cysts had a tendency to clump together. In titanium dioxide at 100mg/L, hatching rate was 41.50% with 67.8% viability. In titanium dioxide at 10mg/L, hatching rate was 54% showing ~90% viability. Gold and silicon dioxide nanoparticles displayed very good viability after hatching. SiO2 nanoparticles at 10mg/L displayed hatching rate and viability equivalent to controls. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic as 80% of nauplii were dead in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12mg/L at 24 hours. The correlation coefficient between hatching rates and mortality was -0.7853. Comparing viability of nauplii with hatching rate showed no statistically significant difference (P=0.683). The standard Artemia toxicity test results were comparable. Silver nanoparticles ranked very high in toxicity, followed by copper and zinc oxide. Titanium dioxide, gold, and silicon nanoparticles showed better survival up to 48 hrs. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed an increase in mortality in the ARC test. The nauplii showed accumulation of eNPs in the gut of Artemia by end of 24 hours. In case of silver nanoparticles, dead nauplii did not show accumulation of material in the gut. Nauplii exposed to silver nanoparticles showed highest staining for ROS and superoxide. Nauplii exposed to other nanoparticles did not show signs of ROS or superoxide. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles did not show gross morphological abnormalities. There were no changes in morphology of nauplii hatched in presence of nanoparticles. Staining of hatched Artemia with DCFDA showed staining for ROS in few still trapped nauplii and the gut of dead nauplii.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality implies hatching rate can be a bioassay. The toxicity of silver and copper oxide could be due to ionic forms. Ionic silver precipitates out due to high salinity but still affected hatching and viability. Silver nitrate and copper sulfate representing ionic forms also showed high toxicity. Silicon nanoparticles at low concentration were very conducive and showed better hatching than control. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed increased mortality in the ARC test. The nanoparticles remained stable in seawater up to one week. The ionic or dissolved component may settle down due to precipitation. Continuous aeration in the hatching test keeps the particles in suspended form. Artemia is a filter feeder and NPs may enter the guts through ingestion. The mortality observed may be due to the uptake of eNPs clogging the gut. Artemia with capacity to homeostasis in variable external salt concentrations appears to be a model organism. Suitability of Artemia for toxicity tests was established. Artemia is often used in pharmaceutical industry and for metal and radiation toxicity. The Artemia hatchability test could be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity. These acute toxicity tests eliminate the need of laboratory maintenance of test species. Use of cysts available in enormous quantities as batch cuts down on variability. This assay can be adopted for the hazard identification of nanomaterial and high throughput methods.

Claims
The toxicity order of the tested nanoparticles on Artemia sp. is Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The order of toxicity was estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The highest toxic effect was seen in silver and copper oxide nanoparticles. The hatching rate dropped to about 29% in silver and copper oxide at 100mg/L. Silver in ionic form was highly toxic as 80% of nauplii were dead in 24 hours. The LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12mg/L at 24 hours. Silver nanoparticles ranked very high in toxicity, followed by copper and zinc oxide. Silicon nanoparticles at low concentration were very conducive and showed better hatching than control. SiO2 nanoparticles at 10mg/L displayed hatching rate and viability equivalent to controls. The toxicity of silver and copper oxide could be due to ionic forms. The nanoparticles remained stable in seawater up to one week. The mortality observed may be due to the uptake of eNPs clogging the gut.
Hatching rate of hydrated cysts can serve as a valid endpoint for nanoparticle toxicity assessment. Both the tests show good inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles. The correlation coefficient between hatching rates and mortality was -0.7853. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed increased mortality in the ARC test. Artemia hatchability test could be used as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity. Hatching of hydrated cysts has not been used as an endpoint for toxicity except in [14]. Few studies have used Artemia sp. for nanomaterial toxicity. These acute toxicity tests eliminate the need of laboratory maintenance of test species. This assay can be adopted for the hazard identification of nanomaterial and high throughput methods. Use of cysts available in enormous quantities as batch cuts down on variability.
There is a strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality in nanoparticle suspensions. The correlation coefficient between hatching rates and mortality was -0.7853. The particles that reduced hatching rate showed increased mortality in the ARC test. The standard Artemia toxicity test results were comparable. Our results correlate with some other toxicity assays performed on Artemia using nanoparticles. Comparing viability of nauplii with hatching rate showed no statistically significant difference (P=0.683). Hatching or emergence of the nauplii has been used as a sensitive bioassay to study the molecular and physiological effects of metals. Lower hatching rate equates with the toxicity of test compound. Artemia with capacity to homeostasis in variable external salt concentrations appears to be a model organism.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The hatching studies have been conducted 6 times. The experiment was repeated six times. Each suspension was analyzed thrice for three days. The data was represented as mean + SEM. The validity criterion for hatching studies was low mortality in the control. The validity criterion for toxicity tests was mortality below 10% in 24 hr. The pH of salt water did not change upon addition of nanoparticles. Hatched nauplii appeared normal and swimming vigorously. There were no changes in morphology of nauplii hatched in presence of nanoparticles. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles did not show gross morphological abnormalities.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the hatching rate, mortality, and viability of Artemia exposed to nanoparticles. Figure 3 shows the hatching rate of brine shrimp altered drastically in presence of nanoparticles. Figure 4 shows the hatching rate was low in presence of other nanoparticles. Figure 5 shows the accumulation of eNPs in the gut of Artemia by end of 24 hours. Figure 6 shows the strong correlation in hatching rates and larval mortality. Figure 1 shows the transmission electron microscope studies show no apparent change in aggregation or dispersion of particles. Figure 2 shows the nanoparticles exhibited different behaviour in salt water. Figure S1 shows the nanoparticles suspended both in Milli Q water and 25%NaCl solution were measured up to 48 hours. Figure S2.1-2.6 shows the nauplii had emerged but were immotile/dead; some were still-dead and trapped in the membrane. Figure S3 shows the staining of hatched Artemia with DCFDA for signs of stress. Table 2 shows the viability of nauplii to various nanoparticles.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the establishment of the toxicity order of the tested nanoparticles on Artemia sp. 2. The strongest evidence is the strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality. 3. The future path is the use of Artemia hatchability test as a pre-screening test for nanoparticle toxicity.

summary.title: An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT homogenization
summary.authors: S. Lucarini and J. Segurado
summary.field_subfield: Computational materials science / FFT-based computational homogenization
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces a new algorithm that imposes a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient history within non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization. The central idea is a modified projection operator in which the null frequencies enforce the type of control (stress or strain) for each component of either the macroscopic first Piola stress or the deformation gradient. The authors argue that this modification lets the resulting problem be solved exactly as the original variational method, requiring no additional iterations compared to the strain control version, neither in the linear iterative solver nor in the Newton scheme. The method is motivated by the need to obtain material responses efficiently for generic loading paths such as uniaxial loading, controlled triaxility, and cyclic stress control tests, which are not direct tasks in FFT homogenization. The authors position their work within the evolution of FFT methods, from the classical Lippmann-Schwinger schemes of Moulinec and Suquet and the projection-tensor approach of Kabel et al. to the reference-free Galerkin framework of Vondřejc, Zeman, and de Geus. They extend the finite-strain variational algorithm of de Geus et al. to stress and mixed control using a direct method based on a modified projection operator while preserving the computational performance of the original method. The efficiency is demonstrated with two numerical benchmarks: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite and a polycrystal with crystal plasticity. In the hyperelastic case, stress and mixed controlled simulations take approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control, and all simulations share the same endpoint within numerical accuracy. In the polycrystal case, a similar tendency is achieved, with the stress-controlled ramp case being clearly faster because most increments are elastic. The authors also highlight that the pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results for nearly incompressible materials, since compressive transverse stresses grow with applied strain. The paper concludes that these algorithms are a very useful tool for FFT-based computational homogenization because they allow solving problems with mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort while sustaining the well-known advantages of FFT methods.

claims.description: The modified projection operator allows imposing a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient history in non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization without additional iterations.
The stress-controlled ramp case is faster than the other cases in the polycrystal because most increments are elastic.
The pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results for nearly incompressible materials.
