The efficiency is demonstrated with two numerical benchmarks: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite and a polycrystal with crystal plasticity. In the hyperelastic case, stress and mixed controlled simulations take approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control, and all simulations share the same endpoint within numerical accuracy. In the polycrystal case, a similar tendency is achieved, with the stress-controlled ramp case being clearly faster because most increments are elastic. The authors also highlight that the pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results for nearly incompressible materials, since compressive transverse stresses grow with applied strain. The paper concludes that these algorithms are a very useful tool for FFT-based computational homogenization because they allow solving problems with mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort while sustaining the well-known advantages of FFT methods.

Research Context
Computational homogenization simulates material response under macroscopic loading by solving a boundary problem in a periodic RVE. The finite element method has traditionally solved boundary value problems while imposing any macroscopic load history. FFT-based homogenization is a popular alternative that replaces differential operators by their Fourier-space counterparts. Imposing a macroscopic stress or mixed loading path is not a direct task in FFT homogenization. Obtaining material responses for generic loading paths is fundamental for uniaxial loading, controlled triaxility, and cyclic stress control tests. Classical FFT schemes require a reference medium whose properties may strongly determine the convergence rate. Under classical mixed control, the full macroscopic strain tensor is imposed and corrected iteratively to obtain the target stress. The corrections to applied strain during iterations significantly increase the number of iterations per step relative to strain control. The Galerkin-based approach uses a weak formulation and projection operators, avoiding a reference medium and using material tangents. The Galerkin framework can be adapted to complex non-linear constitutive equations such as crystal plasticity. The existing Galerkin variational approach was still formulated imposing the history of the macroscopic deformation gradient.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to impose a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient history in non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization. The method is based on a modified projection operator whose null frequencies enforce the type of control for each component of the macroscopic first Piola stress or the deformation gradient. The primary hypothesis is that the modified operator lets the problem be solved exactly as the original variational method without additional iterations. The hypothesis extends to no extra iterations in the linear iterative solver nor in the Newton scheme. The authors predict that stress and mixed controlled simulations take approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control. The authors predict that the stress-controlled ramp case will be clearly faster in the polycrystal because most increments are elastic. The authors predict that the pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results for nearly incompressible materials. The authors predict that all simulations share the same endpoint within numerical accuracy despite different paths. The authors predict that the method preserves the computational performance of the original method.

Methodological Details
The homogenization method finds the deformation gradient and stress on a periodic RVE of a heterogeneous material. The RVE is discretized in nx ny nz voxels and the linear momentum balance is imposed in weak form in the reference configuration. The test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projector operator to enforce compatibility. The discrete linear momentum balance is written as G(P(F, α)) = 0, where P is the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, F the deformation gradient, α internal variables, and G a linear map. The linear map corresponds to a convolution in real space computed as the inverse discrete Fourier transform of the projection operator applied to the field. The system is an algebraic system of 9 nx ny nz equations with the deformation gradient at each voxel as the unknown. The deformation gradient is decomposed into its average value ⟨F⟩ℱ and the fluctuation eF = F − ⟨F⟩ℱ. Under strain control, the value of F = ⟨F⟩ℱ is given, and the problem is to find the fluctuations of the deformation gradient. For non-linear behavior, the macroscopic deformation gradient is split into n increments and a non-linear equation is solved for every time increment k ∈ [1, n]. The stress is linearized around the last iteration of the deformation gradient Fi using Ki = ∂P/∂Fi. The derived linear system is G(Ki : δF) = −G(P(Fi)), solved using the conjugate gradient method. For rate-dependent constitutive equations, the stress depends on both the deformation gradient F and the velocity gradient L. The velocity gradient Lk is given by Lk = [Fk − Fk−1] · F−1_k / (tk − tk−1). The projection operator Ĝ(x) is a fourth-order tensor with a closed form in Fourier space that enforces compatibility via convolution. The Helmholtz decomposition expresses a field as the sum of a curl-free compatible part, a divergence-free incompatible part, and the average. The projection operator returns the compatible part and accomplishes major symmetry Ĝijkl = Ĝklij. The operator is zero at the null frequency ξ = (0,0,0) to return a zero mean field value. At the Nyquist frequency, the operator value is approximated to a null fourth-order tensor to recover frequency symmetry. The final projector operator equals the Green function of the basic scheme for an isotropic reference medium with Lamé constants λ = 0, µ = 0.5. The first benchmark is a non-linear elastic composite: a periodic cubic RVE with a hyperelastic matrix reinforced by stiff spherical particles. The RVE contains 4 particles occupying a volume fraction of 0.2 and the domain is discretized using 64³ voxels. The matrix and particle behavior follow a Saint Venant-Kirchhoff hyperelastic model. The matrix properties are µ = 28 Pa and k = 46.67 Pa (shear and bulk modulus). The particles are one order of magnitude stiffer than the matrix, with both moduli 10 times larger. The uniaxial tensile test reaches an elongation of λend = L/L0 = 0.2, with the other two directions unconstrained. The load is homogeneously divided into 100 load increments, with equilibrium solved in each. Case (1) is a mixed control imposing a deformation gradient ramp in the x direction with the rest of terms stress free. Case (2) is a full stress control applying a linear ramp from 0 to the stress P(1)_end obtained as the solution in the first case. Case (3) is a full strain control test where all the deformation gradient is imposed using a linear ramp. The second benchmark is a polycrystal with loading path and strain rate dependencies, discretized in 64³ voxels with around 200 randomly oriented grains. Each grain follows a crystal plasticity elasto-visco-plastic behavior dependent on orientation and internal variables. A final elongation of λend = 0.02 is imposed in 200 s, corresponding to a strain rate of 5×10⁻⁵ in the strain control case. The time is discretized into 20 regular increments. Case (4) is a pseudo-uniaxial tensile test approaching uniaxial tension using full strain control resulting in an isochoric deformation at the final stage. The convergence criteria for the linear solver is the voxel-averaged L2 norm of the residual, and for the Newton solver the maximum deformation gradient correction relative to the averaged deformation gradient. The tolerances used are 10⁻⁸ for the linear solver and 10⁻⁶ for the Newton solver. The number of conjugate-gradient iterations per load increment includes the sum of all linear iterations performed for each Newton iteration in an increment. The modified stress-control operator Ĝ* equals the identity tensor at the null frequency and zero at the Nyquist frequency. The mixed-control operator Ĝ* uses δikδjl at the null frequency for stress-controlled IJ terms and 0ijkl for strain-controlled ij terms. The non-linear system for mixed control is solved by Newton, with the correction δF including a mean value. The equilibrium under mixed control is expressed as G*(P(Fij + F′, α))_ij = 0 for strain-controlled ij directions and G*(P(Fij + F′, α))_IJ = G*(P)_IJ for stress-controlled IJ directions.

Procedures And Architectures
The procedure splits the macroscopic deformation gradient into n increments and solves a non-linear equation for every time increment k. The stress is linearized around the last iteration Fi as P(Fi + δF) ≈ P(Fi) + Ki : δF. The linear system G(Ki : δF) = −G(P(Fi)) is solved using the conjugate gradient method. The modified stress-control operator is defined as Ĝ* with the null frequency projecting the average part of a field into itself via the fourth-order identity tensor. The null frequency is enforced using the property of the Fourier transform P̂(ξ=0) = ⟨P⟩ℱ to enforce ⟨P⟩ℱ to be the target macroscopic stress. The stress-control iteration solves G*(K : δF) = −G*(P(Fi) − P), where the correction δF includes a mean value. When equilibrium is reached (δF → 0), the average stress reaches the objective. The mixed-control operator is obtained following the same reasoning as for stress control and is used as Ĝ* in the equilibrium equation. The non-linear system for mixed control is solved by Newton, yielding the field F′ with F′_ij = eF_ij and F′_IJ = F_IJ. In the hyperelastic benchmark, the uniaxial tensile test reaches an elongation of λend = 0.2 with the other two directions unconstrained. The load is homogeneously divided into 100 increments, with equilibrium solved in each. Case (1) imposes a deformation gradient ramp in the x direction as a mixed control with the rest of terms stress free. Case (2) applies a linear stress ramp from 0 to the stress P(1)_end obtained as the solution in the first case. Case (3) imposes all the deformation gradient using a linear ramp to reach the final solution of the first simulation. In the polycrystal benchmark, a final elongation of λend = 0.02 is imposed in 200 s, corresponding to a strain rate of 5×10⁻⁵. The time is discretized into 20 regular increments for the polycrystal. Case (4) approaches uniaxial tension using full strain control resulting in an isochoric deformation at the final stage. The performance comparison uses the total number of conjugate-gradient iterations per load increment as a function of the step. The simulation time comparison normalizes the time with respect to the case (3) time.

Key Results
In the hyperelastic benchmark, the stress and mixed controlled simulations took approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control. The jumps in the iteration figure are due to the increase or decrease of one Newton iteration after a given time increment. In the hyperelastic case, the stress and mixed controlled simulations illustrate the very good performance of the approach proposed. In the polycrystal case, a similar tendency is achieved, with most load increments elastic and solved in one Newton iteration. In the polycrystal, when load control is applied using a ramp (case 2), most of the load increments are elastic and solved in one Newton iteration. The plastic regime in the polycrystal corresponds to only a few steps which require much higher numbers of iterations. The stress-controlled ramp case (case 2) in the polycrystal is clearly faster than the others. The fast elastic steps compensate the global time in the polycrystal, making the stress-controlled case faster. The differences in the polycrystal are a consequence of using a fixed time step, and for adaptive time stepping all cases will require very similar simulation times. In the hyperelastic benchmark, all simulations have the same endpoint but follow different paths. Cases (1) and (2) share the path but differ in the size of the strain increments due to the non-linear behavior. Because the hyperelastic behavior is path independent, the macroscopic stress of cases (1) and (2) are superposed. Case (3) follows a slightly different path because a ramp is applied controlling the full deformation gradient. In the hyperelastic material, the behavior depends non-linearly on the deformation gradient value, so the transverse elongation under a stress-free condition depends on the deformation level. Under stress and mixed control the transverse stresses are zero, while under strain control small compressive stresses are developed. Macroscopic and microscopic results at the endpoint for all the cases are the same within the numerical accuracy. In the polycrystal, cases (1) and (2) are not exactly superposed due to the effect of the differences in the strain rate. Case (3) reaches the same point as the previous two cases but with a totally different path and compressive transverse stresses. In the pseudo-uniaxial stress test, the compressive transverse stresses are not zero and grow with the applied strain. The polycrystalline response is very different from a real uniaxial tensile test, especially in the transverse response. The performance comparison is represented in Fig. 3, with the hyperelastic simulations needing almost identical times for every boundary condition. The longitudinal response of the three tests is represented in Fig. 1(b), and the transverse response in Fig. 1(c).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The modified projection operator enforces the type of control for each component of the macroscopic first Piola stress or the deformation gradient. By setting the null frequency to the identity tensor, the average stress is enforced to be the target macroscopic stress. The method preserves the computational performance of the original method, requiring no additional iterations. The stress and mixed controlled simulations take approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control, supporting the hypothesis. The stress-controlled ramp case is faster in the polycrystal because most increments are elastic, confirming the predicted efficiency. The method extends the finite-strain variational algorithm of de Geus et al. to stress and mixed control. The approach avoids the reference medium requirement of classical schemes, which may strongly determine the convergence rate. The Galerkin framework can be adapted to complex non-linear constitutive equations such as the crystal plasticity model. The results show the potential of the approach for two types of constitutive models, but it can be used for any material. The algorithms allow solving problems with mixed boundary conditions without extra computational effort. The algorithms sustain the well-known advantages of the FFT methods for homogenization. The pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results for nearly incompressible materials. The growth of compressive transverse stresses with applied strain indicates the inaccuracy of the pseudo-uniaxial approximation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report the specific number of voxels used in the numerical examples, only the discretization nx ny nz. The paper does not report the specific number of Newton iterations or the total simulation time in absolute terms. The paper does not report the random seed or the exact grain orientations used in the polycrystal. The paper does not report the exact number of grains in the polycrystal, only around 200. The paper does not report the exact number of load increments used in the numerical examples, only 100 for the hyperelastic case. The paper does not report the exact number of degrees of freedom in the numerical examples. The paper does not report the exact number of authors beyond S. Lucarini and J. Segurado.

Claims
The modified projection operator allows imposing a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient history in non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization without additional iterations. The method is based on a modified projection operator with null frequencies enforcing the type of control. The resulting problem is solved exactly as the original variational method. The method does not require additional iterations compared to the strain control version. The stress and mixed controlled simulations took approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control. In the polycrystal, the stress-controlled ramp case requires more iterations in the plastic regime. The pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results. The method enables efficient simulation of uniaxial loading, controlled triaxility, and cyclic stress control tests. The method can be used for any material, including complex non-linear constitutive equations.
The stress-controlled ramp case is faster than the other cases in the polycrystal because most increments are elastic. When load control is applied using a ramp (case 2), most of the load increments are elastic and solved in one Newton iteration. The plastic regime is confined to a few steps which require much higher numbers of iterations. The fast elastic steps compensate the global time, making the stress-controlled case clearly faster. The differences are a consequence of using a fixed time step, and for adaptive time stepping all cases will require very similar simulation times. The method is efficient for simulating stress-controlled tests in polycrystals. The efficiency depends on the time stepping strategy, which affects the comparison.
The pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation can lead to inaccurate results for nearly incompressible materials. In the pseudo-uniaxial stress test, the compressive transverse stresses are not zero and grow with the applied strain. The polycrystalline response is very different from a real uniaxial tensile test, especially in the transverse response. The use of this type of strain control conditions to emulate uniaxial tension can lead to inaccurate results. In the hyperelastic benchmark, the pseudo-uniaxial approximation is less problematic because the behavior is path independent. The method highlights the limitations of the pseudo-uniaxial approximation for nearly incompressible materials. The method enables the study of the effect of the loading path on the material response.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the particle-reinforced RVE (a), the first Piola-Kirchhoff stresses for three load cases in the load direction (b), and the transverse directions (c). Figure 2 shows the polycrystalline RVE (a), the first Piola-Kirchhoff stresses for three load cases in the crystal plasticity model in the load direction (b), and the transverse directions (c). Figure 3 shows the comparative of convergence for each time increment for the particle-reinforced hyperelastic (a) and polycrystal (b), and the simulation time comparative for all examples normalized with respect to case (3) time (c). Figure 1(b) shows that the macroscopic stress of cases (1) and (2) are superposed, while case (3) follows a slightly different path. Figure 1(c) shows that under a stress and mixed control the transverse stresses are zero, while under strain control small compressive stresses are developed. Figure 2(b) shows that cases (1) and (2) are not exactly superposed due to the effect of the differences in the strain rate. Figure 2(c) shows that in the pseudo-uniaxial stress test the compressive transverse stresses are not zero and grow with the applied strain. Figure 3(a) shows that the stress and mixed controlled simulations took approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control. Figure 3(b) shows that in the polycrystal a similar tendency is achieved, with most load increments elastic and solved in one Newton iteration. Figure 3(c) shows that the hyperelastic simulations needed almost identical times for every boundary condition.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a modified projection operator that imposes a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient history in non-linear Galerkin-based FFT homogenization without additional iterations. 2. The strongest evidence is that the stress and mixed controlled simulations took approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control, and the stress-controlled ramp case is clearly faster in the polycrystal. 3. The future path is to use the method for any material, including complex non-linear constitutive equations, and to avoid the pseudo-uniaxial strain-control approximation for nearly incompressible materials.

summary.title: Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies
summary.authors: Martin S King, Paul G Crichton, Jonathan J Ruprecht, Edmund R S Kunji
summary.field_subfield: Structural biology / membrane protein biochemistry
summary.executive_summary: This paper is a pointed critique of a study by Brüschweiler et al., which claimed that the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3 could be refolded to homogeneity from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies using the harsh detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC, Foscholine-12) and maintained in a folded, active state during isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and NMR experiments. The authors of the present letter, who have themselves solved the structure of AAC3 by electron and X-ray crystallography and studied its interactions with the specific inhibitors atractyloside (ATR) and carboxyatractyloside (CATR) by single-molecule force spectroscopy, argue that in their hands DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. They contend that the binding affinities reported for the refolded protein are implausibly weak and inconsistent with the well-established nanomolar affinities of these inhibitors for the membrane-embedded carrier. The central quantitative dispute concerns the dissociation constant (Kd) of CATR binding: the disputed study reported a Kd of ~15 µM by ITC and ~150 µM by NMR chemical shift perturbation, whereas the authors report that published and their own measurements place CATR affinity in the low nanomolar range, with ADP transport half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The authors also flag a unit error in a reference used for comparison, noting that a Kd of 192 µM for ATR was corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. They further question the relevance of NMR relaxation dispersion studies, since CATR binding should lock the protein into a non-dynamic state. To support their position, the authors present their own thermostability data using the thiol-reactive fluorophore CPM, showing that AAC3 in DPC shows no thermal transition, indicating a non-native state. They describe their protein purification protocol, including Ni-Sepharose chromatography, thrombin/Factor Xa cleavage, and reconstitution into liposomes followed by radiolabeled ADP uptake assays. In conclusion, the authors assert that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance, because AAC3 is soluble but non-native in DPC. The paper thus combines a scientific argument with detailed methodological descriptions of the authors' own experimental procedures, including purification, thermostability, ITC, reconstitution, and uptake assays, providing the quantitative details necessary to evaluate the disputed claims.

The central quantitative dispute concerns the dissociation constant (Kd) of CATR binding: the disputed study reported a Kd of ~15 µM by ITC and ~150 µM by NMR chemical shift perturbation, whereas the authors report that published and their own measurements place CATR affinity in the low nanomolar range, with ADP transport half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The authors also flag a unit error in a reference used for comparison, noting that a Kd of 192 µM for ATR was corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. They further question the relevance of NMR relaxation dispersion studies, since CATR binding should lock the protein into a non-dynamic state. In conclusion, the authors assert that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance, because AAC3 is soluble but non-native in DPC. The paper thus combines a scientific argument with detailed methodological descriptions of the authors' own experimental procedures, including purification, thermostability, ITC, reconstitution, and uptake assays, providing the quantitative details necessary to evaluate the disputed claims.

Research Context
The yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3 is a well-characterized membrane protein. Its structure has been solved by multiple methods, establishing its folded state. Its interactions with specific inhibitors have been studied by single-molecule force spectroscopy. The carrier is known to bind inhibitors with very high affinity in the membrane. DPC is a harsh detergent capable of denaturing folded carrier proteins.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether AAC3 can be refolded to homogeneity and kept active in DPC. The disputed study hypothesized that DPC-refolded AAC3 is folded and active. The authors hypothesize that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation. The authors predict that reported Kd values are implausibly weak versus the nanomolar consensus. The authors predict that CATR binding locks the protein into a non-dynamic state.

Methodological Details
The disputed study used DPC, also known as Foscholine-12 from Anatrace, for refolding. The disputed study measured CATR binding by ITC and NMR chemical shift perturbations. The disputed study reported a Kd of ~15 µM by ITC for CATR binding. The disputed study reported a Kd of ~150 µM by NMR for CATR binding. CATR and ATR differ by one carboxylate group and have been studied in 24 binding studies. The comparison reference used a Kd of 192 µM for ATR, later corrected to 192 nM. The authors report ADP transport half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The authors report a Kd of 72 nM for CATR binding to native AAC3. The authors' Kd values are 200 to 2000-fold lower than those reported by Brüschweiler et al. The authors' ITC experiments were difficult, with only 2 of 10 trials succeeding. AAC3 has an isoelectric point of 9.82, making it highly positively charged. The protein was purified using Ni-Sepharose chromatography. The protein was cleaved with Factor Xa after incubation at 10 °C overnight. The protein was snap-frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen. Thermostability was measured using the fluorophore CPM. Thermostability measurements were made from 25 to 90 °C. The CPM dye reacts with protein thiols as they become solvent-exposed during denaturation. The ITC experiments were performed at 10 °C using a NanoITC-LV instrument. The ITC titration used 2-µL injections at 3-min intervals with a stirrer speed of 350 rpm. The reconstitution used a pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent for solubilization. Proteoliposomes were formed by stepwise detergent removal using Bio-Beads SM-2. ADP uptake assays used a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot with a 96-well filter plate. The uptake assays used radiolabeled [14C]-ADP at a final working concentration of 1.5 µM. Transport was stopped at multiple time points up to 15 minutes.

Procedures And Architectures
The disputed study refolded AAC3 from E. coli inclusion bodies using DPC. The disputed study validated integrity via ITC and NMR without transport assays. The authors' thermostability assay used a rotary qPCR machine for fluorescence measurement. The CPM stock was diluted 50-fold into buffer before the assay. Approximately 1.5 µg of purified protein was added to a final volume of 45 µL. Fluorescence was measured with excitation at 440-480 nm and emission at 505-515 nm. The ramp rate was 5.6 °C/min following a 90-second pre-incubation. Melting temperatures were determined as the peak in the derivative of the melting curve. The ITC titrant was 500 µM CATR in a buffer with dodecyl-maltoside and cardiolipin. The ITC protein sample was 25 µM AAC3 at 0.83 mg/mL. Isotherms were fitted to a one-site binding model with ΔH, Kd, and stoichiometry. The reconstitution mixed lipids in a 20:1 (w/w) ratio in chloroform. The internal buffer contained 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, and 5 mM ADP. The protein was diluted 20-fold into DDM or DPC before reconstitution. Detergent was removed by adding Bio-Beads in 20-min intervals overnight. The proteoliposomes were exchanged into external buffer using a PD10 desalting column. The proteoliposomes were diluted 9-fold before ADP uptake assays. The uptake assay used [14C]-ADP at 2.2 GBq/mmol specific activity. The column was washed with buffer containing 20 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 150 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole. Particulate material was removed by ultracentrifugation at 140,000 g for 45 min at 4 °C. The soluble fraction was loaded onto Ni-Sepharose at 1 mL/min on an ÄKTAprime. The column was washed with 40 column volumes of buffer.

Key Results
The disputed study reported a Kd of ~15 µM for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3. The disputed study reported a Kd of ~150 µM by NMR for CATR binding. The authors report ADP transport half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The authors report a Kd of 72 nM for CATR binding to native AAC3. The authors' Kd values are 200 to 2000-fold lower than those reported by Brüschweiler et al. The consensus Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are in the low nanomolar range. The consensus is at least three to four orders of magnitude lower than the reported Kd values. The reference Kd of 192 µM for ATR was corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. The Kd of ADP binding determined by NMR was 500 µM. The NMR ADP Kd is ~85-fold higher than published consensus values in the membrane. The NMR ADP Kd is ~25-fold higher than for the solubilized carrier. Only a limited number of chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding are observed. All observed chemical shift perturbations are dynamic, inconsistent with tight binding. The perturbed residues are not near the known CATR binding site. AAC3 in DPC shows no thermal transition, indicating a non-native state. CATR addition had no effect on AAC3 in DPC, demonstrating no functional binding site. Dilution into DPC before reconstitution resulted in complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake. The disputed study observed clear interpretable density for CATR in the crystal structure. The crystal structure was crystallized in maltoside detergents in the absence of CATR for 5-7 days. The disputed study reported a Kd of 192 µM for ATR from Babot et al., 2012.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors argue that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation. The authors explain that unliganded AAC3 in detergent micelles is prone to unfolding. The authors explain that the transmembrane helices are held together by lateral pressure and counter pressure. The authors explain that binding of CATR cross-links most transmembrane helices together. The authors explain that CATR binding improves stability in detergents. The authors argue that the Kd of CATR binding to the folded carrier is in the low nanomolar range. The authors argue that the low affinity of CATR to refolded AAC3 in DPC questions specificity. The authors argue that CATR binding should lock the protein into a non-dynamic state. The authors argue that the observed dynamics in the presence of substrate do not provide a plausible mechanism. The authors conclude that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance. The authors conclude that AAC3 is soluble but in a non-native state in DPC.

summary.title: Blow-up and global existence for a general class of nonlocal nonlinear coupled wave equations
summary.authors: N. Duruk, H. A. Erbay, A. Erkip
summary.field_subfield: Mathematical analysis of PDEs (nonlocal elasticity / wave equations)
summary.executive_summary: This paper studies the initial-value problem for a general class of nonlinear nonlocal coupled wave equations, in which the spatial operator is a convolution with kernel functions whose Fourier transforms are nonnegative. The authors show that this abstract model reproduces several well-known systems, including coupled Boussinesq-type equations arising in elasticity and in quasi-continuum approximations of dense lattices, by choosing the kernels appropriately. The central mathematical contributions are the establishment of local existence of solutions, the derivation of an energy identity, and the derivation of sufficient conditions for both finite-time blow-up and global existence. Local well-posedness is proved in Sobolev spaces Hs for s > 1/2 under the assumption that the exponents r1, r2 satisfy r1, r2 ≥ 2, with the proof converting the problem into an Hs-valued system of ordinary differential equations and using a standard well-posedness result. The energy identity is obtained by multiplying the transformed equations by the velocities, integrating, and applying Parseval's identity, and it holds under the assumption that the Fourier transforms of the kernels have only isolated zeros. For finite-time blow-up, the authors employ a concavity-type argument with a positive twice-differentiable function Φ(t) satisfying Φ''Φ − (1 + ν)(Φ')² ≥ 0, and they show that if a growth condition on the nonlinear terms holds and the initial energy E(0) is negative, then the solution blows up in finite time. Notably, the proof indicates that blow-up may occur even when E(0) > 0, provided the initial data satisfy a specific inequality involving inner products and norms of the transformed initial data. For global existence, two separate results are proved for two different classes of kernels: sufficiently smooth kernels with r1, r2 > 3, and mildly singular kernels of the form β1(x) = β2(x) = γ(|x|) with a jump in the first derivative, for which the Fourier transform satisfies bβi(ξ) ≤ Ci(1 + ξ²)⁻¹. The global existence proofs rely on Gronwall's lemma applied to appropriate energy-type quantities. The paper is purely theoretical and contains no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational results, and it does not provide a bibliography, so the top influential citations field is empty. The work is situated within the mathematical theory of nonlocal elasticity and wave propagation, and it extends prior single-component and classical Boussinesq results to a coupled, more general system.

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Materials chemistry / green chemistry / agricultural science
summary.executive_summary: This study develops an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, using a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4. The research is grounded in reverse logistics, which the authors describe as an important instrument for applying shared responsibility for the products lifecycle. Eggshells are highlighted as important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite). The milling process was performed with a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7), with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for various durations (15 min to 24 h) and at various speeds (100 to 600 rpm). The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milling, samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content was obtained by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Release essays were conducted in citric acid solution (2 wt%) and in soil (Petri dishes with 78 g of dry soil, 1.2 g.cm^-3 density, 70% water retention). The results indicate that the milling process produces new phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4), which present a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. In soil essays, the concentration of bioavailable calcium increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for the 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery. The P radial diffusion for the 2h/600 rpm sample is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than the precursor at the end of 30 days. The authors conclude that these materials promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The study is based on reverse logistic and green chemistry, using eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The results indicate new phosphate phases that present slower release of potassium and phosphorus in citric acid solution, and faster release compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays indicate the same behavior, but with a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, explained by hydroxyapatite formation, which is an important source of calcium and phosphorus as a long-term slow release fertilizer.

claims.description: A free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning.
The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca.

The essays were performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for various durations (15 min to 24 h) and at various speeds (100 to 600 rpm). The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milling, samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content was obtained by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. Release essays were conducted in citric acid solution (2 wt%) and in soil (Petri dishes with 78 g of dry soil, 1.2 g.cm^-3 density, 70% water retention). The results indicate that the milling process produces new phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4), which present a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. In soil essays, the concentration of bioavailable calcium increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for the 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery. The P radial diffusion for the 2h/600 rpm sample is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than the precursor at the end of 30 days. The authors conclude that these materials promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The study is based on reverse logistic and green chemistry, using eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The results indicate new phosphate phases that present slower release of potassium and phosphorus in citric acid solution, and faster release compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The soil essays indicate the same behavior, but with a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution essays, explained by hydroxyapatite formation, which is an important source of calcium and phosphorus as a long-term slow release fertilizer.

Research Context
Reverse logistics is considered one of most important instruments for applying shared responsibility for the products lifecycle. Reverse logistics is an instrument of economic and social development characterized by a set of actions, procedures and means to enable the collection and restitution of solid waste to the business sector, for reuse, in its cycle or in other cycles productive, or other environmentally appropriate final destination (Tibben and Lembke, 2002). The reverse logistic is perfectly applied in the agriculture context. Eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite) (Byeon, 2016). Everyday millions of tons of eggshells are produced as biowaste around the world, disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and producing odors due to microbial growth. The literature reports the mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) from different precursors to those reported in this study (Chaikina et al., 2019). As far as the authors know, no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4. New technologies of ecological fertilizer production have been prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products (Ivanov et al., 2019; Krishna et al., 2017; Santos et al., 2019; Cichy et al., 2019).

The central research question is whether a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 can produce calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning. The study hypothesizes that the produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, since they provide a delay of the bioavailability of P and K and also improve the bioavailability of Ca. The study hypothesizes that the solid-state mechanochemical activation allows the reactions to occur in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste in the process, ensuring huge savings during the production process. The predicted outcome is that these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium and increasing the calcium bioavailability. The predicted outcome is that the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available, an opposite effect to the delay in nutrient supply for phosphorus and potassium.

The eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed with water and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before the grinding process. The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. The milling process was performed with high-energy ball mill, Fritsch Pulverisette 7, with a 250 ml zirconia bowl, 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The essays were performed using the weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, milled for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. Considering the purity of KH2PO4 and assuming that the eggshells are mainly composed by CaCO3, the mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milled, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance, magic-angle spinning (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Before release essays at citric acid solution (2 wt%), the material has been pelletized to simulated commercial products. The pellets were obtained in steel pelletizer applying the pressure of 5 bar, and the weight was standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in 10 mL beaker, immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring. summary.title: SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model
summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh, Thomas Litfin, Jaswinder Singh, Kuldip Paliwal, Yaoqi Zhou
summary.field_subfield: Computational biology / protein contact-map prediction
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map predictor that improves single-sequence-based prediction by incorporating attention maps from the pre-trained transformer language model ESM-1b. The motivation is that most contact-map predictors rely on multiple-sequence-alignment and evolutionary information, which is unavailable for many proteins lacking homologs, and generating such profiles is computationally intensive. The authors address this gap by feeding ESM-1b's attention maps together with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs into an ensemble of ResNet architectures trained on a large dataset of nearly 35,000 proteins. The central hypothesis is that unsupervised language-model features concatenated with existing single-sequence features will outperform both the single-sequence baseline SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs (Neff). The method was evaluated on three independent test sets: SPOT-2018, Neff1-2018, and CASP14-FM. Key results include a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and 48.7% and 48.5% improvements over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact respectively on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. Feature importance analysis showed that ESM-1b attention maps yield the largest gains, with the last-layer attention maps producing F1, MCC, precision, and AUC of 0.51, 0.50, 0.56, and 0.95. The ensemble of six models improved over the second-best individual model by 4% in F1-score. The method is notably faster than evolutionary methods, requiring 116 seconds versus 2556 seconds for TrRosetta on CASP14-FM. The authors note a limitation that ESM-1b attention maps cannot be used for proteins longer than 1024 amino acids, though this is mitigated by the domain structure of most proteins. The work positions SPOT-Contact-Single as a reasonably accurate, fast screening tool for large-scale contact-map prediction without evolutionary information.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map predictor that improves single-sequence-based prediction by incorporating attention maps from the pre-trained transformer language model ESM-1b. The motivation is that most contact-map predictors rely on multiple-sequence-alignment and evolutionary information, which is unavailable for many proteins lacking homologs, and generating such profiles is computationally intensive. The authors address this gap by feeding ESM-1b's attention maps together with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs into an ensemble of ResNet architectures trained on a large dataset of nearly 35,000 proteins. The central hypothesis is that unsupervised language-model features concatenated with existing single-sequence features will outperform both the single-sequence baseline SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low effective number of homologs (Neff). The method was evaluated on three independent test sets: SPOT-2018, Neff1-2018, and CASP14-FM. Key results include a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred on CASP14-FM, and 48.7% and 48.5% improvements over TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact respectively on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. Feature importance analysis showed that ESM-1b attention maps yield the largest gains, with the last-layer attention maps producing F1, MCC, precision, and AUC of 0.51, 0.50, 0.56, and 0.95. The ensemble of six models improved over the second-best individual model by 4% in F1-score. The method is notably faster than evolutionary methods, requiring 116 seconds versus 2556 seconds for TrRosetta on CASP14-FM. The authors note a limitation that ESM-1b attention maps cannot be used for proteins longer than 1024 amino acids, though this is mitigated by the domain structure of most proteins. The work positions SPOT-Contact-Single as a reasonably accurate, fast screening tool for large-scale contact-map prediction without evolutionary information.

Research Context
The past two decades have seen many developments in the field of protein structure prediction. Improvements in contact-map prediction have contributed to advances in tertiary structure prediction. Most contact-map predictors rely on evolutionary information that is unavailable for many proteins. The reliance on homologs limits performance for proteins lacking homologous sequences. Single-sequence-based methods provide less information for the neural network to learn. Recent unsupervised deep learning methods extract features inspired by NLP language models. ESM-1b is a Transformer-based method that outputs embeddings and attention maps. The gap is the lack of methods that predict contact maps without using homologous information. There is a need to explore features beyond one-hot encoding for single-sequence-based methods. The hypothesis is that unsupervised learning features improve single-sequence-based prediction. The predicted method should outperform SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low Neff. An ensemble of models trained through different approaches should add to the improvement.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether ESM-1b attention maps improve single-sequence-based contact-map prediction. The hypothesis is that language-model features concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs outperform baselines. The predicted outcome is outperformance of SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with low Neff. The authors hypothesize that an ensemble of models trained through different approaches adds to the improvement. The method should provide a faster and reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods. The hypothesis is that ESM-1b attention maps significantly boost performance over one-hot encoding. The authors predict that concatenating all features together further increases the F1-score. The hypothesis is that direct contact-map prediction performs slightly better than distance-based prediction. The predicted outcome is that the ensemble outperforms all individual models. The hypothesis is that SPOT-Contact-Single is 45% higher in F1-score than SPOT-Contact and TrRosetta on proteins without homologs. The authors predict that the method is suitable for genomic scale prediction due to speed. The hypothesis is that the method can be used as a reasonably accurate screening tool.

Methodological Details
The study utilized the benchmark dataset prepared by ProteinNet. The dataset consists of 50914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with high resolution. Proteins were clustered at a sequence identity cut-off of 95% according to MMseqs2 tool. The training dataset was chosen with a sequence identity cut-off of 95% to obtain as much data as possible. 100 proteins were separated from the ProteinNet set for validation. Proteins with hits at an e-value cut-off of less than 0.1 were removed. The final training set contained 34691 proteins. Proteins with a length more than 500 were removed from both sets. The final validation set contained 88 proteins. The test set SPOT-2018 contained 669 proteins. The Neff1-2018 test set contained 46 proteins with Neff=1. The Neff1-2018 test set provides a reliable, stringent and completely independent benchmark.

Procedures And Architectures
The input features included one-hot encoding of amino acids, SPOT-1D-Single output, and ESM-1b attention maps. One-dimensional features were converted into two-dimensional features using an outer concatenation. The model used the probabilities of three-state-secondary-structure and eight-state-secondary structure. The features included Solvent Accessible Surface Area, Half-Sphere-Exposure, and backbone torsion angles. Attention maps were gathered using all twenty attention heads from the last layer of the transformer. Attention maps were also gathered from twenty attention heads from every layer of the ESM-1b model. The attention maps were symmetrized and had average product corrections applied. The neural network architecture was inspired by the success of the ResNet architecture. The study used a 12 block ResNet, which is the maximum depth that could be trained on the available GPU. The study employed a recently published version of ResNet that performs better than vanilla and pre-act ResNet. The convolutional layers used a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. The study trained six models with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations.

Key Results
The method made a significant improvement over SSCpred with 15% improvement in the F1-score for the independent CASP14-FM test set. The method outperformed TrRosetta with 48.7% improvement in the F1-score on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. The method outperformed SPOT-Contact with 48.5% improvement in the F1-score on proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in SPOT-2018. The model trained on one-hot encoding of the fasta sequence only predicted the contact-map with an F1-score of 0.15. Adding SPOT-1D-Single output to one-hot encoding improved the F1-score by 22.90%. The attention maps from the last layer of ESM-1b led to 0.51, 0.50, 0.56, and 0.95 for F1, MCC, precision and AUC of ROC. The last-layer attention maps showed 242% improvement in the F1-score over models trained on one-hot encoding. The last-layer attention maps showed 178% improvement in the F1-score over models trained on SPOT-1D-Single + one-hot encoding. The attention maps from all layers showed continued improvement in the precision of all short-, medium-, and long-range contacts. Concatenating all features together showed an increase of 2.92% in F1-score over using the attention maps (all layers) only. The ensemble improved over the second-best individual model by 4% for the F1-score. The performance gain was consistent across all matrices.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The interpretation is that unsupervised learning features provide valuable information for contact-map prediction. The mechanism is that ESM-1b attention maps capture sequence context that improves prediction. The interpretation is that ESM-1b attention maps significantly boost performance over one-hot encoding. The mechanism is that attention maps from all layers provide continued improvement in precision. The interpretation is that the ensemble of models adds to the improvement. The mechanism is that the ensemble takes the mean of individual models to gain improvement. The interpretation is that the method is a reasonably accurate screening tool for protein contact map prediction. draft_summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
draft_summary.executive_summary: This letter investigates gluon radiation emitted during the hydrodynamic stage of deconfined hot QCD matter, or quark-gluon plasma (QGP), which is central to interpreting relativistic heavy-ion collisions at RHIC. The medium-induced radiation has been extensively studied in the context of final-state partonic energy loss, or jet quenching, where spatially extended nuclear matter affects the fragmentation and hadronization of hard partons, and essentially all high transverse-momentum hadronic observables are affected at collider energies. The degree of medium modification characterizes the hot QCD matter in the deconfined phase, and this effect emerges in principle from thermal QCD, though different approximation schemes yield consistent results. Gluon radiation has also been considered in the context of gluon density saturation in the initial stage, where a strongly interacting gluonic atmosphere is crucial for rapid local thermalization. The time evolution of the RHIC fireball influences observable particle production spectra, and given a strong initial interaction, the resulting state is modeled as a relativistic fluid undergoing hydrodynamic flow, for which generalized fluid mechanics characterizing the long-distance transport of color charges has been developed. The authors previously discovered single skyrmion solutions in color fluid and found an expanding skyrmion case consistent with the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of these non-static configurations is an important characteristic, motivating the calculation of the radiation spectrum in a semiclassical approach. The main results are a fast fall-off in the ultraviolet side of the spectrum, a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and a long tail in the infrared. The paper reviews nonabelian fluid mechanics, calculates the nonabelian current for the soliton solution, computes the semiclassical gluon radiation, and compares the spectrum with other approaches. The color current is derived from a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, with the configuration described by a group element field U and velocity field omega. The equation of state is approximated as epsilon = 3p, describing radiation, and the free energy density is obtained by integrating the ideal fluid formula. The expanding soliton solution is specified with a scale R(t) and a small parameter lambda = tau/R0. The semiclassical amplitude is computed using the lowest-order interaction between the classical current and a free quantum gluon field, and the radiation spectrum is derived from the density of states and energy distribution. The numerical results are presented for lambda = 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5, showing the density of states and energy spectrum as functions of kappa. The comparison with other approaches reveals differences in the infrared behavior, which stems from the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 rather than being infinitely large. The hydrodynamical approach also opens possibilities for addressing the eccentricity of the elliptic flow, which will be the topic of follow-up work. The work was supported by a CUNY Collaborative Research Incentive grant, and the author benefited from mentoring by V. P. Nair.

draft_summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
draft_summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
draft_summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
draft_summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study of a lunar occultation of a carbon-rich AGB star
draft_summary.executive_summary: This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.

draft_summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
draft_summary.executive_summary: This letter investigates gluon radiation emitted during the hydrodynamic stage of deconfined hot QCD matter, or quark-gluon plasma (QGP), which is central to interpreting relativistic heavy-ion collisions at RHIC. The medium-induced radiation has been extensively studied in the context of final-state partonic energy loss, or jet quenching, where spatially extended nuclear matter affects the fragmentation and hadronization of hard partons, and essentially all high transverse-momentum hadronic observables are affected at collider energies. The degree of medium modification characterizes the hot QCD matter in the deconfined phase, and this effect emerges in principle from thermal QCD, though different approximation schemes yield consistent results. Gluon radiation has also been considered in the context of gluon density saturation in the initial stage, where a strongly interacting gluonic atmosphere is crucial for rapid local thermalization. The time evolution of the RHIC fireball influences observable particle production spectra, and given a strong initial interaction, the resulting state is modeled as a relativistic fluid undergoing hydrodynamic flow, for which generalized fluid mechanics characterizing the long-distance transport of color charges has been developed. The authors previously discovered single skyrmion solutions in color fluid and found an expanding skyrmion case consistent with the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of these non-static configurations is an important characteristic, motivating the calculation of the radiation spectrum in a semiclassical approach. The main results are a fast fall-off in the ultraviolet side of the spectrum, a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy, and a long tail in the infrared. The paper reviews nonabelian fluid mechanics, calculates the nonabelian current for the soliton solution, computes the semiclassical gluon radiation, and compares the spectrum with other approaches. The color current is derived from a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, with the configuration described by a group element field U and velocity field omega. The equation of state is approximated as epsilon = 3p, describing radiation, and the free energy density is obtained by integrating the ideal fluid formula. The expanding soliton solution is specified with a scale R(t) and a small parameter lambda = tau/R0. The semiclassical amplitude is computed using the lowest-order interaction between the classical current and a free quantum gluon field, and the radiation spectrum is derived from the density of states and energy distribution. The numerical results are presented for lambda = 1/15, 2/15, and 1/5, showing the density of states and energy spectrum as functions of kappa. The comparison with other approaches reveals differences in the infrared behavior, which stems from the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 rather than being infinitely large. The hydrodynamical approach also opens possibilities for addressing the eccentricity of the elliptic flow, which will be the topic of follow-up work. The work was supported by a CUNY Collaborative Research Incentive grant, and the author benefited from mentoring by V. P. Nair.

claims.description: The expanding skyrmion configuration provides a model for the expanding nature of the RHIC fireball, and the gluon radiation pattern is an important characteristic.
The infrared behavior in this case is softer than in prior work, due to the medium size being characterized by the soliton size R0 rather than being infinitely large.
The hierarchy between the medium-induced gluon radiation and the gluon radiation by the medium reflects the different physical mechanisms.

draft_summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
draft_summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
draft_summary.field_subfield: Astrophysics: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
draft_summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study of a lunar occultation of a carbon-rich AGB star
draft_summary.executive_summary: This paper presents high-speed, multi-wavelength observations of a lunar occultation of the dust-enshrouded carbon star AFGL 5440 (also known as OH 06.86-1.5 and IRAS 18036-2344), obtained on 28 Aug 2001 with the pMIRAS spectrophotometer on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The observations span a continuous wavelength range of 1-4 microns, with a resolving power varying from about 20 at the short end to about 100 at the long end, and a time resolution of 8 msec that yields milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors compare these data with two calibration stars, IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2), which have no detectable circumstellar dust, to characterize the limitations of the observation and analysis process. The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observed signal is a combination of the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. The authors therefore use the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell and fit both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yield a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K +/- 50 K, and an optical depth at 5 microns of 0.5 +/- 0.1. The observations are best fit by models with a density gradient of rho proportional to r^-2, or the gradient derived by Ivezi'c & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The derived dust mass-loss rate is 6.5 x 10^-8 solar masses per year. However, the models cannot fit the observed IRAS 60-micron flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. This work represents the first modeling of this star over the entire infrared wavelength region and separately resolves the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the circumstellar dust shell.

draft_summary.title: Blow-up and global existence for a general class of nonlocal nonlinear coupled wave equations
draft_summary.authors: N. Duruk, H. A. Erbay, A. Erkip
draft_summary.field_subfield: Mathematical analysis of PDEs (nonlocal elasticity / wave equations)
draft_summary.executive_summary: This paper studies the initial-value problem for a general class of nonlinear nonlocal coupled wave equations, in which the spatial operator is a convolution with kernel functions whose Fourier transforms are nonnegative. The authors show that this abstract model reproduces several well-known systems, including coupled Boussinesq-type equations arising in elasticity and in quasi-continuum approximations of dense lattices, by choosing the kernels appropriately. The central mathematical contributions are the establishment of local existence of solutions, the derivation of an energy identity, and the derivation of sufficient conditions for both finite-time blow-up and global existence. Local well-posedness is proved in Sobolev spaces Hs for s > 1/2 under the assumption that the exponents r1, r2 satisfy r1, r2 ≥ 2, with the proof converting the problem into an Hs-valued system of ordinary differential equations and using a standard well-posedness result. The energy identity is obtained by multiplying the transformed equations by the velocities, integrating, and applying Parseval's identity, and it holds under the assumption that the Fourier transforms of the kernels have only isolated zeros. For finite-time blow-up, the authors employ a concavity-type argument with a positive twice-differentiable function Φ(t) satisfying Φ''Φ − (1 + ν)(Φ')² ≥ 0, and they show that if a growth condition on the nonlinear terms holds and the initial energy E(0) is negative, then the solution blows up in finite time. Notably, the proof indicates that blow-up may occur even when E(0) > 0, provided the initial data satisfy a specific inequality involving inner products and norms of the transformed initial data. For global existence, two separate results are proved for two different classes of kernels: sufficiently smooth kernels with r1, r2 > 3, and mildly singular kernels of the form β1(x) = β2(x) = γ(|x|) with a jump in the first derivative, for which the Fourier transform satisfies bβi(ξ) ≤ Ci(1 + ξ²)⁻¹. The global existence proofs rely on Gronwall's lemma applied to appropriate energy-type quantities. The paper is purely theoretical and contains no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational results, and it does not provide a bibliography, so the top influential citations field is empty. The work is situated within the mathematical theory of nonlocal elasticity and wave propagation, and it extends prior single-component and classical Boussinesq results to a coupled, more general system.

draft_summary.title: Maximal abelian extension of a modular curve unramified outside cusps
draft_summary.field_subfield: Number theory / arithmetic geometry (modular curves, abelian extensions)
draft_summary.type_of_paper: Short research note / proof of a theorem
draft_summary.executive_summary: This note addresses the problem of finding a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the open modular curve Y0(p) over Q, where Y0(p) is X0(p) with its two cusps removed. The background is Mazur's theorem that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np = (p−1)/gcd(p−1,12) is the maximal unramified abelian covering of the whole curve X0(p). The gap is that X0(p) is proper, so its two cusps are ramification points; removing them enlarges the pool of available unramified coverings. The authors prove that the maximal unramified abelian covering of Y0(p) is cyclic of degree 2Np, obtained by adjoining a square root of an explicitly constructed rational function Fh^2 on X2(p). The construction uses generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) Eg, whose transformation and cusp-order properties are recalled and applied. The key result is that Fh^2 is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q whose order at every cusp is odd, so that X'2(p) → X2(p) is a degree-two cover ramified exactly at the cusps, and the composite X'2(p) → X0(p) is geometrically maximal unramified over Y0(p). The proof splits into the case p ≢ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) is a genuine intermediate group) and the case p ≡ 11 mod 12 (where Γ2(p) = Γ1(p) and a triplet construction is used). The note is theoretical, with no numerical experiments, datasets, or code. The main quantitative facts are the degree 2Np, the index [Γ0(p):Γ2(p)] = k = Np, the index [Γ2(p):Γ1(p)] = ℓ = gcd(p−1,12)/2, and the order-2 character machinery. The theoretical implication is that the maximal unramified abelian extension over Y0(p) is a quadratic extension of the Shimura field, controlled by the coinvariants of the generalized Jacobian's torsion.

draft_summary.title: Blow-up and global existence for a general class of nonlocal nonlinear coupled wave equations
draft_summary.authors: N. Duruk, H. A. Erbay, A. Erkip
draft_summary.field_subfield: Mathematical analysis of PDEs (nonlocal elasticity / wave equations)
draft_summary.executive_summary: This paper studies the initial-value problem for a general class of nonlinear nonlocal coupled wave equations, in which the spatial operator is a convolution with kernel functions whose Fourier transforms are nonnegative. The authors show that this abstract model reproduces several well-known systems, including coupled Boussinesq-type equations arising in elasticity and in quasi-continuum approximations of dense lattices, by choosing the kernels appropriately. The central mathematical contributions are the establishment of local existence of solutions, the derivation of an energy identity, and the derivation of sufficient conditions for both finite-time blow-up and global existence. Local well-posedness is proved in Sobolev spaces Hs for s > 1/2 under the assumption that the exponents r1, r2 satisfy r1, r2 ≥ 2, with the proof converting the problem into an Hs-valued system of ordinary differential equations and using a standard well-posedness result. The energy identity is obtained by multiplying the transformed equations by the velocities, integrating, and applying Parseval's identity, and it holds under the assumption that the Fourier transforms of the kernels have only isolated zeros. For finite-time blow-up, the authors employ a concavity-type argument with a positive twice-differentiable function Φ(t) satisfying Φ''Φ − (1 + ν)(Φ')² ≥ 0, and they show that if a growth condition on the nonlinear terms holds and the initial energy E(0) is negative, then the solution blows up in finite time. Notably, the proof indicates that blow-up may occur even when E(0) > 0, provided the initial data satisfy a specific inequality involving inner products and norms of the transformed initial data. For global existence, two separate results are proved for two different classes of kernels: sufficiently smooth kernels with r1, r2 > 3, and mildly singular kernels of the form β1(x) = β2(x) = γ(|x|) with a jump in the first derivative, for which the Fourier transform satisfies bβi(ξ) ≤ Ci(1 + ξ²)⁻¹. The global existence proofs rely on Gronwall's lemma applied to appropriate energy-type quantities. The paper is purely theoretical and contains no numerical experiments, datasets, or computational results, and it does not provide a bibliography, so the top influential citations field is empty. The work is situated within the mathematical theory of nonlocal elasticity and wave propagation, and it extends prior single-component and classical Boussinesq results to a coupled, more general system.
